question_text: All are True about fracture neck Talus except?
option_a: Lateral view X-ray is important for diagnosis of fracture
option_b: Avascular necrosis of body is common complication
option_c: Displaced fracture require below knee plaster only
option_d: Displaced fracture require open reduction & internal fixation
explanation:
• FRACTURE NECK TALUS-
    • It results from forced dorsiflexion of the ankle
    • Blood supply to body of talus is often cut following fractures occurring through the neck
    • Diagnosis: AP. lateral & oblique views are essential
    • CT scanning helps to identify associated injuries of the ankle & foot
    • Treatment: If undisplaced, a below knee plaster cast for 6-8 week is sufficient. In a displaced fracture, open reduction & internal fixation of the fracture with a screw is required
    • Complication: Osteoarthritis is the most common complication followed by Avascular necrosis & non-union.
    • The earliest x-ray sign of avascular necrosis of body (often present by the sixth week) is apparent increased density of the avascular segment; in reality it is the rest of the tarsus that has become slightly porotic with disuse, but the avascular portion remain unaffected & therefore looks more dense
    • There is a sign called Hawkin’s sign, which is the appearance of a radiolucent line in the subchondral area of the talus after fracture treatment. Hawkin’s sign is a good sign indicating revascularization of talus.

Reference- Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics 5th edition /165-66

question_text: 35 years old male sustains a closed tibial shaft fracture after falling from a tree. Which of the following measurements would be concerning for an evolving compartment syndrome?
option_a: Anterior Compartment pressure of 25 and diastolic BP of 50mm
option_b: Anterior Compartment pressure of 25 and diastolic BP of 60mm
option_c: Anterior Compartment pressure of 20 and diastolic BP of 60mm
option_d: Anterior compartment pressure of 20 and diastolic BP of 55 mm
explanation:
• This is a question on calculation of Delta P. Delta P is the difference between diastolic BP and Compartmental pressure. It is used for identifying compartment syndrome in hypotensive patients. In hypotensive patients, the traditional use of the formula – compartmental pressure > 30mm does not hold true. In these patients, compartment syndrome is defined as a Delta P < 30.
  • Delta P < 30 is an indication for fasciotomy.
  • In the above question, Delta P is < 30 in option A. Rest all options have delta p greater than 30 mm hg
  • Compartment syndrome: Compartment syndrome results when pressure rises within the closed compartment of a limb, causing a vascular compromise. Apart from limbs it can also develop into buttocks, abdomen and paraspinal muscles.
  • Most common cause is trauma (fracture) Normal compartment pressure is below 10 mm of Hg.
  • Compartment pressure can be measured by Wick or slit catheter technique or an arterial line pressure monitor system.
  • Prevention: Injured limb should be kept elevated to decrease soft tissue swelling and edema. It is important to note that in impending compartment syndrome limb should be kept at heart level because limb elevation also reduces arterial blood flow and thus oxygen delivery to tissues.
  • Supracondylar fracture humerus is the most common cause of compartment syndrome in children. Proximal tibial fracture is most common cause of compartment syndrome in adults and overall.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition, page no 527

question_text: 52 year male comes to trauma centre with 2cm wound on his left leg. His X ray shows multi fragmentary segmental fracture of left tibia and fibula. Classify his fracture.
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Gustilo Anderson class-3A.

The Gustilo Anderson classification is a system for classifying open fractures based on the severity of the soft tissue injury. The classification system has four grades:

  • Grade 1: Clean wound <1 cm long.
  • Grade 2: Laceration >1 but < 10 cm, however more importantly, there must not be any grade 3 features such as gross comminution or segmental fracture, gross contamination, extensive soft tissue loss or vascular injury. If any of these are present then irrespective of the size of the wound, the fracture has to be classified as grade 3
  • Grade 3A: Extensive soft tissue injury with adequate coverage of bone.
  • Grade 3B: Extensive soft tissue injury with inadequate coverage of bone that requires flap or free tissue transfer.
  • Grade 3C: Open fracture with an arterial injury that requires repair.

In this case, even though the wound is small, the fracture is comminuted, so we ignore the size of the wound and classify it as grade 3 open fracture. Again, as there is no mention of significant soft tissue loss or vascular injury in the question, we can sub classify the fracture as grade 3A

Reference: Campbell operative orthopaedics 13th edition, page-2659

question_text: Which area is affected by the fracture shown in the given X-ray?
explanation:
Explanation:

The X-ray shows a fracture at the tibial tuberosity, the site of patellar tendon insertion.

  • A tibial tuberosity fracture involves the anterior projection of the proximal tibia where the patellar tendon inserts.
  • It is commonly seen in adolescent males during growth spurts, often following sudden quadriceps contraction, especially during jumping sports.
  • The fracture typically presents with pain, swelling, and inability to extend the knee, and X-ray reveals a fracture at the tibial tuberosity.
  • While Osgood-Schlatter disease affects the same region, it is a chronic overuse condition, not an acute fracture.

Explanation of other options:

Medial epicondyle of tibia (Option B): This is not a commonly fractured area and lies medially near the tibial plateau; its fracture would not correspond with the tibial tuberosity seen on X-ray.

Gerdy's tubercle fracture (Option C): Located laterally on the proximal tibia as the attachment site of the iliotibial band; fractures here are rare and appear on the lateral side of the tibia, not anteriorly.

Osgood-Schlatter disease (Option D): This is a traction apophysitis, not a true fracture, seen in adolescents with chronic anterior knee pain and swelling at the tibial tuberosity, but without acute disruption of bone continuity as in a fracture.

question_text: The structure indicated by the arrow represents a specific type of epiphysis. What type of epiphysis is shown?
explanation:
Explanation:

A pressure epiphysis is found at the articular ends of long bones, where they bear weight and are involved in joint movement. These epiphyses contribute to the length of the bone and are subjected to compressive forces during movement. Examples include the head of the femur, humerus, and distal end of the tibia.

In the given image, the structure marked is an example of a pressure epiphysis, as it lies at the end of the bone and participates in joint articulation and weight transmission.

Ossification of the Fibula

The fibula ossifies from one primary and two secondary centres.

  • The primary centre for the shaft appears during the eighth week of intrauterine life.
  • A secondary centre for the lower end appears during the first year and fuses with the shaft by about sixteen years.
  • A secondary centre for the upper end appears during the fourth year and fuses with the shaft by about eighteen years.

Violation of the Law of Ossification

The fibula violates the law of ossification because the secondary centre, which appears first in the lower end, does not fuse last.

Reasons for This Violation:

  • The secondary centre appears first in the lower end because it is a pressure epiphysis (according to the law that states pressure epiphyses appear before traction epiphyses).
  • The upper epiphysis fuses last because it is the growing end of the bone. It continues to grow afterwards along with the upper end of the tibia, which is also a growing end.

Explanation of other options:

Traction epiphysis (Option B): A traction epiphysis is associated with the pulling action of muscles and tendons. The fibula's lower epiphysis does not correspond to this type, as it is involved in pressure rather than traction.

Atavistic epiphysis (Option C): Atavistic epiphyses are remnants of ancestral features, not part of the normal developmental process like the fibula's lower epiphysis. The fibula's ossification follows typical epiphyseal development rules, not those of an atavistic feature.

Aberrant epiphysis (Option D): Aberrant epiphyses are abnormal and occur outside the usual developmental pattern. The ossification of the fibula does not fit into this category, as it follows a standard ossification process with some deviations due to its pressure epiphysis nature.

Key Takeaways:

The fibula's lower epiphysis is a pressure epiphysis, as it is the first to ossify and the last to fuse, aligning with the principle that pressure epiphyses typically appear first.

question_text: Which of the below is a feature of Osteogenesis imperfecta?
explanation:
• Osteogenesis imperfecta, also known as brittle bone disease, is due to defective collagen type 1 synthesis.
  • It is inherited mostly as autosomal dominant trait but autosomal recessive pattern is also seen in severe forms of the disease.

Clinical features include

question_text: A 31 yr biker sustained tibia midshaft fracture (displaced) after an RTA. All of the following orthopaedic implants can be used to treat this fracture surgically except:
explanation:
Operative Modalities for Tibia Shaft Fractures

  1. Intramedullary (IM) Nailing
    • Advantages:
      • Preserves periosteal blood supply and minimizes soft tissue damage.
      • Provides control over alignment, translation, and rotation.
      • Suitable for most fracture patterns.
    • Types:
      • Locked Nail: (Option B)
        • Offers rotational control.
        • Prevents shortening in comminuted fractures or those with significant bone loss.
        • Interlocking screws can be removed later to promote fracture healing (dynamization).
      • Non-locked Nail:
        • Allows impaction at fracture site with weight-bearing.
        • Limited rotational control, rarely used.
  2. Flexible Nails (Enders, Rush Rods) (Option C)
    • Exert spring force to resist angulation and rotation with minimal medullary circulation damage.
    • Indications:
      • Rarely used in the U.S. except in:
        • Children or adolescents with open physes.
        • Adults with exceptionally narrow canals.
  3. External Fixation (Option D)

    • Indications:
      • Severe open fractures, compartment syndrome, head injury, or burns.
      • Reduced use in the U.S. due to the preference for reamed nails in open fractures.
    • Outcomes:
      • Union rates up to 90%, with an average union time of 3.6 months.
      • Pin tract infection rate: 10%–15%.

Option A - K-wire is a very weak implant and is usually used for small bones of hands/feet and temporary reduction in large bones.

Option B, C & D: IM locking nail, TENS nail & Illizarov's external fixator all are used in tibia mid shaft fractures.

Key takeaways -

Implant options to treat tibia midshaft fractures surgically are:

  • IM locking nail (most common)
  • Plates
  • IM non locking nails (Ender's nail, TENS, Rush rods etc.)
  • External fixators (Simple/Illizarov's – Usually used in open fractures/non unions)

question_text: A 75-year-old man presents with a fracture of the intracapsular neck of the femur. What is the standard management done in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation :

In this clinical scenario, a 75-year-old patient has sustained a displaced intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck. For an elderly patient with low functional demands, the recommended treatment is hemiarthroplasty.

This is because the blood supply to the femoral head is often disrupted in these fractures, leading to a very high risk of avascular necrosis (AVN) and non-union.

Hemiarthroplasty replaces the damaged femoral head, providing immediate stability, allowing for early mobilization, and eliminating the risk of AVN and non-union.

Indications for Hemiarthroplasty:

  • Displaced sub capital neck fractures
  • Femoral head avascular necrosis (Garden III and IV fractures)
  • Comorbid, less active, older patients(not good surgical candidates for THR)
  • Glenoid dysplasia or bone loss
  • Osteoarthritis (OA)
  • Hip or proximal femoral fracture

Explanation of other options:

Boot and bar cast (Option B): A conservative, non-operative management reserved only for non-ambulatory patients or those with prohibitive surgical risk.

Intramedullary nails (Option C): Used for extracapsular fractures (e.g., intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric fractures), not intracapsular fractures.

Russels traction (Option D): It is used for temporary stabilization and pain relief pre-operatively, not as definitive treatment.

Key Takeaways:

  • Elderly patient + Displaced Intracapsular #NOF → Hemiarthroplasty.
  • Young patient + Intracapsular #NOF → Open Reduction Internal Fixation (ORIF).

question_text: In a 70-year-old female who presents with an extracapsular neck of femur fracture, what is the treatment of choice in this condition?
explanation:
Explanation :

An extracapsular fracture (e.g., intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric) has an intact blood supply to the femoral head. The goal of treatment is anatomical reduction and stable internal fixation.

Cephalomedullary Intramedullary Nailing (e.g., PFN, Gamma nail) is the treatment of choice for most unstable intertrochanteric fractures as it provides superior biomechanical stability compared to a sliding hip screw.

Explanation of other options:

Hemiarthroplasty (Option A): Reserved for intracapsular fractures where the blood supply is compromised.

Boot and bar cast and Russels traction (Option B and D): Non-operative or temporary measures, not definitive treatment for an active elderly patient.

Key Takeaways:

  • Extracapsular #NOF (Intertrochanteric) → Intramedullary Nail.
  • Intracapsular #NOF (Elderly) → Hemiarthroplasty.

question_text: A patient presents with a 5th metatarsal fracture. For how many days he/she would have to wear a cast?
explanation:
Explanation:

A 5th metatarsal fracture typically requires casting for 6-8 weeks to ensure adequate healing and prevent complications like non-union.

  • The 5th metatarsal, especially the proximal portion, is prone to fractures, commonly referred to as Jones fractures when they occur at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction.
  • This region has relatively poor blood supply, so adequate immobilization is crucial to allow proper healing.
  • The standard management involves non-weight-bearing immobilization in a cast or walking boot for 6-8 weeks.
  • Healing is monitored with follow-up radiographs.
  • Surgery is considered if the fracture is displaced, comminuted, or fails to unite (non-union).
  • Early or inadequate immobilization risks delayed healing and long-term dysfunction.

Explanation of other options:

2-3 weeks (Option A): Too short for complete bone healing, especially in a region with poor blood supply like the 5th metatarsal base.

3-5 weeks (Option B): Also inadequate for ensuring solid bone union and may lead to refracture or non-union.

16-20 weeks (Option D): Excessively long for an uncomplicated 5th metatarsal fracture and generally only considered in cases of delayed or non-union.

Reference:

https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/22247-fifth-metatarsal-fracture

question_text: An RTA patient presented to the emergency department with severe pain in the Ankle, an X ray was performed as given below. What is the best next step of management?
option_a: Neurovascular Assessment and Closed reduction and slab application
option_b: Neurovascular Assessment and Closed reduction and cast application
option_d: Neurovascular Assessments and Immediate open reduction
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In all cases of trauma, the first step is neurovascular assessment to check for distal pulses, capillary refill, and nerve function, since dislocations and fractures can compromise vascular supply.
  • The immediate management of a fracture-dislocation of the ankle is closed reduction to restore alignment and relieve pressure on soft tissues and neurovascular structures.
  • After successful reduction, a slab (posterior splint) is applied instead of a complete cast. This is because swelling is common after acute trauma, and a cast may increase the risk of compartment syndrome as it does not allow room for expansion.
  • A slab provides stability while accommodating swelling, serving as the appropriate temporary immobilization until definitive treatment.

Fracture-dislocation of the ankle:

  • First step: Neurovascular assessment.
  • Next step: Immediate closed reduction.
  • Immobilization: Posterior slab preferred in acute phase.
  • Definitive management: If closed reduction is unstable or unsuccessful, open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) is performed once swelling subsides.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Neurovascular Assessment and Closed reduction and cast application (Option B): Incorrect because a cast is contraindicated acutely-it does not allow for swelling and increases the risk of compartment syndrome.

Neurovascular Assessment and Immediate surgery (Option C): Surgery may ultimately be needed, but the initial step is always closed reduction. Immediate surgery is not performed without first attempting closed reduction and temporary immobilization.

Neurovascular Assessment and Immediate open reduction (Option D): Incorrect because open reduction is only considered if closed reduction fails or if there are open fractures or vascular compromise. Initial management is closed reduction with slab.

Key Takeaway:

In an ankle fracture-dislocation following trauma, the priority is neurovascular assessment, immediate closed reduction, and immobilization with a slab to allow swelling. A cast is avoided initially, and surgery is reserved for cases where closed reduction is unstable or unsuccessful.

question_text: Select false statements about achondroplasia.
option_c: Mutation in FGFR2 gene is noted in most cases
option_d: There is a quantitative cartilage defect noted
explanation:
Achondroplasia is a genetic disorder that results in disproportionate dwarfism (Option A) due to abnormal bone growth, especially affecting the long bones. It follows an autosomal dominant inheritance (Option B), though many cases arise from new gene mutations.

Key Features:

  • Physical Characteristics: Short limbs with a relatively normal trunk, large skull, prominent forehead, and flat nose. Hands have short, stubby fingers.
  • Normal Intelligence: Cognitive abilities are unaffected.
  • Complications: Possible spinal canal stenosis, increased lumbar lordosis, and joint mobility issues.
  • Diagnosis: Based on physical traits, X-rays, and genetic testing.
  • Management: No cure, but physical therapy, surgical interventions, and supportive care help manage symptoms. Individuals typically lead normal lives.

Option A: Achondroplasia is the most common form of disproportionate short limbed dwarfism.

Option B: Achondroplasia is autosomal dominant inheritance.

Option C: FGFR2 gene mutation is associated with craniosynostosis.

Option D: Achondroplasia is a Quantitative, not qualitative, cartilage defect.

Key takeaways:

  • Achondroplasia is the most common form of disproportionate short limbed dwarfism.
  • Autosomal dominant condition; 80% of cases caused by a spontaneous mutation in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3)
  • Achondroplasia is categorized as a Quantitative physeal dysplasia (cartilaginous proliferative zone)

question_text: Identify the fracture shown in the image.
explanation:
Explanation:

The X-ray demonstrates a clear indentation at the radial head, the top portion of the radius that articulates with both the capitellum of the humerus and the radial notch of the ulna. This pattern is typical of a radial head fracture.

Explanation for Other Options:

Elbow fracture (Option B): A generic term covering supracondylar, olecranon, and other peri-articular injuries. The given X-ray specifically localises the break to the radial head, not the distal humerus or olecranon.

Medial epicondyle fracture (Option C): Involves the bony prominence on the inner side of the distal humerus, often from valgus stress or elbow dislocation. An X-ray would show a fragment near the medial side, which is absent here.

Lateral epicondyle fracture (Option D): Affects the lateral distal humerus where the common extensor origin attaches. Radiograph would reveal a fragment off the lateral condyle, not the radial head itself.

question_text: All of the following are features of the terrible triad of the elbow, except:
option_d: Fracture of the coronoid process of ulna
explanation:
Explanation:

The terrible triad of the elbow describes a classic injury pattern caused by high-energy trauma-commonly a fall on an outstretched hand with the elbow slightly flexed and subjected to a valgus-posterolateral force.
It involves three key injuries:


Because all three occur simultaneously, the elbow becomes unstable, and early recognition is critical.

Mechanism of Injury

  • Typical scenario: Fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) with the elbow slightly flexed.
  • Force pattern: Axial load combined with valgus and supination causes posterolateral rotatory instability.

Management

  • Urgent closed reduction under anesthesia.
  • Assessment of joint stability.
  • Often followed by surgical fixation (radial head repair/replacement and coronoid fixation) to prevent chronic instability.

question_text: A patient presents with swelling and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on the outstretched hand. The X-ray is provided. Identify the fracture.
explanation:
Explanation:

Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox indicates a scaphoid fracture. This bone lies in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox and is commonly injured by a fall on the outstretched hand (FOOSH) with wrist extension. It is most frequent in young adults, especially males.

Explanation of other options:

Colles's fracture (Option A): Distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement, due to FOOSH with wrist extended.

Smith fracture (Option C): Distal radius fracture with volar displacement, due to fall on back of hand with wrist flexed.

Galeazzi fracture (Option D): Distal radius fracture with dislocation of distal radioulnar joint, often from FOOSH with pronation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Scaphoid fracture = snuffbox tenderness.

question_text: All of these are eponyms of distal radius fractures except:
explanation:
It is a ventrally displaced fracture through the neck of the 5th metacarpal, usually occurs in boxers.


Distal Radius Fracture Types and Mechanisms

  1. Colles Fracture:
    • Involves both extra-articular and intra-articular distal radius fractures with dorsal angulation, dorsal displacement, radial shift, and radial shortening.
    • Commonly results in a “dinner fork” deformity.
  2. Smith Fracture (Reverse Colles Fracture):
    • Description:
      • Fracture with volar angulation of the distal radius, creating a “garden spade” deformity.
      • Hand and distal radius are displaced volarly.
  3. Barton Fracture (Volar/Dorsal):
    • Description:
      • A fracture-dislocation or subluxation of the wrist with displacement of the dorsal or volar rim of the distal radius along with the hand and carpus.
      • Volar involvement is more common.
  4. Radial Styloid Fracture (Chauffeur Fracture, Backfire Fracture, Hutchinson Fracture):
    • Description:
      • Avulsion fracture with extrinsic ligaments attached to the styloid fragment.
      • result from a direct blow or compression of scaphoid against the styloid.
  1. Die- Punch fracture:
    • Depressed fracture of the lunate fossa of distal radial articular surface.
    • ORIF is mandatory to prevent post traumatic arthritis and carpal stability.

Option A - Boxer: It is a ventrally displaced fracture through the neck of the 5th metacarpal, usually occurs in boxers.

Option B - Die-punch is Depressed fracture of lunate fossa of distal radius.

Option C - Chauffeur's fracture is radial styloid fracture.

Option D - Barton's is Intra-articular fractures through the distal articular surface of the radius; further classified as dorsal or volar depending on displacement.

Key takeaways:

Distal Radius Fracture:

  • Colles Fracture - Dorsal Angulation
  • Smith Fracture - Volar Angulation
  • Barton Fractures - Intra Articular, unstable and usually require surgical intervention.
  • Radial Styloid Fracture/chauffer/huthinson - Avulsion Fracture often involves ligamentous injuries.

question_text: A patient was involved in a road traffic accident and presented with the fracture shown in the X-ray. What type of fracture is this?

question_text: A young adult patient presents with a fracture of the neck of the femur. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In young adults, preservation of the natural femoral head is the priority because prosthetic replacements have limited durability in this age group.
  • Therefore, the treatment of choice for a fracture neck of the femur in a young patient is internal fixation (commonly with cannulated cancellous screws or a dynamic hip screw).
  • This preserves the femoral head, allows union, and avoids early prosthetic complications.
  • Arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement) is generally reserved for elderly patients, where the risk of avascular necrosis and nonunion is high.

Explanation of other options:

External fixation (Option A): Rarely used for femoral neck fractures; more common in open fractures of long bones.

Hemiarthroplasty (Option C): Preferred in elderly patients with low activity levels, not in young adults.

Total hip replacement (Option D): Reserved for elderly patients with pre-existing hip arthritis or severely displaced fractures.

question_text: An elderly woman is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. She has difficulty breathing and an altered mental status. X-ray findings reveal a fracture of the femur shaft. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Fat embolism syndrome (FES) is a life-threatening complication seen commonly after long bone fractures (such as the femur, pelvis). Fat globules released from the bone marrow enter the circulation and lodge in the pulmonary and cerebral microvasculature.
  • This leads to the classic triad:
    1. Respiratory distress (hypoxemia, dyspnea),
    2. Neurological abnormalities (confusion, altered sensorium, seizures), and
    3. Petechial rash (usually 24-72 hours later).
  • In this case, the combination of femoral shaft fracture, breathing difficulty, and altered mental status strongly suggests fat embolism syndrome.

Explanation of other options:

Gas gangrene (Option A): Presents with wound infection, severe pain, swelling, foul-smelling discharge, and crepitus, not acute respiratory failure after femur fracture.

Infection (Option C): Post-traumatic infection develops later with fever and local signs, not acute respiratory and CNS symptoms.

Pulmonary embolism (Option D): Presents with dyspnea and chest pain, but in trauma patients with a femur fracture, fat embolism is far more likely within 72 hours.

question_text: Identify the orthopedic implant shown in the image
explanation:
Explanation:

The implant shown is a Dynamic Hip Screw (DHS), commonly used for intertrochanteric fractures of the femur.

  • The Dynamic Hip Screw (DHS) is a sliding screw-plate system used to manage stable intertrochanteric femur fractures, especially in elderly patients.
  • Components:
    • A large lag screw: Inserted into the femoral neck and head.
    • A side plate with barrel: Fixed along the lateral femoral cortex with cortical screws.
  • The "dynamic" mechanism allows for controlled collapse at the fracture site during weight-bearing, which promotes healing by compression.
  • Indications:
    • Stable intertrochanteric fractures (AO/OTA 31-A1 and some A2 fractures)
    • Osteoporotic bone in elderly patients
  • Advantages:
    • Allows for controlled impaction at the fracture site
    • Simple and effective in appropriate fracture patterns

Explanation of other options:

Adynamic Hip Screw (Option B): Not a recognized term in orthopedics-nonexistent terminology.

Condylar Hip Screw (Option C): Used for distal femur (condylar) fractures, not for intertrochanteric fractures.

Intramedullary Nail (Option D): While proximal femoral nails can treat intertrochanteric fractures, the implant in the image is extramedullary, not an intramedullary nail.

Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557514/

question_text: The radiograph below depicts a patient who is experiencing persistent knee pain without any previous injury. Identify the specific condition displayed in the image?
option_b: Bipartite patella, X-ray of the opposite knee
option_c: Fracture of the upper pole of the patella, Cylindrical cast
explanation:
Explanation :

The image shows a non-traumatic, well-corticated fragment at the patella's superolateral pole, characteristic of bipartite patella.

  • Bipartite patella is a congenital condition due to failure of fusion of accessory ossification centers, usually at the superolateral pole of the patella (Type III, most common).
  • It is often bilateral and found in about 1-2% of the population. Although usually asymptomatic, it can present with anterior knee pain, especially after repetitive activity.
  • Radiographs reveal a well-corticated bone fragment, distinguishing it from an acute fracture, which shows irregular, sharp edges.
  • MRI is useful for assessing associated soft tissue injury or bone edema if symptomatic.
  • In this case, absence of trauma and characteristic radiographic findings suggest bipartite patella.
  • The recommended next step is to perform an X-ray of the opposite knee to check for bilateral involvement.
  • Management:
    • Asymptomatic: No treatment required.
    • Symptomatic: Rest, NSAIDs, physical therapy, or in severe cases, surgery (excision of fragment).

Explanation of other options:

Patellar avulsion fracture, TBW (Option A): Avulsion fractures follow trauma and show irregular, non-corticated edges; tension band wiring (TBW) is the treatment of choice.

Fracture of the upper pole of the patella, Cylindrical cast (Option C): Patellar fractures are post-traumatic and rarely managed conservatively unless nondisplaced.

Avulsion fracture, interfragmentary screw fixation (Option D): Involves trauma with sharp fracture lines and requires fixation, not observed in this case.

question_text: Select correct option about treatment for plantar fasciitis:x
option_a: Soft cushion foot sole/ heel pad
explanation:
Plantar Fasciitis is a common condition that causes pain in the heel. It is primarily due to inflammation of the plantar fascia (plantar aponeurosis) at its attachment on the calcaneal tuberosity.

Key Characteristics:

  1. Cause and Pathophysiology:
    • The condition is a result of inflammation where the plantar fascia attaches to the tuberosity of the calcaneus (heel bone).
    • Repeated strain can cause small tears in the fascia, leading to pain and swelling.
  2. Symptoms:
    • Pain Characteristics: The pain is typically sharp and most severe in the morning with the first few steps. It may improve after some activity but can return after prolonged standing or sitting.
    • Tenderness: On examination, there is significant tenderness over the medial aspect of the calcaneal tuberosity at the plantar fascia’s attachment site.
  1. Diagnostic Findings:
    • X-Ray Features: In some cases, an X-ray may reveal a sharp bone spur projecting forwards from the calcaneal tuberosity. This "heel spur" is often associated with plantar fasciitis but is not the cause of the pain.
  2. Management and Treatment:
    • Conservative Treatments:
      • Analgesics: Pain relief with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
      • Heel Pads: Cushioning the heel with a soft pad to reduce strain on the fascia. (Option A)
      • Ice Fomentation: Applying ice to the affected area helps reduce inflammation. (Option B)
    • Steroid Injections: Local corticosteroid injections can be effective in providing relief in cases that do not respond to conservative management. (Option C)
  3. Prognosis:
    • Most cases improve with conservative treatment over time, though the condition can be persistent and may require continued management.

Key Takeaway –

Plantar Fasciitis key points:

  • Pain: Typically worst in the morning, improving with activity.
  • Examination: Marked tenderness over the medial heel at the fascia attachment.
  • X-Ray: May show a bone spur at the heel, although it’s not the primary cause of pain.
  • Treatment: Includes analgesics, heel pads, ice therapy, and corticosteroid injections.

question_text: What surgeon is credited for designing the prosthesis seen in the figure?
explanation:
• Austin Moore developed the most popular long-stemmed prosthesis in the 1950s. The Austin-Moore prosthesis was a large, uncemented femoral stem that didn't use polyethylene. The Austin-Moore prosthesis had fenestrations for self-locking which later became the impetus for biological fixation.
  • These implants were originally used to treat hip fractures and certain cases of degenerative arthritis.
  • The prosthesis has a head with a small neck and a stem. It is available in head sizes ranging from 35 to 59 mm (odd numbers).
  • There is a small hole at the top of the stem for the hook of the extractor, used while removing the prosthesis. The stem has two fenestrations in its middle, through which the bone supposedly grows and helps in fixation of the prosthesis.
  • This prosthesis can thus be used only without cement because the use of cement would make its removal, if required, difficult.
  • Later, in the 1960s, John Charnley introduced the idea of replacing the eroded acetabulum with a Teflon component.
  • Below Figure shows an example of Charnley's "low-friction" total hip arthroplasty, with a stainless-steel head and stem and a polyethylene acetabular component

question_text: Locking of the knee can be due to which of the following?
explanation:
• Locking of knee can be physiological or pathological
  • Physiological locking references to internal rotation of femur over a flexed/ grounded tibia in extended knee. Unlocking occurs when popliteus external rotates the femur and knee can then flex.
  • However, in orthopedics, we usually talk of pathological locking which refers to restriction of terminal few degrees of extension of the knee. This occurs when there is an intra articular obstruction to the normal gliding of the tibial and femoral condyles. The causes can be
    • Torn meniscus (most common),
    • Loose bodies in the knee
    • Osteochondral fractures
    • Fractured osteophytes lying in the joint.
    • Foreign bodies

Reference- Maheshwari, Essential Ortho 5th edition page no 151.

question_text: Which nerve is injured in fracture neck of fibula:
explanation:
• Smaller terminal branch of sciatic nerve, the common peroneal nerve arises in the lower third of thigh. It runs downward through the popliteal fossa(lateral side) closely following the medial border of biceps femoris muscle.
  • It leaves the fossa by crossing superficially the lateral head of the gastrocnemius muscle.
  • It then passes behind the head of the fibula, winds laterally around the neck of the bone, pierces the peroneus longus muscle and divides into two terminal branches superficial and deep peroneal nerve.
  • The common peroneal nerve is extremely vulnerable to injury by direct trauma and fractures of fibula as it winds around the neck of fibula.
  • Injury to common peroneal nerve causes foot drop.
  • Patients with foot drop develop abnormal gait called as "high stepping gait".

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th ed, Pg: 158.

question_text: A patient presents with the fracture shown in the X-ray involving the shaft of the humerus. Which nerve is most likely to be injured in this type of fracture?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The radial nerve spirals around the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus along with the profunda brachii artery.
  • In fractures of the shaft of the humerus, this nerve is highly vulnerable to injury. Damage to the radial nerve causes wrist drop (loss of wrist and finger extension) and sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand.
  • Hence, the most likely nerve injured in this fracture is the radial nerve.

Explanation of other options:

Axillary nerve (Option A): Injured in surgical neck fractures of the humerus, not shaft fractures.

Ulnar nerve (Option B): Commonly injured in medial epicondyle fractures, not in shaft fractures.

Musculocutaneous nerve (Option D): Rarely injured in humeral fractures; injury causes loss of forearm flexion and lateral forearm sensation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Surgical neck fracture → Axillary nerve.
  • Mid-shaft fracture → Radial nerve.
  • Medial epicondyle fracture → Ulnar nerve.
  • Supracondylar fracture → Median nerve.

Patterns of nerve injury:

  • Neuropraxia:
    • Reversible physiological nerve conduction block
    • It is seen in crutch palsy, tourniquet palsy and saturday night palsy
  • Axonotmesis:
    • There is loss of conduction because of axonal interruption but the nerve is in continuity and the neural tubes are intact

question_text: All of the following are the eponymous fractures of the meta-tarsals except:
explanation:
Common Foot Fractures

Aviator's Fracture – Option D

  • Definition: Fracture of the neck of the talus.
  • Historical Context: Referred to as "Aviator’s astragalus," this term originates from the impact of a rudder bar in a crashing airplane on the plantar aspect of the foot, resulting in a talar neck fracture.

Jones Fracture (Option A)

  • Definition: An avulsion fracture of the base of the 5th metatarsal.
  • Injury Classification: Zone 2 injuries are classified as Jones fractures.
  • Mechanism of Injury: Result from adduction or inversion of the forefoot, causing tensile stress along the lateral border of the metatarsal.
  • Treatment Options: Controversial; options include:
    • Weight-bearing or non-weight-bearing in a short leg cast.
    • Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF).
  • Union Concerns: There is often a concern regarding the union of this type of fracture.

March Fracture (Option B)

  • Definition: A fatigue fracture of the shaft of the 2nd or 3rd metatarsal.
  • Mechanism of Injury: Often occurs due to repetitive stress from long hours of walking or running, particularly in military recruits.
  • Relation to Stress Fractures: March fractures are a type of stress fracture, commonly seen in the necks of the second and third metatarsals and the proximal fifth metatarsal.

Dancer's Fracture – Option C

  • Definition: A fracture of the distal shaft of the 5th metatarsal.
  • Injury Classification: Occurs beyond Zone 3.
  • Usually oblique or spiral type fracture due to twisting movements during dancing.

Key takeaways -

  • Aviator's fracture: Fracture of neck of the talus.
  • Jone's fracture: Avulsion fracture of the base of the 5th metatarsal.
  • March fracture: Fatigue fracture of the shaft of 2nd or 3rd metatarsal.
  • Dancer's fracture – Fracture of distal shaft of 5th

question_text: A 14-year-old male presents with a mushroom-like tumor in the distal femur for the past 2 years. Which of the following features suggest malignant transformation?
option_b: Bone marrow is continuous with the parent bone
option_c: The cartilaginous growth goes towards the joint
explanation:
Explanation:

The diagnosis here is osteochondroma, a common benign cartilaginous growth arising from the metaphysis of long bones.

  • The most reliable radiological feature of malignant transformation (usually into chondrosarcoma) is cartilage cap thickness > 2 cm on MRI.
  • This is because benign osteochondromas typically have a thin cartilage cap (<1-2 cm in adults, slightly thicker in children).
  • A thicker cap indicates increased cellular activity, raising suspicion for malignant change.

Osteochondroma:

  • Also called: Exostosis.
  • Epidemiology: Most common benign bone tumor, more common in males, usually during adolescence.
  • Common sites: Distal femur > proximal tibia > proximal humerus.
  • Clinical features: Painless mass; pain occurs due to bursa formation, fracture, or nerve compression.
  • Radiology:
    • X-ray: pedunculated or sessile cauliflower-like mass arising from metaphysis.
    • MRI: measures cartilage cap thickness.
  • Malignant transformation: Rare (<1%), but cartilage cap thickness >2 cm is highly suspicious.
  • Management: Observation if asymptomatic; surgical excision with biopsy if symptomatic or suspicious for malignancy.

Explanation of other options:

Bone marrow is continuous with the parent bone (Option B): This is a diagnostic feature of osteochondroma itself, not of malignancy. It helps differentiate osteochondroma from other bone lesions.

The cartilaginous growth goes towards the joint (Option C): The lesion usually grows away from the joint, but growth direction does not reliably indicate malignant change.

Cartilage thickness > 3 cm (Option D): Although thick cartilage raises suspicion, the accepted threshold for malignant transformation is >2 cm, not 3 cm.

Key Takeaway:

  • Cartilage cap thickness >2 cm on MRI is the most reliable indicator of malignant transformation in osteochondroma.

question_text:
An orthopaedic surgeon wants to give a plaster for Colles fracture. Arrange the following steps in order.
a. Traction
b. Ulnar deviation
c. Palmar flexion
d. POP
explanation:
6 classical deficits in colles fracture are:

  • Dorsal tilt/displacement
  • Lateral tilt/displacement
  • Impaction
  • Supination
Sequence of correction explained below technique.
Technique of closed manipulation:
The muscles of forearm must be relaxed, either by general or regional anaesthesia. The surgeon grasps the injured hand as if he was 'shaking hands'.
The first step is to disimpact the fragments which have often been driven together. This is achieved by firm longitudinal traction to the hand against the counter-traction by an assistant who grasps the arm above the flexed elbow. Some displacements are corrected by traction alone.
 The surgeon now presses the distal fragment into palmar flexion and ulnar deviation using the thumb of his other hand. As this is done, the patient's hand is drawn into pronation, palmar flexion and ulnar deviation. A
Plaster cast is applied extending from below the elbow to the metacarpal heads, maintaining the wrist in palmar flexion and ulnar deviation. This is Colles' cast.

Reference: Essential orthopedics by Maheshwari 7th edition page no 110.

question_text: Match the following with the best mode of management.
explanation:
• Simple bone cyst treatment:- Treatment: The cyst is known to undergo spontaneous healing, particularly after a fracture. One or two injections of methylprednisolone into the cyst results in healing. Some cases need curettage and bone grafting.
  • Osteosarcoma requires wide excision of mass or amputation.
  • Giant cell tumor treatment- Excision or Extended curettage : This is the treatment of choice when the tumour affects a bone whose removal does not hamper with functions e.g., the fibula, lower-end of the ulna etc.

question_text: What is the next step of management in posterior hip joint dislocation?
explanation:
• Hip joint dislocation are reduced closely first under short general anaesthesia. If it cannot be reduced using close reduction and if associated with acetabular fracture then open reduction is required.
  • Hip dislocation with or without acetabular or femoral head fracture is an emergency and must be reduced as early as possible.
  • Most of the times close reduction under general anesthesia is possible. Many methods of close reduction have been described like Allis maneuver, Biglows maneuver (leverage method, can reduce both anterior and posterior dislocations but not used due to high risk of femoral neck fractures), Stimsons gravity method and Modified East Baltimore lift.
  • Allis maneuver is the most commonly used method for closed reduction of hip dislocation. Once a stable closed reduction is achieved, a temporary skin traction can be given for soft tissue healing and gradually the patient can be mobilized.
  • However, if a closed reduction fails (interposed labrum etc., or incarcinated bone fragments) patient should be urgently posted for an open reduction. Patients with concomitant femoral neck or head fractures also usually require primary open reduction.

Reference:Fundamentals of orthopedics by mohindra and jain page no-101

question_text: A 45-year-old patient with a Tibial fracture on cast presents to emergency department with complaints of intense pain. Cast was removed and on examination Passive flexion was painful, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are present and loss of sensation over the first web space was noted. What is the next step in management?
explanation:
Based on clinical history patient is suffering from compartment syndrome ,so first we should confirm our diagnosis by measuring anterior compartment pressure. An intracompartment pressure above 30mm Hg is diagnostic of compartment syndrome.


Diagnosis of compartment syndrome

  • Normotensive patient
    • Compartment pressure >30 mmHg
  • Hypotensive patient
    • Delta P (diastolic BP - compartment pressure) <30mmHg

This patient has clinical symptoms and signs of leg compartment syndrome and should undergo immediate fasciotomies of all 4 leg compartments, followed by external fixation for fracture stabilization.

Tibial fractures are among the most common reasons for compartment syndromes of the leg. A clinical assessment is key in the diagnosis of acute compartment syndrome. If there is uncertainty, intracompartmental pressure measurement has been advocated to help confirm the diagnosis.

5 p's of compartment syndrome

  • pain out of proportion to exam,
  • paralysis
  • Paresthesias
  • Pallor
  • pulselessness

Pain on passive stretch - is the earliest sign

We can not perform intramedullary nailing or open reduction and internal fixation in this case because surgery itself is a predisposing factor for development of compartment syndrome

Reference:Maheshwari ortho 7thedition page number 47.

question_text: Identify the type of fracture shown in the image.
explanation:
Explanation:

  • A depressed fracture is characterized by an inward displacement of a portion of the skull, typically caused by direct trauma with a blunt object.
  • On X-ray, it appears as a circular or irregular indentation of the skull bone, often with overlapping bone margins due to the inward push.
  • These fractures commonly affect the parietal or frontal bones and may be associated with underlying brain injury or dural tear.
  • Immediate neurosurgical consultation is warranted if there are signs of neurological deficit or if the depression is greater than the thickness of the skull.

Explanation of other options:

Linear fracture (Option B): Appears as a single straight or branching line on the skull X-ray without displacement. It is the most common type of skull fracture and usually benign unless it crosses vascular structures or sutures.

Hinge fracture (Option C): Also known as a diastatic or basilar fracture, it involves a fracture through the base of the skull that can cause the base to open like a hinge. Typically identified on CT rather than plain X-ray.

Gutter fracture (Option D): Occurs when a glancing bullet or projectile creates a groove or "gutter" in the skull bone. It has a distinct beveled appearance not consistent with the X-ray of a blunt trauma.

Key Takeaways

A depressed fracture presents with an inward indentation of the skull and is most often due to direct blunt force trauma. Prompt evaluation is essential due to potential brain injury.

References: https://fn.bmj.com/content/94/2/F137

question_text: Chance fracture: Choose the false option.
option_b: Ecchymosis can be seen in the abdominal region
option_c: Mechanism of injury is flexion-distraction force
option_d: Occurs at the level of the cervicothoracic spine
explanation:
Chance Fractures (Seat Belt Fractures)

Definition:

  • Chance Fracture: Also known as a seat belt fracture (Option A), this injury involves a horizontal fracture line that traverses the body of the vertebra and extends through to the posterior elements. It typically results from a flexion-distraction mechanism.

Clinical Presentation:

  • Seat Belt Sign: One of the key physical exam findings is ecchymosis (bruising) (Option B) on the abdominal wall in the region where the seat belt would be worn. This sign is indicative of the trauma that led to the fracture.
  • Associated Risk: The presence of a seat belt sign can be associated with an increased risk of small bowel perforation, with a reported risk increase of approximately 5%.

Mechanism:

  • Flexion-Distraction Injury (Option C): Chance fractures are a type of flexion-distraction injury affecting the thoracolumbar spine (Option D). The injury is caused by a force that is transmitted posteriorly along an anterior-posterior plane, often related to high-energy impacts such as motor vehicle accidents where seat belts are involved.

Option A, B & C: Chance Fracture Also called seat belt fracture causes Ecchymosis in the abdominal region. Mechanism of injury is the flexion-distraction force.

Option D: Occurs at the level of the cervicothoracic spine is false. It's mc at thoracolumbar spine.

Key takeaways:

Chance Fractures / Seat belt fractures:

  • Due to Flexion distraction injury
  • Seat belt sign - Ecchymosis over anterior abdomen
  • MC at Thoracolumbar spine

question_text: Which of the following is a feature of Salter Harris type II physeal injury?
option_c: Open injury with loss of physis
option_d: Transverse fracture of metaphysis with longitudinal extension into the physis
explanation:
• In type II B Salter Harris injuries, there forms a triangular metaphyseal fragment called Thurston Holland Fragment. On an x ray, this appearance is called Thurston Holland sign or sail sign.
  • Salter Harris system remains the most widely used system for describing physeal fractures.

Conveniently the Salter-Harris types can be remembered by the mnemonic SALTER.

Type I- S - Straight across.(5-7%)

Fracture plane passes all the way through the growth plate, not involving bone.

Type II- A- Above (75%) (by far the most common)

Fracture passes across most of the growth plate and exits up through the metaphysis

Type III- L - Lower (7-10%)

Fracture plane passes some distance along with the growth plate and exits down through the epiphysis

Poorer prognosis as the proliferative and reserve zones are interrupted

Type IV- T- Through three zones (intra-articular)

Fracture plane passes directly through the metaphysis, growth plate and down through the epiphysis

Poor prognosis as the proliferative and reserve zones are interrupted

Type V- ER - Erasure of the physis (uncommon <1%)

Crushing type injury that does not displace the growth plate but damages it by direct compression

Worst prognosis.

Reference: https://radiopaedia.org/articles/salter-harris-classification?lang=us

question_text: Three point bony relationship has diagnostic value in:
explanation:
• Three point bony relation is made with medial epicondyle, lateral epicondyle and olecranon process
  • These 3 points will form an isosceles triangle which is congruent with the opposite side when the elbow is in flexion and comes to lie in a horizontal line when the elbow is extended.
  • Three point bony relationship will be disrupted in fractures of olecranon, medial condyle, lateral condyle, intercondylar region and elbow dislocation.
  • In supracondylar fracture, however, three point bony relation is maintained

Reference- Maheshwari Orthopedics, 6thedition, page no 107

question_text: Identify the name of this angle shown in the image which is used to classify as well as assess prognosis of neck of femur fractures.
explanation:
Classification of NOF Fracture:

  1. Anatomical classification –
    1. Sub-capital (Worst prognosis)
    2. Trans-cervical
    3. Basi-cervical (Best prognosis)
  2. Pauwels classification –
    1. Pauwels angle <30 (Best prognosis)
    2. Pauwels angle 30-70
    3. Pauwels angle >70 (Worst prognosis)
  3. Garden’s classification
    1. Trabeculae bending; fracture incomplete
    2. Trabeculae broken; fracture complete but undisplaced
    3. Trabeculae broken and out of alignment; fracture partially displaced
    4. Trabeculae of head parallel with acetabulum; Head completely displaced and rotated.

Option A: Garden Angle doesn’t exist. Garden classification is used for NOF Fractures.

Option B: Neck shaft angle is formed by the femoral shaft and line passing through the centre of the head of the femur. Normal adults have 120-140 degree angles.

Option D: Not Applicable.

Key takeaways -

  • Pauwels classification is based on the angle of inclination of the fracture in relation to the horizontal plane (Pauwels angle). The fractures are divided into three types (type I–III).
  • The more the angle, the more unstable is the fracture, and worse the prognosis.

question_text: Runner's fracture occurs in which of the following bones?
explanation:
• Runner’s fracture: Stress fracture of the distal fibula.
  • Bumper fracture: A fracture of the tibial plateau.
  • Toddler’s fracture: A spiral fracture of the tibial shaft seen in toddlers due to twisting injury.
  • Pott’s fracture: Bimalleolar ankle fracture.
  • Cotton’s fracture: Trimalleolar ankle fracture.
  • Bosworth fracture: A fracture dislocation at ankle where fibula is trapped behind tibia resulting in irreducibility of the ankle by manipulation.
  • Massonneuve’s fracture: Fracture of medial malleolus with fracture proximal third fibula.
  • Pilon fracture: It is a comminuted intra articular fracture of the distal end of tibia.
  • Tillaux fracture: This is avulsion of anterior tibial margin by the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (Salter Harris type III injury).

Reference- Apley’s Orthopedics, 9th edition pg. 724

question_text: Patient met with an accident where the dashboard of the car hits anteriorly over the knee while sitting besides the driver and presents with severe pain and deformity of the hip. Most probable deformity of hip to occur will be:
explanation:
Dashboard Injuries cause Posterior Dislocation of Hip which Presents with Flexion, Adduction and Internal Rotation. (Remembered as FADIR)

Posterior Dislocation of the Hip:

  1. Definition
    • The head of the femur is displaced out of the acetabulum in a posterior direction. In about 50% of cases, this dislocation is associated with a fracture of the posterior lip of the acetabulum, known as a fracture-dislocation.
  2. Diagnosis

Clinical Features:

  • History of severe trauma, such as a car accident.
  • Symptoms:
    • Pain and swelling.
    • Deformity characterized by:
      • Flexion, adduction, and internal rotation of the hip. (Option B)
      • Shortening of the affected leg.
  • Palpation: The femoral head may be felt in the gluteal region.
  • Routine pelvic X-rays are recommended in patients with femoral fractures to rule out associated hip dislocation.

Radiological Features:

  • The femoral head appears displaced out of the acetabulum.
  • The thigh is internally rotated, making the lesser trochanter less visible.
  • Shenton's line is disrupted.
  • Comparison X-ray of the opposite hip may be useful.
  • CT Scan may be required to assess associated fractures.

Option A - ABD +ER is seen in anterior hip dislocation but not FLX.

Option C - Neck of femur & sub trochanteric femur fracture shows Shortening with ER.

Option D - None of the above is incorrect because it presents with Flexion, Adduction and internal Rotation as Given in Option B.

Key takeaways: Dashboard Injuries cause Posterior Dislocation of Hip which Presents with Flexion, Adduction and Internal Rotation. (Remembered as FADIR)

question_text: A labourer fell from 2 meter height and sustained calcaneus fracture. Select true statement about the Bohler's angle in fractures of calcaneum.
option_c: Can be seen in axial view of xray
explanation:
Radiographic Evaluation of Calcaneus Fractures

Initial Radiographic Views

  1. Lateral View of the Hindfoot
  2. Anteroposterior (AP) View of the Foot
  3. Harris Axial View
  4. Ankle Series

Lateral Radiograph

  • Böhler Angle: (Option C)
    • Description: Formed by a line from the highest point of the anterior process of the calcaneus to the highest point of the posterior facet, and another line from the posterior facet to the superior edge of the tuberosity.
    • Normal Range: 20 to 40 degrees.
    • Clinical Significance: A decrease in this angle indicates collapse of the weight-bearing posterior facet of the calcaneus, shifting body weight anteriorly. (Option A, D)
  • Gissane (Crucial) Angle: (Option B)
    • Description: Formed by two cortical struts—one along the lateral margin of the posterior facet and the other anterior to the calcaneal beak.
    • Normal Range: 105 to 135 degrees.
    • Clinical Significance: An increase in this angle indicates collapse of the posterior facet.

Key takeaways -

  • Bohler's angle can be seen in lateral view of x ray calcaneus.
  • Bohler's angle decreases in intra-articular fractures. Normal 20-40 degrees.
  • Criticalcrucial angle of Gissane Increases in calcaneus fractures. Normal 120-145 degrees.

question_text: 41-year-old female feels a pop in her ankle while playing tennis. She is diagnosed with an acute Achilles tendon rupture and elects to undergo nonoperative management. Which of the following is the expected outcome seen with nonoperative management with early functional rehabilitation as compared with operative treatment?
option_a: Decreased incidence of deep venous thrombosis
option_c: No significant difference in functional outcomes
explanation:
• Recent studies have demonstrated no significant difference in functional outcomes or the rate of re-rupture with treatment of Achilles tendon ruptures when nonoperative management consists of early functional rehabilitation.
  • Incorrect Answers:
    • Answer 1: No difference is seen in DVT rates between the two treatments
    • Answer 3: Early functional rehabilitation has been shown to lead to similar rates of re-rupture
    • Answer 4: Earlier return to sport has not been shown when comparing the two treatments
    • Answer 5: Complication rates are increased with operative treatment. Complications seen with surgical treatment include infection, wound failure and sural nerve injury.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 920.

question_text: Identify the structure fractured in the given image:
explanation:
Bones of the Foot

1. Hindfoot:

  • Calcaneus (heel bone): The largest bone, forms the heel.
  • Talus: Sits above the calcaneus and connects to the tibia and fibula to form the ankle joint.

2. Midfoot:

  • Navicular: Boat-shaped bone located medially in front of the talus. (Option D)
  • Cuboid: Cube-shaped bone lateral to the navicular. (Option B)
  • Cuneiforms (3 bones):
    • Medial cuneiform (Option A)
    • Intermediate cuneiform
    • Lateral cuneiform (Option C)
  • These bones form the arch of the foot.

3. Forefoot:

  • Metatarsals (5 bones): Long bones numbered 1 to 5, starting from the big toe (medial side).
  • Phalanges (14 bones):
    • Proximal phalanges (5)
    • Middle phalanges (4) - (Absent in the big toe)
    • Distal phalanges (5)

Key Takeaway -

Cuneiform Bones

  1. Medial Cuneiform:
    • Location: Medial side of the midfoot.
    • Shape: Largest, wedge-shaped.
    • Articulations: With navicular, first and second metatarsals, intermediate cuneiform.
  2. Intermediate Cuneiform:
    • Location: Central in the midfoot.
    • Shape: Smaller, cylindrical.
    • Articulations: With navicular, second metatarsal, medial and lateral cuneiforms.
  3. Lateral Cuneiform:
    • Location: Lateral side of the midfoot.
    • Shape: Smaller, wedge-shaped.
    • Articulations: With navicular, third metatarsal, medial and intermediate cuneiforms.

question_text: In dancers, peroneal muscle weakness has been shown to be the cause of which of the following?
explanation:
• The most common acute skeletal injury in the dancer is the inversion sprain of the ankle and thought to be due to relative peroneal muscle weakness.
  • Sprains may occur in any ligament in the foot or ankle, but most common ones involve the lateral ligament complex (anterior talofibular, calcaneal-fibular, and posterior talofibular ligaments); the anterior tibiofibular, the lateral talocalcaneal ligament; and, occasionally the medial (deltoid) ligament.
  • Regardless of the method of treatment, adequate physical therapy and proper rehabilitation are necessary to restore normal use following injury.
  • Restoration of full peroneal strength is essential to minimize risk of recurrent sprains.

question_text: Which of the following fracture patterns has the least healing potential?
explanation:
Healing potential - Spiral (Option B) >>> Oblique (Option A) >>> Transverse (Option C) >>> Comminuted >>> Open.

The healing potential of fractures generally follows this order:

  • Spiral Fractures: Highest potential for healing due to stability and more contact area.
  • Oblique Fractures: Good healing potential, slightly less stable than spiral fractures.
  • Transverse Fractures: Moderate healing potential; clean breaks can be challenging to maintain alignment.
  • Comminuted Fractures: Lower healing potential due to multiple fragments and instability.
  • Open Fractures: Lowest potential due to high risk of infection and drainage of fracture hematoma

Problems Related to Union in Open Fractures

  1. Bone Loss
  2. Loss of Fracture Hematoma
  3. Inadequate Vascular Cover
  4. Secondary Infection

Proper initial treatment, including wound care and infection prevention, along with adequate surgical intervention, is crucial for promoting successful bone healing in open fractures.

Option D: Open Fracture has the least healing potential.

Key Takeaway:

The healing potential of fractures generally follows this order:

Healing potential – Spiral (Option B) >>> Oblique (Option A) >>> Transverse (Option C) >>> Comminuted >>> Open.

  • Spiral Fractures: Highest potential for healing due to stability and more contact area.
  • Oblique Fractures: Good healing potential, slightly less stable than spiral fractures.
  • Transverse Fractures: Moderate healing potential; clean breaks can be challenging to maintain alignment.
  • Comminuted Fractures: Lower healing potential due to multiple fragments and instability.
  • Open Fractures: Lowest potential due to high risk of infection and drainage of fracture hematoma.

question_text: A patient with fracture of femur shaft develops petechiae, respiratory distress and decreased sPO2, 3 days after injury. What in the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• Fat embolism is often caused by physical trauma such as fracture of long bone, soft tissue trauma and burns.
  • Clinical Features- Triad of respiratory distress, CNS symptoms and Petechial rash.
  • Other features include tachycardia, tachypnea, increased temperature, hypoxemia (decreased sPO2), hypercapnea, thrombocytopenia.
  • Pathognomonic sign: Petechial rash on the upper anterior portion of the body, including the chest, neck, upper arm, axilla, shoulder, oral mucosa and conjunctivae.
  • Crush injury is compression of extremities or other parts of the body that causes muscle swelling and/or neurological disturbances in the affected areas of the body, while crush syndrome is localized crush injury with systemic manifestations. It is Characterized by major shock and renal failure after a crushing injury to skeletal muscle.
  • Hypostatic pneumonia is usually seen in elderly and debilitating patients. It results from infection developing in the dependent portions of the lungs due to decreased ventilation of those areas, with resulting failure to drain bronchial secretions.

Reference: Maheshwari ortho 5thedition, page no. 43

question_text: Which condition produces a Dowager's hump?

question_text: A 37 yr male gives a history of sustaining supracondylar humerus fracture which was treated with plating 3 months back. Since the injury he is not able to hold a card/paper in between extended fingers against pulling force. Select the suitable option.
option_a: Card test for dorsal interossei in ulnar nerve examination
option_b: Card test for palmar interossei in ulnar nerve examination
option_c: Card test for dorsal interossei in median nerve examination
option_d: Card test for adductor pollicis in ulnar nerve examination
explanation:
Ulnar Nerve Tests

Card Test for Palmar Interossei (Adductors) (mnemonics PAD) of the Fingers:

The Card Test is used to assess the strength of the palmar interossei muscles, which are supplied by the ulnar nerve and are responsible for finger adduction. (Option A, C)

Procedure:

  1. The examiner inserts a card between two extended fingers.
  2. The patient is instructed to hold the card as tightly as possible.
  3. The examiner then attempts to pull the card out.

Interpretation:

  • The patient can hold the card firmly indicating normal adductor strength.
  • If the card is easily pulled out, it suggests weakness in the palmar interossei muscles, which could indicate ulnar nerve injury.

Option A & C: Card test is done for palmar Introssei (Not Dorsal Interossei)

Option D: Adductor Pollicis muscle is tested by Book test.- Froment sign (flexion instead of abduction)

Key Takeaway -

Ulnar Nerve Muscle & test:

  • Froment's test/ book test: adductor pollicis muscle.

question_text: Most common site of occurrence of enchondroma is?
explanation:
Enchondroma

1. General Characteristics

  • Most Common Benign Bone Tumor of the upper extremity.
  • Age Group: Typically presents in the 2nd to 4th decades of life.
  • Symptoms:
    • Often asymptomatic and incidentally discovered.
    • May present as a pathological fracture.

2. Location and Spread

  • Origin: Arises from the metaphyseal medullary canal and spreads towards the diaphysis.
  • Common Sites (in order):
    • Proximal phalanx of the hand or metacarpal (Option C) > Feet (Option D) > Distal femur (Option A) > Proximal humerus (Option B) > Tibia.

3. Radiographic Features (X-ray)

  • Appearance: Symmetric fusiform expansion of the bone.
  • Key Findings:
    • Endosteal scalloping.
    • Intramedullary calcifications.

4. Histological Features

  • Hand Enchondromas: Noted for their high cellularity.
  • Potential Malignancy: Presence of mitotic figures may indicate low-grade chondrosarcoma.

5. Treatment

  • Primary Treatment: Curettage.

Explanations of Options:

  • Common Sites (in order):
    • Proximal phalanx of the hand or metacarpal (Option C) > Feet (Option D) > Distal femur (Option A) > Proximal humerus (Option B) > Tibia.

Key Takeaway:

Mnemonic - "ENCHONDROMAS"

  • E: Expansion (symmetric fusiform expansion on X-ray)
  • N: Nonsymptomatic (usually asymptomatic, incidental finding)
  • C: Curettage (primary treatment)
  • H: Hands (most common location - proximal phalanx/metacarpal)
  • O: Occurs in the 2nd to 4th decades of life
  • N: Neoplastic lesion from metaphyseal medullary canal
  • D: Diaphysis spread (from metaphysis)
  • R: Radiographic findings (endosteal scalloping, intramedullary calcifications)
  • O: Overwhelming cellularity in hand enchondromas (histology)
  • M: Mitotic figures may indicate low-grade chondrosarcoma
  • A: Asymptomatic pathological fracture (common presentation)
  • S: Secondary sites: Feet, femur, humerus, tibia

question_text: Which of the following fracture patterns has the best healing potential irrespective of the treatment modality?
explanation:
Spiral fracture has the highest surface area, hence maximum healing potential.

Classification of Fractures Based on Pattern

  1. Transverse Fracture: (Option B)
    • Description: Fracture line is perpendicular to the long axis of the bone.
    • Cause: Typically caused by a tapping or bending force.
  2. Oblique Fracture: (Option A)
    • Description: Fracture line is oblique.
    • Cause: Resulting from a bending force that also has a component along the long axis of the bone.
  3. Spiral Fracture: (Option C)
    • Description: Fracture line runs spirally in more than one plane.
    • Cause: Primarily caused by a twisting force.
  4. Comminuted Fracture: (Option D)
    • Description: Fracture consisting of multiple fragments.
    • Cause: Resulting from a crushing or compression force along the long axis of the bone.
  5. Segmental Fracture:
    • Description: Two fractures in one bone at different levels.
  6. Combination Fractures:
    • Note: A fracture may exhibit a combination of two or more patterns (e.g., a comminuted fracture that is primarily transverse).

Option A, B & D: Sequence of Fracture union Potential: Spiral (Option C) > Oblique (Option A) > Transverse (Option B) > Comminuted (Option D)

Key takeaways: Pattern of fracture in decreasing order of union potential

Spiral fracture (most) >>>> Oblique fracture >>>> Transverse fracture >>>> Comminuted fracture >>>> Segmental fracture >>>> Open fracture (Least).

question_text: Stress fracture occurs most commonly in which of the following bones?
explanation:
• The most common site of stress fracture is tibia followed by metatarsals.
  • Stress fractures often develop from overuse, such as from high-impact sports, army training etc. It is seen due to imbalance between load and resistance on the bone.
  • Most stress fractures occur in the weight-bearing bones of the foot and lower leg. Studies show that athletes participating in tennis, track and field, gymnastics, dance, and basketball are at high risk for stress fractures.
  • Examples of stress fracture:
    • Lower extremity: March - 2nd MT > 3rd MT
    • Upper extremity: Olecranon
  • Note: MC site of stress → lower 3rd tibia > 2nd MT
  • Investigation of choice for unilateral stress fracture is MRI and in bilateral stress fractures is bone scan.
  • MRI is IOC for occult (hidden) fractures.

Reference- Essential Orthopedics Maheshwari, 5th ed. pg. 167

question_text: A 45 yr man collided with a truck while driving on a highway and was brought to emergency with multiple injuries and hypovolemic shock. CT screening shows open book type pelvic injury along with abdominal visceral injuries as well. All of the following are necessary steps in management except:
option_a: Apply pelvic binder as soon as possible to prevent further blood loss
option_b: Insert wide bore cannula and start IV fluids and blood transfusion if necessary
option_c: Open reduction and internal fixation in emergency to stop further bleeding
option_d: Anterior external fixator after abdominal visceral injury is addressed
explanation:
1. Primary Assessment of polytrauma Patient

Standard ABCDE approach for initial assessment

2. Secondary assessment

Extremities and Pelvis Evaluation:

  • Identify all injuries to the extremities and pelvis.
  • Carefully assess distal neurovascular status (pulse, sensation, movement) in each limb.
  • Check for pelvic instability by assessing leg length discrepancy, noting any shortening or abnormal rotation of the lower extremities.

Pelvic Instability Assessment (AP-LC Test):

  • Perform the AP-LC test once, involving gentle internal and external rotation of the pelvis to assess for instability.
  • Be cautious as excessive manipulation can disrupt clot formation.

Hemorrhage and Contusions:

  • Look for signs of significant bleeding, such as massive flank or buttock contusions and swelling.
  • Remember, "The first clot is the best clot". Disruption of the initial clot can complicate subsequent bleeding control due to hemodilution and depletion of clotting factors.

Palpation for Fractures and Defects:

  • Palpate the posterior pelvis for hematomas, defects indicating fractures, or sacroiliac joint dislocations.
  • Check the pubic symphysis for any palpable defects.

Inspection for Open Fractures:

  • Inspect the perineum carefully for signs of open fractures or lacerations.

Rectal and Vaginal Examination:

  • Perform a digital rectal exam in all trauma patients with suspected pelvic ring disruption.
  • For women, a vaginal exam is also necessary to rule out perforations.
  • Missed rectal or vaginal injuries in pelvic trauma can lead to severe complications and poor prognosis.

Secondary assessment:

Options for immediate hemorrhage control in pelvic injuries include:

  1. Application of military antishock trousers (MAST). This is typically performed in the field.
  2. Wrapping of a pelvic binder circumferentially around the pelvis (or sheet if a binder is not available). This should be applied at the level of the trochanters to provide access to the abdomen.
  3. Consider the application of a bean bag.
  4. Consider angiography or embolization if the hemorrhage continues despite closing of the pelvic volume.
  5. Consider application of a pelvic C-clamp (posterior).
  6. Consider an anterior external fixator.
  7. Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF): This may be undertaken if the patient is undergoing emergency laparotomy for other indications but it is frequently contraindicated by itself because loss of the tamponade effect may encourage further hemorrhage.
  8. Open packing of the retroperitoneum is an option in the unstable patient who is brought to the operating room for laparotomy and exploration.

Key takeaways:

Options for immediate hemorrhage control in pelvic injuries include:

  • Wrapping of a pelvic binder circumferentially around the pelvis (or sheet if a binder is not available). This should be applied at the level of the trochanters to provide access to the abdomen.
  • Consider an anterior external fixator.
  • Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF): This may be undertaken if the patient is undergoing emergency laparotomy for other indications but it is frequently contraindicated by itself because loss of the tamponade effect may encourage further hemorrhage.

question_text: Match the following:
explanation:
Types of Casts and Their Uses:

Option A: Glass Holding Cast (Scaphoid Cast)

  • Extends from below the elbow to the metacarpal heads, including the thumb up to the interphalangeal joint.
  • Wrist positioned in slight dorsiflexion and radial deviation (glass holding position).
  • Indications:
    • Used for scaphoid fractures.
    • In cases of widely displaced fractures, open reduction and internal fixation with Herbert's screw may be required.

Option B: PTB Cast (Patellar Tendon Bearing Cast)

  • Purpose: Used for conservative treatment of tibial shaft fractures.
  • Application:
    • After 6 weeks, once the fracture becomes 'sticky', the above-knee cast is replaced with a PTB cast.
    • Modern synthetic casting materials make application more convenient.
  • Follow-Up: As the fracture partly unites, the PTB cast can be replaced with removable plastic braces, allowing joint mobilization.

Option C: Cylindrical Cast

  • Description:
    • Extends from mid-thigh to just above the ankle, keeping the knee in full extension.
  • Indications:
    • Used for patella fractures and post quadriceps tendon repair surgeries.
    • Prevents knee flexion to allow healing.

Option D: U-Slab Cast

  • Description:
    • Extends from the base of the neck, over the shoulder, along the lateral arm, under the elbow, and to the medial side.
    • Molded laterally to prevent angulation and supported with a triangular sling.
  • Indications: Typically used for shoulder and upper arm fractures.
  • Duration: Removed after 6-8 weeks, followed by shoulder exercises.

Key takeaways:

Name of the cast and their use:

  • Minerva cast - Cervical spine disease
  • Risser's cast - Scoliosis
  • Turn-buckle cast - Scoliosis
  • Shoulder spica - Shoulder immobilization
  • U-slab - Fracture of the humerus
  • Hanging cast - Fracture of the humerus
  • Colle's cast - Colle's fracture
  • Hip spica - Fracture of the femur
  • Cylinder cast - Fracture of the patella
  • PTB cast - Fracture of the tibia

Glass holding cast - Scaphoid fracture

question_text: You are the intern on duty and you receive a patient who have been in road traffic accident. For which of the following patient will you urgently call the orthopaedic resident on call?

question_text: False about Tardy Ulnar N palsy
option_a: Seen in fractures of Lateral condyle of humerus

explanation:
• Tardy Ulnar N palsy is a slow onset palsy and it takes months to years for it to develop.
  • Tardy Ulnar N palsy is a delayed complication of nonunion of lateral condyle of humerus fracture.
  • In nonunion of lateral condyle of humerus fracture, because of the growth arrest in the lateral distal physis of the humerus, there will be progressive cubitus valgus deformity. As this deformity worsens, there is stretching of the Ulnar N resulting in its dysfunction after several months or years.

question_text: A 30 year old male sustained injury to left leg in a RTA. O/E there is a wound of size 6cm. X-ray showed transverse fracture of tibia. There is no soft tissue loss. There was arterial bleeder at presentation which was ligated in the casualty. What is the Gustilo Anderson type?

question_text: For the fixation strategy shown in above image, fracture union is likely to proceed by what mechanism?
explanation:
• There are 2 types of bone healing – primary and secondary.
    • Primary Fracture Healing or Direct Fracture Healing (Healing without Callus)
      • It is less common mode of fracture healing. It is seen in rigid internal fixation of fractures (compression plating) and in unicortical fractures (Greenstick fracture).
      • Cutting cones play a part in fracture healing here.
  • Secondary Fracture Healing or Indirect Fracture Healing (Healing by Callus Formation)
    • This is more common method of fracture healing. It is seen in absence of rigid fixation (cast immobilization, intramedullary nailing and bridge plating for comminuted metaphyseal fractures).
  • It is divided into five phases
    • Hematoma organizes by 2-3 days
    • Granulation tissue is fully formed by 2-3 weeks.
    • Provisional callus/Soft callus is seen first around 3 weeks.
    • Woven bone/Hard callus is seen by 3 months or bone consolidates (clinical union) by 3 weeks.
    • Remodelling continues to occur over 2-3 years.

Reference- Maheshwari ortho 5thedition, page no 11

question_text: All are associated with calcaneus except
explanation:

  • Tongue type fracture is a fracture of the calcaneus where the proximal fragment is elevated by the pull of the Achilles tendon (refer image).
