question_text: Not true about osteogenesis imperfecta
explanation:
• Fracture healing is normal in osteogenesis imperfecta. In OI, the bones are fragile and brittle resulting in multiple fractures even with trivial trauma. However, the fracture healing is normal, therefore, these fractures malunite over time and result in deformities.

Clinical features of OI

  • Skeletal system
    • Fractures with slight trauma
    • Multiple B/L symmetrical fractures
    • MC bone # : femur > tibia
    • Normal fracture healing
    • #s Malunites causing deformities
    • Wormian bones
    • Ring shaped epiphysis
  • Ocular signs
    • Blue sclera
    • Saturn ring
    • Arcus Juvenilis
  • Auditory - Deafness

    • Dentigenous imperfecta
    • Normal enamel
    • Discolored, Brittle teeth
    • Lower incisors are most affected

question_text: A 40 year old woman presents 8 weeks after distal radius fracture with a painful swollen hand. The fracture was treated with cast application for 6 weeks. On examination, the hand is cold & cyanosed and shiny with increased temperature sensitivity. The likely diagnosis is?
explanation:
• Sudeck's dystrophy is also called Complex regional pain syndrome or reflex sympathetic dystrophy
  • It usually happens are following the injury around the wrist or foot and ankle
  • The exact mechanism is unknown, however it is thought to be due to an autonomic dysfunction.
  • There are two types of CRPS type 1 and 2
  • The symptoms include continuous burning and throbbing pain, swelling, increased sensitivity to different stimuli like water, touch and vibrations and increased sweating
  • The signs include edema, stiffness of fingers, loss of hair, shiny skin and bluish or pinkish discolouration.
  • It can be treated with physiotherapy, and various drugs like anti-inflammatory drugs, gabapentin, pregabalin, amitryptyline, or sympatholytic drugs (Guanethidine).
  • If all these do not help, we have to give sympathetic block

Other Options:

  • Median nerve injury reduction in temperature sensitivity is usually not seen in association with distal radius fracture and it also does not produce the above symptoms
  • If there is a malunion it has nothing to do with the temperature sensitivity.
  • If compartment syndrome is there for 8 weeks, his hand would have gone into gangrene by now.

question_text: Identify x-ray view taken in below image?

question_text: A 19 year old boy involved in a bike accident is brought to the emergency department. He is unconscious, has a flail chest and restricted movements of neck. First step to be done is.
explanation:
• Whenever we approach a patient with serious injury after RTA, we have to follow the ATLS protocol.
  • And as per ATLS protocol Airway maintenance should be our first priority. However, if we suspect a cervical spine injury, as in this case, we must first stabilize the cervical spine with a collar before securing the airway.
  • This is because most of the time, we will have to manipulate the neck in order to maintain the airway, e.g. for introducing a nasopharyngeal airway or intubation. And if we do not stabilize the neck first, the cervical spine injury may worsen and cause quadriplegia.

question_text: 23 year old male presented to the casualty after RTA. He had sustained a fracture as shown in the x ray given below. On examination, he is also unable to dorsiflex his wrist. What is this fracture known as?

question_text: A 5-year-old boy fell on an outstretched right arm. Which type of fracture is shown on this x-ray?
explanation:

question_text: The 3 point bony relationship is altered in

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 358

question_text:
A 3-year-old child complains of pain and inability to move his left elbow after his mother grabbed his arm and attempted to lead him across the street. Physical exam demonstrates guarding of the extremity with the elbow held in flexed and pronated position. A lateral radiograph is shown in the figure.
What is the most appropriate first step in management ?
option_b: Aspiration of the elbow joint with blood cultures
option_c: Closed reduction via supination and flexion
explanation:
• The clinical scenario above describes a pulled elbow/ nursemaid's elbow.
  • This injury occurs commonly in children under 5 years of age as a result of a quick pull on an extended and pronated arm and results in subluxation of the annular ligament.
  • Figure is a lateral radiograph of the elbow which shows normal ossification pattern in a pediatric elbow, without any obvious fracture or dislocation.
  • Lateral radiograph of a nursemaid's elbow will show a normal collinear relationship between capitellum & central axis of the radius.
  • Reduction typically includes elbow flexion and supination while placing a finger on the radial

head to feel the snap of the reducing annular ligament.

Above image shows the elbow flexion and forearm supination technique used to reduce the subluxated radial head.

Reference: Maheshwari ortho 5th edition page no 105

question_text: What mechanism most likely led to this injury?
explanation:
• Image shows distal end radius fracture with Volar angulation known as smith fracture
  • Smith fracture is fracture of the distal radius with associated volar angulation of the distal fracture fragment(s). Classically, these fractures are extra-articular transverse fractures and can be thought of as a reverse Colles fracture.
  • Smith fractures usually occur in one of two ways:
    1. A fall onto a flexed wrist
    2. Direct blow to the back of the wrist
  • Malunion of Smith fractures produces garden spade deformity

Reference- Fundamentals of Orthopedics Mahindra 1stedition, page no 70

question_text: A 60-year-old man presents to the trauma bay after falling onto his flexed wrist. What is the eponymous name of the fracture shown in the image below?
explanation:
• The x ray shows an extra-articular transverse fracture through the distal radius with volar angulation of distal fracture fragment representing a Smith fracture.
  • The direction of displacement can be assessed on an x ray by looking at the thickness of soft tissue shadow around the forearm bones on the lateral x ray. The volar soft tissue shadow will always be thicker than the dorsal soft tissue shadow. So wherever the soft tissue shadow is thicker, it is volar and the thinner side would be dorsal.
  • Note, there is no intra-articular extension of the fracture line. An avulsion fracture of the ulnar styloid process is also noted.

SMITH'S FRACTURE (Reverse of Colles' Fracture)

  • This uncommon fracture is seen in adults and in elderly people.
  • Its importance lies in differentiating it from the commoner Colles' fracture which occurs at the same site.
  • It differs from Colles' fracture in that the distal fragment displaces and tilts volarly.
  • Treatment is by closed reduction and above elbow plaster cast immobilisation for 6 weeks. Grossly displaced fractures might need ORIF.

Reference: Maheshwari ortho 5th edition page no 111

question_text: Which of the following is true about fracture shown in the image?
option_a: Volar angulation with radial deviation occurs
option_b: It is an intra articular fracture
option_c: It may lead to gunstock deformity due to malunion
option_d: It is associated with dorsal angulation
explanation:
• Above image is of Colles fracture
  • Colles fractures are very common extra-articular fractures of the distal radius that occur as the result of a fall onto an outstretched hand. It is defined as a fracture of cortico cancellous junction of distal radius with dorsal angulation and impaction, but without the involvement of the articular surface. Colles fractures produce the classical dinner fork deformity. They are particularly common in patients with osteoporosis, and as such, they are most frequently seen in elderly women.
  • Garden spade deformity is seen in volar angulation type fracture (smith fracture)
  • Gunstock deformity is seen in malunited Supracondylar humerus fracture.

Reference- Fundamentals of Orthopedics Mahindra 1stedition, page no 70

question_text: 63 year old female presents with severe hip pain without any history of trauma. Her x ray shows a lytic lesion of around 7cm in peritrochantric area of right femur. What should be the management for this patient?
explanation:
This patient has a large lytic lesion in the proximal femur. As the lesion is in a weight bearing area, there is a high risk of a pathological fracture occurring there. In order to prevent this, we must perform prophylactic fixation of the bone. In prophylactic fixation, we fix a bone without a fracture, to prevent a fracture. The decision as to whether we need to fix a bone with lytic lesion is made with the help of MIREL’S score.

Reference: Rockwood and green adult fracture 8ᵗʰ edition, page-673

question_text: What is Hoffa's fracture?
option_b: Epiphyseal injury of the distal femur
option_c: Fracture of femoral condyle in the sagittal plane
option_d: Fracture of femoral condyle in the coronal plane
explanation:
• Hoffa's fracture is a fracture of the femoral condyle in the coronal plane.

Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 2084

question_text: A 35 year old alcoholic male was admitted 48 hours back with fracture shaft of  femur. He was planned for intramedullary nailing today, but he suddenly developed aggressive and altered behavior. O/E there is tachypnea and petechial rashes in the axilla. The probable diagnosis is
explanation:
• Altered behavior after 48 hours can be seen in both alcohol withdrawal and fat embolism syndrome. However the triad of CNS symptoms (altered behavior), respiratory symptoms (tachypnea) and rashes is pathognomonic of fat embolism.
  • Fat embolism syndrome
    • It is a systemic disorder characterized by organ damage due to fat particles in micro circulation.
    • Causes
      1. Trauma (90%) - # Shaft of Femur , # Tibia
      2. Surgeries
        • Joint reconstruction surgeries
        • Liposuction
      3. Diseases
        • Diabetes
        • Acute pancreatitis
        • Sickle cell disease
      4. Burns
    • There is always a 24- 72 hour time delay in the onset of symptoms.

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 48

question_text: Identify the angle shown in the calcaneal radiograph exhibit below, which is formed between the anterior process, posterior facet, and tuberosity (normal range 20°–40°) and is decreased in calcaneal fracture:
explanation:
Bohler’s angle and angle of Gissane are used for the evaluation of calcaneum fractures. They are evaluated on a lateral radiograph of calcaneum.

  • Bohler's angle:
    • Angle between line from highest point of anterior process to highest point of posterior facet + line tangential to superior edge of tuberosity
    • Normal 20-40°
    • Decreases in calcaneal fractures
  • Angle of Gissane:
    • Angle between line along lateral margin of posterior facet + line anterior to beak of calcaneus
    • Normal 120-145°
    • Increases in calcaneal fractures

Reference- Maheshwari ortho 5thedition, page no. 164

question_text: Erlenmeyer flask deformity of the femur is seen in which of the following conditions?
explanation:
• Osteopetrosis (also known as Marble bone disease, Albers- Schonberg disease) Defect is in bone resorption due to abnormal function of osteoclasts. Defective bone resorption results in uniformly thickened dense bones, often without distinction between cortical and cancellous regions.
  • The bones are dense but brittle therefore known as marble bone disease. Inheritance is both AD & AR. The AR form dies early in the life. The AD form is of milder variety.
  • Classical types:
    • Autosomal recessive(infantile and malignant)
    • Autosomal dominant(adult and benign) type I and type II
    • Autosomal recessive intermediate form
  • Clinical features in osteopetrosis are caused by an increased tendency to fractures and osteomyelitis.
  • Defect in bone modelling produces loss in hematopoietic function and resultant anemia and immunodeficiency, skull foramina fail to expand resulting in various cranial nerve palsies and blindness.
  • X-RAY FEATURES:
    1. Generalized osteosclerosis of bones.
    2. Loss of cortico medullary differentiation
    3. Grossly narrowed/absent medullary canal
    4. Cube-like bones(carpals and tarsals)
    5. Erlenmeyer flask deformity of distal femur Sandwich vertebra
    6. Endobone formation(bone within bone appearance)

Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney, 1st Edition, Page no. 96.

question_text: What is Lisfranc fracture dislocation ?
option_a: Fracture dislocation through tarso metatarsal joints
option_d: Fracture dislocation through inter metatarsal joints.
explanation:
• A Lisfranc dislocation or injury describes a spectrum of injuries involving the tarsometatarsal joints of the foot.
  • The Lisfranc joint is comprised of the articulation between the first, second, and third metatarsals bones and the cuneiform bones.
  • Injuries of the joint can range from complete tarsometatarsal displacement with associated fractures and ligamentous tears to partial sprains with no displacement.
  • Mechanism of injury- injuries occur mostly because of high energy injuries like forced hyper flexion of ankle in road traffic accident.

Reference- Essential Orthopedics Maheshwari 5th edition, page no 54.

question_text: The ligaments connecting the menisci to the tibia are known as?
explanation:
• Ligaments Related to Menisci
  • Coronary Ligaments:
    • These ligaments attach the periphery of both the menisci to the periphery of tibial condyles.
    • The coronary ligaments of the knee (also known as meniscotibial ligaments) are portions of the joint capsule which connect the inferior edges of the fibro cartilaginous menisci to the periphery of the tibial plateaus.
  • The coronary ligaments function to connect parts of the outside, inferior edges of the medial and lateral menisci to the joint capsule of the knee.
  • Meniscofemoral Ligaments:
    • These ligaments attach the posterior part of lateral meniscus to the femur.
    • These are of two types:
      • Anterior meniscofemoral ligament (Ligament of Humphrey): Runs anterior to PCL.
      • Posterior meniscofemoral ligament (Ligament of Wrisberg ): Runs posterior to PCL.
  • Option ‘B’: Arcuate ligament
    • Arcuate ligament is the ligament between the posterolateral femoral condyle to the fibular head. It covers the popliteus tendon.
  • Option ‘C’:Transverse Ligament:
    • It attaches the anterior edges of medial and lateral meniscus to each other.
  • Option ‘D’: Oblique ligament
    • Oblique popliteal ligament is the ligament from semimembranous to lateral femoral condyle and it is derived from semimembranous.

Reference- Apley’s ‘System of Orthopaedics and Fractures’; 9/e, p-583

• In the x ray we can observe that the big toe is directed laterally away from the midline. This deformity is called hallux vagus.
  • Hallux Valgus, commonly referred to as a bunion, is a complex valgus deformity of the first ray that can cause medial big toe pain and difficulty with shoe wear.
  • Diagnosis is made clinically with presence of a hallux that rests in a valgus and pronated position. Radiographs of the foot are obtained to identify the severity of the disease and for surgical planning.
  • Treatment can be nonoperative with bunion splint and shoe modifications for mild and minimally symptomatic cases. Surgical management is indicated for progressive deformity and difficulty with shoe wear.

Other options-

  • Hallux rigidus is a common foot condition characterized by pain and loss of motion of the 1st MTP joint in adults due to degenerative arthritis.
  • Freiberg's Disease is a rare foot condition characterized by infarction and fracture of the metatarsal heads.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 1275.

question_text: Select the false statement about Hangman's fracture
option_a: It is a fracture through the pedicle at pars interarticularis of atlas
option_b: It is due to distraction extension force
option_d: Mild injuries can be treated with rigid cervical support
explanation:
Hangman's fracture is defined as a traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2 over C3. This means that there is fracture through the pars inter articularis of C2 and not C1.

Reference: Ebnezar, 5th edition, Page no. 308

question_text: A lady presented in emergency with history of trauma to neck region. Identify the shown fracture in image.
explanation:
The shown image is a case of atlanto-axial dislocation

  • Atlantoaxial dislocation commonly present with fracture, as compared to pure dislocation of C1 (Atlas) and C2 (Axis)
  • Pure dislocation is commonly associated with neurological deficit
  • MC type of atlanto-axial dislocation: Anterior
  • Treatment: Skull traction followed by immobilisation using Minerva jacket.
  • Hangman fracture: Fracture through pedicle and lamina of C2 vertebra, with subluxation of C2 over C3. This type of fracture seen in judicial hangings.
  • Jefferson fracture: Fracture of C1 vertebra
  • Clay-shoveler fracture: Avulsion fracture of spinous process of one or more of the lower cervical or upper thoracic vertebra. Name is given as it is caused by muscular action in shovelling by labourers.

Reference- Maheshwari Orthopedics, 5thedition, page no 273

question_text: Regarding Hangman's fracture true statement is
explanation:
• This is a fracture of the isthmus part of axis(pars inter-articularis) characterized by forward slipping of C2 over C3 (spondylolisthesis), originally described in patients subjected to judicial hanging. The mechanism in judicial hanging is extension of the spine with distraction.
  • Hangman's fracture is nowadays, more commonly seen in road traffic accidents where it is caused by extension of the spine with axial loading(when head strikes to dash board). Mostly there is no neurological deficit as the fracture of the posterior arch tends to decompress the spinal cord and acute post admission mortality is low
  • Most of these fractures heal rapidly and union is almost never a problem.

Reference: Essential Orthopaedics Maheshwari, 5th edition, Page no. 3.

question_text: Which of these is a false statement
explanation:
• Periosteum does not contain osteoclasts. Osteoclasts are seen in endosteum
  • Endosteum is made up of a single layer, however it is thicker than the periosteum.

Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 27.

question_text: Barlow test is used for testing
explanation:
• Special tests designed for early detection of CDH are 1) Barlow test 2) Ortolani test
  • Barlow test: Consists of 2 parts
    • 1st part: Hip & knee flexed & thighs gently adducted. Feel for abnormal posterior movement & sometimes dislocation with a distinct ‘clink’ of femoral head.
    • 2nd part: Thighs are gently abducted. If the hip was dislocated earlier, a distinct clink will be heard & felt indicating reduction of dislocated hip.

Ortolani’s test: Similar to 2nd part of Barlow’s test. Hip & knee flexed and thighs gently abducted. A click of entrance will be felt as the femoral head slips back into the acetabulum from the position of dislocation.

Reference- Maheshwari 5th ed. Page no 220

question_text: A 40-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because she has pain in the right arm two hours after she fell in her home. Physical examination shows swelling and deformity of the right arm. The patient is unable to dorsiflex the wrist. X-ray studies show a spiral mid-shaft fracture of the humerus. Which of the following nerves is most likely affected by this fracture?
explanation:
• This clinical vignette describes the classical wrist drop occurring in association of humerus fractures due to injury to Radial N.
  • The radial nerve courses posterior to the middle third of the humeral shaft and is prone to injury with fractures of the midshaft of the humerus. Sensory distribution of the radial nerve includes the first dorsal web space of the hand, and motor innervation includes the dorsal forearm extensor muscles, including those of the wrist.
  • Radial N involvement is more common in distal third humerus fractures, and such fractures associated with Radial N injury is called Holstein Lewis fracture.
  • Option (A)- Axillary, is incorrect because this nerve is located posterior to the humeral neck. It provides sensation over the deltoid region and innervates the deltoid muscle.
  • Option (B)- Median, is incorrect because this nerve courses through the medial aspect of the arm between the biceps brachii and brachialis muscles. It provides sensation to the radial aspect of the palm and fingers as well as the distal dorsal surfaces of the thumb, index finger, long finger, and the radial aspect of the ring finger. Motor innervation within the hand includes the muscles of the thenar eminence.
  • Option (C)- Musculocutaneous, is incorrect because this nerve does not innervate any muscles involved in motor function of the wrist or hand.

Reference- Maheshwari Ortho 5th edition, page no 63

question_text: IDENTIFY TUMOR SHOWN IN XRAY IMAGE?
explanation:
• GCT The X-ray depicts the diagnostic Soap bubble appearance of a Giant cell tumor which is one of the commonest tumors to be seen in distal end of radius.
  • However, the commonest sites for the GCT per say are: Distal femur Proximal tibia Distal radius.

Giant cell tumor:

  • AGE (YR): 20-40 Slight female predominance
  • SITE: Distal femur>Proximal tibia>Distal radius
  • PRESENTATION: Pain, Pathologic fracture(10%-30%), Egg shell cracking sound on tapping the lesion is heard

IMAGING:

  • Eccentrically located in epiphysis
  • Purely radiolucent(no matrix formation) Soap bubble appearance
  • Usually, no rim of reactive bone
  • Abuts subchondral bone
  • May exhibit cortical destruction with softtissue extension
  • Metaphyseal in skeletally immature patients

HISTOLOGY:

  • Multinucleated giant cells in sea of mononuclear cells
  • Nuclei of mononuclear cells identical to nuclei of giant cells

TREATMENT:

  • Extended curettage Resection if residual bone stock inadequate
  • Consider radiation for spinal/sacral tumors Resection of pulmonary metastases

Reference: Maheshwari, Essential Ortho, 5th edition, Page no. 237.

question_text: Which is incorrect about perilunate dislocation?
option_a: Tavernier manoeuvre is used for closed reduction
option_c: Lunate remains in position and the carpals dislocate dorsally
option_d: Lunate dislocates ventrally and carpals remain in position
explanation:
• In Lunate dislocation the lunate dislocates out of the carpus while in Perilunate dislocation the lunate stays in its place while all other carpal bones dislocate out of the carpus.
  • In other words, in lunate dislocation long axis of radius passes through the capitate and in perilunate dislocation long axis of radius passes through the lunate.
  • The most common nerve injured in perilunate dislocation as well as in fracture of lunate is the Median nerve.
  • X-ray of perilunate dislocation shows discontinuity of Gilula’s arc. In lateral view of lunate dis- location, lunate is seen palmarly rotated and no longer articulates with capitate (Spilled teapot sign).
  • Treatment- In reducible perilunate dislocation close reduction and percutaneous pinning is recommended. Close reduction is achieved by Tavernier manoeuvre. For irreducible peri- lunate dislocations open reduction and repair is required.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition, page no 1648.

question_text: Shish kebab osteotomy is used for the treatment of which condition?
explanation:
• Shish kebab osteotomy is used for the treatment of osteogenesis imperfecta.
  • In OI, there is severe deformities of long bones of the body. These occur due to recurrent fractures of the fragile bones which malunite to produce gross deformities.
  • Surgical correction of any deformity of bone requires cutting the bone and straightening it and fixing it in the corrected position. This procedure is called osteotomy.
  • In OI, because of the severe deformities, a single bone may have to be osteotomised at multiple places and realigned to achieve correction. This procedure is similar to preparing shish kebab, where multiple pieces of meat are threaded on a skewer.

Reference: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics 5th edition page no. E621

question_text: What is the usual presenting feature of Jefferson's Fracture?
option_a: Sensory loss below the point of injury
explanation:
• In Jefferson's fracture(burst fracture of the atlas) the patient usually presents with neck pain but no neurological deficit. This is because Jefferson's fracture is a burst fracture, hence the fracture fragments will displace outward away from the spinal cord. But, rarely if there is a retro-pulsed fragment spinal cord injury may occur.
  • The fracture is identified on the open-mouth X-ray view(odontoid view) with displacement of C1 relative to C2.
  • Jefferson fracture:
    • A burst fracture of C1 ring resulting from an axial load is known as Jefferson's Fracture.
    • The fracture is identified on the open-mouth X-ray view with displacement of C1 relative to C2, i.e., overhang of the lateral processes. A CT scan will confirm and define the fracture.
    • If undisplaced, the injury is stable and the patient is managed with a semi-rigid collar.
    • If C1 overhang on C2>7mm on the open mouth view, the transverse ligament is likely to be ruptured(rule of Spence), making the injury unstable and should be treated by halo-vest for several weeks. And if there is persistent instability on X-ray then posterior C1/2 fixation and fusion is needed.
    • There is seldom a neurological injury. Fractures of the atlas are associated with injury elsewhere in the cervical spine in up to 50% of cases.

Reference: Ebnezar, 5th edition, Page no. 307.

question_text: What type of physeal injury is Tillaux fracture?
explanation:
• Tillaux fracture is a type III physeal injury.
  • It occurs due to the avulsion of the anterior talo fibular ligament.

Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 2148

question_text: In which condition is Thurston Holland fragment seen?
explanation:
• Thurston Holland fragment is seen in type II physeal injuries.
  • It is a triangular metaphyseal fragment of bone that is formed due to the fracture
  • When seen on x-ray it is also called the sail sign

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 58

question_text: A 5 year old child presents to the casualty with pain in the right wrist after fall. His x ray is given. What is the diagnosis?
option_a: SH type I injury of distal radius
option_b: SH type II injury of distal radius
option_c: SH type III injury of distal radius
option_d: SH type IV injury of distal radius
explanation:
• The x ray shows a triangular metaphyseal fragment which is called the Thurston Holland fragment and it is seen in type II physeal injuries.
  • Moreover the fracture line is seen to pass through the physis and exit through the metaphysis.
  • Type II injuries usually have good prognosis.

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 58

question_text: What type of physeal injury is Triplane fracture?
explanation:
• Triplane fracture is a type IV physeal injury of the distal tibia where the distal fragment gets displaced in all 3 planes.

Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 2148

question_text: Which of the following structures can be injured in a dashboard injury?
explanation:
• PCL can be injured in dash board injuries.
  • There are 2 mechanisms in which the PCL can be torn
    • RTA - Dash Board injury
    • Sports - Hyperflexion injury
  • In dashboard injuries, the proximal part of the tibia may impact against the dashboard of the car. This will result in a posterior thrust of the tibia against the femur, causing the PCL to rupture.

Reference: Koval's Handbook of fracture's 5th edition, page no. 647

question_text: False about cubitus varus deformity in supracondylar fracture is.
option_d: French osteotomy is used for correction
explanation:
• Cubitus varus in supracondylar fracture is not progressive.
  • Cubitus varus is the deformity in which the forearm is deviated towards the midline at the elbow.
  • It is also called the gun stock deformity
  • The most common cause for cubitus varus is the malunion of supracondylar fractures of humerus in children
  • Carrying angle is the angle between the long axis of arm and long axis of fore arm with elbow in full extension. In cubitus varus, the carrying angle will decrease
  • Baumann angle is the humero-capitellar angle which is measured on an x ray. In cubitus varus this angle will increase.
  • The treatment of choice for cubitus varus is Lateral closing wedge osteotomy.
  • French osteotomy is the most commonly used form of Lateral closing wedge osteotomy.

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 102

question_text: Stress fracture in Metatarsals is most common at
explanation:
• STRESS FRACTURES-
    • Bone is a dynamic structure and, unlike the scaffolding of a building, it adapts to the stresses placed upon it according to “Wolff’s law”.
    • A stress fracture is a break in a bone cause by repetitive stress.
    • Stress fractures can be either ‘fatigue fractures’ (normal bone) or ‘insufficiency fractures’ (abnormal bone).
    • Common sites: tibial shaft, the metatarsal shafts, the femur, and the bones of the pelvis.
    • The distribution of stress fractures amongst runners is: - Tibia 49%, Tarsals 25%, Metatarsals 9%, Femur 7% and Fibula 7%.
    • The tarsal navicular and metatarsal stress fractures are the bane of the armed forces owing to marching, but particular care must be taken of the base of fifth metatarsal fracture as it has a high rate of delayed union or nonunion.
    • Stress fractures are not confined to the lower limb and may occur in the ribs, clavicle, acromion, olecranon and metacarpals.
    • The second and third metatarsals are the most commonly affected.
    • Bone scintigraphy, or MRI if it is available, is the investigation of choice to demonstrate the earliest changes of marrow hypervascularity and trabecular microfracture.

Reference- Fundamentals of Orthopaedics Mohindra and Jain 1st edition page no 35

question_text: Bankart's lesion involves the avulsion of labrum from
explanation:
Though the original definition of Bankart lesion is that of an avulsion of labrum from the anterior glenoid, now we know that almost all Bankart lesions involve the antero-inferior labrum. Hence, option D is a better answer than option A.

  • Bankart’s lesion: this is the commonest lesion being present in almost 90-98% cases. There is detachment of anteroinferior labrum from margin of glenoid that produces recurrent anterior dislocations.
  • Bony Bankart’s lesion: this refers to the avulsion fracture of anteroinferior glenoid rim.
  • HAGL (humeral avulsion of glenohumeral ligaments) lesion: Here the glenohumeral ligaments (a static restraint) are avulsed from the humeral neck with failure of the ligaments to heal up.
  • Hill-Sach’s lesion: A defect is excavated on the posterolateral aspect of humeral head due to repeated impact against the anterior glenoid rim in patients who have had several episodes of dislocations. In throwing positions (90 degrees abduction and external rotation) this defect engages the glenoid rim and causes instability which may result in recurrent dislocations of shoulder.
  • Some special X-ray views used for shoulder joint are:
    • For Bankart’s lesion: West point axillary view
    • For Hill sach’s lesion: Internal rotation view and Stryker notch view

Reference- Essential Orthopaedics, Maheshwari, 5th ed. P 90

question_text: 32 year old pregnant female with 2 months of amenorrhea comes with mid clavicle fracture. What is your treatment of choice?
explanation:
• Clavicle fracture is commonly managed conservatively but in young female for cosmetic reasons, some surgeons prefer to perform plate fixation. But in case of young pregnant female, it is an absolute contraindication to operate any fracture in first trimester of pregnancy.

Reference- Campbell operative procedure 13ᵗʰ edition, page-3054

question_text: Turn buckle cast is used for
explanation:
• Turnbuckle cast: This device is used to immobilize the entire trunk, one upper arm to the elbow, and the upper legs to the knee.
  • It is constructed of plaster of Paris or fiberglass and incorporates a lateral hinge at the apex of the spinal deformity along its convexity and a turnbuckle (a threaded screw with a wing nut) on the concave side.
  • Opening the hinge by distraction of the concave side, via the turnbuckle, would result in corrective lateral bending forces placed on the deformity, straightening the primary curve.
  • Other important casts used in orthopedics
    • Minerva cast- Cervical spine disease
    • Risser's cast -Scoliosis
    • Turn-buckle -cast Scoliosis
    • Shoulder spica-Shoulder immobilisation
    • U-slab -Fracture of the humerus
    • Hanging cast -Fracture of the humerus
    • Colles’ (hand shake) cast- Colles’ fracture
    • Hip spica -Fracture shaft of the femur in children
    • Cylinder cast- Undisplaced fracture of the patella
    • PTB cast - Fracture of the tibia

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics 5th edition, page no 17

question_text: The 'terrible triad' injury of the elbow consists of radial head fracture, elbow dislocation and which of the following fracture?
explanation:
The terrible triad of the elbow is a severe elbow fracture-dislocation pattern with the following features:

  • Posterior elbow dislocation
  • Coronoid process fracture
  • Radial head fracture

Reference: Manish kumar varshney 1st edition page no 978

question_text: The malunion of supracondylar fracture of the humerus most commonly leads to:
explanation: B i.e. Cabitus Varus Malunion : - It is the commonest complication of supracondylar fracture and results in cubitus varus (Gun stock deformity). Cubitus valgus is rare and may occur occasionally in posterolateral displacement.

question_text: Which classification is used for the fracture shown in the image?
explanation:
Above image clearly shows intra articular radial head fracture. Mason classification is used for classifying radial head fractures.

  • Mason's classification:
    • Type I, nondisplaced fracture.
    • Type II, displaced partial articular fracture with or without comminution.
    • Type III, comminuted radial head fracture involving the whole head.
  • Bado classification - used for monteggia fracture.
  • Mayo classification - used for olecranon process fracture.
  • Malone classification - used for distal end radius fracture.

Reference: Postgraduate Orthopedics by Manish Kumar Varshney, 1st Edition, Page Number-980.

question_text: Not a classical displacement in supracondylar fracture humerus

question_text: External fixation is used most often for which of the following?
option_a: Definitive treatment of type I open tibia fractures
option_b: Definitive treatment of pediatric femur fractures
option_c: Temporization of open fractures or fractures with soft tissue compromise
explanation:
External Fixator

Overview

An external fixator is a medical device used to stabilize fractures by holding the bone in a steel frame outside the limb. This technique is particularly useful for managing open fractures where internal fixation is not feasible due to the risk of infection. The fixator consists of pins inserted percutaneously into the bone, which are then connected externally to a bar using clamps.

Types of External Fixators

  1. Pin Fixators
    • Description: Utilizes 3-4 mm sized pins inserted through the bone.
    • Configuration: Pins are stabilized outside the bone using a system of tubular rods and clamps (see Fig-3.5a).
    • Applications: Commonly used for simple and complex fracture patterns where strong stability is needed.
  2. Ring Fixators
    • Description: Employs thin 'K' wires (1-2 mm) passed through the bone.
    • Configuration: Wires are secured externally using circular rings, which allow for precise adjustments and dynamic corrections.
    • Applications: Often used in complex fractures, deformity corrections, and limb lengthening procedures.

Advantages

  • Minimizes Infection Risk: Particularly beneficial in open fractures where traditional internal fixation may pose a higher risk of infection.
  • Versatility: Can be adjusted externally, allowing for dynamic correction of alignment and rotation during the healing process.

Considerations

  • Requires careful monitoring of pin sites to prevent infection.
  • Regular adjustments may be needed to maintain optimal alignment and stability.

Option A, B & D: Although external fixators are used for all the situations (options A, B, C and D) given, external fixation is primarily used for temporization of fractures (Option C) and occasionally for definitive treatment these days as better implants are available.

Key takeaways:

Indications

  • Open fractures with a high risk of infection.
  • Severe soft tissue injuries where internal fixation is not possible.
  • Situations requiring gradual bone transport or deformity correction.

question_text: A 20-year-old male with a spiral midshaft femur fracture from a high velocity injury presents to the emergency department for evaluation. He is 66 inches tall and weighs 66 kg. The best option for treatment would be:
explanation:
Nonoperative Management: Skeletal Traction

  • Indication: Used in adult patients with significant medical comorbidities where surgery is contraindicated.
  • Usage: Temporary measure before surgery; traction should be 15% of body weight (20-40 lb).
  • Complications: Knee stiffness, limb shortening, heterotopic ossification, prolonged hospitalization, respiratory/skin issues, malunion.

Operative Management

  • Standard of Care: Operative stabilization for most femoral shaft fractures, ideally within 24 hours after resuscitation.

Intramedullary Nailing (IM Nailing)

  • Standard for Femoral Shaft Fractures:
    • Benefits: Less exposure, lower infection rates, less quadriceps scarring, lower tensile/shear stresses.
    • Advantages: Maintains fracture hematoma and periosteum; early functional use; high union rates (>95%).
  • Surgical Approach:
    • Antegrade:
      • Positioning: Supine or lateral; either piriformis fossa or greater trochanteric starting point.
      • Consider reaming for better outcomes; all nails should be statically locked.
    • Retrograde:
      • Easier identification of starting point.
      • Relative indications include ipsilateral injuries and bilateral fractures; contraindications include restricted knee motion.

External Fixation

  • Indication: Limited use as definitive treatment; often provisional (damage control).

Plate Fixation

  • Decreasing Use: Due to IM nailing popularity.
  • Advantages:
    • Anatomic reduction possible.
    • Minimal trauma to distant structures.
    • Newer minimally invasive techniques available.
  • Indications:
    • Narrow medullary canal, malunion fractures, obliteration due to infection, proximal/distal extension fractures, and associated vascular injuries

Option A: Long-leg casts are not typically used for adults because of high malunion rates.

Option B: Traction and long leg cast is also not a very feasible option as it will involve prolonged bed rest which increases the chances of DVT, bed sores etc.

Option C: Retrograde IM nailing is not very popular nowadays as it involves opening the fracture site or knee joint which drains fracture hematoma and attracts complications like non-union, infection and knee stiffness.

Option D: An antegrade IM nail with trochanteric starting point would be best choice as it is a minimally invasive procedure and gives good stability and allows early mobilization.

Key takeaways:

Femoral Shaft fractures in adults are managed with an antegrade IM nail with trochanteric starting point as it is a minimally invasive procedure and gives good stability and allows early mobilization.

question_text: Volkmann's ischemic contracture mostly involves which of the following mucles ?

VOLKMANN ISCHEMIC CONTRACTURE-

  • It is a consequence of ischemic necrosis of muscles and nerves of forearm which are then replaced by fibrous tissue. Any obstruction to brachial artery caused by tight plaster, improper use of tourniquet, or compartment syndrome can lead to Volkmann ischemic contracture (VIC).

  • Supracondylar humerus fracture is the most common fracture associated with vascular injury (Brachial artery) and is the most common cause of compartment syndrome and Volkmann’s ischemia in children.
  • Volkmann ischemic contracture most commonly involves FDP and median nerve.
  • A turn buckle splint is most commonly used for mild deformities.

question_text: After injury to the thumb MCP joint ulnar collateral ligament, what is the significance of a Stener lesion?
option_a: Represents a bony avulsion that will likely necessitate pin fixation for stability
option_b: Represents displacement of the torn ulnar collateral ligament superficial to the adductor aponeurosis, which can prevent proper healing of the ligament back to the insertion site and will likely necessitate surgical intervention
option_c: Represents an area of a chronic nonunion that will likely necessitate open reduction and screw fixation
option_d: Represents an incidental radiographic finding that has no clinical relevance
explanation:
Thumb Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) Joint Dislocation

Anatomy and Mechanism of Injury

  • The thumb MCP joint primarily facilitates flexion and extension but also allows for abduction-adduction and limited rotational movement (pronation with flexion).
  • Collateral Ligament Injury:
    • A one-sided collateral ligament injury can cause the phalanx to subluxate volarly in a rotatory manner, pivoting around the intact opposite ligament.
    • Ulnar Collateral Ligament (UCL) Injury:
      • May present as a two-level injury with a fracture at the ulnar base of the proximal phalanx and a ruptured ligament detached from the fracture fragment.

Stener Lesion (Option A,B,C and D)

  • Definition: The proximal edge of the adductor aponeurosis forms the anatomic basis of the Stener lesion.
    • The torn UCL stump displaced dorsally to the adductor aponeurosis, preventing natural healing to its anatomic insertion at the volar, ulnar base of the proximal phalanx.
  • Incidence: The true incidence of the Stener lesion is unclear due to varied reporting in literature.

Diagnosis

  • Clinical Assessment:
    • If the MCP joint opens >30 degrees or >15 degrees compared to the contralateral side (tested at 30 degrees of flexion), it suggests a complete collateral ligament injury.

Treatment

  1. Nonoperative Management:
    • Indicated for partial collateral ligament injuries.
    • Options:
      • Thumb spica cast or splint for 6 weeks.
  2. Operative Management:
    • Indicated for complete UCL injuries, while surgical management for radial collateral ligament injuries is controversial.
    • Surgical Techniques:
      • Ligament Repair: Using a bone suture anchor.
      • Chronic Injury: If the ligament is not viable for repair, a free tendon graft through bone tunnels may be used.

Key takeaways:

Stener lesion: Occurs in 85% of complete UCL tear injuries when the adductor pollicis aponeurosis is interposed between the avulsed UCL and its insertion site on the base of the proximal phalanx.

  • Treatment: Surgical reattachment of ligament through drill holes, suture anchor, or interference screw is necessary and can't be treated conservatively.

question_text: A male patient presented with the fracture of Tibia following a road traffic accident. He was managed appropriately, but after 2 days he developed dyspnea, petechiae involving the whole body, and a fall in oxygen saturation. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The classic triad of dyspnoea, hypoxemia, and petechial rash appearing 24–72 hours after a long bone fracture strongly suggests fat embolism syndrome (FES).
  • It occurs due to fat droplets released from the bone marrow into the bloodstream after trauma. These emboli lodge in pulmonary and systemic capillaries, leading to respiratory failure, neurological changes, and skin/mucosal petechiae.
  • This is a life-threatening condition requiring prompt recognition and supportive management (oxygen therapy, fluids, sometimes steroids).

Fat embolism syndrome:

  • Common causes: Long bone fractures (femur, tibia), pelvic fractures, orthopaedic surgery, burns.
  • Clinical features:
    • Respiratory distress (dyspnoea, tachypnoea, hypoxemia).
    • Neurological changes (confusion, agitation, seizures).
    • Petechial rash (chest, axilla, conjunctiva, oral mucosa).
  • Diagnostic criteria (Gurd and Wilson):
    • Major: Respiratory insufficiency, cerebral signs, petechial rash.
    • Minor: Tachycardia, pyrexia, retinal changes, jaundice, renal dysfunction, sudden anemia, thrombocytopenia, ↑ESR, fat macroglobulinemia.
  • Treatment: Supportive care-oxygen, fluids, mechanical ventilation if needed, DVT prophylaxis, and sometimes corticosteroids.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Air embolism (Option B): Usually occurs after trauma to large veins, surgery, or catheter procedures. Presents acutely with respiratory collapse, not with a delayed rash and neuro signs.

Venous thromboembolism (Option C): Can occur after fractures but causes pulmonary embolism without petechial rash. Typically presents with chest pain, tachypnoea, and hypoxemia.

Pulmonary hypertension (Option D): A chronic condition of elevated pulmonary artery pressure, not an acute complication of fracture with petechiae.

Key Takeaway:

In a patient with long bone fracture who later develops dyspnea, altered mental status, and petechial rash, the diagnosis is fat embolism syndrome, confirmed clinically and managed with supportive care.

Fat Embolism Clinical Presentation: History, Physical Examinationhttps://emedicine.medscape.com/article/460524-clinical#showall?form=fpf

question_text: All of the following are radiological features of fracture non-union except:
explanation:
Delayed and Non-Union of Fractures

Definition:

  • Delayed Union: When a fracture takes longer than expected to heal but eventually unites.
  • Non-Union: When a fracture fails to unite after 6 months, with no further progression towards healing.

Clinical Features:

  • Delayed Union: Persistent fracture line visible on X-rays with inadequate callus formation.
  • Non-Union: Visible fracture line with minimal or absent bridging callus. The fracture ends may be smooth, rounded, and sclerotic, with possible obliteration of the medullary cavity.

Signs & Symptoms:

  • Persistent pain or pain on stressing the fracture.
  • Mobility at the fracture site (in non-union).
  • Increasing deformity.

Common Sites:

  • Neck of the femur
  • Scaphoid
  • Lower third of the tibia
  • Lower third of the ulna
  • Lateral condyle of the humerus

Types of Non-Union:

  1. Atrophic: Minimal or no callus formation.
  2. Hypertrophic: Callus is present but does not bridge the fracture site.

Diagnosis:

  • Clinical Findings: Persistent pain, abnormal mobility, and deformity.
  • Radiological Features:
    • Delayed Union: Visible fracture line with inadequate callus.
    • Non-Union: Smooth, sclerotic fracture ends with little bridging callus.
    • Advanced Imaging: 3D CT scans, stress X-rays, and weight-bearing X-rays may be required for detailed evaluation.

Consequences:

  • Persistent pain, deformity, abnormal mobility.
  • Refracture risk if stressed.

Treatment Options:

  1. Conservative Management: Continue physiotherapy and monitoring in delayed unions.
  2. Surgical Intervention:
    • Bone Grafting: Commonly used with internal fixation, using grafts from the iliac crest.
    • Excision of Fragments: Used where removal does not affect function (e.g., distal ulna).
    • Prosthetic Replacement: For non-union of the femoral neck in elderly patients.
  3. Ilizarov's Method: Ring external fixation for complex cases.
  4. No Treatment: In asymptomatic non-unions, especially in the scaphoid.

Option A, B & D: The fracture line is visible (Option B). There is little bridging callus (Option A). The fracture ends may be rounded, smooth and sclerotic (not lytic) (Option C). The medullary cavity may be obliterated (Option D).

Key takeaways:

The following are some of the radiological features suggestive of these complications:

  • Delayed union: The fracture line is visible. There may be inadequate callus bridging the fracture site.
  • Non-union: The fracture line is visible. There are little bridging calluses. The fracture ends may be rounded, smooth and sclerotic (not lytic). The medullary cavity may be obliterated.

question_text: Traumatic AVN of Neck of femur occurs due to injury to which vessels?
explanation:
• The most important blood vessel supplying the head and neck of femur is the Lateral retinacular branch of the Medial circumflex femoral A
  • The blood supply of Femoral head comes from 2 branches of deep femoral A - medial and lateral circumflex femoral A.
  • Both of these vessels anastomose at the base of the neck forming an arterial ring.
  • This ring send off ascending cervical arteries (Retinacular arteries) which ascend up the neck and supplies the head of femur.
  • These retinacular arteries are end arteries, so in fracture neck of femur, there is complete disruption of blood supply to head of femur resulting in AVN.

question_text: 6 years old child has an accident and had fracture over his elbow before 4 years. Now he is presented with tingling and numbness over little and ring fingers. Diagnose the fracture child had before 4 yrs.
explanation:
• From the history, the child has tingling of little and ring fingers, indication Ulnar N palsy. There is also a delay of 4 years from the point of injury and development of Ulnar N palsy. This kind of late onset Ulnar N palsy is called tardy ulnar N palsy. The most common cause of tardy Ulnar N palsy is progressive cubitus valgus deformity produced by nonunion of lateral condyle of humerus fracture.
  • Fracture lateral condyle humerus can undergo nonunion if not treated surgically because of the pull of common extensor muscles. This will cause growth arrest in the lateral half of distal humeral physis.
  • Diminished growth at the lateral side of distal humerus epiphysis results in a overgrowth of medial side resulting in a cubitus valgus deformity.
  • This may result in late ulnar nerve palsy (tardy ulnar nerve palsy) because of stretching of the ulnar nerve as it moves over the medial epicondyle, every time the elbow is flexed and extended.
  • Treatment-anterior transposition of ulnar nerve

• Here, the child has suffered a nonunion of the lateral condyle of humerus, which has result in a cubitus valgus deformity.
  • Because of this deformity, the Ulnar N gets stretched slowly and over time cause it to stop functioning resulting in a Tardy (late onset) Ulnar N palsy.
  • Ulnar N is the one which innervates the palmar interossei, which are the finger adductors.
  • So Tardy Ulnar N palsy will result in inability to adduct the fingers.

A lateral condyle fracture which does not show signs of healing by 3 months is said to be in nonunion. Early nonunion fracture presents with pain and instability. These patients are treated by open reduction and internal fixation with bone grafting.

Late presentation of nonunion is either a painless mass or a cubitus valgus deformity. With increasing valgus tardy ulnar nerve palsy may develop (due to stretching of ulnar nerve with increasing valgus). Severe cases are treated by corrective osteotomy (Milch osteotomy) with or without ulnar nerve transposition.

Option a) ape thumb deformity is seen in median nerve injury

Option b) pointing index is seen in median nerve injury

Option c) kiloh nevin sign is seen in median nerve and anterior interosseus nerve injury

Reference:Campbells operative orthopedics 14thedition page no 1508

question_text: A 42-year-old construction worker sustains a crush injury to the hand at a job site. He immediately develops pain and significant swelling, and is taken to the local emergency department for evaluation. Radiographs do not demonstrate any fracture or dislocation. On examination, he experiences severe pain with passive extension of the metacarpal phalangeal and interphalangeal joints Otherwise, he has intact sensation and appropriate capillary refill. What is the next best step in treatment?
explanation:
• All signs and symptoms show patient is having compartment syndrome of the hand. A history and clinical exam are the best tools to identify the diagnosis, and the treatment consists of emergent fasciotomies.
  • Compartment syndrome of the hand may be secondary to trauma, burn, IV drug use, extravasation of IV fluids, or major limb revascularization.
  • The diagnosis is usually made with pain not responding to analgesics, particularly with passive stretch of the digits. It is possible to have compartment syndrome without neurovascular changes (paresthesia, pallor, pulselessness), particularly earlier in the presentation.
  • Compartment measurements may be obtained and are considered diagnostic with an absolute value greater than 30mmHg or when the compartment pressure is within 30mmHg of the patient's diastolic blood pressure.
  • However, pressure testing is not necessary in most cases, but may be particularly important in the patient who is obtunded, intubated, or who had a regional block, as the physical findings will be confounded. There are ten hand compartments: hypothenar, thenar, adductor pollicis, four dorsal interosseous, and three palmar interosseous; and emergent surgical release of all ten compartments is indicated.

Reference- Maheshwari ortho 5th edition, page number 47.

question_text: A 17-year-old boy falls on an outstretched hand and now complains of pain and swelling at the base of the thumb. Which carpal bone is most likely fractured?
explanation:
Explanation:

The scaphoid bone is the carpal bone that is most likely fractured.

Mechanism of injury: Classically follows a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) with the wrist extended (dorsiflexed).

  • Typical site:
    • Waist of scaphoid – most common
    • Distal pole – least common
    • Proximal pole – highest risk for avascular necrosis due to retrograde blood supply.
  • Clinical features:
    • Localised pain and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, the triangular depression at the base of the thumb, bordered by the tendons of extensor pollicis longus and the abductor pollicis longus/extensor pollicis brevis.
    • Swelling and pain, or reduced wrist motion.
  • Investigations:
    • An X-ray may show a fracture line at the waist, cortical disruption, or displacement.
    • MRI or bone scan is more sensitive if initial X-rays are negative, but suspicion remains.
  • Management:
    • Immobilisation in a thumb-spica (scaphoid) cast for 6–12 weeks or longer, depending on healing.
    • Surgical fixation is required displaced joint or if there is non-union.
  • Complications:
    • Avascular necrosis (especially proximal pole).
    • Delayed union, non-union.
    • Chronic wrist arthritis and "humpback" deformity.

Explanation for other options:

Lunate (Option A): Injured mainly by hyperextension trauma or collapse of a weakened lunate (Kienböck disease). In perilunate dislocation, the other carpal bones dislocate dorsally while the lunate stays in place; in lunate dislocation, the lunate itself moves volarly. Presents with median nerve symptoms and deformity, not isolated snuffbox pain.

Pisiform (Option C): A rare fracture, usually caused by a direct blow to the ulnar side of the wrist or by avulsion from the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon. Pain is localised to the hypothenar region, not the radial (thumb) side.

Trapezoid (Option D): One of the least commonly fractured carpal bones. Typically results from an axial load on the second metacarpal, producing dorsal pain at the index-metacarpal base rather than snuffbox tenderness.

question_text: A 79-year-old lady presents with a history of fall. There is a right sided intertrochanteric fracture of the hip evidenced by the given X-ray. Best management for this patient is-
explanation:
• X-ray image shows intertrochanteric femur fracture which is more common in elderly people with osteoporotic bones.
  • In elderly population, the intertrochanteric fracture is usually sustained by a sideway fall or a blow over the greater trochanter.
  • Most of these undisplaced fractures unite by themselves if femoral neck-shaft angle is maintained. Done by conservative means like traction (require bed rest of 3-4 months).
  • In elderly population, internal fixation in the form of Dynamic hip screw (DHS) or Proximal femoral nailing (PFN) is the treatment of choice. Prolonged bed rest in elderly is best avoided as it can cause further complications like pneumonia, bed sores etc.

question_text: What is not required in an emergency management of an open femur fracture?

  • Once wound gets healed and infection is cleared thereafter open reduction and internal fixation is done.

For open fractures gustilo and Anderson classification is used for grading.

For open fractures like 3B - antibiotics coated intramedullary nails are preferred over K wires.

  • With the evolution of available nails like antibiotic impregnated nails, intramedullary nailing is now performed even in 3B fractures.
  • Although there was initial phobia for the use of intramedullary nails, their usage has become widespread not only in grade 1 and 2 but even in grade 3 injuries.

question_text: A 24-year-old male sustained a shaft of femur fracture after a road traffic accident, and internal fixation was done for the same. Two days later, he developed shortness of breath with confusion and a petechial rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given clinical features of the development of dyspnea and petechial rash after a long bone fracture suggest a diagnosis of fat embolism.

  • Fat embolism commonly follows limb fractures, with fat globules often appearing in the blood after closed long bone fractures, and histological evidence of fat can be found in the lungs and other organs.
  • In some cases, it causes symptoms resembling ARDS, but a history of limb fractures and development of petechiae helps to differentiate between the two. (Option D ruled out)
  • The fat source is likely bone marrow, and the condition is more frequent in patients with multiple fractures.
  • Early signs within 72 hours include mild temperature and pulse elevation, progressing in some to breathlessness, mental confusion or restlessness, and in severe cases, respiratory distress and coma due to brain emboli and lung hypoxia.
  • Distinguishing signs are petechiae on the trunk, axillae, conjunctiva, and retina.
  • Diagnosis has no definitive test but may involve detecting fat globules in urine, monitoring blood PO2 (with levels below 8 kPa within 72 hours raising suspicion), and a chest X-ray for lung changes.
  • Management is supportive, with high inspired oxygen early after injury, prompt long-bone fracture stabilisation, and patient positioning in sitting to improve lung ventilation-perfusion.

Explanation of other options:

Tension pneumothorax (Option B): Tension pneumothorax occurs when a 'one-way valve' air leak develops from either the lung or the chest wall, allowing air to enter the thoracic cavity but preventing its escape. This causes the affected lung to fully collapse and compress, while shifting the mediastinum to the opposite side, reducing venous return and compressing the other lung. Common causes include penetrating chest injuries, blunt trauma with an unsealed parenchymal lung air leak, and iatrogenic damage such as from central venepuncture and mechanical positive-pressure ventilation.

Air embolism (Option C): Air can inadvertently enter the venous system through injection or be drawn into an open vein during procedures such as head and neck surgery or from penetrating trauma to the neck. It can also result from Fallopian tube insufflation or illegal abortion. When a significant volume of air reaches the right side of the heart, it can create an airlock in the pulmonary artery, leading to acute right-sided heart failure.

question_text: Fracture after trivial fall in elderly patient. Identify the cause?
explanation:
Explanation for answer:

A pathological fracture occurring after minimal trauma (a trivial fall) in an elderly patient is most commonly due to bony metastasis.

Common primary cancers that metastasize to bone include :

  • In males: Lung carcinoma
  • In females: Breast carcinoma
  • Prostate carcinoma: Typically causes bone-forming (osteoblastic) lesions
  • Thyroid carcinoma

These metastases weaken the bone structure, making it susceptible to fracture under normal physiological loads.

Clinical Features

  • Bone pain, often in spine, ribs, and long bones.
  • Pathological fractures, frequently in spine and hip.

Common Sites of Bone Metastasis:

  • Vertebral bodies
  • Ribs
  • Pelvis
  • Humerus
  • Femur

Explanation of other options:

TB hip (Option B): The patient typically presents with a more chronic history of pain, swelling, and constitutional symptoms before a fracture might occur.


Brown tumour (Option C): A lesion seen in hyperparathyroidism, which is a less common cause of pathological fracture than widespread metastasis in the elderly.


Eosinophilic granuloma (Option D): A benign bone lesion of Langerhans cell histiocytosis that primarily affects children and young adults, not the elderly.

Key Takeaways:

  • In an elderly patient, a pathological fracture is most often due to metastatic bone disease.

question_text: In hypertrophic nonunion which of the following is the most appropriate treatment ?
explanation:
HYPERTROPHIC NONUNION

  • Hypertrophic nonunion occurs because of inadequate immobilization. The quality of bone is very good and union is not taking place just because of the mobility at the fracture site. So a simple fixation of fracture is enough to induce bone healing.
  • Hypertrophic nonunions are characterized by vascularized bone ends. Callus formation is generally seen and may be abundant but this callus is non bridging in nature. Types of hypertrophic nonunion include.
    • Elephant's foot—rich in callus-it results from insecure fixation and early weight bearing in a reduced fracture
    • Horse's hoof-less abundant callus-it is seen in moderately unstable fracture fixation
    • Oligotrophic-minimal or no callus but vascularized bone ends. It is seen in distracted/displaced bone ends.

question_text: A mass casualty is reported in a tertiary care centre with a history of a passenger bus involved in an RTA. The emergency department should be ready for initial radiologic imaging of the poly-trauma patients which includes:
option_a: Chest radiograph + anteroposterior (AP) view of pelvis
option_b: Chest radiograph, AP view of pelvis, and CT of cervical spine
explanation:
General Considerations in Polytrauma Management

Polytrauma Overview

  • Definition: Polytrauma refers to multiple traumatic injuries resulting from high-energy trauma, often associated with significant morbidity and mortality.
  • Management Protocols: Adherence to Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) protocols is critical for effective assessment and treatment.

ATLS Primary Survey (ABCs of Resuscitation)

  1. A-Airway Maintenance with Cervical Spine Protection:
  2. B-Breathing and Ventilation:
  3. C-Circulation with Hemorrhage Control:
  4. D-Disability and Neurologic Assessment:
  5. E-Exposure and Environmental Control:

Initial Radiologic Workup

  • During or Immediately After the Primary Survey:
    • Standard Imaging Includes: (Option A, B, C and D)
      • Anteroposterior (AP) chest radiograph.
      • AP pelvis radiograph.
      • Lateral cervical spine radiograph (must include C7-T1 junction for adequacy).

Advanced Imaging

  1. Computed Tomography (CT) Scan:
    • Advantages:
      1. Superior availability and processing speed.
      2. Replacing lateral cervical spine radiographs for trauma evaluation.
      3. Sagittal views detect approximately 85% of cervical spine fractures.
    • Indications:
      1. Evaluation of C1 fractures.
      2. Assessing bone integrity in the spinal canal.
    • Limitations:
      1. May miss axial plane fractures (e.g., Type II odontoid fractures).
  2. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI):
    • Benefits:
      1. Superior for detecting soft tissue abnormalities.
      2. Evaluates the integrity of the posterior longitudinal complex (PLC).
      3. Detects disc herniations, canal compromise, spinal cord injury, edema, and epidural hematomas.
    • Controversial Use:
      1. Increasingly used for cervical spine "clearance", but its routine use remains debated.

Secondary Survey

  • Performed After Primary Survey and Initial Imaging:
    • Comprehensive head-to-toe evaluation of each body region.
    • Focus:
      • Neurological Examination:
        • Assess the lowest remaining functional level.
        • Check for sacral sparing, indicating an incomplete spinal cord injury.
        • Neurologic level defined by the most cephalad level with normal bilateral motor and sensory function
      • Investigate:
        • Facial injuries.
        • Hypotension.
        • Localized tenderness or muscle spasm.

Additional Imaging Based on Secondary Survey

  • Complete Cervical Spine Series (C1-T1):
    • Indicated if there are findings from the secondary survey that suggest further spinal injury.
    • Multiple-Level Injuries:
      • Occur in 10%-20% of trauma cases.

Reassessment

  • If the patient's condition deteriorates during the secondary survey, reinitiate the primary survey to reassess and stabilize the patient.

Key takeaways:

CT of the cervical spine has replaced the lateral cervical spine radiograph in the standard trauma series for spine clearance. Radiography of the pelvis and chest remains the standard. The other examinations may be indicated by the clinical scenario.

question_text: In atrophic nonunion following a fracture, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment ?
explanation:
ATROPHIC NONUNION

  • Atrophic nonunion is characterized by absence of callus formation at fracture site. This occurs because of the poor quality of bone fracture ends/ loss of blood supply or infections. Bone scan will show avascular fracture ends.
  • Atrophic nonunions have to be treated using fixation and bone grafting. Bone graft will supply stem cells and osteoinductive factors which will induce and promote bone healing.
  • Infected nonunions are usually treated using Ilizarov fixation.

question_text: All are true regarding osteopetrosis except
explanation:
• Fracture healing is normal in osteopetrosis.
  • Osteopetrosis is also called Marble bone disease/Albers Schonberg disease
  • It is a congenital condition characterized by defective osteoclastic resorption of immature bone resulting in its accumulation through out the skeleton, causing increased frequency of long bone fractures, cranial nerve palsies, pancytopenia and low back pain.
  • Clinical feature include
    • Low back pain
    • Pathological fractures
    • Progressive anemia
    • Severe infections : Mandible osteomyelitis
    • Easy bruising
    • Failure to thrive
    • Cranial N 2, 7, 8 palsy leading to blindness and deafness

question_text: 3 year old child presented with progressive anemia, hepatosplenomegaly and osteomyelitis of jaw with pathological fracture. His x-rays show diffuse sclerosis of bones. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Osteopetrosis(also known as Marble bone disease, Albers-Schonberg disease):

  • Defect is in bone resorption due to abnormal function of osteoclasts.
  • Defective bone resorption results in uniformly thickened dense bones, often without distinction between cortical and cancellous regions.
  • The bones are dense but brittle therefore known as marble bone disease.
  • Inheritance is both AD & AR. The AR form dies early in the life. The AD form is of milder variety.
  • Due to abnormal thickening of bone, there will be narrowing of cranial nerve foramina resulting in cranial N palsies causing blindness and deafness.
  • The medullary canal usually gets obliterated by bone deposition leading to bone marrow failure. This causes pancytopenia. Neutropenia manifests as recurrent infections especially mandibular osteomyelitis. Thrombocytopenia presents as easy bruising and bleeding. The anemia will be classically progressive as more and more of medullary canal gets filled up with bone.

Reference: Manish kumar varshney, 1st edition, Page no. 96.

question_text: A 7 year old child fell from a tree and sustained injury to the right ankle. X-ray taken did not show any fractures and was treated with crepe bandage. At 10 years of age the child presents with valgus deformity of right ankle. What could be the cause?
explanation:
• This child has sustained a type V physeal injury.
  • In type V injuries there is crushing of a part or whole of the physis.
  • Many a time these injuries will not be visible on the initial x ray.
  • These injuries will get revealed only later when the child grows and deformities develop in the affected bone due to physeal arrest.

Surgical Osteotomies in DDH:

  1. Salter's Osteotomy (Option D)
    • Type: Iliac bone osteotomy above the acetabulum.
    • Procedure: The acetabular roof is rotated with the pubic symphysis as the fulcrum.
    • Purpose: Increases horizontal coverage of the femoral head by the acetabulum.
  2. Chiari's Pelvic Displacement Osteotomy (Option B)
    • Type: Transverse osteotomy of the iliac bone above the acetabulum.
    • Procedure: The lower fragment (with the acetabulum) is displaced medially, allowing the upper fragment to add depth to the acetabulum.
    • Purpose: Enhances acetabular depth and coverage of the femoral head.
  3. Pemberton's Pericapsular Osteotomy (Option A)
    • Type: Curved osteotomy near the acetabulum.
    • Procedure: The acetabular roof is deflected downwards over the femoral head, with the triradiate cartilage as the fulcrum.
    • Purpose: Improves coverage of the femoral head by changing the angle of the acetabulum.

Option C: Pauwels osteotomy is used for old neglected/ non united/ malunited neck of femur fractures and not DDH.

Pauwels Osteotomy:

  • Type: Valgus osteotomy at the level of the lesser trochanter.
  • Procedure: Creates a valgus effect at the fracture site, converting shearing forces into compression forces, which aids in fracture healing.
  • Fixation: Done using a double-angle blade plate.

question_text: A 70 yr old lady presents with complaints of easy fatigability and back pain. Her DEXA scan shows T score of -3.5 SD. Which bone is most commonly fractured in this condition?
explanation:
Osteoporosis and Pathological Fractures:

  • Condition:
    • Osteoporosis is a condition characterized by weakened bones, making them more prone to fractures.
  • Pathological Fractures:
    • Definition: Fractures that occur in bones weakened by disease, often from minimal trauma or even spontaneously.
    • Common Cause: Osteoporosis is the most frequent cause of pathological fractures.
  • Diagnosis of Osteoporosis:
    • Test Used: Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) scan.
    • Measurement: Bone density is measured and reported as a T-score.
    • T-score Interpretation:
      • A T-score of less than -2.5 standard deviations (SD) is indicative of osteoporosis.

Options A, B, C and D-

Common pathological fractures due to osteoporosis are as follows:

Thoracic vertebrae >>> Lumbar vertebrae >>> Neck of femur >>> Distal radius.

Key Takeaway -

  • The bones most often affected in osteoporosis are the vertebral bodies (thoracic > lumbar). Other common fractures associated with osteoporosis are fracture of the neck of the femur and Colles' fracture.
  • DEXA scan measures T score and Z score. But only the T score is used as a quantitative measure of osteoporosis.

question_text: What could be the likely diagnosis based on the x-ray image of a 22-year-old female?
explanation:
Explanation:

An eccentric, expansile lytic lesion in the epimetaphyseal region of a skeletally mature adult is characteristic of a Giant Cell Tumor (GCT).

  • Giant Cell Tumor (GCT), also called Osteoclastoma, is a benign but locally aggressive bone tumor that typically occurs after skeletal maturity (20-45 years) and predominantly affects females.
  • It arises in the epiphyseal region of long bones, most commonly the distal femur, proximal tibia, and distal radius.
  • Clinically, patients present with swelling, pain, and occasionally pathological fractures.
  • Radiographic features:
    • Eccentric, expansile lytic lesion in the epiphysis (may extend to metaphysis).
    • Non-sclerotic margins, "soap bubble" appearance in some cases.
    • No periosteal reaction unless fractured.
  • Histologically, the lesion is composed of multinucleated giant cells dispersed uniformly in a stromal background.
  • Management:
    • Extended intralesional curettage with bone grafting or cementing is the standard.
    • Recurrence can occur.
    • Denosumab is used in certain recurrent or inoperable cases.
    • Rarely, pulmonary metastasis can occur (benign metastasizing GCT).

Explanation of other options:

Chondroblastoma (Option A): Occurs in adolescents and children (before closure of growth plates). Appears as an epiphyseal lesion but in skeletally immature patients. Biopsy shows characteristic chicken wire calcification.

Osteochondroma (Option B): Arises from the metaphysis and presents as a painless bony outgrowth. Radiographs show a pedunculated or sessile lesion with a cartilage cap.

Aneurysmal bone cyst (Option D): Seen in younger patients (first two decades). X-ray shows a multiloculated, expansile, lytic lesion with a soap-bubble appearance. Histology reveals blood-filled spaces separated by septa containing fibroblasts and giant cells.

question_text: This is the typical appearance of?
explanation:
This is an osteoid osteoma. CT is the modality of choice and typically shows a focally lucent nidus within surrounding sclerotic reactive bone. A central sclerotic dot may also be seen.

Osteoid osteoma:

  • Benign bone forming lesion considered to be the most common true benign tumor of the bone
  • Age group - 2nd-3rd decades
  • Male : female = 3 : 1
  • Lower extremity, long bones, Posterior elements spine, Diaphyseal/metaphyseal
  • Pain - worse at night
  • XRAY - Cortical radiolucent nidus <1.5 cm with marked cortical thickening
  • High levels of cyclooxygenases and prostaglandins in the lesion
  • Frequently responds to NSAIDs
  • HISTOLOGY - Trabeculae surrounded by loose fibrovascular tissue
  • TREATMENT - NSAIDs, Burr down technique, Radiofrequency ablation.

Reference: Maheshwari Essential ortho, 5th edition, Page no. 236.

question_text: Identify the false statement about treatment of Ewing's sarcoma:
option_a: Though Ewing's sarcoma is highly radio-sensitive, chemotherapy can be used to treat metastasis
option_b: Combination chemotherapy of vincristine, adriamycin and cisplatin is preferred
option_c: Combination chemotherapy of vincristine, adriamycin and cyclophosphamide is preferred
option_d: Surgical resection is not of much use as metastasis is very common before diagnosis
explanation:
Ewing Sarcoma Management:

Ewing's sarcoma is a highly radiosensitive tumor (Option A), meaning it responds well to radiotherapy. However, despite this sensitivity, the tumor is known for its tendency to recur and spread.

  • Radiotherapy:
    • The tumor responds quickly to radiotherapy, with a typical dose of 6000 rads used for local tumor control.
    • While radiotherapy is effective in reducing the tumor size, recurrence is common.
  • Chemotherapy:
    • Due to the high likelihood of distant metastasis at the time of diagnosis, chemotherapy is crucial. (Option D)
    • The standard chemotherapy regimen involves a combination of:
      • Vincristine
      • Cyclophosphamide
      • Adriamycin
    • This regimen, known as the VAC regimen (Option C), is administered in cycles, typically repeated every 3-4 weeks.
    • The total treatment course usually spans 12-18 cycles, depending on the patient's response and overall health.
  • Combination Therapy:
    • Effective treatment requires a combination of local control (via radiotherapy) and systemic control (via chemotherapy) to manage both the primary tumor and any metastasis.

Prognosis

The prognosis for Ewing's sarcoma remains challenging, though advancements in chemotherapy have improved outcomes over the years.

Prognostic Features:

  • Recurrence and Metastasis:
    • Ewing's sarcoma is notorious for bone-to-bone metastasis, contributing significantly to poor survival rates.
  • 5-Year Survival Rate:
    • In the past, the 5-year survival rate was only around 10%. However, with the introduction of potent chemotherapy protocols, this has improved.
    • Currently, the 5-year survival rate ranges between 30-40%.
  • Factors Influencing Prognosis:
    • Early diagnosis, tumor size, location, and the presence of metastasis at diagnosis play critical roles in determining the survival rate.

Option A, C & D: All Three are Correct Statements.

Option B: Combination chemotherapy of vincristine, adriamycin and cisplatin is a false option because VAC Regimen Contains Vincristine, Adriamycin and Cyclophosphamide.

Key Takeaway -

Mnemonic - "EWING'S PAIN"

  • E: EWS-FLI1 fusion gene (genetic mutation)
  • W: White ethnicity (more common)
  • I: Involves long bones (femur, pelvis)
  • N: Night pain and swelling (common symptoms)
  • G: Group affected: children & young adults (10-20 years)
  • S: Sensitive to radiotherapy
  • P: Pelvis, ribs, spine (common locations)
  • A: Aggressive nature
  • I: Involves chemotherapy (VAC regimen - Vincristine, Adriamycin and Cyclophosphamide)
  • N: Notorious for metastasis (especially bone-to-bone)
