question_text: What three injuries make up the "terrible triad" of the elbow?
option_a: Olecranon, elbow dislocation (LCL injury), radial head
option_b: Olecranon, elbow dislocation (LCL injury), medial collateral ligament
option_c: Medial collateral ligament,elbow dislocation (LCL injury), radial head
option_d: Coronoid, elbow dislocation (LCL injury), radial head
explanation:
Elbow Dislocation

Overview

  • Most Common Direction: Posterolateral
  • Types:
    • Simple Dislocation
    • Complex Dislocation (with associated fractures)

Initial Management

  • Closed Reduction: Performed promptly after assessing neurovascular status.

Treatment Protocols

  • Simple Dislocations:
    • Early Range of Motion (ROM) initiated within 3 weeks of injury.
  • Persistent Instability:
    • If instability is noted within 30 degrees of full extension, consider acute ligamentous repair.
    • LCL is always repaired, followed by Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL) repair if instability persists.

Common Complications

  • Most Common Complication After Closed Treatment: Loss of terminal extension.

“Terrible Triad” Injury

  • Components:
    • Elbow dislocation
    • Radial head fracture
    • Coronoid process fracture
  • Treatment:
    • Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF) of coronoid process.
    • ORIF or prosthetic replacement of radial head.
    • Lateral and ± medial ligamentous repair.

Persistent Instability Management

  • Options:
    • Hinged external fixator.
    • Transarticular ulnohumeral pinning.
  • Early ROM Protocol:
    • Start with an intraoperative arc of stability.

Positioning for Stability

  • LCL Repaired and MCL Intact:
    • Elbows kept in forearm pronation to increase stability (decreases stress on LCL).
  • LCL Repaired but MCL Deficient:
    • Elbows kept in forearm supination to increase stability (decreases stress on MCL).
  • Both LCL and MCL Repaired:
    • Elbow kept in neutral position.

Option A, B & C: Terrible triad includes Coronoid, elbow dislocation (LCL injury), radial head thus all 3 are incorrect.

Key takeaways:

Structures Involved in terrible triad of elbow:

  • Coronoid Fracture
  • Elbow Dislocation (Lateral Collateral Ligament Injury)
  • Radial Head Fracture

Implications:

  • The combination of these injuries, often resulting from a fracture-dislocation, indicates an unstable elbow.
  • Such instability necessitates surgical stabilization to restore joint integrity.
  • Worse functional outcomes.

question_text: A 22-year-old woman who is a professional tennis player presents to her physician because of pain on the lateral aspect of her elbow radiating down her forearm. She describes the pain as shooting and constant. Repetitive use of which of the following muscles most likely led to this patient's condition?
explanation:
• This patient suffers from lateral epicondylitis, better known as tennis elbow.
  • This condition stems from overuse of the superficial extensor muscles of the forearm and wrist, including the extensor carpi radialis muscle.
  • This muscle also inserts at the lateral epicondyle.
  • The repeated forced extension and flexion of the forearm at the elbow causes an inflammation of the common extensor tendon.
  • Patients exhibit pain over the lateral epicondyle that may radiate down the posterior aspect of the forearm.
  • Treatment options include rehabilitation, which may include exercises, motion analysis and straps or braces; medication; open surgery; and arthroscopic(minimally invasive) surgery.
  • Answer A is incorrect. The biceps muscle functions to supinate and flex the forearm.
  • Answer C is incorrect. The extensor carpi ulnaris muscle functions to extend and adduct the hand at the wrist but does not extend the forearm.
  • Answer D is incorrect. The flexor carpi ulnaris muscle functions to flex and abduct the hand at the wrist.

question_text: A 45 yr housewife presents with pain in the dorsal aspect of distal one third of the forearm which aggravates while lifting heavy utensils in the kitchen and is relieved with rest and medications. Xray of the forearm are normal and finkelstein's test is negative. Probable diagnosis?

Intersection Syndrome:

  • Condition: Inflammatory condition at the crossing of:
    • 1st extensor compartment (APL and EPB).
    • 2nd extensor compartment (ECRL and ECRB).

Option A - Radial Tunnel Syndrome:

  • Pain Location: Deep aching pain in the dorso-radial proximal forearm, 3-5 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle.
  • Cause: Compressive neuropathy of the Posterior Interosseous Nerve (PIN).

Option C - DeQuervain’s Disease:

  • Presenting Symptoms: Pain and tenderness at the radial styloid.
  • Clinical Examination: Finkelstein's test is postive, used for diagnosis

Key Takeaway -

It is important to differentiate between 2 closely related pathologies. Finkelstein’s test is typically positive in deQuervain’s tenosynovitis. Tenderness point in intersection syndrome is proximal to that in deQuervain’s tenosynovitis.

question_text: Select false statement about myositis ossificans:
option_a: Hip is the most commonly affected joint
option_b: Prophylaxis Indomethacin is given to prevent MO
option_c: Post op massage is one of the triggering factors
option_d: Surgical excision if necessary should only be done after MO bone matures
explanation:
Myositis Ossificans (Post-Traumatic Ossification)

Overview

Myositis ossificans is the ossification of the hematoma surrounding a joint, resulting in a mass of bone that restricts joint movement, often completely.

Causes

  • Severe Joint Injury: Particularly when the joint capsule and periosteum are stripped from the bones due to violent displacement of fragments.
  • Age Factor: More common in children due to the loosely attached periosteum.
  • Common Sites: Frequently occurs around the elbow joint.
  • Associated Conditions: Higher incidence in patients with prolonged or permanent neuronal damage (e.g., from head injuries) and those with paraplegia.
  • Exacerbating Factors: Massage following trauma can aggravate myositis. (Option C)

Consequences

  • Joint Stiffness: Bone formation leads to stiffness, either from capsule thickening or from bone obstructing movement.
  • Extreme Cases: In severe cases, bone may bridge the joint, resulting in complete loss of movement (extra-articular ankylosis).

Radiological Features

  • Active Myositis: Characterized by fluffy margins of the bone mass.
  • Mature Myositis: Appears trabeculated with well-defined margins.

Treatment

  • Initial Care: Rest the limb and avoid massage. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may be prescribed in the early active stage. (Option B)
  • Physiotherapy: In late stages, physiotherapy may help regain movement.
  • Surgical Options: Surgical excision of the matured myositic mass may be considered to restore movement (Option D)

Option A: It is particularly common around the elbow joint. hence Option A is false.

Option B: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may be prescribed in the early active stage.

Option C: Massage following trauma can aggravate myositis.

Option D: Surgical excision of the matured myositic mass may be considered to restore movement.

Key takeaways:

  • Myositis ossification is ossification of the haematoma around a joint, resulting in the formation of a mass of bone restricting joint movements, often completely.
  • It is particularly common around the elbow joint.
  • Massage following trauma is a factor known to aggravate myositis.
  • In the early active stage of myositis the limb should be rested, and NSAID (Indomethacin 75mg SR/25 mg TDS) is given.
  • In some cases, once the myositic mass matures, surgical excision of the bone mass may help regain movement.

question_text: A 33-year-old man sustains blunt trauma to his forearm and presents with the injury seen in Figure. Definitive management of this injury involves the following:
option_a: Perform closed reduction of the radius, then immobilize the forearm in a long arm cast in supination
option_b: Perform open reduction and internal fixation of the radius, then assess the proximal radioulnar joint  for instability, and percutaneously fix the proximal radioulnar joint if instability persists.
option_c: Perform open reduction and internal fixation of the radius, then assess the distal radioulnar joint for instability, and percutaneously fix the distal radioulnar joint if instability persists.
explanation:
• The picture shown above is a Galeazzi fracture dislocation (reverse Monteggia/Piedmont fracture).
  • There is a fracture of the lower third of radius and subluxation of the distal radio-ulnar joint.
  • The treatment of choice is open reduction and internal fixation with compression plates.
  • The counterpart of Galeazzi is Monteggia fracture-dislocation where there is a fracture of the upper third of ulna with dislocation of the radial head.

question_text: A 4yr child while playing, suddenly pulled back her elbow from nanny's hand and started crying and not allowing anyone to touch the elbow. She is keeping the elbow extended and pronated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
PULLED ELBOW (NURSE MAID ELBOW)

This condition occurs in children between 2-5 years of age. The head of the radius is pulled partly out of the annular ligament when a child is lifted by the wrist. The child starts crying and is unable to move the affected limb.

The forearm lies in an attitude of pronation. There may be mild swelling at the elbow. It is not possible to see the subluxated head on an X-ray because it is still cartilaginous; X-rays are taken only to rule out any other bony injury.

Treatment: The head is reduced by fully supinating the forearm and applying direct pressure over the head of the radius. A sudden click is heard or felt as the head goes back to its place. The child becomes comfortable and starts moving his elbow almost immediately

Reference: Maheshwari textbook of orthopedics 7th edition, pg no 105

question_text: A patient was involved in a RTA and sustained fracture of the humerus following which there is loss of sensation over lateral side of forearm, difficulty in flexion of elbow and supination of forearm. Which nerve is most likely injured?
explanation:
Musculocuatneous nerve supplies:

  • Biceps brachi
  • Brachialis
  • Coracobrachialis

These muscle are responsible for flexion and supination at elbow joint

Also musculocuatneous nerve continues as lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm

So, Musculocutaneous nerve injury causes loss of flexion and supination at elbow and sensory loss along the lateral aspect of forearm seen in fracture of humerus

Reference: maheshwari textbook of orthopedics 7th edition, pg no 65

question_text: A 4 year boy presents to the OPD with history of sudden onset pain around the left elbow while playing with his elder sibling. O/E, the child is holding the elbow in pronation and extension. X ray taken is normal. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• Nursemaid’s elbow, Babysitter’s elbow or Pulled elbow is a dislocation of the elbow joint caused by a sudden pull on the extended pronated arm, such as by an adult tugging on an uncooperative child, or swinging the child by the arms during play.
  • The technical term for the injury is radial head subluxation.
  • It is common in children below 5 years of age. Symptom wise, the child stops using the arm, which is held in flexed and pronated position. Minimal swelling may be present. All movements except supination will be normal. The child usually cries inconsolably
  • Treatment: The affected arm must be held by the attending physician with one hand/finger on the radial head and the other grasping the hand. While applying compression between these two hands, the forearm of the patient is gently supinated and the arm flexed. The physician will usually feel a “click’' if the maneuver is done properly, the child will feel momentary pain, and usually within 5 minutes, the forearm will thereafter function well and painlessly.

Reference- Apley’s 8th ed p. 603

question_text: A 3 year old boy is brought with the history that he had a fight with his older sister, who pulled his hand forcefully to get her favorite toy from him. After this, the boy started crying with pain on the elbow. O/E the boy is keeping his forearm pronated. X ray did not show any fractures. The next step is
option_a: MRI to rule out occult fractures
option_b: Manipulate the elbow into supination and flexion
option_c: Apply crepe bandage and repeat x ray after 1 week
option_d: Apply a plaster cast and repeat x ray after 1 week
explanation:
• This is a case of pulled elbow also called the nursemaid’s elbow.
  • It is a subluxation of radial head caused due to an axial pull distal to the elbow.
  • Seen in children < 5 years
  • Clinical features
    • Minimal inflammation
    • Pronated forearm
  • X ray - normal
    • Treatment - flexion and supination of the forearm will reduce the radial head and correct the subluxation.

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 105

question_text: A patient presents with decreased sensation over the radial aspect of the forearm, thumb, index and middle finger. There is weakness of Extensor carpi radialis longus. Which nerve root has been damaged here?
explanation:
• C6 root damage - Decreased sensation over the radial aspect of the forearm, thumb, index and middle finger with the weakness of extensor carpi radialis longus and extensor carpi radialis brevis activity.
  • C7 root damage - Decreased sensation over the ulnar border of the ring and little fingers with the weakness of triceps and finger extensors.
  • C8 root damage - Decreased sensation over the ulnar border of hand and forearm with decreased flexor digitorum superficialis or flexor digitorum profundus activity.

Reference: Apley's system of Orthopaedics & Fractures, 9th ed, Pg: 229, 272.

question_text: A 15-year-old boy fell from a bicycle and sustained a supracondylar fracture of the humerus. An above-elbow cast was applied. After cast removal, he now complains of weakness and inability to extend his fingers. His forearm appears thin and wasted, and his hand is fixed in a claw-like position. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Volkmann's ischemic contracture occurs due to ischemia of forearm muscles, most commonly following tight casts, compartment syndrome, or brachial artery injury in a supracondylar fracture. The resulting ischemia leads to:

  • Wasting of forearm muscles
  • Flexion deformity of the wrist and fingers
  • Inability to extend fingers
  • A characteristic claw-like deformity

Volkmann's contracture is caused by ischemic necrosis of flexor muscles (especially flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus) due to compromised circulation. Typical features include:

  • Pain out of proportion (early)
  • Tight or rigid forearm
  • Weakness or paralysis of finger extension
  • Flexion deformities of wrist and fingers
  • Muscle atrophy
  • Claw-like fixed hand posture

Common causes in children:

  • Supracondylar fracture with brachial artery compression
  • Tight plaster cast
  • Untreated compartment syndrome

Dupuytren contracture (Option B): Fibrosis of palmar aponeurosis causing flexion of ring and little fingers; not related to trauma or ischemia.

De Quervain's disease (Option C): Stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment; causes radial wrist pain, not clawing.

Trigger finger (Option D): Stenosis of flexor tendon sheath causing clicking or locking; no muscle wasting or fixed claw deformity.

question_text: A 42 years old lady complains of nocturnal pain over the thumb, index finger and middle finger. Which of the following tests is required to reach a diagnosis?
explanation:
• Lady is suffering from carpal tunnel syndrome.
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome(tardy median palsy) is the result of compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel as it passes beneath the flexor retinaculum.
  • Clinical findings:
    • Carpal tunnel syndrome is most common in the fourth to the sixth decades of life and occurs more often in women than in men.
    • Carpal tunnel syndrome consists predominantly of tingling and numbness in the typical median nerve distribution in the radial three and a half digits (thumb, index, long and radial side of ring).
    • Tingling is more prominent during sleep. Frequently causes the patient to awaken several hours after falling asleep with burning and numbness of the hand that is relieved by exercise.
    • Pain, described as deep, aching or throbbing, occurs diffusely in the hand and radiates up the forearm.
  • Tests for carpal tunnel syndrome are:
    • Percussion test(Tinel sign): Tapping over the median nerve at the mid axis of the wrist elicits electric-shock like discomfort at the site of the tap with paresthesias that radiate distally into the median nerve distribution(positive Tinel sign).
    • Phalen test(or Phalen maneuver): The Phalen maneuver provokes median nerve compression by active hyperflexion of the wrist; this test is considered positive if paresthesias in a median nerve distribution develop within 60 seconds.
    • Tourniquet test: The development of numbness and tingling in the fingers in median nerve distribution after an inflated blood pressure cuff is placed on the upper arm suggests carpal tunnel syndrome.
    • Durkan compression test: Compression is applied to the median nerve for 30 seconds with the thumbs or an atomizer bulb attached to a manometer. Patients with carpal tunnel syndrome usually have symptoms of numbness, pain, or paresthesia in the median nerve distribution.
  • Other options:
    • Cozen test- used for diagnosis of tennis elbow
    • Finkelstein test - used for diagnosis of dequverian tenosynovitis.

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th edition, Page no. 303.

question_text: In which of the following injuries, will 3 point bony relation be maintained?
explanation:
Three bony points relationship: The three prominent bony points around the elbow i.e., the medial epicondyle, lateral epicondyle and tip of the olecranon are important landmarks in the diagnosis of injuries around the elbow.

Normally, in an elbow flexed to 90°, these three bony points form a near-isosceles triangle , but they lie in a straight horizontal line in an extended elbow.

The base of the triangle (between the two epicondyles) is the longest arm. The side between the medial epicondyle and olecranon tip is the shortest.

The head of the radius, also considered the 4th bony point, can be palpated in a semiflexed elbow, just distal to the lateral epicondyle. It can be better felt moving during supination pronation of the forearm


Reference: maheshwari textbook of orthopedics 7th edition, pg no 96

question_text: Identify the injury of the thumb shown in the image.
explanation:
Rolando's Fracture

Definition:

  • A complete, comminuted intra-articular fracture of the base of the first metacarpal, typically shaped like a "T" or "Y".

Characteristics:

  • Involves greater force than a Bennett fracture.
  • Can have dorsal and palmar fragments.
  • Sometimes the term ‘Rolando’ is also used to describe a comminuted Bennett fracture.

Clinical Presentation:

  • Unstable fracture requiring immediate treatment.

Treatment Options:

  1. Closed Reduction and Percutaneous Pinning (CRPP):
    • Used for less complex fractures.
  2. Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF):
    • Recommended for more severe fractures or when CRPP is not feasible.
  3. External Fixation:
    • Considered in cases with severe comminution or when other methods are unsuitable.

Immobilization:

  • Post-reduction, immobilize in a thumb spica cast for 3 weeks.

Option A – Rolando fracture - This is a complete articular, ‘T’ or Y’ shaped fracture of the first metacarpal.

Option B – Bennet’s fracture dislocation - It is an oblique intra-articular fracture of the base of the first metacarpal with subluxation or dislocation of the metacarpal.

Option C - Stener lesion occurs when the adductor pollicis aponeurosis becomes interposed between the retracted ulnar collateral ligament in chronic Gamekeeper’s thumb, and this hinders healing.

Key takeaways:

Rolando’s Fracture is A complete, comminuted intra-articular fracture of the base of the first metacarpal, typically shaped like a "T" or "Y".

question_text: Identify the test name shown in the image below.
explanation:
Thomas test is used to assess a fixed flexion deformity of the hip joint.

  • With the patient positioned flat on the bed, place a hand below their lumbar spine with your palm facing upwards (this helps to prevent the patient from masking a fixed flexion deformity by increasing lumbar lordosis).
  • Passively flex the hip of the unaffected leg as far as you are able to and observe the contralateral limb.
  • Repeat the assessment on the contralateral hip.

Interpretation- The test is positive (abnormal) if the affected thigh raises off the bed, indicating a loss of the hip joint extension. This would suggest a fixed flexion deformity in the affected hip.

question_text: "Piano key sign" is positive in

question_text: What is the name of the test performed in the image given below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image demonstrates Allen's test, a bedside maneuver used to check the patency of the radial and ulnar arteries supplying the hand.

Allen's Test

  • How it is performed:
    • The examiner compresses both radial and ulnar arteries at the wrist while the patient clenches their fist to drain blood from the hand.
    • The patient then opens the fist, and the examiner releases pressure on one artery.
    • Normal finding: rapid return of hand color, confirming good collateral circulation from the released artery.
  • Clinical importance:
    • Performed before arterial blood gas (ABG) sampling or radial artery harvest (e.g., coronary artery bypass grafting).
    • Confirms adequate collateral supply through the palmar arch.

Explanation of other options:

Adson test (Option B): Used in suspected Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS). The patient extends the neck and rotates the head while taking a deep breath; loss of the radial pulse suggests compression of the subclavian artery.

Barbeau test (Option C): Another method for assessing palmar arch patency, but it relies on pulse oximetry and plethysmography, not visual color return.

Homan's test (Option D): A bedside maneuver for deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Pain in the calf on forced dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee extended is considered a positive sign.

Key Takeaway:

  1. Allen's test evaluates collateral circulation of the hand and is crucial before radial artery interventions such as ABG sampling or graft harvesting.

question_text: Durkan's test is used for the diagnosis of:
explanation:
Durkan Test:

  • Purpose: Used to diagnose carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS).
  • Procedure:
    • The test is performed by applying direct pressure to the carpal tunnel area at the base of the palm.
    • The examiner uses their thumb to compress the area over the median nerve.
  • Positive Test Result:
    • A positive result is indicated by the reproduction of symptoms such as pain, tingling, or numbness in the distribution of the median nerve (typically the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and half of the ring finger).
    • The test can be used as part of a comprehensive diagnostic approach including history, physical examination, and possibly electrodiagnostic studies.
  • Sensitivity and Specificity:
    • The test has varying sensitivity and specificity but is generally useful as a preliminary assessment tool for CTS.

Clinical tests used in CTS

Option A - DeQuervain's tenosynovitis - The Finkelstein test usually is positive in this condition: "on grasping the patient's thumb and quickly abducting the hand ulnarward, the pain over the styloid tip is excruciating." Finkelstein stated that this test is "probably the most pathognomonic objective sign,"

Option B - Carpal tunnel syndrome - A carpal compression test (Durkan test), in which direct compression is applied to the median nerve for 30 seconds with the thumbs or an atomizer bulb attached to a manometer, was found to be more specific (90%) and more sensitive (87%) than either the Tinel or Phalen test.

Option C - Tennis elbow: COZEN'S test - Pain is aggravated by putting the extensor tendons to a stretch; for example, by palmar-flexing the wrist and fingers with the forearm pronated.

Option D - Golfer’s elbow – There is no named test for this condition. But clinically provocative tests can be done by fully supinating the forearm and passively extending the elbow, wrist and fingers which causes pain over medial epicondyle of humerus (common flexor origin).

Key Takeaway -

Carpal Tunnel Syndrome test:

  • Durkan test - Most specific
  • Tinel sign
  • Phalen & Reverse Phalen test

The anatomical snuff box is defined laterally by the Extensor pollicis brevis and Abductor pollicis longus, medially by the Extensor pollicis longus. The tendon indicated in the image is the Extensor pollicis brevis, which is key for thumb extension and abduction.

question_text: Apparent lengthening of the limb is seen in which stage of TBhip?
explanation:
STAGES OF TB HIP

The disease process progresses through the following clinical stages:

  • Stage 1 (Stage of tubercular synovitis): Due to synovitis, there is joint effusion and the joint is held in position of maximum capacity, i.e., flexion, abduction and external rotation causing apparent lengthening. On X-ray all that is visible is a widened joint space due to effusion and generalized osteopenia.
  • Stage 2 (Stage of early arthritis): With advancement of the disease process, there is destruction of articular cartilage. With spasm of flexors and adductors of hip, there is flexion, adduction and internal rotation deformity with apparent shortening. True shortening is also present due to damage to articular cartilage but is less than 1 cm. X-ray shows decrease in joint space and osteopenia.
  • Stage 3 (Stage of late arthritis): With further destruction, clinical signs of flexion, adduction, internal rotation deformities and apparent shortening are exaggerated. True shortening is more than 1 cm. Here is gross restriction of movements and muscle wasting. X-rays may show complete loss of joint space with destruction of head/acetabulum.
  • Stage 4 (Late arthritis with subluxation/dislocation): There are flexion adduction and internal rotation deformities with gross shortening. With destruction of acetabulum, femur head and ligaments, the upper end of femur may displace upwards and dorsally leaving the lower part of acetabulum empty but forming a false acetabulum higher up (wandering acetabulum).

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 7th edition, Page no. 194.

question_text: 40-year-old male after RTA sustains a cervical spine injury. His lower limb power is greater than that of upper limb and sacral sensations are present. What type of spinal cord lesion is this?
explanation:
• Central Cord Syndrome This is the most common incomplete spinal cord injury(SCI) syndrome. It results from hyperextension injury in older person with pre-existing osteoarthritis of spine.
  • There is initial flaccid weakness followed by a lower motor neuron type of paralysis of the upper limbs and upper motor neuron(spastic) paralysis of the lower limbs, with preservation of bladder control and perianal sensations (sacral sparing).
  • The spinal cord is pinched between the vertebral body anteriorly and the buckled ligamentum flavum posteriorly with pressure getting concentrated around the cord area lying in vicinity of central canal.
  • Due to typical arrangement of spinal tracts(the arm fibres medially and the leg fibres laterally, the arms are more severely affected than the legs, resulting in a disproportionate motor impairment.
  • Clinical presentation depends on the site of involvement. In cervical spine involvement(most commonly affected area) patients present with quadriparesis with weakness involving the upper limbs(flaccid paralysis, due to LMN type lesion at the level of spinal injury) more than lower limbs(spastic paralysis due to UMN type lesion below the level of injury), varying degree of sensory loss below the level of spinal injury with or without bladder involvement. Prognosis is good with more than 50% patients recovering bladder/bowel function and ambulation.

Reference: Essential orthopaedics Maheshwari, 5th edition, Page no. 277.

There may be a palpable thickening of the sheath.

question_text: Perkin's line on X-ray is used for diagnosis of ?
explanation:
• Radiological features of DDH/CDH-
  • In Von Rosen’s view following parameters should be noted
    • Perkin’s Line: Vertical line drawn at the outer border of acetabulum
    • Hilgenreiner’s line: Horizontal line drawn at the level of tri-radiate cartilage
    • Shenton’s line: Smooth curve formed by inferior border of neck of femur with superior margin of obturator foramen.
    • Acetabular index: Normally is < 30°

question_text: All of the following are predictive findings for correctly diagnosing carpal tunnel syndrome EXCEPT:
option_b: Abnormal Semmes-Weinstein testing in wrist-neutral position
option_c: Positive median nerve compression test(Durkan's sign)

Option B: A2 and A4 Pulleys are Crucial for preventing flexor tendon bowstringing.

question_text: Identify the structure marked in the given image:
explanation:
Explanation :

On a standard Posteroanterior (PA) chest X-ray:

  • Posterior ribsappear more horizontal and are the primary ribs used for counting.
  • Anterior ribshave a more steep, downward-sloping course and are less distinct.
    The marked horizontal structure is, therefore, a posterior rib.

Identification of Anterior and Posterior Ribs on Chest X-ray

Rib Anatomy:

  • Upper border:Smooth and well-defined.
  • Lower border:Thin and less distinct.
  • Symmetry:Compare ribs on both sides at the same level—symmetry usually indicates normal anatomy.
  • Sternal attachment:Anterior rib ends connect to the sternum via costal cartilage, which may calcify with age (normal finding).

Rib Counting on X-ray:

  • Posterior ribs:More distinct and run horizontally.
  • Anterior ribs:Less prominent and slope downward.
  • The first ribcan be difficult to identify due to crowding near the apex.
    • Locate the anterior partof the first rib first.
    • Then trace it backward to its posterior end.
  • Continue counting posterior ribsdownward from the first rib.

Key Takeaways:

  • On a PA CXR, count the horizontal posterior ribs.

question_text: Codman's triangle is typically seen in which of the following conditions?
explanation:
Explanation:

Codman's triangle is typically seen in Osteogenic sarcoma

Codman's Triangle

  • Represents a triangular periosteal elevation where a rapidly expanding lesion lifts the periosteum from the cortex.
  • It is most characteristic of osteogenic sarcoma (osteosarcoma), although other aggressive bone lesions can rarely produce it.

Osteogenic Sarcoma

  • The most common primary malignant bone tumour of non-hematopoietic origin.
  • Typical sites: Metaphysis of long bones (distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal humerus).
  • Age group: Adolescents and young adults; smaller peak in older adults.
  • Clinical features: Progressive pain (often worse at night), swelling, limitation of joint motion.
  • Imaging:
    • Sunburst/sun-ray pattern from spiculated new bone formation.
    • Codman's triangle from periosteal lifting at tumour margins.
  • Management: Limb-salvage surgery or amputation plus multi-agent chemotherapy (doxorubicin, cisplatin, high-dose methotrexate, ifosfamide).

Explanation for Other Options:

Osteomyelitis (Option A): It is a Bacterial infection of bone producing sequestrum and involucrum. X-ray shows lytic areas and periosteal reaction, but classic Codman's triangle is not a typical feature.


Aneurysmal Bone Cyst (Option B): It is a Benign, blood-filled, expansile cyst, usually in the metaphysis. Radiographs demonstrate an "eggshell" or "soap-bubble" appearance rather than a periosteal triangle.



Chondrosarcoma (Option D): It is a Malignant cartilage-forming tumour of adulthood.

Imaging reveals "rings and arcs" or stippled calcifications; Codman's triangle is not characteristic.

question_text: Which is not a correct constellation of markers for post arthroplasty prosthetic joint infection?
option_d: CRP, ESR, Neutrophil count of synovial fluid
explanation:
Markers for post arthroplasty joint infection

  1. ESR and CRP currently remain as first-line screening tests for periprosthetic joint infection (PJI). They have high sensitivity and low specificity. CRP is more sensitive and specific than ESR.
  2. Interleukin-6 (IL-6)- IL-6 is an inflammatory cytokine produced by stimulated monocytes and macrophages. It induces the production of acute-phase proteins, including CRP. Its sensitivity, specificity and diagnostic accuracy is comparable or higher than CRP.
  3. White blood cell count (WBC)- While synovial WBC count and differential is one of the main diagnostic criteria for PJI, serum WBC count has very little utility.
  4. Procalcitonin (PCT)- It is a protein produced by neuroendocrine cells and the parafollicular cells of the thyroid under physiological conditions. In sepsis, the main producers of PCT are macrophages and monocytic cells of different organs, especially the liver. PCT has a high diagnostic accuracy for the identification of systemic infection but for joint infection it has low sensitivity and diagnostic accuracy.
  5. D-dimer- Serum D-dimer has been shown to outperform other conventional tests such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein in diagnosis of PJI. It has sensitivity and specificity higher than the ESR and CRP and has emerged as a promising tool for diagnosis of PJI.
  6. Tumor necrosis factor-alfa (TNF-alfa)- It has high specificity and low sensitivity for PJI. Technical drawbacks include long processing times (over two hours) and the instability of the sample, which means it needs to be processed within 60 minutes of being drawn. Therefore, based on these results, TNF-a is not an ideal serum screening test for PJI.
  7. Intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) is a membrane glycoprotein that plays a key role in leukocyte migration and activation that has also been studied in the context of PJI. It may also be considered as good markers of infection, as measurement of its levels allows for differentiating patients with and without infection, and between patients with infection and those with previous infection, since marker levels quickly return to baseline values after clearance of the infection.

Reference: Manish kumar varshney 1st edition chapter 11 page no 435.

question_text: Knee dislocations can be associated with which of the following?
explanation:
Injury Considerations

  • Knee Dislocation:
    • Requires significant soft tissue injury.
    • Typically involves ruptures of at least three of four major ligamentous structures:
      • Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL)
      • Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL)
      • Collateral ligaments
      • Capsular elements and menisci may also be injured.

Vascular Anatomy

  • Popliteal Vascular Bundle:
    • Courses through a fibrous tunnel at the adductor hiatus.
    • In the popliteal fossa, five geniculate branches are given off.
    • Runs deep to the soleus muscle through another fibrous canal.
    • Vulnerable to tenting and injury during dislocation.

Associated Fractures

  • Common associated fractures include:
    • Tibial eminence
    • Tibial tubercle
    • Fibular head or neck
    • Capsular avulsions

Option A & B: There is an increased risk for vascular injury with an associated dislocation, and by definition a ligament must tear for the knee to dislocate.

Option C: Although less common than ligamentous injury, bony injuries, especially compression and avulsion fractures, do occur.

Key takeaways:

  • Knee dislocations are often the result of complex forces acting across the joint. They can occur with low-energy mechanisms, particularly in obese patients.
  • There is an increased risk for vascular injury with an associated dislocation, and by definition a ligament must tear for the knee to dislocate.
  • Although less common than ligamentous injury, bony injuries, especially compression and avulsion fractures, do occur.

question_text: A 45 yr female sustained a high velocity road traffic accident after which she complains of severe pain in her left hip region. The hip is in flexion, adduction internal rotation with gross shortening. She is not able to move her ankle or knee joint as well. Best investigation to do in this case is?
explanation:
Posterior Dislocation of the Hip

Overview:

  • Occurs when the femoral head is displaced posteriorly out of the acetabulum.
  • Often associated with a fracture of the posterior acetabular lip, known as a fracture-dislocation.

Mechanism of Injury:

  • Caused by a force along the femoral shaft with the hip flexed.
  • Commonly seen in motor vehicle accidents (dashboard injury) when the knee strikes the dashboard, transmitting force to the femur and dislocating the hip.

Diagnosis:

  • Clinical Features:
    • Severe trauma history with pain, swelling, and deformity (hip in flexion, adduction, and internal rotation).
    • Affected leg appears shortened, and the femoral head may be palpable in the gluteal region.
    • Often missed in patients with other severe injuries or in unconscious patients.
  • Radiological Features:
    • Femoral head displaced out of the acetabulum with the thigh internally rotated, obscuring the lesser trochanter.
    • Shenton's line is disrupted.
    • Look for bony fragments from the posterior acetabulum or femoral head.
    • CT scan may be needed to assess associated fractures.

Treatment:

  • Emergency Reduction:
    • Prompt reduction is essential to prevent avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
    • Most cases can be managed with closed reduction under general anesthesia.
    • Acetabular chip fractures often realign with successful reduction.
  • Open Reduction Indications:
    • Failure of closed reduction, especially in delayed cases.
    • Presence of intra-articular loose fragments hindering accurate reduction.
    • Large acetabular fragments from the weight-bearing area, causing hip instability.

Option A: USG has no role in identifying pelvic fracture and associated dislocation.

Option B: CT is the best modality for dislocations, also to see if it is associated with any fracture of the acetabulum or femoral head. (more likely) in this case.

Option C: MRI Is helpful in identifying associated Spinal Cord injury. However to check associated acetabulum, or femoral head fracture or Sciatic nerve injury CT Scan is a better Choice.

Option D: Though x rays are primary investigations done in all trauma cases, specific views like Judet views are not possible due to severe pain. Hence CT scan is always a better choice.

Key takeaways: FADIR deformity of hip and inability to move knee and ankle as well points towards posterior dislocation of hip with sciatic nerve injury which is Diagnosed with CT scan.

question_text: Anterior cruciate ligaments prevent?
explanation:
• The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) stretches from the lateral condyle of femur to the anterior intercondylar area.
  • The ACL is critically important because it prevents the tibia from being pushed too far anterior relative to the femur. It is often torn during twisting or bending of the knee.
  • If there is ACL tear, reconstruction is most commonly done by autograft, meaning the tissue used for the repair is taken from the patient’s body.
  • The two most common sources for tissue are the patellar tendon and hamstrings tendon.
  • The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) stretches from medial condyle of femur to the posterior intercondylar area. This ligament prevents posterior displacement of the tibia relative to the femur

question_text: False about ACL anatomy is
option_a: AM bundle is longer than PL bundle
option_b: AM bundle is taut in flexion
option_c: PL bundle is taut in extension
option_d: PL bundle is bulkier and longer than AM bundle
explanation:
• The ACL is an intra-articular but extrasynovial ligament. Proximally, it takes origin from the posteromedial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle. It runs inferomedially to get inserted on the tibia between two spines.
  • The ACL has two bundles:
    • The anteromedial (AM) bundle and the posterolateral (PL) bundle. They are named according to their relative insertion sites onto the tibia.
    • In extension, the AM and PL bundles are parallel and both are relatively taut, however the PL bundle is more taught than the AM bundle.
    • With knee flexion AM bundle remains taut but PL bundle relaxes. The AM bundle is longer and bulkier than the PL bundle.
  • Primarily ACL prevents anterior tibial translation on the femur. The ACL is a secondary restraint to internal rotation of the tibia and resist varus displacement at full extension.

question_text: A 60-year-old woman with history of Colle's fracture 8 months ago, attained menopause at the age of 52, comes with a T score of -2.5 on DEXA Scan, she is currently asymptomatic. What treatment that you will give her?
explanation:
Here T score of -2.5 on DEXA scan is diagnostic of osteoporosis.

What is T-score?

The T-score is the relevant measure when screening for osteoporosis. It is the bone mineral density (BMD. at the site when compared to the young normal reference mean. It is a comparison of a patient's BMD to that of a healthy thirty-year-old.

The criteria of the World Health Organization are:

  • Normal is a T-score of -1.0 or higher
  • Osteopenia is defined as between -1.0 and -2.5
  • Osteoporosis is defined as -2.5 or lower. meaning a bone density that is two and a half standard deviations below the mean of a thirty-year-old man/woman

Osteoporosis can cause back pain, deformities and high chance of fractures. Hence it is important to treat osteoporosis.

The drug of choice of osteoporosis is bisphosphonates such as Alendronate.

Problems of using bisphophonates:

  • Prolong fracture healing
  • Chronic use causes atypical fractures (subtrochanteric fractures of femur)
    • Prevention: by giving drug holiday (bisphosphiantes stopped after 5yr use and restarted after 2-3yrs bridged with teriperatide in absence of bisphophonates)

Supplements used in osteoporosis:

  • Calcium-800-1200mg/day
  • Vitamin D- 400-800 IU/day

Calcitonin (nasal spray)- 200-400 IU/day (mainly used for pain relief

question_text: A 46-year-old male presents with a lesion in the epiphyseal region of the lower end of the femur. Histopathology shows multinucleated giant cells along with mononuclear stromal cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A lesion in the epiphysis of the lower end of the femur in a skeletally mature patient, showing multinucleated giant cells on histopathology, is highly suggestive of a Giant Cell Tumor (GCT).

Giant cell tumour

  • Benign but locally aggressive tumor of bone. Rarely (<1%) undergoes malignant transformation, slightly more common in females.
  • Most common between 20-45 years.
  • GCT typically involves the metaphysis and epiphysis of long bones.
  • Common locations: distal femur, proximal tibia, distal radius (most common), and proximal humerus.
  • Presents with pain, swelling and /or a pathological fracture.
  • Radiology:
    • X-ray: Eccentric, expansile, lobulated lytic lesion with a narrow transition zone.
    • May extend into soft tissues with a thin sclerotic rim.
    • Minimal or absent matrix calcification, new bone formation, or periosteal reaction.
  • Histopathology:
    • Shows numerous osteoclast-like giant cells interspersed with round or spindle-shaped mononuclear stromal cells.

Treatment:

  • Wide excision is preferred, as curettage alone has a high recurrence rate.
  • Lesions may be packed with polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA).
  • Large resections may require allograft or vascularized fibula reconstruction.

Explanation of other options:

Chondrosarcoma (Option B): Chondrosarcoma typically occurs in adults aged 40-70 years and is more common in men. It usually involves the metaphysis of large bones, including the pelvis, proximal femur, proximal humerus, distal femur, scapula, and proximal tibia. Histologically, chondrosarcomas are composed of malignant chondrocytes embedded in a cartilaginous matrix.

Osteosarcoma (Option C): The most common primary malignant bone tumour. It shows a bimodal age distribution, peaking in adolescence (10-14 years) and in the seventh decade. It typically arises in the metaphysis of long bones, most commonly the distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal femur, and humerus. Radiographs show a sunburst pattern and Codman triangle, while biopsy reveals highly anaplastic, pleomorphic cells producing osteoid and primitive woven bone in a permeative pattern.

Aneurysmal bone cyst (Option D): An aneurysmal bone cyst is a locally aggressive, multiloculated lesion that typically arises in the metaphysis of long bones in patients aged 10-20 years, most commonly the distal femur and proximal tibia. The cyst is blood-filled and presents as a painful, rapidly enlarging swelling. Radiographs show an expansile, lytic, multiloculated metaphyseal lesion.

Treatment:

  • Wide excision is preferred, as curettage alone has a high recurrence rate.
  • Lesions may be packed with polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA).
  • Large resections may require allograft or vascularized fibula reconstruction.

Explanation of other options:

Chondrosarcoma (Option B): Chondrosarcoma typically occurs in adults aged 40-70 years and is more common in men. It usually involves the metaphysis of large bones, including the pelvis, proximal femur, proximal humerus, distal femur, scapula, and proximal tibia. Histologically, chondrosarcomas are composed of malignant chondrocytes embedded in a cartilaginous matrix.

Osteosarcoma (Option C): The most common primary malignant bone tumour. It shows a bimodal age distribution, peaking in adolescence (10-14 years) and in the seventh decade. It typically arises in the metaphysis of long bones, most commonly the distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal femur, and humerus. Radiographs show a sunburst pattern and Codman triangle, while biopsy reveals highly anaplastic, pleomorphic cells producing osteoid and primitive woven bone in a permeative pattern.

Aneurysmal bone cyst (Option D): An aneurysmal bone cyst is a locally aggressive, multiloculated lesion that typically arises in the metaphysis of long bones in patients aged 10-20 years, most commonly the distal femur and proximal tibia. The cyst is blood-filled and presents as a painful, rapidly enlarging swelling. Radiographs show an expansile, lytic, multiloculated metaphyseal lesion.

question_text: A 7-year-old male presents to the orthopedic clinic with leg pain that has been present for the past 6 months. On physical exam, the patient appears malnourished. There is tenderness to palpation of the distal femur. Additionally, the gums have a bluish-purple hue with areas of hemorrhages. A radiograph of the patient's knee is demonstrated in figure. Given the most likely diagnosis, which of the following is true regarding this condition?
option_c: Result of increased chondroitin sulfate and collagen synthesis
option_d: Causes widening of the zone of provisional calcification
explanation:
• The clinical presentation and radiograph are consistent with scurvy. Scurvy leads to widening of the zone of provision calcification which is demonstrated on radiograph as a dense band(White line of Frankl) at the growing metaphysis.
  • Scurvy is a disease resulting from a deficiency of vitamin C(ascorbic acid), which is required for the synthesis of collagen in humans. This leads to decreased chondroitin sulfate synthesis which causes defective collagen growth and repair in the metaphyseal region of the long bone.
  • This defect in type I collagen synthesis primarily affects osteoblastic function. As a result, this decreased osteoblastic activity leads to defective primary and secondary spongiosa of the growing long bone.
  • Histologically, the primary trabeculae of the bone is replaced with granulation tissue causing thin cortices. Additionally, impaired collagen synthesis in scurvy leads to fragile capillaries, resulting in abnormal bleeding, ecchymosis and joint effusions. The treatment for scurvy is prompt administration of vitamin C.
  • Incorrect Answers:
    • Answer A: Decreased osteoclast function is the primary pathology seen in osteopetrosis
    • Answer B: Scurvy is caused by vitamin C deficiency, not vitamin D
    • Answer C: Chondroitin sulfate and collagen synthesis is decreased in scurvy

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Ortho, 5th edition, Page no. 315.

question_text: A 25-year-old male presents to the emergency department with pain and swelling of the right knee. Radiographs are shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given Xray knee shows a patella fracture with the bone divided into two fragments.

Patellar fracture

  • Patella fractures can result from direct trauma, such as a fall onto the knee or dashboard injury, or from indirect trauma due to forceful quadriceps contraction when the foot is fixed.
  • Clinical features
    • Pain, swelling, and haemarthrosis
    • Abrasion or bruising over the anterior knee
    • Tenderness
    • Palpable gap in displaced fractures
    • Crepitus in comminuted fractures

Radiological examination

  • Anteroposterior and lateral knee X-rays are usually sufficient to diagnose patella fractures.
  • Skyline view of pattella is the xray view of choice in patellar fractures.
  • Fractures with wide fragment separation are easily seen on lateral X-rays
  • Transverse fracture with a gap >3 mm indicates significant displacement.

Management

  • Undisplaced: Cylinder cast from ankle to mid-thigh
  • Displaced: Tension band wiring using reduction, K-wires, and figure-of-eight stainless steel wire to achieve compression
  • Comminuted (shattered): Patellectomy with excision of fragments and repair of the extensor mechanism

Explanation of other options:

Tibial fracture (Option B): Tibial fractures usually result from direct trauma or twisting injuries. Patients present with pain, tenderness, swelling, and inability to bear weight. Deformity may be present in displaced fractures. Diagnosis is confirmed on X-ray, which shows a fracture line along the tibial shaft.

Foreign body (Option C): Foreign body can be excluded due to the absence of penetrating injury and characteristic fracture line.

Femur fracture (Option D): Fracture of the femoral shaft typically occurs due to high-energy trauma, presenting with severe thigh pain, tenderness, swelling, deformity, abnormal mobility, and limb shortening. Diagnosis is confirmed on X-ray, which shows a fracture line in the femoral shaft.

question_text: A 50-year-old male with long-standing type 1 diabetes presents with redness, swelling and crepitus in his foot two weeks after a twisting injury. Elevation of the extremity reduces the hyperemia. A radiograph is shown in the Figure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The x ray shows complete destruction, disorganization and sclerosis of mid tarsal joint along with loose bodies. This is a classical finding of Charcot’s arthropathy. The patient being diabetic and hyperemia that regresses with elevation etc. also point towards Charcot’s joint.
  • Charcot’s joint is also called neuropathic joint. It occurs when the pain and proprioceptive sensations of the joint is lost. We must realize that pain has a very important protective function in the body. Presence of pain prevents us from aggravating any injury. This protective function is lost in sensory neuropathies (like diabetic neuropathy) resulting in reccurent and persistant damage to the bones of the joint resulting in its destruction. The clinching point here is that, even though there is so much destruction going on, the patient will be painfree.
  • Neuropathy has the greatest effect on diabetic foot pathology

Reference: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter: 17, Pg: 261

question_text: In which condition is Pisani sign seen?
explanation:
• Pisani sign is seen in meniscal cysts.
  • Pisani sign is when the meniscal cyst swelling disappears on knee flexion and then reappears on extension.
  • Meniscal cyst can be seen on the medial or lateral aspect of knee
  • It is caused because of a tear in the meniscal which causes the synovial fluid to escape into the periarticular tissue to form a cyst.
  • MC meniscus involved is the Lateral meniscus

question_text: Which ligament is tested in the following test?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The anterior drawer test evaluates the integrity of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).
  • With the knee flexed at 90° and the foot stabilised, the examiner pulls the tibia forward. In a normal knee, the ACL resists anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur.
  • Excessive forward movement compared to the opposite knee indicates ACL injury. Thus, the test directly checks the stability provided by the ACL.

Knee Ligament Tests:

question_text: Structural integrity of collateral ligaments is best tested by
option_a: Varus/Valgus stress test in full flexion
option_b: Varus/Valgus stress test in full extension
explanation:
• Collateral ligaments are best tested by stress tests.
  • Varus stress test is for LCL
  • Valgus stress test is for MCL
  • Examiner keeps one hand on knee of patient which is flexed to 30 deg and with other hand holds the leg to give a varus or valgus stress to the knee.
  • Performing the tests at 30 degrees knee flexion relaxes other structures in the knee and one can specifically isolate the collateral ligaments for testing.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 878.

question_text: False statement is
option_a: SACH foot has a rigid keel.
option_b: Squatting is possible with Jaipur foot.
option_c: SACH foot allows for walking barefoot.
option_d: Jaipur foot is more life like.

question_text: A 3-month-old patient with clubfoot who you've been treating with the Ponseti Method has returned to your clinic. On examination, the foot appears as it does in Figure A. What treatment error has been made?
option_c: Tried correcting equinus before heel varus
option_d: Used below knee casts instead of above knee casts
explanation:
• Rocker bottom foot deformity occurs when equinus is corrected before heel varus and forefoot pronation.
  • Congenital clubfoot, or talipes equinovarus, consists of four main parts: midfoot cavus, metatarsus adductus, varus hindfoot, and equinus contracture. The goal of manipulation is to rotate the foot around a fixed talus. This must be done in the order described by Ponseti.
  • The mnemonic C-A-V-E is an easy method to remember the order of treatment (Cavus, metatarus Adductus, Varus, Equinus). If equinus is addressed before the cavus and varus hindfoot, dorsiflexion occurs through the midfoot instead of treating the hindfoot equinus, thus creating a rockerbottom foot.
  • Answer A: Under-correction of foot pronation can lead to residual cavus deformity
  • Answer B: Over correction of metatarsus adductus would lead to an abduction deformity of the forefoot.
  • Answer D: Below knee casts are not considered sufficient immobilization to fully take advantage of the manipulations you perform

Reference- MAHESHWARI ORTHO 5TH EDITION PAGE NO 214.

question_text: Which of the following is the most common mechanism of meniscus injuries?
explanation:
• Mechanism of injury to Meniscus-
    1. Damage to the meniscus is due to rotational forces directed to a flexed knee (as may occur with twisting sports).
    2. A valgus force applied to a flexed knee with the foot planted and the femur rotated externally can result in a lateral meniscus tear.
    3. A varus force applied to the flexed knee when the foot is planted and the femur rotated internally can result in a tear of the medial meniscus.
  • Symptoms of meniscus injury The patient's chief complaints are usually knee pain and swelling. Another typical complaint is joint locking, when the patient is unable to straighten the leg fully. This can be accompanied by a clicking feeling. Cooper's sign is a subjective symptom of pain in the affected knee when turning over in bed at night
  • The tests for meniscus injury include
    1. The McMurrav test
    2. Steinmann test
    3. Apley grind test
    4. Apley’s distraction test
    5. Thesaly test
    6. Ege’s test

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 902.

question_text: An athlete sustains an injury around the knee joint while training. The consulting doctor suspects a cartilage injury and decides to further evaluate the patient. Which of the following is the investigation of choice in this scenario?
explanation:
• Investigation of choice for knee ligament injury is MRI as it will clearly show injuries of both the cruciates (intra articular) and the collaterals (extra articular)
  • However, the investigation of choice for intra articular knee structures such as, ACL, PCL, menisci and cartilage is diagnostic arthroscopy. This is because, when we put an arthroscope in the knee joint, we can visualize the intra articular structures in 5 to 10 times magnification.

Reference- Maheshwari, Essential ortho 5th edition page no 151.

question_text: Most common level to undergo IVDP is?
explanation:
The commonest level of disc prolapse is between L4-L5 in the lumbar spine and C5-C6 in the cervical spine. In the lumbar spine, it is uncommon above L3-L4 level. (Option B)

Clinical Features

  • Patient Profile: Usually an adult between 20-40 years of age with a sedentary lifestyle.
  • Common Symptoms:
    • Low Back Pain:
      • Acute Backache:
        • Severe, with spine held rigid by muscle spasm.
        • Painful movement; patient may be incapacitated.
      • Chronic Backache:
        • Dull, diffuse pain worsened by exertion, forward bending, sitting, or standing for long periods.
        • Relieved by rest.
  • Sciatic Pain:
    • Often associated with low back pain, but may be the sole symptom.
    • Pain radiates to:
      • Gluteal region
      • Back of the thigh and leg
    • Radiation Patterns:
      • S1 Root Compression: Pain radiates to the postero-lateral calf and heel.
      • L5 Root Compression: Pain radiates to the anterolateral aspect of the leg and ankle.
      • Higher Disc Prolapse (L2-L3 etc.): Pain may radiate to the front of the thigh.
    • Pain often begins with walking and is relieved by rest (neurological claudication).
  • Neurological Symptoms:
    • Paraesthesias: 'Pins and needles' sensation corresponding to the dermatome of the affected nerve root.
    • Numbness and Weakness:
      • Numbness in the leg or foot.
      • Muscle weakness.
    • Cauda Equina Syndrome (if large disc material compresses the theca and roots):
      • Irregular LMN type paralysis in lower limbs.
      • Bilateral absent ankle jerks.
      • Hypoaesthesia in L5 to S4 dermatomes.
      • Urinary and bowel incontinence.

Key takeaways:

  • Overall most common is IVDP at the lumbar spine at L4-L5 level.
  • Investigation of choice is MRI.
  • Most common symptom is lower back pain.

Tags:

Spine injuries and pathologies

Must know

NEET 2021

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopedics page no. 253

question_text: A pedestrian was hit by the bumper of a car at high velocity while he was walking on the road. His x-ray was normal but he was having gross knee swelling. MRI revealed injury to ACL, MCL and medial meniscus. What is this injury called?
explanation:
• Often the injury to medial collateral ligament, medial meniscus and anterior cruciate ligament occur together. This is called the O'Donoghue triad. Aka as Unhappy / Terrible triad of knee.

Knee Ligament Injury

Specific Ligament Injuries

  • Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL):
    • Injury Mechanism: Result of an abducting force on the leg (valgus force).
    • Common Rupture Site: Typically ruptures from its femoral attachment.
  • Lateral Collateral Ligament (LCL):
    • Injury Mechanism: Result of adduction of the tibia on the femur (varus force).
    • Common Rupture Site: Often avulsed from the head of the fibula with a piece of bone.
  • Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL):
    • Injury Mechanism: Most commonly ruptured due to twisting forces on a semi-flexed knee.
    • Associated Injuries: Frequently occurs alongside tears of the MCL and/or lateral collateral ligaments.
    • O'Donoghue Triad (Option A): Injury to the MCL, medial meniscus, and ACL occurring together.
  • Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL):
    • Injury Mechanism: Damaged when the anterior aspect of the tibia is struck while the knee is semi-flexed, forcing the tibia backwards on the femur.

Key takeaways:

  • Often the injury to medial collateral ligament, medial meniscus and anterior cruciate ligament occur together. This is called the O'Donoghue triad.
  • These are actually very rare and very difficult to treat as well as associated with inferior outcomes as well. Hence this combination of injury is also called the Unhappy/Terrible triad of knee as well.
  • However in common practice, combination injury of ACL, MCL and lateral meniscus is more commonly seen than this triad.

Tags:

Sports injuries

Must know

FMGE dec 2021 / NEET 2020 / Inicet May 2022

Reference: J. Maheshwari's, 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics, page no. 149

question_text: An 18-year-old male sustains a right hip injury after being tackled on the football field. Figure shows his radiograph upon presentation to the emergency room three hours later. On physical exam, he is noted to have a foot drop and decreased sensation globally throughout his entire lower leg. Closed reduction under conscious sedation is immediately performed, and the hip is able to be ranged through a stable arc of motion following reduction. A post-reduction radiograph is shown in Figure. Shortly after the reduction, the patient continues to have a foot drop, but his sensation is slightly improved. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
option_c: CT scan of his right hip
option_d: Skeletal traction on the distal femur to relax tension on the sciatic nerve
explanation:
• Following successful reduction of a traumatic hip dislocation, a CT scan must be obtained to evaluate for any entrapped osteochondral fragments.
  • Traumatic hip dislocations are typically the result of high-energy trauma and are frequently associated with posterior wall acetabular fractures. Initial management of a traumatic hip dislocation, with or without a fracture, is immediate closed reduction under conscious sedation.
  • If closed reduction is unsuccessful, immediate open reduction in the operating room should be performed.
  • Following successful reduction, a CT scan is necessary to rule-out intra-articular osteochondral fragments, even in the absence of fracture on radiographs. The incidence of sciatic nerve palsy following a traumatic hip dislocation is roughly 10%.
  • Incorrect Answers:
    • Answer A: Acute exploration of the sciatic nerve is controversial, and shouldn't be entertained before a CT scan has been completed.
    • Answer B: EMG scan may be useful if the sciatic nerve fails to recover after a period of weeks to months.
    • Answer D: Skeletal traction is not necessary if the hip is stable after concentric reduction and there are no associated fractures.

Reference- Maheshwari Ortho 5thedition, page no 130

question_text: Rocker bottom foot is due to
explanation:

question_text: A patient sustained twisting injury to the knee 2 days back. He has developed pain and swelling of the knee since 1 day. He also complains of restriction of extension of knee. On examination McMurray test is positive. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
• McMurray test is positive in meniscus injuries.
  • McMurray test for the medial meniscus.
    • Hold the knee with one hand and palpate the medial joint line
    • Hold the foot with other hand
    • Externally rotate the tibia
    • Flex and extend the knee
    • Positive - Pain/Click is felt
  • McMurray test for the lateral meniscus.
    • Hold the knee with one hand and palpate the lateral joint line
    • Hold the foot with other hand
    • Internally rotate the tibia
    • Flex and extend the knee
    • Positive - Pain/ Click is felt

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 149

question_text: Patient presents with knee pain after RTA. Dial test was positive. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
• Dial test is positive in PLC injuries
  • PLC is Postero Lateral Corner complex.
  • PLC is a group of ligaments in the posterolateral aspect of the knee which plays a very important role in the rotational stability of the knee.
  • Dial test
    • Patient is put in prone position
    • Then the clinician flexes the patient knees to 30° and places both hands on the feet of the patient, cupping his heels. A maximal external rotation force is then applied, and the foot-thigh angle is measured and compared with the other side.
    • the test is positive when there is more than 10° of external rotation in the injured knee compared to the uninjured knee

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 154

question_text: Identify the brace shown in the image.
explanation:
• The image shows a CROW i.e. Charcot restraint orthotic walker.
  • It is used in Charcot's joints of foot especially in those associated with diabetes.
  • Its is a below knee brace made up of tough sturdy material intended to support the foot and ankle during walking.

Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1297

question_text: A patient undergoes serial casting for the foot abnormalities shown in Figure A and achieves excellent correction. Unfortunately, the patient returns at 22 months of age with a recurrence which will require repeat casting and posteromedial releases. What is/are the risk factor(s) for recurrence in this condition?
explanation:
• Noncompliance with foot abduction orthosis (FAO) and parental education level of high school or below are risk factors for recurrence after correction of idiopathic clubfoot using the Ponsetti method.
  • The Ponsetti method of serial manipulation and casting is >90% successful in correcting clubfoot and preventing the need for surgical releases other than Achilles tenotomy. After serial casting and tenotomy, the patient is fitted for a foot abduction orthosis (FAO) which is worn for 23 hours per day for the first few months after casting and then nightly until around age 4 year.
  • Compliance with FAO usage is the most important factor in preventing clubfoot recurrence and this is influenced by the parent's education level.

Reference- MAHESHWARI ORTHO 5TH EDITION PAGE NO 214.

question_text: An army recruit has pain over both of his feet for the last 3 months since he started training. He has point tenderness and pain in the forefoot which is aggravated by activity. However, his x rays are normal. What is the next line of investigation?
option_d: No further investigations are required as his x-rays are normal
explanation:
• From the history, the person has stress fractures. Stress fracture is sometimes not seen on x-ray in early stages. Hence we need further investigations to confirm our diagnosis. For suspected stress fracture in one site, the investigation of choice is MRI. But for B/L stress fractures or multiple stress fractures, bone scan is recommended over MRI as it is easy, effective and economical.

Reference- Rockwood and green adult fracture 8ᵗʰ edition, page-653

question_text: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department with foot pain after landing on his foot improperly while playing basketball last night. His X-ray is shown here. What is the correct diagnosis in this patient?
explanation:
• JONES FRACTURE- A Jones fracture is a fracture of the proximal metadiaphyseal junction of the fifth metatarsal bone.
  • Aviator - neck of talus
  • Lovers -calcaneum

question_text: Pigmented villo-nodular synovitis most commonly occurs at
explanation:
Pigmented villonodular synovitis: Pigmented villonodular synovitis(PVNS) is a rare benign disease of the synovial membrane which is characterised by hypervascular neoplastic proliferation of the synovium with deposition of macrophages, multinucleated giant cells and hemosiderin.

Knee joint is most commonly involved joint. On arthroscopy typical brownish pigmentation of synovium is seen due to deposition of hemosiderin pigment.

Two varieties have been described:

  • Diffuse variety and localized nodular variety. Chances of recurrence are higher in diffuse variety. Low dose external beam radiotherapy and arthroscopic/open synovectomy have been tried with varying success for the treatment.

Malignant transformation has been reported but very rare.

Reference: Fundamentals of Ortho Mohindra and Jain, Page no. 268.

question_text: A 24-year-old professional soccer player presents with discomfort and pain while walking, and unstable knee joint following an injury during the match. The patient heard a popping sound at the time of injury. Physical examination reveals swelling of the knee joint and tibia could be moved excessively forwards on the femur. Which of the following knee structures is most likely damaged?
explanation:
LIGAMENTOUS INJURY OF KNEE JOINT -Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)

  • Attachments of ACL In tibia immediately behind anterior horn of medial meniscus Pass upwards, backwards and laterally Posterior part of medial surface of lateral femoral condyle
  • It is intra-synovial.
  • Limits forward gliding of tibia on femur and limits hyper extension.
  • Significant contribution to lateral stability & limits antero lateral rotation of tibia on femur
  • ACL is most commonly injured with valgus, external (lateral) rotation, hyper extension, deceleration, and rotational knee movements
  • ACL injuries commonly are associated with sports such as football, hockey, basketball, lacrosse, gymnastics, wrestling, and volleyball.
  • ACL injury rate is 4-6 times higher in females than males in competitive sports. The injury often is associated with immediate pain and an audible "pop". Swelling of the knee is noted within a few hours (acute hemarthrosis). The patient often states that the knee feels too unstable to continue playing and that weightbearing is difficult.
  • Most difficult action to perform in injury of Anterior Cruciate ligament (ACL) is: Walking downhill
  • Typically, full knee extension is limited secondary to pain, effusion, hamstring spasm, and ACL stump impingement. Flexion often is limited by effusion.
  • The Lachman test is the most sensitive examination for acute ACL injuries.

Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)

  • Attachments of PCL In tibia behind posterior horn of medial meniscus. Passes upwards, forwards and medially. Postural part of lateral surface of medial femoral condyle.
  • It is intra capsular, extra synovial and stouter ligamentous structure. It limits backward glide of tibia of femur (posterior translation). It Checks hyperextension only after the ACL is ruptured. Classically, PCL is injured by high velocity trauma with posterior dislocation of tibia on a flexed knee as in a 'dash board impact' in a motor car.
  • In Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL): Climbing stairs is difficult.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 878.

question_text: Patient sustains twisting type of injury followed by locking of knee. Most likely structure to be injured is?
explanation:
• Locking is the phenomenon in which the patient is unable to fully extend the knee due to intra articular block by a torn meniscus. Hence, when the patient has locking of knee, it means he/ she has sustained a meniscus injury.
  • Locking is most common in bucket-handle type of longitudinal tears of meniscus, where the inner segment of the meniscus is caught in the intercondylar notch and cannot return to its former position.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 901.

question_text: Unhappy triad of O'Donoghue is?
option_a: Rupture of the medial collateral ligament, damage to the medial meniscus, and rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament
option_b: Rupture of the Lateral collateral ligament, damage to the medial meniscus, and rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament
option_c: Rupture of the lateral collateral ligament, damage to the lateral meniscus, and rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament
option_d: Rupture of the medial collateral ligament, damage to the medial meniscus, and rupture of the posterior cruciate ligament
explanation:
• The unhappy triad was described by American orthopedic surgeon D H O'Donoghue, in 1950.
  • He described simultaneous occurrence of tear of ACL, MCL and medial meniscus tear when lateral force applied to knee while the foot is fixed to the ground.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 889.

question_text: Not a part of Unhappy triad of the knee
explanation:
• Unhappy triad of O'Donoghue or the Unhappy triad of the knee is composed of tears of
    • ACL +
    • MCL +
    • Medial meniscus

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 149

question_text: A dial test that is positive in 30-degree knee flexion suggests injury to which of the following structures?
option_c: Posterior cruciate ligament as well as PLC
explanation:
• Dial test is used for checking posterolateral instability of knee joint.
  • The posterolateral corner is a complex that includes the lateral collateral ligament, popliteus tendon, fabellofibular ligament, arcuate ligament, popliteofibular ligament, and the short lateral ligament.
  • “Tests for posterolateral instability include dial external (lateral) rotation (of tibia) test, external rotation recurvatum test, reverse pivot shift test of Jakob, Hassler and Staubli and posterolateral drawer test."
  • Dial test: -
    • With the leg dangling over the edge of the couch, one hand of the examiner stabilizes the distal femur and another hand holds the heels.
    • The examiner, then flexes the knee to 30°, and externally rotates the leg maximally, holding it through the heel, and notes the position of tibial tuberosity. Same maneuver is repeated on the other side.
    • If external rotation is more by 15° as compared to the other side, a posterolateral corner injury (PLC) is suspected.
    • The test is then repeated with the knee flexed further to 90°. Increased external rotation indicates (as compared to 30°) concomitant PLC with PCL injury.

Reference- Apley's 9/e p 881

question_text: Which of the following structure is intracapsular and extrasynovial?
explanation:
• Both the anterior and posterior cruciate ligamnets are intracapsular but extrasynovial.
  • In the knee, the extra capsular structures are the MCL and LCL
  • The Intracapsular structures are
  • Intrasynovial - Menisci
  • Extrasynovial - ACL, PCL

Reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy-Volume 1, Edition 6th, page no. 144.

question_text: A 20 years old male presents with history of gradual onset pain and swelling in left knee for 6 months. Now since last 1 month patient has started limping while walking and also has flexion deformity of knee. Ultrasonography shows presence of synovial thickening. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Unilateral monoarticular knee involvement with gradual onset pain swelling and flexion deformity, with synovial thickening is most probably suggestive of tuberculosis of knee.

Tuberculosis of knee clinical features:

  • Presenting complaints: The patient, usually in the age group of 10-25 years, presents with complaints of pain and swelling in the knee. It is gradual in onset without any preceding history of trauma. Subsequently, pain increases and the knee take an attitude of flexion. The patient starts limping. There is severe stiffness of the knee.

Examination:

  1. Swelling: The joint is swollen, which may be due to synovial hypertrophy or effusion.
  2. Muscle atrophy: Atrophy of the thigh muscles is more than what can be accounted for by disuse alone. This is an unexplained feature of joint tuberculosis.
  3. Cold abscess: There may be swelling due to a cold abscess, either around the knee or in the calf.
  4. Sinus: There may be discharging or healed sinuses.
  5. Deformity: In early stages, there is a mild flexion deformity of the knee because of effusion in the knee and muscle spasm. Later, triple deformity(flexion, posterior subluxation and external rotation) occurs due to ligament laxity.
  6. Movements: The movements at the joint are limited. There is pain and muscle spasm on attempting movement.

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th edition, Pg: 200-201.

question_text: A 20 yr old footballer sustained an injury to left knee while playing football. He is having pain and feeling of giving away over back and outer aspect of the knee. MRI shows injury to PCL and PLC both. Which clinical test will be positive in this patient?
explanation:
Tibial External Rotation (Dial) Test for Posterolateral Knee Instability

Purpose:

  • Assesses posterolateral instability of the knee by measuring the external rotation of the tibia relative to the femur at different angles of knee flexion.

Procedure:

  1. Patient Position:
    • Can be performed with the patient in a supine or prone position.
  2. Measurement Points:
    • External rotation is measured at 30 degrees and 90 degrees of knee flexion.
  3. External Rotation Measurement:
    • Use the medial border of the foot in its neutral position as a reference.
    • Apply an external rotational force to the foot and measure the foot-thigh angle relative to the femur axis.
    • Compare the degree of external rotation with the opposite (uninjured) leg.

Interpretation of Results:

  1. A difference of 10 degrees or more in external rotation between the injured and uninjured knees is considered pathologic.
  2. Increased External Rotation at 30 Degrees Only:
    • Indicates an isolated injury to the posterolateral corner.
  3. Increased External Rotation at Both 30 and 90 Degrees:
    • Indicates injury to both the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) and the posterolateral corner.

Special Considerations:

  1. Results of the dial test may be unreliable in the presence of medial instability, such as a torn medial collateral ligament (MCL).
  2. Reduction with Anterior Force:
    • Applying an anterior force to reduce the tibia can enhance detection of posterolateral rotatory instability, especially in the presence of PCL injuries.

Option A: Lachman test is done for Checking ACL Injuries.

Option B: Mc murray test Is done for Checking Meniscal Pathologies.

Option D: Pivot shift test is done for Checking ACL Injuries.

Key takeaways:

  • The purpose of the Dial Test is to diagnose Posterolateral Knee injury, as well as to differentiate between isolated Postero-lateral corner (PLC) injury and combination of PLC and Posterior Cruciate Ligament injury (PCL).
  • For an isolated PCL tear, the posterior drawer test or sag tests are more relevant.
