question_text: A 40-year-old female presents with chronic left plantar forefoot pain, exacerbated by narrow-toed shoes. She has a history of polyarthropathy. Physical exam demonstrates no palpable lesion, but pain is reproduced with forefoot squeeze. She is RF negative but ANA positive. Surgical excision of the painful lesion is performed, and frozen section pathology demonstrates perineural fibrosis without fibrinoid necrosis. These findings are consistent with which of the following diagnoses:
explanation:
• The clinical and histological findings are consistent with Morton’s neuroma. A physical exam will demonstrate pain with squeezing of the metatarsals, sometimes with a painful click (Mulder's click), and pathology will characteristically show perineural fibrosis with entrapment of the interdigital nerve.
  • Morton’s interdigital neuroma is an entrapment neuropathy that affects the common digital nerves of the lesser toes.
  • While the pathogenesis is incompletely understood, cumulative microtrauma is thought to result from a combination of repetitive compression of the interdigital nerve between neighbouring metatarsals as well as the intermetatarsal ligament in toe-off and traction from tethering between the more fixed medial and more mobile lateral metatarsals.
  • As a result, symptoms are exacerbated by high heels and a narrow toe box. Treatment initially involves metatarsal pads and a wider shoebox; though most patients go on to require surgical management consisting most commonly of transverse intermetatarsal ligament release and neurectomy.
  • Incorrect Answers:
    • Answer 2: Neurofibromas may similarly present in association with a peripheral nerve, but pathology will show distorted neural histology with a hypocellular, predominantly fibroblastic network of wire-like collagen and scattered myxoid regions.
    • Answer 3: Benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors (or Schwannomas) may share a similar clinical presentation. However, histologically they demonstrate a characteristic encapsulated, well-circumscribed lesion with alternating areas of densely-packed palisading spindle cells (Antoni A) and hypocellular mucinous stroma with fibrillar collagen (Antoni B).
    • Answer 4: Plantar fibromatosis arises from the plantar fascia, and would not be exacerbated by the physical exam maneuvers described. The lesions are usually asymptomatic but may become painful. Pathology is significant for dense fibrous tissue with mature collagen and interdigitated fibrocytes

question_text: A 40-year-old man presents with acute onset pain on his left great toe. X ray of the left foot shows punched out lesions with overhanging margins on the 1st metatarsal head.  What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• G sign/Martel sign: Punched out lesion of bone with overhanging bony edges.
  • GOUT-
  • It is a disorder of purine metabolism characterized by hyperuricemia (uric acid >7 mg/dL) that leads to deposition of monosodium urate crystalsin joints and periarticular tissues and thereby precipitates recurrent attacks of acute synovitis and eventually leads to arthritis
  • The hyperuricemia in gout may be due to:
    • Underexcretion of uric acid (90%)
    • Overproduction of uric acid (10%)
  • Factors predisposing to gout:
    • Obese, alcoholic middle-aged (usually over 30 years) male patient
    • Dietary excess of purine-rich foods: Meat, beans, peas, cauliflower, lentils, spinach, mushrooms, alcohol.
    • Trauma, post-surgery
  • Pathogenesis of gout is the high body total urate levels that cause deposition of monosodium urate crystals (called as tophi) into the synovium of joints
  • Acute gout: It is characterized by sudden onset, severe joint pain with red, hot, swollen, shiny overlying skin that mimics septic arthritis. The most common site of involvement is the MTP joint of the great toe (podagra)
  • Chronic gout: Recurrent acute attacks in due course lead to chronic gout. It is asymmetric and polyarticular. Joints become eroded, painful and eventually stiff and deformed.
  • X-ray changes include:
    • Soft tissue swelling (may be the only sign during acute attack)
    • Periarticular deep erosions – Rat/Flea bitten appearance
    • Joint space narrowing
    • G sign/Martel sign- Punched out lesion of bone with overhanging bony edges.

question_text: A 22-year-old football player sustained an injury to left thumb. Radiographic evaluation shows a Bennett fracture at the base of his thumb. Which muscle provides the predominant deforming force?
explanation:
Bennett Fracture

Overview

  • Definition: A Bennett fracture is an intraarticular fracture-dislocation of the base of the first metacarpal bone (see Fig. 7.26).
  • Pathophysiology: Characterized by a single large volar-ulnar fragment that remains attached to the trapezium via the anterior oblique or “beak” ligament, while the remainder of the metacarpal shaft is displaced.

Deforming Forces

  • Abductor Pollicis Longus (APL): Option A
    • Pulls the metacarpal shaft proximally, dorsally, and radially.
    • Causes supination and adduction of the metacarpal shaft.
  • Thumb Extensors: Option C
    • Contribute to the proximal and dorsal displacement of the metacarpal shaft.

Treatment Options

  • Closed Reduction and Percutaneous Pinning (CRPP):
    • Indicated for small or minimally displaced fragments.
  • Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF):
    • Recommended for larger fragments or when adequate reduction cannot be achieved through closed means.

Reduction Technique

  • Steps:
    1. Apply traction to the thumb.
    2. Perform palmar abduction.
    3. Induce pronation of the metacarpal shaft.
  • Goal: Achieve less than 1–2 mm of articular step-off to restore joint congruity and minimize the risk of post-traumatic arthritis.

Key takeaways -

Bennett fracture: Intraarticular fracture-dislocation 1st metacarpal base

  • Deforming forces: Abductor pollicis longus (APL) and thumb extensors cause proximal, dorsal, and radial displacement of the metacarpal shaft.
  • APL causes supination and adduction of the metacarpal shaft.
  • Anterior oblique or “beak” ligament keeps the volar-ulnar base fragment reduced to the trapezium.
  • Treatment: CRPP (percutaneous pinning) or ORIF based on the size of fragment

question_text: A 30 year old female patient presents to you with pain over right knee along with instability while walking. H/o hit by a 2 wheeler over the outer aspect of the right knee 1 day back. Clinical examination reveals a positive valgus stress at 30 degree flexion. Your diagnosis is:
explanation:
Mechanism of Knee Ligament Injuries

  1. Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL) - Option A
    • Mechanism: Injured by a valgus force (abduction of the leg on the femur).
    • Common Injury Site: Often ruptured from its femoral attachment.
  2. Lateral Collateral Ligament (LCL) - Option C
    • Mechanism: Damaged by a varus force (adduction of the tibia on the femur), opposite to the mechanism for MCL injury.
    • Common Injury Site: Usually avulsed from the head of the fibula along with a piece of bone.
  3. Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) - Option B
    • Mechanism: Commonly ruptured due to a twisting force on a semi-flexed knee.
    • Associated Injuries: Often occurs with tears of the medial or lateral collateral ligaments.
    • O'Donoghue Triad: A combination of injuries involving the medial collateral ligament, medial meniscus, and anterior cruciate ligament.
  4. Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL) - Option D
    • Mechanism: Damaged when the anterior aspect of the tibia is struck while the knee is semi-flexed, pushing the tibia backwards relative to the femur.

Key takeaways:

  • Medial collateral ligament: It is damaged if the injuring force has the effect of abducting the leg on the femur (valgus force). It ruptures most commonly from its femoral attachment. Diagnosed by Valgus stress test at 30 degree Knee Flexion.

question_text: Which of the following components of the clubfoot deformity should be addressed first when using the Ponsetti method?
explanation:
PONSETI METHOD-

  • Ponsetti method of choice now with a success rate of >95%. This procedure consists of manipulating the foot for 1-3 minutes into corrected position, followed by holding the correction in an above knee cast (applied with knees flexed to 90°).
  • After 7 days, cast is removed, foot re-manipulated, and recasted for another week in successively more corrected position. Usually, 5 to 7 casts are sufficient and deformity gets corrected.
  • The order of correction is very important. It can be remembered by the pneumonic 'CAVE'. Cavus is corrected in the 1st cast by supinating the forefoot and dorsiflexing the 1st metatarsal.
  • Forefoot must never be pronated as it will increase the cavus deformity.
  • Adduction and varus are then corrected simultaneously in the subsequent casts by abducting the forefoot in supination with counter pressure being applied at talar head.
  • Lastly, equinus is corrected, by dorsiflexing the fully abducted foot.
  • In case dorsiflexion is difficult beyond neutral then a percutaneous tenotomy of Tendo Achilles is done to achieve adequate dorsiflexion.

Reference- MAHESHWARI ORTHO 5TH EDITION PAGE NO 214.

question_text: Identify the radiological sign pathognomonic of this foot injury.
option_a: Avulsion sign seen in a TFL injury
option_b: Gissane sign seen in calcaneal fracture
option_c: Hawkins's sign seen in talar neck fracture
option_d: Fleck sign seen in injury at the Lisfranc joint
explanation:
Lisfranc (Tarsometatarsal) Joint Injuries

Epidemiology

  • Rare injuries, often missed (20% initially overlooked).
  • High incidence in polytraumatized patients.

Mechanism of Injury

  1. Twisting: Forceful abduction of the forefoot; seen in motor vehicle accidents.
  2. Axial Loading: Force applied to a fixed foot; e.g., a heavy object striking the heel.
  3. Crushing: Common in industrial injuries; can lead to compartment syndrome.

Clinical Evaluation

  • Symptoms: Pain, swelling, tenderness on dorsum of foot; pathognomonic plantar ecchymosis.
  • Requires high suspicion; 20% are misdiagnosed.
  • Watch for potential complications like compartment syndrome or neurovascular damage.
  • Stress testing (forefoot abduction/pronation) helps diagnose instability.

Radiographic Evaluation

  • Standard AP, lateral, and oblique X-rays typically diagnostic.
  • Key signs: Misalignment of the second metatarsal, dorsal displacement, "flake fractures." (Option D)
  • Weight-bearing and stress views, CT, and MRI may be needed for complex cases.

Treatment

  • Nonoperative: For stable, non-displaced injuries; involves casting or boots and gradual weight bearing.
  • Operative: For displacements >2 mm; involves anatomic reduction and fixation (screws/K-wires).
    • Postoperative care includes immobilization and gradual weight-bearing.

Postoperative Management

  • Immobilization for 6–8 weeks, followed by progressive weight bearing.
  • Removal of lateral column stabilization at 6–12 weeks; medial fixation may remain longer.

Complications

  • Posttraumatic arthritis, compartment syndrome, infection, CRPS, neurovascular injury, hardware failure.
  • Management includes orthotics, arthrodesis, or inter positional arthroplasty for severe cases.

question_text: A patient suffers an inversion injury to the ankle during a football match. Which structure is most likely to get injured?
explanation:
Explanation:

The anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) is the most commonly injured structure in inversion ankle sprains due to its anatomical location and relative weakness among lateral ligaments.

  • The anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) is part of the lateral ligament complex of the ankle, which also includes the calcaneofibular and posterior talofibular ligaments.
  • It extends from the anterior margin of the lateral malleolus (fibula) to the neck of the talus.
  • During an inversion injury, the foot rolls inward, placing excessive strain on the lateral side of the ankle-especially the ATFL.
  • This ligament is most commonly injured in low ankle sprains, particularly during sports or missteps.
  • Injury Grading:
    • Grade I: Mild stretching
    • Grade II: Partial tear
    • Grade III: Complete rupture
  • Clinical Features:
    • Pain and swelling over the lateral malleolus
    • Positive anterior drawer test
    • Bruising, tenderness, and instability of the ankle joint
  • Diagnosis:
    • Clinical examination (anterior drawer test)
    • X-rays to rule out fracture
    • MRI for soft tissue injury assessment
  • Treatment:
    • Grades I & II: RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation), bracing, physiotherapy
    • Grade III: May require surgical repair

Explanation of other options:

Tibialis anterior tendon (Option A): Primarily involved in dorsiflexion and inversion of the foot; not typically injured in lateral (inversion) sprains as it lies anterior-medially.

Tibialis posterior tendon (Option B): Supports the medial longitudinal arch and assists in inversion; more commonly injured in medial ankle injuries or overuse, not lateral inversion sprains.

Extensor hallucis longus tendon (Option C): Involved in extension of the big toe and dorsiflexion; lies on the anterior ankle and is not subjected to strain during inversion.

question_text: Sudden dorsiflexion of foot may lead to which of the following injuries?
explanation:
• Achilles tendon injury-
    • Achilles tendon is the thickest and strongest tendon in the body and is also the one of the most commonly injured tendons in the body.
    • The most common Achilles tendon injuries are-
      1. Achilles tendinosis (formerly called Achilles tendonitis)
      2. Achilles tendon rupture
  • Achilles tendon rupture-
    • A rupture of the Achilles tendon occurs when the tendon is stretched outside beyond its capacity.
    • The most common site of rupture is the “watershed” less vascular area of tendon, which is 4 cm proximal to its insertion on calcaneum.
  • Achilles tendinosis (Achilles tendonitis)-
    • Achilles tendonitis is a condition that develops over time and is associated with degeneration of the tendon and inflammation that causes pain.
    • Achilles tendonitis is described as insertional or non-insertional-
      1. Insertional achilles tendonitis-Occurs where the achilles tendon inserts into the calcaneum, i.e., at tendon-bone interface.
      2. Non-insertional achilles tendonitis-Occurs about one to two inches (2-5 cm) proximal to the site of insertion of the tendon.
  • “Achilles tendonitis is a chronic problem; “The etiology of Achilles tendonitis is overuse” - Essential sports medicine Achilles tendonitis occurs more commonly in Athletes, joggers and hikers.

Reference: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter: 17, Pg: 257

question_text: A 30-year-old marathon runner presents with persistent pain over the dorsum of the foot on weight bearing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
March/Stress fracture

  • March fractures are metatarsal fractures, most commonly second and third metatarsal fractures caused by an overuse injury. The repetitive impact to the metatarsals with weight-bearing exercises cause microfractures, which consolidate to form stress fractures.
  • The most common location of metatarsal stress fractures is the second metatarsal neck.
  • High-risk populations include runners, military recruits, ballet dancers, basketball players, or those with a recent increase in activity or training.
  • Distal second metatarsal stress fractures are the most common due to the high bending and shear forces. Further risk factors include a long 2nd metatarsal, hypermobile first ray, and women. Radiographs may be negative or may show callus formation.
  • Advanced imaging of a bone scan or an MRI can be obtained to confirm the diagnosis in cases of negative radiographs.
  • Initial treatment usually involves activity modification with a gradual return to sport over 6-8 weeks when asymptomatic.
  • Use of a walking boot, cast, or limiting weight-bearing can be used in patients whose symptoms do not resolve with activity modification or cannot comply with the recommendations.

Reference: Essential Orthopaedics: Maheshwari & Mhaskar, 5th Edition, Page Number-3.

question_text: A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department following a motorbike accident and is found to have a closed midshaft fracture of the left tibia. Six hours later, he develops severe leg pain that is disproportionate to the injury and worsens with passive dorsiflexion of the foot. The pain is not relieved by analgesics. On examination, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are present, but there is no sensation over the first dorsal web space. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given scenario of development of pain disproportionate to injury not relieved by analgesics and loss of sensation is suggestive of compartment syndrome, and the most appropriate next step in management is immediate fasciotomy.

  • Compartment syndrome may occur following fractures of the arm or leg, even without major vessel injury, due to bleeding, swelling, or infection that increases pressure within an osseofascial compartment.
  • This pressure reduces capillary flow, causing muscle ischaemia, swelling, and further pressure increase, leading to necrosis of nerve and muscle within hours.
  • Muscle infarction results in permanent replacement by fibrous tissue known as Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.
  • Similar effects can result from swelling inside a tight plaster cast. High-risk injuries include fractures of the elbow, forearm bones, proximal tibia, multiple fractures of the hand or foot, crush injuries, and circumferential burns.
  • The classic ischaemia signs are pain, paraesthesia, pallor, paralysis, and pulselessness, but in compartment syndrome, pulses may remain, and skin may not be pale.
  • Severe pain, often bursting in nature, is typically the earliest and sometimes only sign. Altered sensation and weakness of active muscle contraction may also occur, requiring repeated skin sensation checks.
  • Ischaemic muscles are sensitive to stretch, so pain increases when toes or fingers are passively hyperextended.
  • Diagnosis is confirmed by measuring intracompartmental pressure, with early detection being critical. Continuous pressure monitoring is advised in high-risk cases, especially in unconscious patients.
  • A split catheter is used to measure compartment pressure near the fracture, and a differential pressure (diastolic minus compartment pressure) below 30 mmHg indicates the need for immediate decompression through fasciotomy. (Option A ruled out)
  • Casts, bandages, and dressings must be fully removed, as simply splitting the plaster is completely ineffective. (Option D ruled out)
  • The limb should be kept flat, since elevating it further lowers end-capillary pressure and worsens muscle ischaemia. (Option B ruled out)

question_text: A 35 year old man with a history of lifting weights, presents the next day with back pain, right sided radiculopathy, loss of bladder function, loss of sensation of the feet, weakness of extensor hallucis longus. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• The clinical profile described fits a case with intervertebral disc prolapse with a cauda equina presentation, for the following reasons.
  • The patient is usually a fit adult between 20-45 years. Typically, while lifting or stooping, he has severe back pain and is unable to straighten up. A day or two later pain is felt in the buttocks and lower limb(Sciatica).
  • L5 impairment causes weakness of knee flexion and big toe extension as well as sensory loss on the lateral side of the leg and the dorsum of the foot. Normal reflexes at the knee and ankle are characteristic of L5 root compression.
  • Paradoxically, the knee reflex may appear to be increased, because of weakness of the antagonists which are supplied by L5.
  • SI impairment causes weak plantar-flexion and eversion of the foot, a depressed ankle jerk and sensory loss along the lateral border of the foot.
  • Occasionally an L4/5 disc prolapse compresses both L5 and SI.
  • Cauda equina compression causes urinary retention and sensory loss over the sacrum.

Reference: Apley's System of Orthopaedics AMI Fractures, 9th edition, Page: 479.

question_text: A 34 yr old body-builder presents with complaints of severe pain in lower back radiating to the whole left lower limb, anaesthesia over left buttock, weakness in legs and loss of bladder control for the last 2 days after the history of weight lifting. Choose the correct option.
option_a: MRI to be done for cauda equina syndrome
option_b: MRI to be done acute for disc prolapse
option_c: Xray to be done for burst fracture of vertebrae
explanation:
The history and findings fits perfect for Cauda equina syndrome

Cauda Equina Syndrome

  • Causes:
    • Large extruded disc
    • Surgical trauma
    • Hematoma
  • Symptoms:
    • Bilateral buttock and lower extremity pain
    • Bowel or bladder dysfunction (usually urinary retention)
    • Saddle anesthesia
    • Varying degrees of lower extremity motor or sensory dysfunction
  • Initial Diagnosis:
    • Digital rectal examination:
      • Assess rectal tone
      • Evaluate perianal sensation
      • Check for volitional control and contraction
      • Perianal sensation evaluation is crucial for immediate diagnosis
    • Imaging:
      • Urgent/emergent MRI: (Option A)
        • Helps assess cauda equina compression
      • Surgical Decompression:
        • Timing:
          • Controversial, but earliest possible decompression is generally indicated to prevent progression of neurologic loss
        • Best Outcomes:
          • Surgical decompression within the first 48 hours has been associated with the best recovery outcomes, although prognosis remains guarded in most cases

Option B - Acute disc prolapse won't cause so much neurological involvement suddenly.

Option C - There is no history of trauma to cause burst fracture of vertebrae

Option D - As bowel and bladder are involved, urgent steps have to be taken to find the cause. Observation alone doesn't suffice.

Key takeaways

Cauda Equina Syndrome - Mnemonic - "SADDLE BAGS"

  • Saddle anesthesia
  • Abdominal or lower extremity pain
  • Dysfunction in bowel or bladder (urinary retention)
  • Digital rectal examination (for initial diagnosis)
  • Loss of motor or sensory function in lower extremities
  • Emergent MRI (for assessing compression)
  • Best outcomes with decompression within 48 hours
  • Assessment of perianal sensation
  • Guarded prognosis if not treated early
  • Surgical decompression is key

question_text: A football player sustains a twisting injury to the ankle and knee during a match. There are no bony injuries detected on examination. The examiner is performing the test shown in the image to evaluate knee stability. Which test is being performed?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Lachman test is the most sensitive clinical test for diagnosing anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury, performed with the knee flexed to 20-30°.

  • The Lachman test is the gold standard clinical test for ACL integrity, especially in acute injuries like the twisting trauma described here:
  • Position: Patient lies supine, knee flexed to 20-30°.
  • Maneuver: Examiner stabilizes the distal femur with one hand and applies anterior force to the proximal tibia with the other.
  • Positive Test: Excessive anterior translation of the tibia compared to the uninjured leg, usually >5 mm.
  • Significance: Indicates partial or complete ACL tear.
  • Advantage: Preferred over the anterior drawer test because hamstrings are less active in 30° flexion, reducing false negatives.

Explanation of other options:

Posterior drawer for PCL (Option A): Assesses PCL by pushing the tibia posteriorly with the knee at 90°. Not appropriate for suspected ACL injury.

McMurray (Option B): Evaluates meniscal tears, not ligament injuries. Involves rotation of the tibia during knee flexion-extension.

Anterior drawer for ACL (Option D): Also tests the ACL, but less sensitive than the Lachman test due to influence from hamstring tension. Done at 90° flexion.

Reference:

Anterior Cruciate Ligament Knee Injury - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf (nih.gov)

Lachman Test - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf (nih.gov)

question_text: A 65 years old postmenopausal female came with persistent backache not responding to conservative treatment. History of lifting heavy weight 4 months back with progressively increasing pain that worsens on walking. The pain starts radiating down her legs after walking for around 100m distance, she however feels no pain on climbing up the stairs, most probable diagnosis is?
explanation:
In most condition pain will increase on climbing up stairs. The one exception is lumbar canal stenosis, where there is relief in pain when the patients climb up stairs.

LUMBAR CANAL STENOSIS

  • Chronic condition characterised by narrowing of lumbar spinal canal causing compression of spinal cord or its emerging nerve roots
  • Most common location: L4-L5
  • Age- >65 yrs
  • Lumbar Canal stenosis is the most common reason for lumbar spine surgery in patients >65yrs
  • Males>females
  • Causes of lumbar canal stenosis:
    • Degenerative/spondylotic changes (most common)
    • Intervertebral disc prolapse
    • Post surgical
    • Vertebral fractures
    • Inflammatory: ankylosing spondylitis
    • Secondary to systemic disease- paget disease, acromegaly, fluorosis

Clinical features of lumbar canal stenosis:

  • Back pain
  • Radiation to one\both lower limbs
  • Buttock pain
  • Bowel bladder symptoms
  • Neurogenic claudication

Neurogenic claudication:

  • In lumbar canal stenosis, neurogenic claudication pain is the hall mark (i.e. pain arising in the lower back radiating down the buttock, thigh, leg to the foot especially on prolonged physical activity).
  • Pain worsens on standing or walking but is generally relieved by either bending forwards (trunk flexion) or sitting. Posture related pain in LCS is due to the fact that the available space in the central canal decreases in axial loading and extension and increases in axial distraction and flexion. this also explains that why do patients get more relief in lying on the side (allowing flexion posture) than lying flat.

For the same reason patients and walking uphill easier and pushing a shopping cart gives them relief (positive shopping cart sign) . Since they mostly remain stooped forwards to relieve pressure on their neural structures, their posture is said to be Ape like.

Differentials

An important differential is vascular claudication pain (i.e. pain due to a peripheral artery disease). Pain on standing alone is the most sensitive symptom to differentiate neurogenic claudication from vascular claudication.

Reference:Fundamentals of orthopedics by mohindra and jain page no 186.

question_text: A heavy lifter presents with lower back ache. Identify the nerve compressed in the following disc prolapse?
explanation:
Explanation:

L5 nerve root is the most commonly compressed nerve in lumbar disc prolapse, especially at the L4-L5 level, causing dorsiflexion weakness and pain over the anterolateral leg and dorsum of the foot.

  • Lumbar disc prolapse commonly affects individuals involved in repetitive heavy lifting or strenuous physical activity.
  • In this case:
    • L4-L5 disc prolapse compresses the L5 nerve root.
  • Symptoms include:
    • Lower back pain
    • Radiating leg pain (sciatica) down the lateral thigh, anterolateral leg, and dorsum of the foot
    • Motor weakness: especially of extensor hallucis longus (difficulty lifting the big toe or foot-foot drop)
    • No reflex loss (ankle and knee jerks are typically preserved)
  • Radiographic findings:
    • X-Ray : Useful to rule out bony pathology.
    • CT : Reveals disc shape abnormalities, loss of pre-thecal fat, and herniated material pressing on nerve roots or theca.
    • MRI : Gold standard. Clearly shows the prolapsed disc, nerve roots, and thecal sac.
    • Myelography : Useful when CT or MRI is unavailable. Shows dye flow block, indentation, or root cut-off sign in lateral prolapse.

question_text: A 30-year-old female presents with back pain radiating to the right lower limb. Based on the MRI findings provided, which is the most commonly affected nerve root?

Explanation:

question_text: For the treatment of new onset plantar fasciitis, which of the following modalities results in the highest patient satisfaction at 8 weeks of follow-up?
explanation:
• A plantar fascia-specific stretching program has the highest patient satisfaction at the 8-week follow-up interval.
  • Symptoms of plantar fasciitis include “start-up” inferior heel pain with patients often preferring to walk on their toes for the first few steps when getting out of bed.
  • The pain lessens with ambulation and then increases again with increased activity.
  • Illustration A depicts a patient performing plantar fascia-specific stretching. Illustration B displays a patient performing an achilles tendon–stretching program.
  • The purpose of plantar fascia–specific stretching is to recreate the windlass mechanism and achieve a tissue tension through a controlled stretch of the plantar fascia.
  • Corticosteroids (Answer 2) should be used rarely as they can cause fat atrophy and even plantar fascia rupture. The FDA has approved extracorporeal shock-wave therapy (Answer 3) for plantar fasciitis lasting greater than 6 months. Surgical release of medial third of plantar fascia can be done is resistant cases.

question_text: A 44 yr carpenter presents with adduction deformity and arthritis in right hip with true shortening of 2cm in right lower limb. He had a past history of TB hip for which he has taken full course of ATT 5 yrs back. His family is dependent on him financially. Least preferred treatment option for him will be:
option_d: All of these are preferred options
explanation:
Treatment for TB of the Hip

Objectives:

  • Control disease activity.
  • Preserve joint movement.

Early Stages (Stages I and II):

  • Conservative Treatment:
    • Antitubercular Chemotherapy: As per standard regimens.
    • Care of the Hip:
      • Immobilization: Below-knee skin traction for rest and pain relief.
      • General Care: Follow specific guidelines.

Later Stages (Stage III and beyond):

  • Operative Treatment:
    1. Joint Debridement:
      • Remove pus, necrotic tissue, and dead cartilage.
      • Post-op: Traction and joint mobilization.
    2. Girdlestone Arthroplasty:
      • Excise the head and neck of the femur.
      • Post-op: Skeletal traction followed by hip mobilization.
    3. Arthrodesis:
      • Fuse the hip joint if a stiff hip in a functional position is preferred.
    4. Corrective Osteotomy:
      • Subtrochanteric osteotomy for unacceptable bony ankylosis positions.
    5. Total Hip Replacement:
      • Effective for quiescent TB; alternative in cost-sensitive regions is excision arthroplasty.

Option A - Arthrodesis was previously done where the patient needs stability and can compromise on mobility but it is difficult to carry out day to day activities and hence not preferred these days.

Option B - If infection is quiescent >>>>> patient needs mobility >>>>>  Girdlestone arthroplasty (unaffordable)

Option C - If infection is quiescent >>>>>patient needs mobility >>>>> THR (if affordable)

Key takeaways:

  • If infection is active without arthritis >>>>> Debridement + ATT
  • If infection is active with arthritis >>>>>> Girdlestone arthroplasty + ATT

question_text: A mother brings her 5-year-old kid with high grade fever with chills. The child has severe pain in right hip and is unable to move the lower limb. On palpation there is fullness of scarpa's triangle. IOC in this condition?
explanation:
Clinical Presentation of Septic Arthritis (Pediatric Case)

Investigations:

Radiological Examination:

  • X-ray Findings (early stages):
    • May appear normal
    • Possible increased joint space and soft tissue shadow (due to swelling)
  • X-ray Findings (later stages):
    • Narrowing of joint space
    • Irregular joint margins
    • Potential subluxation or dislocation of the joint
  • Ultrasound: Useful for detecting effusion, especially in deep joints (e.g., hip, shoulder). Can guide joint aspiration.
  • MRI: May be useful in low grade infections. (Option A)

Laboratory Findings:

  • Blood Tests:
    • Neutrophilic leukocytosis
    • Elevated ESR
    • Blood culture may grow the causative organism (Option D)
  • Joint Aspiration:
    • Best and quickest diagnostic method for septic arthritis
    • Fluid shows features of acute septic inflammation
    • Gram stain provides early clues to the causative organism before culture results are available

Option A: MRI May be useful in low grade infections. However Septic arthritis diagnosed with USG guided Aspiration.

Option B: Joint aspiration is the quickest and the best method of diagnosing septic arthritis. The fluid may show features of acute septic inflammation. USG guided aspiration is the IOC. USG Alone won't suffice.

Option D: Blood culture may grow the causative organism. However Septic arthritis diagnosed with USG guided Aspiration.

Key takeaways

  • Joint aspiration is the quickest and the best method of diagnosing septic arthritis. The fluid may show features of acute septic inflammation. USG guided aspiration is the IOC.
  • Treatment typically involves joint drainage and appropriate antibiotic therapy, guided by culture and sensitivity reports.

question_text: A Patient had difficulty climbing upstairs, when he was made to bear weight on right lower limb, the pelvis of the left side dropped down. Which is the structure involved causing this problem?
explanation:
• The test mentioned in the question is the Trendelenburg test. In a positive test the ‘normal side sags down’.
  • Here the left side sags down, so the problem is with the right side. The common cause of positive Trendelenburg test is the weakness of the gluteus medius, is supplied by the Superior gluteal N.
  • So on this case the injured nerve is the right superior gluteal N.

Common causes of positive Trendelenburg test are:-

Defect in fulcrum:Hip dislocation, advanced cases of TB hip and septic arthritis of hip joint, developmental dysplasia of hip, Perthes disease, advanced cases of AVN hip.

Defect in liver arm: Fracture head or neck of femur, coxa vara and trochanteric fractures.

Defect in power: Abductor paralysis due to poliomyelitis or superior gluteal nerve injury, tensor fascia lata and iliotibial tract palsy and L5 radiculopathy

  • During one legged stance of gait cycle, when one stands on one leg (i.e. left leg), the right side pelvis is lifted up to clear the ground.
  • This is done by contraction of abductors on the left side (mainly gluteus medius that is running between ilium and greater trochanter on lateral aspect of hip) with an intact lever arm and fulcrum.
  • If left side abductor mechanism is defective the opposite side of pelvis will dip down by virtue of gravity (positive Trendelenburg sign)
  • In this case while walking patient lurches to same side i.e. he shifts all his weight to the left side to prevent the right pelvis from dipping down and keep the pelvis leveled (Trendelenburg gait).
  • When patient lurches on both sides (positive Trendelenburg sign on both hips), it is known as "waddling gait"

question_text: A 50 year old male on walker support presents with back pain and weakness of both lower limbs for 1 month. MRI reveals TB spine with abscess compressing the spinal cord. Next line of action is?

• In, India we follow the middle path regime for treatment of TB paraplegia.

question_text: A 40 yr old gym trainer with a frequent history of heavy weight lifting complains of chronic lower back pain and recently the pain has started radiating to the left lower limb. MRI shows L4-L5 disc prolapse. Correct sequence of progression of intervertebral disc prolapse is:
option_a: Stage of displacement > stage of degeneration > stage of sequestration > stage of extrusion
option_b: Stage of degeneration > stage of sequestration > stage of displacement > stage of extrusion
option_c: Stage of degeneration > stage of displacement > stage of extrusion > stage of sequestration
option_d: Stage of extrusion > Stage of degeneration > stage of sequestration > stage of displacement
explanation:
Intervertebral Disc Prolapse

a) Nucleus Degeneration

  • Definition: The initial phase of disc degeneration before any displacement of the nucleus occurs.
  • Characteristics:
    • Softening of the Nucleus: The nucleus pulposus (the gel-like center of the disc) becomes softer and more pliable.
    • Fragmentation: The nucleus begins to fragment or break down into smaller pieces.
    • Weakening of Annulus: The annulus fibrosus (the tough outer ring of the disc) weakens, particularly the posterior part, leading to disintegration.

b) Nucleus Displacement

  • Definition: The movement or bulging of the nucleus pulposus due to internal pressure and structural weaknesses in the disc.
  • Characteristics:
    • Disc Protrusion: The nucleus bulges through a weakened area of the annulus fibrosus. This is often due to the degeneration of the annulus, which may occur spontaneously or due to trauma.
    • Disc Extrusion: As the disc continues to degenerate and the annulus becomes more compromised, the nucleus can push out of the annulus and lie beneath the posterior longitudinal ligament. At this stage, it may still remain attached to the parent disc.

c) Stage of Extrusion

  • Definition: A specific phase where the nucleus pulposus has moved beyond the confines of the annulus fibrosus.
  • Characteristics:
    • Extruded Nucleus: The nucleus exits through the annulus and is located under the posterior longitudinal ligament.
    • Irreversibility: Once the nucleus is extruded, it does not naturally return to its original position. The posterior longitudinal ligament alone is usually insufficient to prevent further displacement.

d) Stage of Sequestration

  • Definition: The final stage where the extruded disc material becomes a separate fragment from the main disc.
  • Characteristics:
    • Sequestrated Disc: The extruded nucleus may lose its connection with the parent disc and become a free fragment within the spinal canal.
    • Location: This fragment can end up lying behind the posterior longitudinal ligament or elsewhere in the spinal canal.

Key takeaway:

Correct order of progression of pathology in IVDP is:- Stage of degeneration > stage of displacement > stage of extrusion > stage of sequestration

question_text: A young mother brings her 5 month old baby with complaints of clicking on the left hip while trying to wear clothes and the child not actively using the left limb. Choose the correct statement.
option_a: USG can be used for screening of DDH and alpha angle is increased
option_b: X-ray can be used for screening of DDH and alpha angle is increased
option_c: USG can be used for screening of DDH and alpha angle is decreased
option_d: USG can be used for screening of DDH and beta angle is decreased
explanation:
Important Radiological Parameters in Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH)

1.Acetabular Index (AI)

  • Definition: The acetabular index is the angle formed by Hilgenreiner's line and a line from a point on the lateral triradiate cartilage to the lateral margin of the acetabulum.
  • Normal Range: In children older than 6 months, the AI should be less than 25°.
  • Imaging Modality: X-ray.
  • Significance: An increased acetabular index indicates insufficient acetabular development, a key feature in diagnosing DDH.

2. Alpha (α) Angle

  • Definition: The alpha angle is formed by the intersection of the baseline (along the ilium) and the acetabular roof line.
  • Normal Range: Greater than 60°. (Option A,B)
  • Imaging Modality: Ultrasound (USG). (Option C)
  • Significance: A smaller alpha angle suggests a shallow acetabulum, indicating hip dysplasia.

3. Beta (β) Angle

  • Definition: The beta angle is formed by the intersection of the baseline (along the ilium) and the inclination line (along the labrum).
  • Normal Range: Less than 55°. (Option D)
  • Imaging Modality: Ultrasound (USG).
  • Significance: A larger beta angle may indicate hip instability or dislocation.


4. Ultrasound Considerations for Newborns

  • Limitations: Ultrasound findings before 6 weeks of age can be unreliable due to ligamentous laxity in the early newborn period.

5. Radiographic Lines and Measurements in DDH

  • Hilgenreiner's Line B. Perkin's Line C. Shenton's Line

6. Center-Edge Angle of Wiberg

  • Definition: The angle between a vertical line (Perkins' line) and a line drawn from the lateral edge of the acetabulum to the center of the femoral head.
  • Normal Range: Greater than 10° in children between 6 and 13 years. This angle increases with age.
  • Significance: It is a useful measure of hip position in older children. A lower angle suggests under coverage of the femoral head, characteristic of hip dysplasia.

Option A, B & D: DDH is diagnosed with USG in which alpha angle is decreased and beta angle is increased.

Key takeaways

  • USGis used for screening of DDH
  • AI - In children older than 6 months, the AI should be less than 25°.
  • Alpha angle: Normal Range: Greater than 60° - Decreased in DDH.
  • Beta angle: Normal Range: Less than 55° - Increased in DDH.
  • CE angle of Wiberg - Normal Range: Greater than 10° in children between 6 and 13 years. This angle increases with age

question_text: A 30-year-old male suffers a severe crush injury to his right leg after being run over by a car. To aid in the decision between limb salvage and amputation, the surgical team calculates the Mangled Extremity Severity Score (MESS). This score incorporates all of the following parameters EXCEPT:
option_b: Severity of soft tissue and skeletal injury
option_d: Degree and duration of limb ischemia
explanation:
Explanation:

The Mangled Extremity Severity Score (MESS) is an objective scoring system used to predict the likelihood of amputation following severe limb trauma. It is based on four specific clinical parameters. The mechanism or velocity of the trauma is not a direct variable in the score. However, high-velocity trauma (e.g., gunshot wound) will result in a higher score for the "Injury severity" component.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Presence and degree of shock (Option A): The patient is scored based on their systolic blood pressure, reflecting their hemodynamic status.
  • Severity of soft tissue and skeletal injury (Option B): This is the first component, graded on a 1 to 4 scale based on the energy imparted to the limb (low energy, medium energy, high energy, and massive crush).
  • Degree and duration of limb ischemia (Option D): This is a critical component, reflecting the perfusion status of the limb. The score is doubled if the ischemia time is greater than 6 hours, highlighting the importance of timely revascularization.

Key Takeaways:

The four components of the MESS score can be remembered easily:

  1. Injury severity (skeletal/soft tissue)
  2. Shock
  3. Age of the patient
  4. Ischemia of the limb

A score of 7 or more is highly predictive of the need for amputation and is a common threshold used in clinical decision-making.

Reference:

  • Johansen K, et al. Objective criteria accurately predict amputation following lower extremity trauma. J Trauma. 1990;30(5):568-73.

question_text: An 8-year-old male child presents with fever and tenderness in the left lower limb. The limb is warm to the touch, and ESR is raised. An X-ray reveals periosteal elevation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Fever, localized warmth, raised ESR, and periosteal elevation on X-ray are classic indicators of acute osteomyelitis.

  • Osteomyelitis is an infection of the bone, commonly caused by pyogenic bacteria in children.
  • caused by pyogenic bacteria in children. The metaphysis of long bones is the usual site due to its rich vascular supply and sluggish blood flow, which predisposes to bacterial seeding.
  • Clinically, it presents with fever, localized pain, warmth, tenderness, and systemic signs of infection.
  • Raised ESR and CRP are common laboratory findings. On radiography, periosteal elevation appears by 7-10 days due to subperiosteal abscess formation.
  • Early radiographs may be normal, so MRI is more sensitive in the early phase (within 24 hours) as it can detect bone marrow edema.
  • Confirmation of diagnosis is through aspiration and culture of the infected site.

Explanation of other options:

Ewing sarcoma (Option A): A malignant small round cell tumor seen in children and adolescents; presents with fever, pain, and swelling but is less likely to show acute signs of infection like warmth and raised ESR early. Onion-skin periosteal reaction is more characteristic.

Osteosarcoma (Option B): Malignant bone tumor of adolescence; typically presents with pain and swelling. X-ray shows sunburst appearance and Codman's triangle-not just simple periosteal elevation.

Giant Cell Tumor (Option D): Benign, locally aggressive tumor seen in skeletally mature individuals (usually after closure of epiphyses); rare in children and not associated with fever or signs of infection.

question_text: Most common type of lesion in Pott's spine:
explanation:
There are 4 patterns of vertebral involvement in Pott's spine:

  1. Paradiscal(due to arterial spread) - This is the commonest In this, the contiguous areas of two adjacent vertebrae along with the intervening disc are affected.
  2. Central(due to venous spread) - In this type, the body of a single vertebra is affected. This leads to early collapse of the weakened vertebra. The nearby disc may be normal.
  3. Anterior(due to subperisteal spread) - In this type, infection is localised to the anterior part of the vertebral body. The infection spreads up and down under the anterior longitudinal ligament.
  4. Appendiceal and posterior type(occur in isolation involving pedicles, laminae, transverse process and spinous process or in conjunction with typical paradiscal variant).

question_text: A man presents with back pain following a road traffic accident. There was no history of neurological deficit. X-ray spine is done. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The absence of neurological deficits and X-ray findings of isolated posterior element involvement point to a spinous process fracture.

  • Spinous process fractures occur due to direct trauma or hyperextension injuries and involve the posterior bony projection of a vertebra.
  • These fractures are often stable, and because the spinal canal and neural structures remain unaffected, there are usually no neurological deficits.
  • X-ray typically shows a clear fracture line through the spinous process without vertebral body collapse or disruption of alignment.
  • In the context of trauma with localized pain and preserved neurologic function, this diagnosis is most consistent.

Explanation of other options:

Chance fracture (Option B): Horizontal fracture through the vertebra due to flexion-distraction injuries (e.g., seatbelt injury). Often involves the vertebral body and posterior elements, more severe, and commonly associated with neurological deficits.

Fracture of base of vertebrae (Option C): Refers to more generalized vertebral body fractures (e.g., endplate or pedicle); may involve instability or neurological compromise, not limited to the spinous process.

Compressed fracture (Option D): Involves anterior wedging or collapse of the vertebral body, often due to axial loading; may present with vertebral body height loss on imaging-not consistent with isolated spinous process injury.

question_text: A 36 year old female is brought to the emergency department with history of RTA. She is unconscious and has swelling around her cervical spine. What is the first step in management?
explanation:
• In any seriously injured patient, we must follow the ATLS protocol
  • Advance trauma life support (ATLS) is a periodically updated, evidence-based training course for physicians and surgeons who are involved in care of trauma patients. Concept behind ATLS is that save the life by addressing the most dangerous threat to life first.
  • Patients are rapidly assessed on the basis of 'ABCDE' resuscitation system
    • Airway control with stabilization of the cervical spine.
    • Breathing assessment-management of respiratory distress.
    • Circulation-assessment of shock and management of external hemorrhage.
    • Disability or neurological status-management of head injury.
    • Exposure or undressing of the patient.
  • In this case, as the patient has swelling in the cervical spine, we presume an injury there. So before doing any maneuvers for securing the airway or intubating the patient, we must apply a Philadelphia collar. If we donot do that, we may aggravate a cervical spine injury and cause quadriparesis/ quadriplegia.

Reference- Fundamentals of Orthopedics Mohindra and Jain, page no 41

question_text: In tuberculosis of spine, which one of the following is not a cause for Paraplegia?
option_a: Stretching of spinal cord in gibbus deformity
explanation:
Pott's paraplegia occurs because of pressure on the neural tissues within the canal by products from the diseased vertebrae. It could occur in the following ways:

  • Inflammatory oedema: The neural tissues become oedematous because of vascular stasis in the adjacent diseased area.
  • Extradural pus and granulation tissue: This is the commonest cause of compression on neuralstructures. The abscess formed around the diseased vertebrae may compress the neural structures from the front, much the same way as an extradural tumour.
  • Sequestra: Devascularised bone and extruded disc material may be displaced into the canal.
  • Internal 'gibbus': Angulation of the diseased spine may lead to formation of the bony ridge on the anterior wall of the spinal canal(Fig-23.10). This is called the internal gibbus
  • Infarction of the spinal cord: This is an unusual but important cause of paralysis. It results from blockage of the anterior spinal artery, caused by the inflammatory reaction.
  • Extradural granuloma: Very rarely, an extradural granuloma may form without any damage to the osseous structures. Such a patient presents with a clinical picture of a spinal tumour - the so-called 'Spinal tumour syndrome'.

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 7th edition, Page no. 190.

question_text: A 65 year old female presented to the OPD with complaints of back pain for the last 2 years. X-ray of her lumbar spine is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• X-ray shows codfish/biconcave vertebra which is seen in osteoporosis.
  • Osteoporosis is a condition characterized by reduction in bone mineral density. Here all the biochemical parameters will be normal only the quantity of bone tissue diminishes throughout the body.
  • Loss of bone mass leads to loss of strength so that a trivial trauma is sufficient to cause a fracture.
  • Dorso-lumbar spine is the most frequent site or pathological fracture in osteoporosis.

RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES

Radiological evidence of decreased bone mass is more reliable, but about 30 per cent of the bone mass must be lost before it becomes apparent on X-rays. Following features may be noticed on X-rays:

  • Loss of vertical height of a vertebra due to collapse.
  • Cod fish appearance: The disc bulges into the adjacent vertebral bodies so that the disc becomes biconvex.

question_text: Which of the following is the most commonly injured tarsal bone?
explanation:
• Calcaneum is the most commonly fractured tarsal bone
  • In 5-10% of cases fracture is bilateral
  • Most common mechanism of injury is fall from height, often from a ladder, onto one or both heels. The calcaneum is driven up against the talus and is split or crushed. About one fifth of these patients suffer associated injuries of the spine, pelvis or hip.
  • Calcaneal fracture is also known as 'lover fracture'
  • Plain x-rays done for calcaneal fracture include lateral, oblique and axial views. Axial view of calcaneum is also called Haris view.
  • CT is the investigation of choice
  • With severe injuries and especially with bilateral fractures - it is essential to take x-rays of the knees, the spine and the pelvis. Many cases of fractures of the calcaneum are associated with a compression fracture of a vertebral body (usually in the dorsolumbar region), fractures of the pubic rami, or an atlanto-axial injury.

question_text: According to the WHO, which investigation is included in the diagnosis of TB spine?
explanation:
Explanation :
CBNAAT/Xpert MTB-RIF is included in WHO diagnostic algorithms for extrapulmonary TB, including spinal TB, because it is a rapid nucleic acid amplification test that detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance in a few hours, guiding early therapy. It has higher sensitivity than smear in paucibacillary disease and is recommended on tissue/aspirate from the suspected vertebral lesion.

Explanation of other options:
X-ray (Option A): Helpful screening (wedging, end-plate erosion, paradiscal involvement), but not sufficient nor specific; radiographs lag behind pathology.
CT scan (Option B): Excellent for bony detail and guiding biopsy but CT alone is not the WHO-included molecular diagnostic.
Culture and sensitivity (Option D): Definitive but slow (weeks); limited yield in paucibacillary disease. WHO still includes Xpert as part of rapid diagnostic work-up.

Key Takeaways:

WHO endorses Xpert MTB/RIF for extrapulmonary TB, including spine.

Imaging suggests diagnosis; microbiologic/molecular tests confirm and detect resistance.

Culture is the gold standard for drug susceptibility but slow.

Diagnosis of Spondylolisthesis

Physical Examination:

  • Visible or palpable 'step' deformity above the sacral crest due to forward displacement of the spinal column.
  • Increased lumbar lordosis may be noted.
  • Sciatic nerve stretch signs, such as a positive straight leg raising test (SLRT), may indicate nerve involvement.

Radiological Examination:

  • X-ray Findings:
    • Lateral view of the spine shows anterior displacement of one vertebra over the other. (Option B)
    • Grading of spondylolisthesis based on severity of vertebral slip:
      • Grade I: Displacement up to 25% of the antero-posterior width of the lower vertebral body.
      • Grade II: Displacement of 26-50%.
      • Grade III: Displacement of 51-75%.
      • Grade IV: Complete forward displacement (100%).
    • Oblique view: (Option C)
      • Helps visualize the pars interarticularis.
      • In a normal vertebra, the pars interarticularis resembles a "Scottish dog".
      • Spondylolysis (defect without vertebral slip):
        • Appears as a "Scottish dog wearing a collar", indicating a defect in the isthmus (pars interarticularis).
      • Spondylolisthesis (defect with vertebral slip):
        • Appears as the "head of the Scottish dog separated from the neck", indicating a defect with slippage of the vertebra.

Option A: X Ray AP view is not of much use in diagnosing spondylolisthesis.

Option B: Lateral view of the spine shows anterior displacement of one vertebra over the other and thus helps in Grading spondylolisthesis.

Option C: Oblique view Helps visualize the pars interarticularis thus giving beheaded Scottish Appearance in spondylolisthesis.

Key takeaways

Interpretation of Lumbosacral Spine Oblique X Ray view:

  1. Normal Vertebra:
    • The pars interarticularis appears as a well-formed "Scottish dog" with no abnormalities.
  2. Spondylolysis (defect without vertebral slip):
    • The "Scottish dog" appears to be "wearing a collar".
    • This indicates a defect in the isthmus (pars interarticularis), but no vertebral displacement.
  3. Spondylolisthesis (defect with vertebral slip):
    • The head of the "Scottish dog" appears separated from the neck.
    • This indicates a defect with slippage of the vertebra.

question_text: A 51-year-old male reports difficulty with urination and numbness in his bilateral buttocks. His symptoms began 12 hours ago. Which of the following statements about his condition is true?

explanation:
• Based on clinical profile patient is having cauda equine syndrome.
  • Cauda equina syndrome(CES) is caused by severe compression of lumbar and sacral nerve roots, occurs in approximately 2% of all patients with LDH.

Symptoms include:

  • Severe bilateral leg pain
  • Numbness in buttocks, back of legs and sole(Saddle anesthesia)
  • Perineal sensory deficit
  • Decreased rectal tone

question_text: A 66-year-old female presents with chronic lower back pain. An oblique lumbar spine X-ray is done and shown below. Based on the radiological findings, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical scenario of chronic lower back pain along with a scottie dog with collar sign on oblique spine x-ray is spondylolysis.

  • Spondylolysis refers to a defect in the pars interarticularis, which may be unilateral or bilateral and can be linked to spondylolisthesis.
  • Spondylolisthesis describes the forward displacement of one vertebra over the one below it, sometimes with angular deformity such as kyphosis.
  • This condition is most often seen at the L5-S1 level, less commonly at L4-L5, but may occur at other lumbar or multiple levels.
  • Spondylolysis likely develops from a stress fracture at the pars interarticularis, with repetitive extension and lateral flexion increasing shear forces.
  • Higher rates are seen in female gymnasts, football linemen, and backpack-carrying soldiers, and it is also associated with Scheuermann kyphosis. Familial clustering suggests possible genetic factors.
  • Congenital abnormalities at the lumbosacral junction, sacrum, or facet joints, as well as spina bifida occulta, may predispose to the condition.
  • Symptoms vary with age and type. Adults usually have low back pain radiating to the buttocks or thighs, sometimes with L5 radiculopathy.
  • Children more often present with gait changes, postural deformity, and hamstring tightness, which may lead to pelvic tilt, short stride length, and difficulty raising the leg when supine.
  • Imaging involves standing PA and lateral radiographs from L3 to the sacrum, with cone-down lateral and spot lateral views best showing pars defects, usually at L5-S1. L4 defects are more common in those with sacralization of L5.
  • The normal spine in oblique view shows the Scottish dog sign, and If plain films are inconclusive in spondylolysis, oblique views may reveal the classic Scotty dog sign with a broken neck or collar sign.
  • Spondylolisthesis refers to the forward slipping of one vertebral segment over the one beneath it and shows the beheaded Scottish terrier sign. (Option B ruled out)

Explanation of other options:

Crush vertebral fracture (Option C): When the vertebral body is crushed in a neutral neck position, it produces a burst fracture. On plain X-ray, burst fractures appear as a crushed vertebral body, as shown below.

Klippel Feil syndrome (Option D): Klippel-Feil syndrome is a generalised disorder marked by bilateral failure of scapular descent, cervical spine anomalies, and occipital bone fusion defects, giving patients an appearance of having no neck. It is characterised by a low hairline, bilateral neck webbing, and severely restricted neck movement, and can be differentiated from bilateral sternomastoid muscle shortening by the absence of associated congenital anomalies.

question_text: A 30-year-old individual presents with restricted hip mobility along with hip pain and discomfort. Which test is used to detect a flexion deformity of the hip?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Thomas test evaluates hip flexion contracture by assessing hip extension, where elevation of the opposite knee from the table indicates the presence of a contracture.


Explanation of other options:

Telescopy (Option C): Telescopy is used to assess hip instability by rotating the patient's leg in a circular motion, during which abnormal movement of the hip joint is noted, along with visible and palpable displacement of the greater trochanter.

Lasegue test (Option B): The Lasegue test is used to detect lumbar radiculopathy or sciatica by raising the patient's straightened leg while they lie flat, with the onset of pain suggesting nerve root compression.

McMurray test (Option D): The McMurray test is performed to evaluate meniscal tears in the knee by flexing, rotating, and extending the joint, where pain or a palpable "click" indicates a possible tear.

Thomas test:-

Kanavel's Signs in Suppurative Tenosynovitis

Suppurative tenosynovitis is an infection of the flexor tendon sheath of the fingers. (Option B) Kanavel's signs are a set of clinical features used to diagnose this condition. They are indicative of infection within the tendon sheath and require prompt medical attention. The key signs given above in image

Management:

  • Emergency Treatment:
    • Intravenous (IV) Antibiotics:
      • Immediate administration of IV antibiotics is essential to combat the infection. The choice of antibiotic may be guided by the suspected or confirmed pathogen and its antibiotic sensitivity.
    • Debridement and Washout:
      • In cases where the infection is severe or if there is a collection of pus, surgical intervention may be required. This involves debridement (removal of infected tissue) and washout (irrigation) of the tendon sheath to clear the infection and prevent further tissue damage.

Option C - Durkan's test is the most specific test for carpal tunnel syndrome.

Option D - Piano key sign is for DRUJ instability. (distal radio ulnar joint instability)

Key takeaway:

Kanavel's signs which is typically seen in suppurative tenosynovitis of fingers includes following features

  • The finger is swollen (fusiform) throughout its length
  • Acutely tender over the flexor tendon sheath
  • Finger is held in semi-flexed position, and
  • Active or passive extension at the interphalangeal joint is painful.

question_text: A child with a history of recurrent respiratory infections presented with complaints of pain around the knee along with high fever. X -ray shows lytic and sclerotic bone. His peripheral blood smear is shown in the image below. The organism most likely involved is?
explanation:
Explanation

  • The peripheral smear shows features of sickle cell anemia, such as sickled red cells.
  • In children with sickle cell disease, osteomyelitis is common due to bone infarction and poor splenic function.
  • Salmonella is the most frequent cause of osteomyelitis in these patients, particularly involving the diaphysis of long bones.
  • This differs from the general population, where Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism.

Osteomyelitis: Important Associations

  • Most common overall in adults and children: Staphylococcus aureus (Option A).
  • In HIV patients: MRSA
  • In intravenous drug users: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is common.
  • In sickle cell anemia: Salmonella species (Option C).
  • In children aged 1-4 years: Haemophilus influenzae.
  • Following an upper respiratory tract infection in children: Kingella kingae.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Staphylococcus aureus (Option A): This is the most common organism in the general population for both acute and chronic osteomyelitis, but in sickle cell patients, Salmonella is more characteristic.

Escherichia coli (Option B): Typically associated with urinary tract infections and gastroenteritis, not bone infections.

Streptococcus (Option D): Can cause skin, throat, or lung infections but is less common as a cause of osteomyelitis compared to Salmonella in sickle cell disease.

Key Takeaway:

In patients with sickle cell anemia presenting with osteomyelitis, the most likely causative agent is Salmonella, whereas Staphylococcus aureus remains the most common cause in the general population.

question_text:
The pathognomonic sign of chronic OM is persistent discharging sinus. Identify the suitable cause for this feature of this condition. (multiple correct options)
A. Resistance to antibiotics
B. Inadequate follow up and treatment
C. Sequestrum
D. Reduced blood supply in affected bone
explanation:
Pathology of Osteomyelitis

Progression from Acute to Chronic Osteomyelitis

Acute osteomyelitis commonly progresses to chronic osteomyelitis due to several factors:

  1. Delayed and Inadequate Treatment (Option B)
    • Cause: Delay in treatment allows pus to spread within the medullary cavity and subperiosteally.
    • Consequences:
      • Death of bone tissue, leading to sequestrum formation. (Option C)
      • Destruction of cancellous bone creates cavities within the bone.
      • Persistent infection due to "non-collapsing" bone cavities and sequestra.
  2. Type and Virulence of Organism
    • Cause: Highly virulent organisms may not be controlled even with early and adequate treatment.
    • Consequences:
      • Persistent infection despite effective initial treatment.
  3. Reduced Host Resistance
    • Cause: Malnutrition or compromised defense mechanisms.
    • Consequences:
      • Persistent infection due to weakened body defenses.

Key takeaways:

Acute osteomyelitis commonly progresses to chronic osteomyelitis due to

  • Delayed and inadequate treatment
  • Type and virulence of organism
  • Reduced host resistance

Option A and D: they are not directly related to chronic pus discharge.

question_text: A child from a small village of Bihar has long bone pain, is weak and lethargic and on examination he has bow legs. The X-ray reports shows increase in bone density, osteophytes and dismorphic joint space. Possible diagnosis:
explanation:
• Hint in the question is child from a village of Bihar with Genu varum/bow legged, long bone pain and X-Rays showing increased bone density, this characteristically focuses towards Fluorosis.
  • Fluorine in very low concentration- 1 part per million (ppm) or less is used to reduce the incidence of dental caries. At slightly higher levels (2–4 ppm) it may produce mottling of teeth.
  • In some parts of India and Africa, where fluorine concentration in the drinking water may be above 10 ppm- chronic fluorine intoxication (fluorosis) is endemic and results in skeletal anomalies.
  • Characteristic pathological feature is subperiosteal new bone accretion and osteosclerosis (increased bone density), most marked in vertebrae, ribs, pelvis, forearm and leg bones, together with hyperostosis at the bony attachments of ligaments, tendons and fascia.
  • Despite the apparent thickening and density of skeleton, tensile strength is reduced and the bones fracture more easily.
  • First clinical manifestation is usually a stress fracture, back pain, bone pain, joint stiffness and neurological defects (due to hyperostosis encroaching vertebral canal).
  • Characteristic X-ray features are osteosclerosis, osteophytosis and ossification of ligamentous and fascial attachments. It can be radiologically mistaken for other osteosclerotic conditions as Paget’s disease, osteopetrosis, renal osteodystrophy, idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis etc.
  • Note: Fluorine stimulates osteoblastic activity; fluoroapatite crystals are laid down in bone and these are usually resistant to osteoclastic resorption. This leads to calcium retention impaired mineralization and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Reference: Maheshwari, 5th ed. pg. 314

question_text: Felon means infection of:
explanation:
Felons/Whitlow are closed-space infections of the fingertip pulp. Infection occurring within these compartments can lead to abscess formation, edema and rapid development of increased pressure in a closed space. This increased pressure may compromise blood flow and lead to necrosis of the skin and pulp.

Clinical feature: Felons are characterized by marked throbbing pain, tension and edema of the fingertip pulp.

Causes: Staphylococcus aureus, is the most common cause.

Management: The felon should be incised in the area of maximum tenderness. The incision should not cross the distal interphalangeal(DIP) joint to prevent formation of a flexion contracture at the DIP flexion crease. Probing is not carried out proximally to avoid extension of infection into the flexor tendon sheath.

Complication of felon: Osteomyelitis > Tenosynovitis

question_text: All are true about chronic osteomyelitis except -
option_b: Cloaca is an opening in involucrum
explanation:
Pathology in chronic osteomyelitis

  • Chronic osteomyelitis occurs most commonly in long bones.
  • Bone is destroyed or devitalized in the affected part. Cavities containing pus and pieces of dead bone(sequestra) are surrounded by vascular tissue and beyond that by areas of sclerosis due to reaction new bone formation, which may take the form of a distinct bony sheath(involucrum).
  • Often sinus track leads to the skin surface; the sinus tends to heal and present down recurrently, but if a sequestrum is present it never heals permanently.
  • This is because sequestra act as substrate for bacterial adhesion in much the same way as foreign implants, ensuring the persistence of infection until they are removed or discharged through perforations in the involucrum and sinuses that drain to the skin.

Sequestrum

  • Sequestrum is a piece of dead bone, surrounded by infected granulation tissue trying to eat the sequestrum away.
  • The sequestrum is hard, rough, porus, light in weight and lighter in colour than normal. Normal pattern of bone is lost. (Note: Sequestrum in syphilis and TB is heavier than normal bone because sclerosis usually precedes the death of the bone)
  • On x-ray, sequestra show up as unnatural dense fragments, in contrast to the surrounding osteopenic bone.

Involucrum

  • Involucrum is reactive new bone overlying a sequestrum.
  • There may be some holes in the involucrum for pus to drain out. These holes are called cloaca.

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 172

question_text: Rickets is associated with
explanation:
• Two important terminologies in association with rickets are osteoid maturation time and mineral apposition rate.
  • Osteoid maturation time - rate at which osteoid matures into osteon.
  • Mineral apposition rate - rate at which minerals are deposited on the osteon so that it matures into an osteoid.
  • Maturation is the process by which osteoid (which is the organic part of bone) is transformed into osteon (which is the basic structural unit of bone). Osteoid maturation takes place by deposition of minerals on it. In rickets, the minerals are deficient, hence the process of maturation is slowed down.
  • This means that the mineral apposition rate decreases and the osteoid maturation time increases.

question_text: A 13 yr old boy presents with pain and swelling in the mid thigh region with no history of trauma or fever. Xray shows cortical destruction with new bone formation in layers in the diaphysis of femur bone as seen in the image below. Probable diagnosis would be:
explanation:
Ewing's Sarcoma

  • Description:
    • A type of bone tumor that primarily affects the diaphysis (the mid-shaft) of long bones.
  • Common Location:
    • Most frequently occurs in the femur.
  • Age Group:
    • Predominantly affects adolescents.
  • Radiological Features:
    • X-ray Appearance:
      • Lytic Lesion: Characterized by a destructive area in the medullary zone of the midshaft of the long bone.
      • Cortical Destruction: The tumor often leads to the breakdown of the cortical bone.
      • New Bone Formation: Observable as layers of new bone growth.
      • Onion-Peel Appearance: The layered new bone formation gives a distinctive appearance resembling an onion skin.
  • Biopsy - The tumour has sheets of round cells resembling lymphocytes. Often, the tumor cells surround a central clear area, forming a pseudo-rosette
  • .Treatment - Highly radio-sensitive tumor
    • Local Tumor Control: Radiotherapy (6000 rads).
    • Metastasis Control: Chemotherapy.
  • Prognosis - It is very poor. Bone to bone secondaries are very common. With the availability of potent chemotherapeutic drugs, 5-year survival has now improved to 30-40 % from 10 % before.

Option B - Osteosarcoma commonly occurs in the metaphysis of long bones.

Option C - Absence of fever and trauma rules out OM

Option D: Non Applicable.

Key Takeaway-

Ewing sarcoma which mimics Acute Osteomyelitis clinically. Xray shows cortical destruction with new bone formation in layers in the diaphysis of femur bone.

question_text: Which of the following organisms is very rarely involved in chronic osteomyelitis?

question_text: A child presents with growth failure. Biochemical analysis shows normal Ca2+, normal PTH, reduced phosphate, and increased ALP. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Hypophosphatemic rickets presents with low phosphate, elevated ALP, and normal calcium and PTH, due to defective renal phosphate reabsorption.

  • Hypophosphatemic rickets (especially X-linked) is the most common hereditary cause of rickets.
  • It results from renal phosphate wasting despite normal vitamin D and calcium levels.
  • In these patients:
    • Serum phosphate is low due to proximal renal tubular phosphate loss.
    • Calcium remains normal because intestinal absorption is preserved.
    • PTH is normal or mildly elevated, unlike in nutritional rickets.
    • ALP is elevated due to increased osteoblastic activity during defective bone mineralization.
  • The child presents with growth failure, a key clinical feature.
  • Radiographic features of rickets such as metaphyseal fraying, cupping, and splaying are usually seen.

Explanation of other options:

Nutritional rickets (Option A): PTH is elevated, and calcium is often low or low-normal due to vitamin D deficiency. Also, 25(OH)D is decreased.

Type 1 VDDR (Option C): Caused by 1-alpha hydroxylase deficiency, leading to low 1,25(OH)2D, low calcium and phosphate, elevated PTH, and ALP. It does not show normal calcium and PTH.

Type 2 VDDR (Option D): Due to end-organ resistance to 1,25(OH)2D. Despite normal or elevated 1,25(OH)2D, calcium and phosphate are low, PTH is elevated, and ALP is raised.

question_text: Identify the most commonly affected region of the hip joint in tuberculosis.
explanation:
Explanation:

The most commonly affected area in hip tuberculosis is the acetabulum, marked as ‘3’ in the image.

  • Skeletal TB accounts for 10–20% of all TB cases.
  • The spine is the most commonly affected skeletal site (30–50%), particularly the thoracolumbar region.
  • Infection typically spreading from the anterior vertebral body through subligamentous burrowing to adjacent vertebrae.
  • In the appendicular skeleton, major weight-bearing joints are usually involved, most commonly the hip and knee, followed by the ankle, foot, and upper extremity joints.
  • The hip is the most frequently affected large joint, with the acetabulum (subchondral region) being the most commonly involved part.
  • Tuberculosis in the hip affects weight-bearing areas, leading to articular cartilage destruction, subchondral bone involvement, and progressive joint degeneration.

question_text: Tuberculosis of spine - All of these statements are true except:
option_c: Paradiscal is the commonest type  of vertebral TB
option_d: TB spine is always secondary and occurs due to hematogenous spread
explanation:
Kyphosis is commonly seen in later stages of TB spine and not scoliosis.

Types of Vertebral Tuberculosis

  1. Paradiscal:
    • Description: Most common type.
    • Affected Areas: Contiguous areas of two adjacent vertebrae and the intervening disc.
  2. Central:
    • Description: Affects the body of a single vertebra.
    • Impact: Leads to early collapse of the weakened vertebra; nearby disc may remain normal.
    • Collapse Types:
      • Wedging: More common.
      • Concertina: Less common.
  3. Anterior:
    • Description: Infection is localized to the anterior part of the vertebral body.
    • Spread: Moves up and down under the anterior longitudinal ligament.
  4. Posterior:
    • Description: Affects the posterior complex of the vertebra.
    • Affected Areas: Pedicle, lamina, spinous process, and transverse process.

Option A: In late stages, a significant part or whole of the vertebral body may be destroyed, leading to angular kyphotic deformity. (Option A)

Option B: TB spine patients can develop a psoas abscess. As it tracks down the inguinal canal it causes flexion deformity of the hip. As this deformity is not due to hip pathology but due to spine pathology, it is called pseudo flexion deformity of the hip.

Option C: Paradiscal: This is the commonest type. In this, the contiguous areas of two adjacent vertebrae along with the intervening disc are affected.

Option D: TB of the spine is always secondary. The bacteria reach the spine via the haematogenous route, from the lungs or lymph nodes.

Key takeaways:

TB Spine:

  • Secondary via hematogenous route
  • Mc Paradiscal
  • Causes Pseudo Flexion deformities of hip
  • Causes Kyphosis in later stages.
