question_text: A 35 yr gentleman sustained a humerus mid-shaft fracture following an RTA. All of these treatment modalities can be used to treat this fracture except:
explanation:
Screws and k wires alone will not give adequate stability to a long bone like humerus and may lead to non union/ mal union. So it's an incorrect option.

Humerus Fracture Management:

  • Conservative methods
    1. U-slab: (Option A)
      • A plaster slab extending from the base of the neck over the shoulder to the lateral side of the arm and under the elbow to the medial side.
      • Removed after 6-8 weeks once the fracture heals, followed by shoulder exercises.
    2. Hanging Cast
      • Used for lower-third humerus fractures.
      • The weight of the limb and cast provides traction to keep the fracture aligned.
    3. Chest-Arm Bandage
      • Used for humerus fractures in children under five.
      • The arm is strapped to the chest, providing sufficient immobilization.
    4. Functional (Sarmiento) Brace
      • Used for closed humerus fractures that can be managed without surgery.

Operative Methods

Required when closed reduction is not possible or the fracture is unstable. 

  1. ORIF with plates and screws
    • Usually gives high union rates.
    • Allows exploration of radial nerves as well.
    • Weight-bearing tolerance is safe after plate fixation.
  2. CRIF with intramedullary nailing (Option B)
    • Mostly used for segmental or pathologic fractures.
    • Complications include a higher rate of reoperation and shoulder pain.
    • Higher chances of nerve injury as compared to ORIF.
  3. External fixators(Option D)
    • Usually reserved for open/contaminated fractures.

Option C: Screws and k wires alone will not give adequate stability to a long bone like humerus and may lead to non union/ mal union. So it's an incorrect option.

Key takeaways:

Most preferred method of surgical management of humerus shaft fractures is through plate and screws as it gives high rates of union and allows exploration of radial nerves.

Other methods include

  • U Slab / hanging cast for conservative management
  • IM nailing
  • External fixators (in polytrauma, contaminated/infected fractures)

question_text: Which part of the meniscus has the least vascularity?
explanation:
• White white zone of the meniscus has the least vascularity.
  • The blood supply to the meniscus is derived from the peri-capsular capillary plexus situated at the menisco-capsular junction. The blood vessels from this plexus will enter the meniscus at the periphery and proceed towards the center. However these blood vessels will reach roughly till the middle of the meniscus and stops. This means that the peripheral 1/3rd of the meniscus has good blood supply, the middle 1/3rd has less blood supply and the inner 1/3rd has no blood supply at all and is dependent on the synovial fluid for nutrition.
  • Based on this the meniscus is divided into 3 zones.
    • Red red zone - peripheral 1/3rd of the meniscus
    • Red white zone - middle 1/3rd of the meniscus
    • White white zone - inner 1/3rd of the meniscus

Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 739

Treatment of SCH Fractures in children

1. Undisplaced Fractures

  • Immobilization:
    • Use an above-elbow plaster slab. (Option B)
    • Position the elbow in 90° flexion.

2. Displaced Fractures

  • Treatment Methods:
    • a) Closed Reduction and Percutaneous K-Wire Fixation: (Option C)
      • Procedure:
        • Displaced fractures are usually reduced by closed reduction.
        • To prevent slippage, fixation with one or two K-wires is performed.
        • K-wires are inserted percutaneously under image intensifier guidance.
      • Alternative:
        • If an image intensifier is unavailable, careful monitoring of the fracture position in plaster is essential.
      • b) Open Reduction and K-Wire Fixation: (Option D)
        • Indications:
          • When closed methods fail to achieve or maintain proper positioning.
          • If the fracture displaced after reduction.
          • Used as a first-line treatment for some open fractures.
          • Necessary for exploration of the brachial artery if there is suspected injury.
        • Procedure:
          • Involves surgical intervention to directly visualize and correct the fracture.
          • K-wires are used for fixation to stabilize the fracture.
          • Refer to Figure 14.9 for illustrative details.
        • c) Continuous Traction:
          • Indications:
            • Employed in cases with late presentation involving excessive swelling or severe wounds around the elbow.
          • Purpose:
            • To manage and stabilize the fracture while addressing complications associated with swelling or wound issues.

Option B, C & D: Closed reduction and cast application, Closed reduction and pinning and Open reduction and pinning all three are management options for SCH Fractures.

Key takeaways

  • Gartland classification is used to classify SCH fractures in children
  • Classical clinical sign is S sign of the arm and elbow
  • Most common injury in children following fall on an out-stretched hand is SCH fractures.
  • If undergoes mal-union; SCH fractures can cause gun stock deformity.

question_text: A classical clinical sign of grossly displaced supracondylar humerus fractures in children is:
explanation:
In type III SCH fractures, gross displacement of the elbow is evident leading to S shaped deformity as seen in the image.

Pathoanatomy of Supracondylar Humerus Fracture

  • Location: Transverse fracture line through the distal metaphysis of the humerus, just above the condyles.

Types:

  1. Extension Type:
    • Description: The distal fragment is tilted backwards (extended) in relation to the proximal fragment.
    • Prevalence: More common of the two types.
  2. Flexion Type:
    • Description: The distal fragment is tilted forwards (flexed) in relation to the proximal fragment.
    • Prevalence: Less common.

Displacements:

  • Posterior or Backward Shift: Distal fragment shifts posteriorly.
  • Posterior or Backward Tilt: Distal fragment tilts backwards.
  • Proximal Shift: Distal fragment moves proximally.
  • Medial or Lateral Shift: Distal fragment shifts medially or laterally.
  • Medial Tilt: Distal fragment tilts medially.
  • Internal Rotation: Distal fragment rotates internally.
  • Option A, B & C: The S-shaped configuration is created by the anterior prominence of the proximal fragment's spike and extension of the distal fragment. It's not C, U or J Shaped so Option A, B & C are wrong.

Key takeaway:

  • In type III SCH fractures, gross displacement of the elbow is evident leading to S shaped deformity.
  • Deformity in malunited SCH fractures is called gun stock deformity.

  3. Duration: Long standing paraplegia has a worse prognosis.

explanation:
In SH type II fractures the epiphyseal fragment thus comprises all of the epiphysis and some portion of the peripheral metaphysis (the Thurston-Holland fragment or sign).


Salter-Harris Classification of Growth Plate Fractures

Salter and Harris classification: Epiphyseal injuries in children have been classified into 5 types based on their X-ray appearance. The higher the classification the more severe the injury.


Salter-Harris Classification Types:

  1. Type I (Slip)
    • Description: A fracture that occurs straight across the growth plate (physis) without involving the metaphysis or epiphysis.
    • Characteristics: The physis is separated or slipped, but the surrounding bone remains intact.
    • Prognosis: Generally, a good prognosis with proper treatment, as the growth plate remains largely undamaged.
  2. Type II (Above) (Option B,C)
    • Description: A fracture through the growth plate and metaphysis, sparing the epiphysis.
    • Characteristics: The most common type, it extends across the physis and into the metaphysis, creating a triangular fragment of the metaphysis.
    • Prognosis: Good, as the growth plate is still relatively unharmed; usually does not result in growth disturbances.
  3. Type III (Lower) (Option A,D)
    • Description: A fracture through the growth plate and epiphysis, sparing the metaphysis.
    • Characteristics: The fracture extends from the physis into the articular surface of the bone.
    • Prognosis: Can affect growth and joint function if not properly treated, as it involves the articular cartilage and growth plate.
  4. Type IV (Through)
    • Description: A fracture through the metaphysis, growth plate, and epiphysis.
    • Characteristics: The fracture passes vertically through all three elements, potentially damaging the growth plate and joint surface.
    • Prognosis: Risk of growth disturbance and joint dysfunction is higher; requires precise anatomical reduction to prevent complications.
  5. Type V (Rammed)
    • Description: A compression fracture of the growth plate.
    • Characteristics: The growth plate is crushed or compressed, often leading to growth arrest.
    • Prognosis: Poor, due to the significant damage to the growth plate; high risk of growth arrest and deformity.

Option A, C & D:

In Children SH type II fractures the epiphyseal fragment thus comprises all of the epiphysis and some portion of the peripheral metaphysis (the Thurston–Holland fragment or sign). Thus Option A, C & D Are wrong.

Key takeaways:

  1. In SH type II fractures the epiphyseal fragment thus comprises all of the epiphysis and some portion of the peripheral metaphysis (the Thurston-Holland fragment or sign).
  2. Mnemonic - SALTe R and its example

Slip (Type I) -SCFE

Above (Type II)-supracondylar humerus #

Through (Type IV)-lateral condylar humerus#

question_text: An 11 yr old boy presents with grossly displaced SCH fracture and absent pulse or perfusion in the emergency room. Gentle traction for sometime followed by CRIF using pins in the operating room restores the perfusion but the pulse is still absent (pulseless perfused hand). What will be the next step?
option_b: Exploration and vascular repair by vascular surgeon
explanation:
The management plan for pulseless SCH fractures is as follows


Management of Pulseless Supracondylar Humerus Fracture (SCH Fx)

1. Assessment and Admission:

  • Initial Step: Admit the patient and closely observe the condition of the limb. In the Emergency Department (ED), gentle traction and flexing the elbow to 30-45 degrees are applied to stabilize the fracture initially.
  • Apply plaster if undisplaced or pin in OR if displaced

2. Evaluation of Perfusion and Pulses:

  • Well Perfused with Good Pulse:
    • Management: Continue monitoring and assess for any changes. No immediate intervention is required if the pulse is strong and the limb is well-perfused.
  • Well Perfused with No Pulse:
    • Management: Although the limb is well-perfused, the absence of a pulse requires further evaluation. Admit the patient and do continuous pulse and perfusion monitoring.
  • Poorly Perfused with No Pulse:
    • Management: Immediate action is required. Please consult with a vascular specialist to assess for any potential vascular injuries and explore their presence. Do ORIF for fracture and vascular repair if necessary.

Option B: Exploration and vascular repair by vascular surgeon is done if Poor perfusion symptoms develop in pulseless syndrome.

Option C: Re-apply traction and CRIF again is not required. Observation and further evaluation of pulse is the next step in management.

Option D: Re-apply traction and ORIF Is done in poor perfusion patients.

Key takeaways:

Pulseless Supracondylar Humerus Fracture is managed with Observation & Evaluation. If Poor Perfusion symptoms develop immediate action and Consulting Vascular surgeon required.

question_text: A 6 year old child presents to he casualty with a type III supracondylar fracture of humerus. His radial and ulnar pulses are not palpable. His hand is pink and capillary filling is adequate. Next line of management
option_c: Arteriogram of Brachial A and proceed as per findings
option_d: Closed reduction of the fracture, slab application and monitoring for reappearance of pulse
explanation:
• In type III supracondylar fracture of humerus, very often the fracture fragment will press against the Brachial A and cause it to undergo spasm. This will cause the loss of Radial and Ulnar pulses.
  • However thankfully most of the time the collateral circulation around the elbow becomes active and maintains the perfusion of the limb. Hence, the capillary filling will be normal and the limb will be pink in colour.
  • This pink limb in the absence of pulses is called the 'Pink pulseless hand'
  • In such a case, the treatment is to reduce the fracture and put a plaster and keep the limb in elevation. Then the child is monitored for adequate capillary filling and return of pulses. Most of the time, when the fracture is reduced, the pressure on the Brachial A stops and the spasm get relieved causing the pulses to return. This usually happens within a few hours.
  • If there is no return of pulse even after 6 hours, then surgery needs to be done.

Reference: Rockwood and Wilkin's Fractures in Children's 8th edition, page no. 609.

question_text: A 1 yr child who just completed Ponseti's cast treatment for CTEV has been advised to wear CTEV orthotic shoes for maintenance of correction. All of these are characteristics of orthotic CTEV shoes except:
explanation:
Option D - Medial arch support is used for treating flat feet.

Methods for Maintaining CTEV Correction

Once the correction of Congenital Talipes Equinovarus (CTEV) is achieved, it's crucial to maintain that correction to prevent relapse. Here are the common methods used:

CTEV shoes: These are modified shoes, used once a child starts walking.

  • Before Walking: The splint is worn throughout the day to maintain the correction.
  • After Walking Begins: Once the child starts walking, the DB splint is worn at night while CTEV shoes are used during the day.
  • CTEV Shoes

CTEV shoes are specialized footwear introduced when the child begins to walk. These shoes are modified to maintain the correct foot alignment with the following features:

These shoes are typically worn until the child reaches 5 years of age, providing ongoing support during crucial developmental years.

  • Option A - Outer Shoe Raise: Helps prevent foot inversion.
  • Option B - Straight Inner Border: Prevents forefoot adduction by ensuring the foot remains in proper alignment.
  • Option C - No Heel: Avoids the recurrence of equinus by keeping the foot flat.
  • Option D - Medial arch support is used for treating flat feet.

Key Takeaway -

The following modifications are made in the CTEV shoe which are used until the child is 5 years old:

  • Straight Inner Border: Prevents forefoot adduction by ensuring the foot remains in proper alignment.
  • Outer Shoe Raise: Helps prevent foot inversion.
  • No Heel: Avoids the recurrence of equinus by keeping the foot flat.

question_text: Select the false statement in view of Kite's and Ponseti's method of correction of CTEV:
option_a: Order of correction in Ponseti's method is - cavus, adductus, varus, equinus
option_b: Total duration of treatment by Kite's method is 5-6 weeks
option_c: Kite method is rarely used because of the inability of others to match his results
option_d: Casts are changed every week in Ponseti technique
explanation:
Clubfoot Treatment Methods

Kite Method:

  • Principle: Forefoot should be slightly overcorrected into a mild flatfoot position before correcting equinus.
  • Historical Context: Kite's method was once popular but is now rarely used due to:
    • Inconsistent Results: Difficulty replicating Kite's results. (Option C)
    • Lengthy Treatment: Requires 26 to 49 weeks of casting. (Option B)
  • Current Status:Outdated due to the success of more modern methods.

Ponseti's Philosophy of Clubfoot Treatment

Understanding Pathoanatomy:

  • Key Insight: The deformity involves internal rotation (adduction) of the calcaneo-cuboid-navicular complex beneath the plantarflexed talus.
  • Correction Approach:
    • Manual Correction: Apply thumb pressure over the talar head, not the calcaneo-cuboid joint.
    • Objective: Externally rotate the calcaneo-cuboid-navicular complex under the talar head by stretching tight structures.

Treatment Protocol:

  1. Initiation:
    • Timing: Begin treatment within the 1st week of life.
  2. Deformity Correction Sequence: (Option A)
    • Cavus: Correct first.
    • Adduction: Address next.
    • Varus: Correct after adduction.
    • Equinus: Correct last.
  3. Casting:
    • Procedure: After each manipulation, apply an above-knee plaster of Paris (POP) cast.
    • Frequency: Change casts every 5-7 days with total duration being 5-6 weeks. (Option D)
    • Duration: Typically, all components of the deformity are corrected within 6 weeks.
  4. Residual Equinus:
    • Treatment: Often remains undercorrected.
    • Management: Treat with percutaneous tenotomy of the tendoachilles.
    • Outcome: The cut tendoachilles regenerates spontaneously.

Option A, C & D: All three are correct statements.

Option B: Total duration of treatment by Kite's method is 24-48 weeks thus option b is false.

Key takeaways:

Order of correction in CTEV - Mnemonic - CAVE:

  • C: Cavus
  • A: Adductus
  • V: Varus
  • E: Equinus

question_text: Identify the surgery shown in the image that is used to treat CTEV.
explanation:
1. Postero-medial Soft Tissue Release (PMSTR)
This procedure involves releasing tight soft tissues on the posterior and medial sides of the foot. It is typically performed on younger children under the age of 3. In older children, additional bony procedures may be needed.

2. Limited Soft Tissue Release

Specific releases are done based on the component of the deformity:

  • Posterior release for equinus
  • Medial release for adduction
  • Plantar release for cavus
    This approach is used when the foot is partially corrected after conservative treatment.

3. Tendon Transfers

The tibialis anterior is transferred to the outer side of the foot to counteract the weak peroneal muscles. This method is suitable for children over 5 years of age.

4. Dwyer's Osteotomy (Option B)

An open-wedge osteotomy of the calcaneum is performed to correct heel varus. It is generally carried out in children aged 3 years and older.

5. Dilwyn Evans Procedure (Option A)

This technique combines soft tissue release with calcaneo-cuboid fusion to correct neglected or recurrent clubfoot. It is recommended for children aged 4-8 years.

6. Wedge Tarsectomy (Option C)

A wedge of bone is removed from the mid-tarsal area to correct the deformity. This procedure is usually performed on children aged 8-11 years with neglected clubfeet.

7. Triple Arthrodesis (Option D)

Fusion of the subtalar, calcaneo-cuboid, and talo-navicular joints is performed, typically in children over 12 years of age. This procedure addresses deformities when the bones have matured.

8. Ilizarov's Technique

Utilizes an external fixator for gradual correction of deformities, which is maintained with plaster casts. This method is applied for neglected or recurrent clubfeet.

9. JESS Fixation

A simplified technique based on Ilizarov's principles, developed by Dr. B.B. Joshi. It is used for similar indications as Ilizarov's technique.

Key takeaways:

Dwyer's osteotomy: This is an open-wedge osteotomy of the calcaneus, performed in order to correct varus of the heel. Minimum age at which this operation can be performed is 3 years, as prior to this the calcaneum is mainly cartilaginous. Some prefer a closed-wedge osteotomy on the lateral side.

question_text: You visit a new born near your house & identify that the child has CTEV. When will you advice the baby's parents to seek consult to put a cast?
explanation:
• Ideally, the treatment of a child with CTEV, should be started as early as possible.
  • In the first 2 weeks of life, the mother is advised to do gentle corrective manipulation of the foot.
  • From 2 weeks onwards the child should be under the care of an orthopaedic surgeon, who will put weekly corrective casts.
  • The technique we currently use for correcting CTEV is the Ponseti technique.

Ponsetti's philosophy:

  • This philosophy is based on better understanding of the pathoanatomy of the deformed foot.
  • Serial manipulation and casting
  • Above knee casts changed every week
  • Order of correction: cavus—> adduction—> varus—> equinus
  • According to Ponsetti, the calcaneo-cuboid-navicular complex is internally rotated (adducted) under the plantarflexed talus,
  • Hence, the deformity can be corrected by bringing the complex back under the talus by gradually stretching the tight structures.
  • This is done by putting thumb pressure over the talus head (and not over calcaneo-cuboid joint as in Kite's method).
  • By doing this, the calcaneocuboid-navicular complex is externally rotated under the talar head.

Maintainable of correction:

Dennis brown splint

  • Foot maintained in abduction and dorsiflexion
  • Full time wearing till 1 year of age
  • Night time wearing till 5 years of age

CTEV shoes: day time wearing from the time starts to walk till 7 years


Features of CTEV shoes:

  • Straight inner border
  • Outer raiser
  • No heel

  • guided by the distance between shoulders and changed with the growth of child. Feet are typically placed in 60–70° of external rotation or in case of unilateral deformity the normal foot is placed in 30–40° of external rotation.
  • The Denis Browne Split utilizes an L-shaped bracket to hold the foot in significant dorsiflexion and is connected to open-toe boots.
  • It is used throughout the day before the child starts walking. Once he starts walking, a DB splint is used at night and CTEV shoes during the day.

question_text: The most common deformity in Rickets is?

The most common deformity in rickets is genu varum followed by genu valgum.

  • Deformities: Deformities of the long bones develop, once the child starts walking. The most common deformity is bilateral genu varum, also called bow legs.

question_text: First deformity corrected in CTEV?

According to Ponseti technique cavus is corrected first. The order of correction is given by the mnemonic - CAVE- Cavus followed by Adductus and varus and equinus is corrected as the last step

Treatment is started within 1st week of life. The cavus aspect of the deformity is corrected first, followed by the adduction, then varus and lastly equinus. After every manipulation, an above-knee POP cast is applied, which is changed every 5-7 days. It is usually possible to correct all components of the deformity within 6 weeks. The equinus deformity often remains undercorrected, and can be treated by percutaneous tenotomy of tendoachilles. The cut tendoachilles regenerates spontaneous

question_text: A 7-year-old child presents with genu varum. An X-ray of the wrist reveals classical radiological findings. Based on the clinical presentation and radiographic features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Rickets is the most likely diagnosis in a 7-year-old with bow legs and wrist X-ray showing cupping and fraying of the metaphysis.
  • Rickets is a disorder caused by vitamin D deficiency, leading to defective mineralization of growing bones in children.
  • Classic radiographic findings include:
    • Cupping, fraying, and widening of the metaphyseal ends (especially at the wrist and knees).
    • Bow legs (genu varum), delayed milestones, rachitic rosary, and frontal bossing may also be present clinically.
    • It typically affects children between 6 months and 2 years but can be seen later if deficiency persists.

Explanation of other options:

Scurvy (Option B): Caused by vitamin C deficiency, scurvy presents with bleeding gums, pseudoparalysis, subperiosteal hemorrhages, and white line of Frankel on X-ray, not cupping and fraying.

Hypophosphatemia (Option C): Hypophosphatemic rickets can show similar signs to nutritional rickets, but the history often includes family history or persistent rickets despite vitamin D therapy. Diagnosis requires lab confirmation of low serum phosphate with normal calcium.

None (Option D): This is incorrect as the classical signs clearly indicate rickets.

Key Takeaways:

Rickets is characterized radiographically by cupping, fraying, and widening of the metaphysis, and clinically by bow legs in children due to vitamin D deficiency.

question_text: A 7 yr old boy presents with mild pain and limping in right hip. He is not able to swing the leg outwards and away from the body while trying to ride a bicycle. MRI reveals signs of early Perthes disease. Select false statements.
option_a: Pain is usually mild but may radiate to anterior thigh/knee
option_b: Limitation of internal rotation and abduction movements
option_c: Xray shows collapse and sclerosis in femur head epiphysis
option_d: Surgical osteotomy should be done in this case
explanation:
Perthes Disease

Demographics

  • Common Age Group: Boys aged 5-10 years.

Clinical Presentation

  • Symptoms:
    • Pain in the hip, often radiating to the knee. (Option A)
    • Limping or hip stiffness.
  • Examination Findings:

      • Limitation of hip abduction.

Radiological Findings

  • Imaging Characteristics:

Treatment

  • Primary Goals:
    • Relieve pain.
    • Restore hip movements.
    • Prevent further deformity of the femoral head.
  • Treatment Methods:
    • Non-Surgical:
      • Use of casts and braces.
      • Offloading with crutches.
    • Surgical:
      • Reserved for patients older than 8 years or in cases with poor prognostic signs. (Option D)
      • Includes osteotomies to correct or prevent further damage.

Option A, C & D: Pain is usually mild but may radiate to anterior thigh/knee, Limitation of internal rotation and abduction movements and Xray shows collapse and sclerosis in femur head epiphysis all three are correct statements.

Key takeaways:

Perthes disease is managed mostly with cast and braces. Surgical management is Reserved for patients older than 8 years or in cases with poor prognostic signs. It Includes osteotomies to correct or prevent further damage.

question_text: A pediatrician refers a child to an orthopedician with probable diagnosis of sprengel's shoulder from his clinical examination. On detailed examination and history, it is confirmed to be sprengel's shoulder. Select the false statement:
option_a: Can be associated with cervical ribs
option_c: Extra bone between scapula and cervical vertebrae is the main culprit
explanation:
Sprengel Deformity

Definition:

  • Sprengel deformity is a congenital condition characterized by the upward elevation of the scapula relative to the thoracic cage.
  • The affected scapula is often hypoplastic (underdeveloped) and misshapen.

Associated Congenital Anomalies:

  • Cervical Ribs: Extra ribs that originate from the cervical vertebrae.
  • Rib Malformations: Structural abnormalities in the ribs.
  • Cervical Vertebrae Anomalies: Includes conditions like Klippel-Feil syndrome, which involves the fusion of cervical vertebrae.

Key Features:

  • In 50% of cases, an omovertebral bone is present:
    • This extra ossicle connects the superior angle of the scapula to the spinous process, lamina, or transverse process of one or more lower cervical vertebrae.
    • The presence of this bone restricts the descent of the scapula.

Option A- Sprengel’s deformity is associated with cervical ribs.

Option B- It is a congenital anomaly and not a developmental disorder.

Option C- Omovertebral bone which is an extra ossicle is the main culprit.

Option D – Presence of extra bone restricts the descent of scapula resulting in upward elevation.

Key Takeaway -

  • Sprengel shoulder is also called undescended scapula, Congenital Condition.
  • Extra ossicle called omovertebral is mostly present
  • Often associated with cervical ribs and other rib malformations.

question_text: A 30 yr individual developed discharging sinus after a chronic treatment for a fracture. His x rays shows sequestrum formation due to chronic osteomyelitis. Identify the cause of chronic OM?
explanation:
The above Image is showing ring sequestrum which is seen in external fixators.

Sequestrum and Involucrum in Bone Infections

Sequestrum

  • Definition: A sequestrum is a piece of dead bone that has become separated from the living bone due to an infection, typically in the context of osteomyelitis.
  • Appearance:
    • The sequestrum appears pale.
    • It has a smooth inner surface and a rough outer surface.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • The outer surface is rough because it is continuously eroded by surrounding infected granulation tissue. This granulation tissue is the body's attempt to "eat away" or remove the dead bone (sequestrum).

Involucrum

  • Definition: An involucrum is the layer of new bone growth that forms around a sequestrum.
  • Characteristics:
    • It is dense and sclerotic, providing a protective layer over the sequestrum.
    • The involucrum may develop holes, known as cloacae, through which pus can drain from the infected site.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • The bony cavities within the involucrum are lined with infected granulation tissue, which continues to be involved in the inflammatory and healing process.

Option A: Tuberculosis Shows Sandy Sequestrum in chronic OM.

Option B: Perthes disease shows Coralliform sequestrum in Chronic OM.

Option C: Amputation stumps shows Crown Sequestrum in Chronic OM.

Key takeaways:

  • Sequestrum is the dead bone. Involucrum is the new bone that forms around the sequestrum
  • Different types of Chronic osteomyelitis show Different Sequestrum.

Option B- It may recover spontaneously as the deposits may disappear and become asymptomatic.

question_text: In congenital Knee dislocation, the knee joint is in which position?
explanation:
• Congenital dislocation of the knee is characterized by forward displacement of the proximal tibia on the femoral condyles, with sever hvperextension of the knee joint.
  • Rx depends on the severity of the knee dislocation, age of patient, and presence of associated deformities. Immediate reduction or serial casting should be tried when the patient is seen early after birth, especially when younger than 2 days. If the patient is seen late and serial casting proves to be unsuccessful, traction in the Bryant position or in a prone position may be used for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by closed reduction. In a recalcitrant case, an arthrogram may be performed with open reduction. Surgical Rx has also been suggested for patients in whom 3 months of casting fails, without reduction of the subluxation or without obtaining 45° of flexion.
  • Surgery involves lengthening of the quadriceps tendon with a V-Y-shaped plasty, enlarging the suprapatellar pouch by anterior capsulotomy, and reducing the dislocation. Operative findings show quadriceps muscle fibrosis; abnormal anterior cruciate ligament; hypoplastic, dislocated patella; and anteriorly dislocated hamstrings and iliotibial band.

Ankylosing Spondylitis (Marie Strumpell Disease)

Overview:

  • Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease primarily affecting the spine and sacroiliac (SI) joints.

    • Technique:
      • With the patient supine, the examiner fully flexes the hip and knee on the affected side.
      • The affected knee is then brought across the chest towards the opposite shoulder.
    • Positive sign: Pain on the affected side, indicating SI joint involvement.

Option A, B & C:

Option D - Lasegue test is used for examination of PIVD/ nerve root compression/ Sciatica.

Key takeaways

  • HLA-B27 is positive in most cases of AS

  • A common congenital deformityof the foot characterized by inward (medial) and downward (plantar) positioning.
  • One of the most frequent congenital malformations, showing varying severity and predictable contractures.
  • Four primary components:

    • Pathophysiology:
      • Deformity primarily involves the tarsal bones, which are fixed in maximal flexion and adduction.
      • Talus: medially deviated.

      • Navicular and cuboid: displaced medially.
    • Associated Conditions:

      • Amniotic band syndrome
      • Spina bifida

Posteromedial soft tissue release (Option B): Soft tissue release used in 1-3 years, not infants.

Triple arthrodesis (Option C): Triple arthrodesis reserved for >10 yrs.

Evan's procedure (Option D): Evans procedure for 3-5 yrs age group.

question_text: Apparent lengthening of the lower limb is seen in which condition?
explanation:
Stages of TB of the Hip

Tuberculosis of the hip is clinically divided into three stages based on its progression.

Stage I: Stage of Synovitis

  • Key Features:
    • Effusion into the joint causes the hip to assume a position of flexion, abduction, and external rotation for maximum joint capacity.
    • Deformities of flexion and abduction are subtle and compensated by pelvic tilt.
    • The affected limb appears longer due to the compensatory pelvic tilt (apparent lengthening), though true limb lengths are equal. (Option B)
  • Clinical Presentation:
    • The limb remains in external rotation.
    • Rarely diagnosed at this early stage.
    • Also called the stage of apparent lengthening.

Stage II: Stage of Arthritis

  • Key Features:
    • Articular cartilage involvement leads to muscle spasms, with the more powerful flexor and adductor muscles overpowering the extensors and abductors.
    • The hip adopts a position of flexion, adduction, and internal rotation.
    • The adduction deformity causes the pelvis to tilt upwards, making the affected limb appear shorter (apparent shortening), though true limb lengths remain equal.
  • Clinical Presentation:
    • Internal rotation is evident.
    • Also referred to as the stage of apparent shortening.

Stage III: Stage of Erosion

  • Key Features:
    • Destruction of the cartilage and erosion of the head of the femur and/or acetabulum.
    • Possible pathological dislocation or subluxation of the hip.
    • The position of the limb remains in flexion, adduction, and internal rotation, but the deformities are exaggerated.
    • There is true shortening of the limb due to actual bone destruction, alongside further apparent shortening caused by the adduction deformity.

Option A and C - Apparent lengthening is not seen in Perthes disease or neglected DDH instead both will have true shortening.

Option D: There is true shortening of the limb due to actual bone destruction, alongside further apparent shortening caused by the adduction deformity.

Key takeaways

There is generally a true shortening in TB of the hip, except in Stage I, in which an apparent lengthening occurs. Limb length discrepancy can occur at this joint not only because of actual shortening of the bones (true length) but also because of the adduction-abduction deformity, which results in pelvic tilt and thus affects the length of the limb (apparent length).

question_text: Which condition is this brace typically used to manage?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows the Pavlik harness brace, which is used in the management of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) in infants.

Developmental dysplasia of hip

  • DDH represents abnormal development or dislocation of the hip due to capsular laxity and mechanical factors.
  • Most common congenital anomaly worldwide.
  • Clinical features inculde limitation of hip abduction, asymmetric thigh folds, shortening of the affected limb, and limping.
  • The risk factors for developmental dysplasia of the hip include:
    • Firstborn child
    • Female sex
    • Fetal malposition (most commonly breech)
    • A positive family history
    • Oligohydramnios

Clinical Examination

  • Barlow Test:
    • The Barlow test is a provocation test used to assess hip dislocatability or instability.
  • Ortolani Test:
    • The Ortolani test detects a hip that is already dislocated.
  • Later Signs:
    • Asymmetrical thigh or gluteal folds
    • Leg-length discrepancy (Galeazzi test)
    • Limited hip abduction

Management

Explanation of other options:

Slipped capital femoris (Option B): Slipped capital femoris is a transphyseal separation where the femoral epiphysis slips posteriorly and inferiorly relative to the proximal femur. It usually occurs in adolescents aged 12–16. Treatment is surgical, typically with in-situ fixation, and a Pavlik harness is not used because it cannot stabilize the slipped epiphysis.

Perthes disease (Option C): Perthes disease is avascular necrosis of the proximal femoral epiphysis in children aged 4–8 years. Treatment involves activity restriction, physiotherapy, or containment braces.

Congenital coxa vara (Option D): Congenital coxa vara is a deformity of the proximal femur present at birth or early childhood, caused by an ossification defect in the inferior femoral neck. The Hilgenreiner-epiphyseal (H.E) angle is used to guide treatment: angles <60° are observed, while angles >60° require subtrochanteric valgus osteotomy. Braces like the Pavlik harness are ineffective.

question_text: All of the following are true about slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) except:
option_c: Schamm's loss of dense triangular appearance in infero-medial neck
explanation:
Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE)

Overview:
SCFE is a condition where the upper femoral epiphysis slips at the growth plate, typically in a postero-medial direction, resulting in coxa vara. The slip usually occurs gradually, though it can be sudden.

Causes:
The exact cause is unknown, but it is thought to involve trauma in the presence of an underlying abnormality. It is more common in:

  • Obese and sexually underdeveloped children
  • Tall, thin children with normal sexual development

Clinical Features:

  • Age: Common between 12-14 years of age, typically during puberty.
  • Sex: More frequent in boys.
  • Side: Affects both sides in 30% of cases.
  • Trauma: A history of trauma may be present in some cases.
  • Endocrine Abnormalities: More common in children with endocrine issues.

Symptoms:

  • Pain in the groin radiating to the thigh and knee.
  • Early limp that becomes constant.
  • Symptoms may initially be mistaken for a sprain.

Examination Findings:

  • Leg is externally rotated and may be 1-2 cm short.
  • Limited hip movements: restricted abduction and internal rotation, with increased adduction and external rotation.
  • During hip flexion, the knee may move towards the ipsilateral axilla.
  • Muscle bulk may be reduced.
  • Positive Trendelenburg's sign.

Radiological Features:

  • AP View: Displacement of the growth plate towards the metaphyseal side; Trethowan's sign (the line along the superior surface of the neck remains superior to the head).
  • Steel's metaphyseal blanch sign and Scham's loss of dense triangular appearance of inferomedial articular neck is seen in SCFE.
  • Lateral View: Head is angulated on the neck, detectable early.

Treatment:

  • Acute Slip: Closed reduction and pinning, similar to treatment for a femoral neck fracture.
  • Gradual Slip:
    • For slips less than 1/3 of the femoral neck diameter: Internal fixation in situ.
    • For slips greater than 1/3: Corrective osteotomy at the intertrochanteric region.
  • Unilateral Cases: Prophylactic pinning of the unaffected side is recommended due to a 30% chance of bilateral involvement.

Option A&C:

Steel's metaphyseal blanch sign and Scham's loss of dense triangular appearance of inferomedial articular neck is seen in SCFE.

Option B: In infantile coxa vara, neck-shaft angle is reduced.

Option D: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is a disease of adolescence, commonly associated with endocrine disorders.

Key takeaways:

SCFE:

  • Trethowan sign
  • Steel's metaphyseal blanch sign and Scham's loss of dense triangular appearance
  • A/w Endocrine disorders

Overview of Perthes Disease

Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH) (Option A): This condition involves abnormal development of the hip joint, which may lead to dysplasia, subluxation, or dislocation due to capsular laxity and mechanical instability. It is more frequently observed in females and typically presents before 2 years of age.

Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) (Option B): SCFE occurs when the femoral metaphysis slips relative to the epiphysis, most commonly affecting obese adolescent males. Unlike Perthes disease, SCFE is usually painless.

Congenital Coxa Vara (Option D): This condition, either congenital or post-traumatic, is characterised by a decreased femoral neck-shaft angle (usually <120°) and presents with a waddling gait.

question_text: A 30-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging swelling around the wrist that has been progressing over the past three months. An X-ray of the wrist reveals the lesion, as shown in the attached image. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Explanation:

An X-ray demonstrates an eccentric, expansile, lytic lesion involving the epiphysis, findings that are typical of a giant cell tumour (GCT), also known as osteoclastoma. The recommended treatment is extended curettage followed by bone grafting.


Explanation for other options:

Osteosarcoma (Option A):

  • Nature: Primary malignant tumour of bone, most frequently seen in children and teenagers.
  • Typical Presentation: Progressive pain and swelling, most often around the metaphyseal region of long bones such as the femur or tibia.
  • Imaging Clues:
    • Aggressive bone destruction.
    • Irregular, disorganised new bone formation.
    • Classic "sunburst" periosteal reactionon X-ray.

Ewing's sarcoma (Option B):

  • Nature: Highly aggressive small round-cell malignancy of bone, usually affecting the pediatric and adolescent age group.
  • Clinical Features: Painful swelling with a firm or tender mass; may be associated with fever or systemic symptoms.
  • Radiographic Findings:
    • Moth-eaten or permeative pattern of bone destruction.
    • Lamellated ("onion-skin") periosteal reaction.
    • Often extends into adjacent soft tissues.

Osteochondroma (Option D):

  • Nature: Most common benign bony projection (exostosis); arises from the metaphysis and is capped by cartilage.
  • Clinical Features: Usually asymptomatic, presenting as a painless, hard lump. Pain or growth after skeletal maturity may suggest malignant change.
  • Imaging Characteristics:
    • Sessile or pedunculated outgrowth continuous with the cortex and medullary cavity.
    • Cartilage cap thickness exceeding ~2 cmraises suspicion for secondary chondrosarcoma.

question_text: Which of the following is an important marker of recurrence of osteosarcoma?
explanation:
Importance of Serum ALP in Osteosarcoma

1. Diagnostic Marker

  • Serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels are often elevated in osteosarcoma patients.
  • High ALP reflects increased bone turnover, characteristic of the rapid and abnormal bone growth in osteosarcoma.

2. Indicator of Tumor Activity

  • Elevated ALP indicates aggressive tumor behavior.
  • Tumors with high metabolic activity tend to show higher ALP levels.

3. Prognostic Value

  • High ALP at diagnosis is linked to poorer prognosis.
  • Patients with persistently elevated ALP levels typically have lower overall survival and higher risk of metastasis.

4. Treatment Response Monitoring

  • A decrease in ALP levels during treatment suggests a positive response.
  • Persistent elevation may indicate incomplete treatment response or residual disease.

5. Recurrence Indicator

  • Rising ALP levels post-treatment can signal early disease recurrence, prompting further investigations and timely interventions.

Option A: Serum ALP is a useful serum marker in osteosarcoma.

Option B: LDH is a useful serum marker in Ewing's sarcoma.

Option C: Beta-2 microglobulin is a useful serum marker in MM.

Option D: Reversed A/G ratio and normal ALP in multiple myloma

Key Takeaway -

ALP Importance In Osteosarcoma

  • Prognostic Marker
  • Diagnostic Marker
  • Monitoring Marker
  • Recurrence Marker

question_text: A 45-year-old male patient presents to the OPD with complaints of increasing pain in his right hand over the past few months. On examination, there is a palpable lump, and an x-ray was done which is given below. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis
explanation:
Explanation:

The given hand X-ray shows popcorn calcifications, characteristic of chondrosarcoma, supported by the clinical presentation.

Chondrosarcoma

  • Aggressive malignant tumour arising from cartilaginous tissue.
  • Its the second most common primary malignant bone tumor.
  • Affects adults aged 30-80 years, peak 40-70 years.
  • Typically, a metaphyseal tumor, with the pelvis and proximal femur being the most common sites.
  • Presents as gradually enlarging mass with deep-seated

X-ray Findings:

  • Large radiolucent lesion with abundant calcifications, including popcorn-like calcifications (also seen in enchondromas)
  • May show endosteal scalloping and punctate calcifications

Treatment:

  • Surgical excision is the primary treatment
  • Chemotherapy and radiotherapy are generally ineffective.

Explanation of other options:

Osteosarcoma (Option A): Osteosarcoma, the most common malignant bone tumor, usually affects adolescents aged 10-20 years, typically arises in the metaphysis of long bones (distal femur, proximal tibia), presents with rapidly growing painful swelling, and X-ray shows a metaphyseal lesion with Codman's triangle and sunburst periosteal reaction.

Ewing's sarcoma (Option B): Ewing's sarcoma is a highly malignant but radiosensitive bone tumour, most commonly affecting children and adolescents (5-20 years). It typically involves the diaphysis of long bones and presents with pain, swelling, and sometimes fever. X-rays show a diaphyseal lytic lesion with an "onion-skin" periosteal reaction.

Osteoclastoma (Option C): Osteoclastoma (giant cell tumour) is a benign but locally aggressive tumour occurring in the epiphysis of skeletally mature individuals aged 20-40; X-ray shows an eccentric, expansile lytic lesion often extending into the metaphysis with a classic soap bubble appearance due to internal trabeculations.

question_text: Most common site for osteomyelitis?
explanation:
• Blood vessels in the metaphyseal zone are arranged in the form of a loop(hair-pin arrangement). The blood stasis resulting from such an arrangement is probably responsible for the metaphysis being a favourite site for bacteria to settle and thus a common site for osteomyelitis.
  • Hematogenous osteomyelitis is an infection caused by bacterial seeding from the blood.
  • Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis is characterized by an acute infection of the bone caused by the seeding of the bacteria within the bone from a remote source. This condition primarily occurs in children.
  • The most common site is the rapidly growing and highly vascular metaphysis of growing bones. The apparent slowing or sludging of blood flow as the vessels make sharp angles at the distal metaphysis predisposes the vessels to thrombosis and the bone itself to localized necrosis and bacterial seeding
  • MC site of OM in child: Lower end of femur
  • MC site of OM in adults: Thoraco-Lumbar vertebra(Thoracic > Lumbar)
  • MC site of OM in infants: Hip

question_text: A 4-year-old child is brought to the clinic with a gradually increasing, painless swelling of the right index finger over the past few months. There is no history of trauma. An X-ray of the hand reveals a cystic, expansile lesion in the proximal phalanx with thinning of the cortex. What is the most likely causative organism for this condition, known as "Spina ventosa"?
explanation:
Explanation:

This is a two-step question. The clinical and radiological findings are classic for tuberculous dactylitis, which is specifically referred to as spina ventosa. This condition is caused by a hematogenous infection of the short tubular bones of the hands and feet by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Key Features:

  • Clinical Presentation: Typically seen in children under 5 years of age. It presents as a painless or mildly painful, spindle-shaped swelling of a digit.
  • Radiological Appearance: The term "spina ventosa" (spina = short bone, ventosa = expanded with air) perfectly describes the characteristic X-ray finding: a central, cystic, lytic lesion causing balloon-like expansion of the phalanx or metacarpal with significant cortical thinning.

Explanation of other options:

Staphylococcus aureus (Option B): This is the most common cause of acute pyogenic osteomyelitis, which typically presents with acute pain, fever, and erythema. The X-ray findings would more likely show aggressive bone destruction, periosteal reaction, and sequestration, not the slow, expansile lesion of spina ventosa.

Treponema pallidum (Option C): Syphilitic dactylitis is a manifestation of congenital syphilis. While it causes swelling of the digits, the radiological appearance is different, usually showing diaphyseal osteomyelitis with a marked periosteal reaction.

Sarcoidosis (Option D): Sarcoidosis is a key differential diagnosis for dactylitis, especially in adults. However, sarcoid dactylitis radiologically presents with a different pattern, typically a "lacy" or reticular pattern of trabecular bone loss, and lacks the dramatic cystic expansion seen in spina ventosa.

Key Takeaways:

  • Spina ventosa is the specific term for tuberculous dactylitis of the short tubular bones (phalanges, metacarpals).
  • It is most common in children under 5 years of age.
  • Classic presentation: Painless, spindle-shaped finger swelling.
  • Classic X-ray: Cystic, "balloon-like" expansion of the bone.
  • The main differential is sarcoid dactylitis, which presents with a "lacy" bone pattern and is more common in adults.

    • Chronic Discharging Sinus:Continuous pus discharge through sinus tracts that develop to drain infection.
    • Tissue Changes:Scarring causes thickening, puckering, or inward folding of nearby soft tissues.
    • Bone Deformity or Non-union:Common in post-traumatic cases due to improper bone healing.
    • Systemic Manifestations:Usually mild; flare-ups may produce fever, chills, and general malaise.

Osteomalacia (Option A): Shows generalized osteopenia and Looser's zones, not a sequestrum.

Osteosarcoma (Option B): Appears as a destructive bone lesion with a sunburst periosteal reaction and Codman's triangle.

Ewings sarcoma (Option C): Appears as a moth-eaten lytic lesion with an onion-skin periosteal reaction.

question_text: For evaluation of which of the following condition is Mirel's criteria used for ?
option_c: Risk of pathological fracture after metastasis
explanation:
• Pathological fracture occurs in a bone which is abnormally weak either by systemic affection or by a localized disease. Trivial trauma/stress which would have left the normal bone intact can cause pathological fracture in weak bone. Osteoporosis is the most common cause of pathological fracture in elderly.
  • Causes of pathological fracture are-
    1. Reduced bone mass: Osteoporosis
    2. Neoplastic: Primary bone tumor (benign and malignant), metastatic bone lesions.
    3. Tumor-like lesions: Simple bone cyst, aneurysmal bone cyst, fibrous dysplasia, non-ossifying fibroma
    4. Metabolic and hormonal imbalance: Osteomalacia, rickets, scurvy, Cushing’s syndrome, hyperparathyroidism
    5. Developmental disorders and bony dysplasias: Osteogenesis imperfecta, osteopetrosis, achondroplasia, diaphyseal aclasis (multiple exostosis), Ollier’s disease
    6. Defect of bone remodeling: Paget’s disease, osteopetrosis
    7. Infections: Osteomyelitis, hydatid disease of bone
    8. Marrow cell disorders: Histiocytosis, Gaucher's disease.
  • When a bone develops a metastatic lesion, there is a high chance that the bone can fracture. We however do not want a fracture to occur as this will result is nonunion which is very resistant to treatment. Moreover the patient will also have to suffer pain and poor function on the affected limb. So we try and prevent fracture by nailing a bone with a lytic lesion. This procedure is called prophylactic fixation. There is a criteria, which helps us decide what lesions should be fixed prophylactically and what lesions can be left alone. This is called MIREL's score. A Mirel's score more than 8 is an indication for prophylactic fixation.

Reference- Fundamentals of orthopedics Mohindra and Jain page no 37

question_text: Select the false statement about osteomalacia:
option_a: It is the counterpart of rickets in adults
option_b: It is a disease of deficiency of bone matrix
option_c: Can be diagnosed by bone biopsy from iliac crest
option_d: Looser's zones are characteristic x ray findings
explanation:
Osteoporosis is a disease of deficiency of bone matrix. Thus Option B is False.

Definition:

  • Osteomalacia is the adult counterpart of rickets (Option A), characterized by the softening of bones due to vitamin D deficiency.

Symptoms and Signs:

  • Bone Pain: Persistent pain in bones.
  • Muscle Weakness: Decreased muscle strength.
  • Spontaneous Fractures: Fractures occurring with minimal trauma.

Diagnostic Findings:

  • Bone Biopsy: Performed on the iliac crest to confirm diagnosis (Option C) >>> Characteristic finding: Excessive uncalcified osteoid.
  • X-Ray: Shows Looser's zones (pseudo-fractures) (Option D) as radiolucent areas at stress sites, commonly in:
    • Pubic rami
    • Axillary border of scapula
    • Ribs
    • Medial cortex of the neck of the femur
  • Treatment – Calcium and Vit D supplementation.

Option A, C & D: It is the counterpart of rickets in adults, Can be diagnosed by bone biopsy from iliac crest and Looser's zones are characteristic x-ray findings, all three are Correct Statements.

Option B: Osteoporosis is a disease of deficiency of bone matrix. Thus Option B is False.

Key Takeaway –

  • Osteoporosis Involves a deficiency in bone matrix whereas Osteomalacia and Rickets Caused due to deficiency in bone mineralization.

question_text: Fill in the blank: __________is used for quantitative assessment of osteoporosis on a DEXA scan according to WHO.
explanation:
Osteoporosis: Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disease characterized by low bone mass and deterioration of bone tissue, leading to increased bone fragility and a higher risk of fractures. The bone condition is often diagnosed using a DEXA scan, which measures bone mineral density (BMD).

DEXA Scan:

  • Full Form: DEXA stands for Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry.
  • Purpose: The DEXA scan is the most commonly used method to measure bone mineral density (BMD) and assess bone health.
  • How it Works: The scan uses two low-energy X-ray beams to measure the density of bones, typically at the hip and spine. It is quick, painless, and involves minimal radiation exposure.
  • Key Usage: Primarily used for diagnosing osteoporosis and assessing fracture risk, especially in postmenopausal women and elderly individuals.

T-Score

The T-score compares an individual's bone density to the optimal bone density of a healthy young adult (ages 20-29). It indicates how much higher or lower your bone density is compared to this standard.

  • WHO Diagnostic Criteria for Osteoporosis:
    • A T-score of -1.0 or above: Normal bone density.
    • A T-score between -1.0 and -2.5: Indicates low bone mass (osteopenia).
    • A T-score of -2.5 or below: Diagnostic of osteoporosis. (Option A)

If the BMD measurement is more than or equal to 2.5 standard deviations below the young adult reference value (T-score ≤ -2.5), the individual is diagnosed with osteoporosis.

Option B: A Z-score compares a person’s bone density to others of the same age, sex, and body size. It helps identify if factors other than aging are causing bone loss. A Z-score of -2.0 or lower suggests the need for further investigation. The Z-score is particularly relevant for younger individuals, men, and premenopausal women, where age-matched comparisons provide more accurate insights.

Option C: there is no such assessment score called O score.

Option D: calcium scoring is done in coronary arteries through CT scan to assess the level of calcification.

Key Takeaway –

A DEXA scan is the gold standard for diagnosing osteoporosis, based on WHO criteria using the T-score which Compares BMD to Younger healthy individuals aged 20-29 years. A T-score of -2.5 or below is Diagnostic of osteoporosis.

explanation:
• Osteomalacia, which means softening of bones, is the adult counterpart of rickets. It is primarily due to deficiency of vitamin D.
  • This results in failure to replace the turnover of calcium and phosphorus in the organic matrix of bone. Hence, the bone content is demineralised and the bony substance is replaced by soft osteoid tissue.

CLINICAL FEATURES: Bone pain, muscular weakness and spontaneous fractures.

RADIOLOGY:

  • Diffuse rarefaction of bones.
  • Looser zone(pseudo-fractures): These are radiolucent zones occurring at sites of stress. Common sites are the pubic rami, axillary border of scapula, ribs and the medial cortex of the neck of the femur.
  • Triradiate pelvis in females.
  • Codfish vertebrae
  • Protrusio-acetabuli i.e., the acetabulum protruding into the pelvis.

Serum: The serum calcium level is low, the phosphates are low, PTH is high and alkaline phosphatase high.

  • When osteomalacia is due to defective intake, vitamin D supplementation therapy, as for rickets, brings dramatic results. Vitamin D in daily maintenance doses of 400 I.U. is sufficient. If there is mal-absorption, higher dose or intramuscular dose may be needed.

question_text: What bone disease would result from a loss of osteoprotegrin(OPG) protein?
explanation:
• Osteoprotegerin(OPG) is a member of the TNF receptor family but it is secreted and acts like a cytokine.
  • OPG has bone protective properties by inhibiting osteoclast development and activation. Osteoprotegerin is a decoy receptor which binds and thereby opposes RANK ligand. RANK ligand is the primary agent that activates osteoclasts and causes bone resorption.
  • Hence, the loss of OPG will result in excessive bone resorption by osteoclasts causing osteoporosis.

Reference: Manish kumar varshney, 1st edition, Page no. 67.

question_text: The drug, Denosumab is used in the treatment of osteoporosis, as well as in the treatment of giant cell tumor of bone. Which of the following is the mechanism by which Denosumab acts?
explanation:
• Bone resorption in the human body is mediated via RANK ligand, which when produced by osteoblasts(under PTH influence)/tumor cells, attaches to the RANK receptor on the osteoclast and causes its activation.
  • Denosumab(AMG 162) is a recombinant human immunoglobulin G2(IgG2) antibody functionally similar to OPG with affinity and specificity for RANKL.
  • Denosumab inhibits the RANKL/RANK formation on the osteoblast and hence preventing the osteoblast-osteoclast interaction decreasing bone resorption.
  • The effect is an increase in bone mass and strength in both cortical and trabecular bone primarily by antiresorptive action.

Reference: Manish kumar varshney, 1st edition, Page no. 87.

question_text: All of the following causes osteopenia except?

• Osteopenia- It is a condition where bone mineral density is lower than normal. It is considered to be a precursor to osteoporosis. However, not every person diagnosed with osteopenia will develop osteoporosis. Technically, Osteopenia is defined as a bone mineral density T-score between -1.0 and -2.5.
  • What is T-score?
    • T score is a value that we get when we compare the BMD of a patient with the BMD of a normal 30 year old person of the same gender and race.
  • World Health Organization classification based on T score are:
    • Normal is a T-score of -1.0 or higher
    • Osteopenia is defined as between -1.0 and -2.5
    • Osteoporosis is defined as -2.5 or lower.
  • CAUSES OF OSTEOPENIA-
    • Metabolic bone disease

question_text: In the following conditions, Bone mass is reduced except?
explanation:
Osteoporosis:

  • It is characterized by an abnormally low bone mass, normal mineral to matrix ratio and defects in bone structure, a combination which renders the bone unusually fragile and at greater than normal risk of fracture in a person of that age, sex and race.
  • In X-rays characteristic signs of osteoporosis are loss of trabecular definition, thinning of the cortices and insufficiency fractures.
  • Compression fractures of the vertebral bodies, wedging at multiple levels or biconcave distortion of the vertebral end-plates due to bulging of intact intervertebral discs are typical of severe post-menopausal osteoporosis.

Osteomalacia:

  • It is a manifestation of Vitamin D deficiency in adults.
  • There is inadequate mineralisation of hone.
  • It is characterized by a decreased ratio of bone mineral to matrix. Thus, there is a decrease in bone mineral mass.

Hyperparathyroidism:

  • It is characterized by a general loss of bone substance.
  • In severe cases, osteoclastic hyperactivity produces subperiosteal erosions, endosteal cavitation and replacement of the marrow spaces by vascular granulations and fibrous tissue(osteitis fibrosa cystica).
  • Haemorrhage and giant-cell reaction within the fibrous stroma may give rise to brownish, tumour like masses, whose liquefaction leads to fluid-filled cysts.

Osteopetrosis:

  • It is characterized by sclerosis and thickening of the bones which appear with increased radiographic density.
  • In osteopetrosis, there is failed bone resorption due to a defect in osteoclast production and/or function.
  • As a result of this bone mass is increased in this condition.
  • This does not translate into increased strength but causes increased brittleness and susceptibility to pathological fractures. This condition is also called marble bones disease or Albers-Schonberg Disease.

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Ortho, 5th edition, Page no. 313.

question_text: Which of the following X-ray findings is typically seen in a patient with fluorosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

In skeletal fluorosis, the bones typically show generalized osteosclerosis on X-ray due to excessive fluoride deposition.

Skeletal Fluorosis

  • Skeletal fluorosis is a chronic toxic metabolic bone disease caused by excessive fluoride intake over a long period, usually in endemic regions where water or food has high fluoride content.
  • It represents the severe end of the fluorosis spectrum, which also includes dental and non-skeletal forms.
  • Characteristic X-ray features include:
    • Generalized osteosclerosis (increased bone density throughout the skeleton).
    • Ossification of ligaments and tendons, leading to stiffness.
    • Osteophytosis (bone spur formation).
    • Ossification of the interosseous membrane of the forearm, which is highly diagnostic.

Explanation of other options:

Osteomalacia (Option A): Osteomalacia is the softening of bones due to vitamin D deficiency in adults. X-rays typically show looser zones (pseudofractures) rather than generalised sclerosis.

Osteoporosis (Option B): Osteoporosis is characterised by reduced bone mass and density, leading to fragile bones. X-rays show thinning of cortical bone and decreased trabecular pattern, which is the opposite of fluorosis.

Osteopetrosis (Option D): Osteopetrosis is a genetic disorder of defective bone resorption, leading to very dense bones. While it also shows sclerosis, it is congenital, often affects the entire skeleton, and has different clinical features like anemia, cranial nerve compression.

Reference:

https://www.ijoro.org/index.php/ijoro/article/view/1819

question_text: All of the following are markers of bone formation except:
explanation:
Bone Formation Markers

  1. Osteocalcin
    • Function: A protein secreted by osteoblasts that binds calcium and aids in bone mineralization.
    • Clinical Use: Indicates osteoblastic activity and bone formation. Elevated levels are used to assess conditions like osteoporosis and monitor treatment efficacy.
    • Normal Levels: Varies by age, sex, and assay methods. Higher levels suggest increased bone formation.
  2. Osteonectin
    • Function: A glycoprotein that binds collagen and hydroxyapatite, aiding in bone mineralization and matrix organization.
    • Clinical Use: Reflects bone metabolism changes, though less commonly used in routine practice compared to other markers.
    • Normal Levels: Varies; typically assessed in research rather than clinical settings.
  3. Bone-Specific Alkaline Phosphatase (BSAP)
    • Function: An enzyme produced by osteoblasts that facilitates bone mineralization by breaking down phosphate compounds.
    • Clinical Use: Indicates bone formation rates and is used to diagnose and monitor diseases like osteoporosis and Paget’s disease.
    • Normal Levels: Reference ranges vary, with elevated levels indicating increased osteoblastic activity.

These markers provide essential information about bone formation, health, and the effectiveness of treatments for bone disorders.

Option A, B & C: Serum bone specific ALP, Serum osteonectin, Serum osteocalcin all 3 are markers of Bone Formation.

Option D: Serum N and C telopeptides are markers for bone resorption.

Key Takeaway -

Markers of bone formation: Mnemonic – BONC

  • Bone-specific ALP, (alkaline phosphate)
  • Osteocalcin/nectin,
  • N & C terminal propeptide of type I Collagen

question_text: Regarding bone densitometry, a T-score of -3.5 is defined as which of the following?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • According to the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for Bone Mineral Density (BMD) measured by DXA (Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry), a T-score of -2.5 or lower is defined as Osteoporosis.
  • Since -3.5 is lower than -2.5, the correct diagnosis is osteoporosis.

Explanation of Other Options:

question_text: Which of the following is the earliest radiological sign in Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS)?

explanation:
• X-RAY FINDINGS IN ANKYLOSING SPONDYLITIS
  • Bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis is the hallmark of AS.
  • X-ray signs develop first on the iliac side of SI joint. Haziness and widening of SI joint due to subchondral erosions are the earliest X-ray signs. This is usually accompanied by variable osteoporosis around the SI joint.
  • As the disease progresses sclerosis, new bone formation and calcification of SI and sacrotuberous ligaments around SI joint occurs leading to ankylosis (fibrous then bony) of the SI joint as the end result.
  • Radiographs of the lumbosacral spine show loss of lumbar lordosis, diffuse osteoporosis, calcification of anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments, squaring of the vertebral bodies and bridging osteophytes (k/a syndesmophytes).
  • Eventually, the spine in advanced stages gives the classical bamboo spine appearance


  • Dagger sign refers to a single central radio dense line in the anteroposterior (AP) radiographs of spine related to ossification of supraspinous and interspinous ligaments

question_text: Which of the following does not cause secondary hyperparathyroidism?
explanation:
• Hyperparathyroidism can be primary or secondary
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism is always pathological and is seen in parathyroid tumors, which secrete large amounts of PTH without any control. So, parathyroid adenoma is a cause of primary hyperparathyroidism.
  • Secondary hyperparathyroidism is, however, usually physiological and occurs as a response to reduced calcium levels in the blood.
  • So any condition that lowers the serum calcium can trigger secondary hyperparathyroidism. E.g.
    • Vitamin D deficiency
      • Rickets
      • Osteomalacia
    • Calcium deficiency, especially in preterm infants
    • Chronic Renal failure leading to renal calcium loss

question_text: A 39 yr old male patient presents with non traumatic wrist pain, with an osteolytic area over distal radius on xray. Serum evaluation reveals high Ca, low phosphate and elevated ALP. Probable diagnosis would be?
explanation:
Primary Hyperparathyroidism

Definition:

  • Excessive parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion from the parathyroid glands, leading to high serum calcium levels.

Causes:

  • Parathyroid adenoma (most common)
  • Parathyroid hyperplasia
  • Parathyroid carcinoma (rare)

Pathophysiology:

  • Increased PTH causes elevated serum calcium through enhanced bone resorption, intestinal absorption, and renal reabsorption.

Clinical Features:

  • Bone: Osteoporosis, fractures
  • Renal: Kidney stones
  • Gastrointestinal: Nausea, abdominal pain
  • Neurological: Fatigue, depression

Diagnostic Markers:

  • Elevated PTH
  • Elevated serum calcium
  • Normal or low serum phosphorus
  • Elevated ALP

Imaging:

  • Ultrasound or sestamibi scan to locate parathyroid adenoma.

Management:

  • Surgical: Parathyroidectomy
  • Medical: Bisphosphonates, calcimimetics
  • Lifestyle: Adequate hydration, monitoring calcium levels

Prognosis:

  • Generally favourable with treatment, especially when managed early.

Option A: Calcium and phosphate are normal in Paget's disease but ALP is markedly elevated.

Option B: In renal osteodystrophy, calcium is normal/low, phosphate is low and ALP is high.

Option C: In secondary hyperparathyroidism -ca low/normal, phosphate is increase,ALP increased.

Key Takeaway -

  • Brown's tumor is an expansile bone lesion, a collection of osteoclasts. It commonly affects the maxilla or mandible, though any bone may be affected. Serum calcium is high, phosphates low and alkaline phosphatase high. All these are features of primary hyperparathyroidism.

question_text: Keinbocks disease is?
explanation:
• It is osteochondritis of lunate that occurs possible due to a chronic stress injury.
  • Affected patients are in the age group 15–40 years, mostly being manual laborers who present with pain usually in the dominant wrist.
  • The etiology is unknown, but it is associated with negative ulnar variance.
  • On examination, one may find tenderness over lunate. X-rays are done that initially may be normal but later on show increased density of lunate followed by evident collapse and fragmentation.
  • MRI provides the earliest diagnosis and is the investigation of choice.
  • Management in early stages (before collapse) involves radial shortening/ulnar lengthening procedures to correct ulnar variance along with a vascularized pronator quadratus based muscle pedicle graft to increase vascularity. In advanced stages with collapse, arthrodesis of the wrist is performed.

question_text: A 43 yr gentleman with complaints of dull aching pain and swelling in thigh and multiple lytic area on x-ray in femur bone was diagnosed with Paget's disease. Which statement is false?
option_a: Also known as marble bone disease
option_b: Affected bone becomes thick and spongy
option_c: The disease has a malignant potential
explanation:
Osteopetrosis Is Also known as marble bone disease so Option A is False.

Paget's Disease (Osteitis Deformans) is a chronic bone disorder characterized by the progressive thickening (Option B) and deformity of one or more bones.

Types of Paget's Disease

  1. Monostotic Paget's Disease:
    • Description: Affects only one bone.
    • Common Sites: Often the tibia or femur.
    • Features: less severe compared to polyostotic forms.
  2. Polyostotic Paget's Disease:
    • Description: Involves multiple bones.
    • Common Sites: Frequently affects the pelvis, spine, femur, and skull.
    • Features: Symptoms can be more widespread, including bone deformities, pain, and complications like fractures.

Key Features:

  • Bone Changes:
    • Initially, bones become soft and spongy.
    • Over time, bones become dense but irregular in structure.
  • Commonly Affected Bone:
    • Tibia is the most frequently affected bone.
  • Cause:
    • The exact cause is unknown, but it is associated with defects in osteoclast function, leading to irregular bone resorption and increased bone turnover.
  • Age of Onset:
    • Typically begins after the age of 40.
  • Symptoms:
    • Dull pain in the affected bone(s).
    • Bowing and thickening of the affected bone(s).
  • Diagnostic Findings:
    • X-Rays: Reveal multiple confluent lytic areas with interspersed new bone formation.
    • Bone Scan: Shows increased uptake of the radiotracer.
    • Serum Alkaline Phosphatase: Elevated levels indicate increased bone turnover.
  • Complications:
    • Pathological fractures.
    • Potential for malignant transformation. (Option C)
  • Treatment:
    • First Line: Bisphosphonates. (Option D)
    • Second Line: Calcitonin.

Option A: Osteopetrosis Is Also known as marble bone disease so Option A is False.

Option B, C & D: Affected bones are thick & spongy, Premalignant and Treatment with alendronate all three are Correct Statements.

Key Takeaway -

  • Marble bone disease – Osteopetrosis
  • Brittle bone disease – Osteogenesis imperfecta
  • Osteitis deformans – Paget’s disease

X-Ray Examination in Hyperparathyroidism

  1. General Features:
    • Irregular, Diffuse Rarefaction: Bones appear less dense and irregularly porous.
  2. Specific Signs:
    • Salt and Pepper Appearance (Option A)
      • Description: Skull bones exhibit stippling with small opaque areas resembling salt and pepper.
    • Loss of Lamina Dura:
      • Description: The lamina dura, a thin white line surrounding the teeth, is absorbed, leading to loss of cortical bone.
    • Subperiosteal Resorption (Option D):
      • Description: Resorption of phalanges and possibly the lateral end of the clavicle.
    • Spinal Changes:

    • Pelvis and Other Bones:
      • Description: Coarse striations with cyst-like spaces visible on X-ray.
    • Brown's Tumour (Option B):
      • Description: Expansile lytic bone lesion resembling a tumor, typically affecting the maxilla or mandible.
    • Extra-Osseous Features:
      • Description: Possible presence of renal calculi and other features.

Option A, B & D: Salt & Pepper Appearance, Brown's Tumor and Subperiosteal resorption all three are seen in hyperparathyroidism.

Option C: Frontal Bossing is Typically seen in rickets, not hyperparathyroidism.

Brown's Tumour (Osteitis Fibrosa Cystica) is A lytic bone lesion associated with hyperparathyroidism, appearing as expansile, cyst-like areas. Caused by elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) leading to increased bone resorption and fibrous tissue replacement. Typically in the maxilla, mandible, and can also affect long bones and vertebrae.

question_text: Not true about Paget's disease?
option_d: Elevated serum calcium/phosphate level in osteolytic phase
explanation:
Paget's disease: Paget's disease is a disorder of abnormal bone turnover. There is increased osteoblastic activity followed by increased osteoclastic activity leading to deformed and brittle bones(osteitis deformans) that easily fracture.

  • The most common age group is more than 40 years and males and females are equally affected.
  • Etiology of the disease is still unknown, although paramyxovirus and respiratory syncytial virus have been implicated.

The course of the disease, however is divided into three phases:

  • First phase(osteolytic phase): Characterized by increased bone resorption and hyper vascularization seen on radiograph as an advancing blade of grass appearance.
  • Second phase(phase of bone formation): The resorbed bone is replaced by structurally weak bone that is brittle and breaks easily.
  • Third phase(sclerotic/burnout phase): Bone resorption declines progressively resulting in hard, dense, avascular pagetic/mosaic bone.

SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS:

  • Pelvis followed by tibia is the most commonly affected bone, but other bones like the femur, clavicle, spine and skull are also affected. The disease can be monostotic(affecting single bone) or polyostotic(multiple bones involved). Patients are usually asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally with increased serum ALK phosphatase level.
  • Pain is usually a dull ache but still the most common presenting symptom. The patient presents with a short neck because of a flattened base of skull, kyphotic deformity and bowing of tibia and femur or at times with pathological fractures.
  • Rarely, features of cranial nerve compression or spinal stenosis may also be seen. Deafness results due to VIII nerve compression and otosclerosis. So in Paget's disease, the hearing loss is both conductive and sensorineural.
  • In patients with Paget's disease an increase in blood flow to extremities involved by Paget's disease can lead to vascular steal phenomenon, wherein blood is diverted from internal organs to skeleton leading to cerebral ischemia and spinal claudication.

LAB INVESTIGATIONS: Serum calcium and phosphorus levels are usually normal. Markers of bone formation and bone resorption show elevated levels. Urinary N-telopeptide(bone resorption marker) is a sensitive marker and can be used to monitor response to treatment.

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Ortho, 5th edition, Page no. 317.

question_text: A 50-year-old woman reports months of dull bone pain. Skull radiograph is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis for the given clinical scenario is Paget's disease of bone.

Paget's disease of bone

  • Pathology: Accelerated osteoclastic resorption followed by chaotic osteoblastic bone formation, creating enlarged, vascular, and poorly organised bone.
  • Key Skull Finding: "Cotton-wool" appearance on X-ray due to patchy sclerosis and thickened trabeculae.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Often asymptomatic, discovered on X-ray or raised serum alkaline phosphatase.
    • Bone pain that is dull and worse at night.
    • Bony enlargement/deformity (e.g., larger hat size, bowing of long bones, platybasia).
  • Other Imaging Signs: Early “flame-shaped” osteolytic lesions, coarse trabecular thickening, and possible stress or pathologic fractures.

Sunburst pattern : This is seen in osteosarcoma, where aggressive bone growth produces a characteristic spiculated appearance due to new bone formation.

Ground-glass appearance: This is typically associated with fibrous dysplasia, where bone appears hazy due to disorganised fibrous tissue replacing normal bone.

Explanation for Other Options:

Osteosarcoma (Option A): Primary malignant bone tumour of adolescents/young adults; presents with painful metaphyseal mass, most often around the knee. X-ray shows sunburst/spiculated periosteal reaction and Codman's triangle, not cotton-wool skull changes.

Osteochondroma (Option B): Benign exostosis arising from the metaphysis of long bones. Appears as a bony outgrowth with a cartilage cap, usually near the knee or proximal humerus, and not as diffuse skull sclerosis.

Ewing's sarcoma (Option D): Aggressive small-round-cell tumour of children or teenagers, typically in the diaphysis of long bones or pelvis. Imaging reveals an onion-skin periosteal reaction, not the fluffy sclerotic patches seen in Paget's disease.
