question_text: What is the probable diagnosis for a child brought to the orthopedics OPD with a lower limb deformity and hyperpigmented skin lesions, based on the presented X-ray of her thigh?
explanation:
Explanation:

A ground-glass lesion with shepherd's crook deformity and hyperpigmented skin lesions strongly suggests fibrous dysplasia, particularly the polyostotic form seen in McCune-Albright syndrome.

  • Fibrous Dysplasia is a non-inherited developmental anomaly caused by a postzygotic activating mutation in the GNAS1 gene.
  • This leads to the replacement of normal bone with fibro-osseous tissue, resulting in structural weakness, deformity, and risk of fractures.
  • Age group affected: Most commonly presents in children and adolescents (typically in the 2nd decade).
  • Clinical features:
    • Progressive limb deformity
    • Bone pain
    • Skin lesions: Café-au-lait spots (especially in McCune-Albright syndrome)
    • Pathological fractures
  • X-ray findings:
    • Ground-glass appearance of the bone
    • Shepherd's crook deformity of the proximal femur (varus angulation)
  • Types:
    • Monostotic: Involving a single bone
    • Polyostotic: Multiple bones involved
    • McCune-Albright Syndrome: Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia + café-au-lait macules + endocrine abnormalities (e.g. precocious puberty)
  • Management:
    • Medical: Bisphosphonates to reduce bone pain and lesion progression
    • Surgical: Correction of deformity or fixation of pathological fractures

Explanation of other options:

Non-ossifying fibroma (Option A): Typically asymptomatic and incidentally found on X-ray as eccentric, well-demarcated lytic lesions in the metaphysis of long bones. No ground-glass appearance or associated skin lesions.

Paget's disease (Option C): Occurs in older adults, not children. Characterized by disorganized bone remodeling, cortical thickening, and bowing, but does not present with skin lesions or ground-glass appearance.

Osteogenesis imperfecta (Option D): A genetic disorder of collagen synthesis leading to brittle bones and multiple fractures. Features include blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and hearing loss-but not ground-glass lesions or café-au-lait spots.

question_text: Which of the following conditions produce the x-ray finding given in the image below?

• This is a typical x-ray of the Rugger jersey spine. Rugger jersey spine describes the prominent endplate densities at multiple contiguous vertebral levels to produce an alternating sclerotic-lucent-sclerotic appearance.
  • This mimics the horizontal stripes of a rugby jersey.
  • Rigger jersey spine is classically seen in renal osteodystrophy. Renal osteodystrophy is the bone damage that occurs in chronic renal failure.
  • Pathology - In renal osteodystrophy, there will be secondary hyperparathyroidism because of calcium loss through the kidneys. The excess PTH will cause bone resorption throughout the body. In response to this, osteoblasts form an increased amount of osteoid that does not contain hydroxyapatite but does appear opaque on radiographs.
  • The sclerotic bands on the superior and inferior endplates of the vertebral bodies represent accumulations of excess osteoid and appear opaque because of their increased volume when compared to normal bone.

question_text: A woman during her routine examination presents with the following Xray finding. What is her most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The X-ray shows multiple benign cartilaginous growths arising in small bones of the hand, consistent with enchondromas.
  • When enchondromas occur in multiple sites, the condition is called multiple enchondromatosis.
  • If lesions are unilateral, it is known as Ollier's disease; if associated with soft tissue haemangiomas, it is called Maffucci syndrome.
  • These are benign tumours of hyaline cartilage, usually diagnosed in childhood, and most frequently involve the phalanges and metacarpals.

Multiple enchondromatosis:

  • Clinical features: Asymmetric limb shortening, finger swelling, impaired joint movement, pathological fractures.
  • Course: Tumours usually stop developing after puberty; growth in adulthood may suggest malignant transformation.
  • Malignant potential: 20-30% risk of secondary chondrosarcoma, especially if lesions enlarge after puberty.
  • Treatment: Observation for stable lesions; surgery if deformity, fractures, or malignancy suspected.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

  • Multiple brown tumour (Option A): Seen in hyperparathyroidism due to excessive osteoclastic activity. X-rays show osteolytic lesions with fibrous tissue and haemorrhagic areas, not enchondromas.
  • Fibrous dysplasia (Option B): Appears as a ground-glass/smudged radiographic lesion, not discrete cartilaginous tumours. It results from replacement of normal bone with fibro-osseous tissue.
  • Multiple exostoses (Option D): Also known as hereditary multiple osteochondromas, these appear as bony outgrowths (exostoses) projecting from the bone surface, not intramedullary cartilage tumours as seen in enchondromas.

Key Takeaway:

Multiple enchondromas, often seen in Ollier's disease or Maffucci syndrome, present as benign cartilaginous tumours of small bones. They carry a significant risk of malignant transformation into chondrosarcoma, warranting lifelong follow-up.

question_text: Which of the following is a complication of intermittent administration of teriparatide?
explanation:
Explanation:

Teriparatide, a recombinant parathyroid hormone, carries a Black Box Warning for the risk of osteosarcoma based on rat studies.

This risk is considered very low in humans but is a recognized potential complication, leading to contraindications in patients with predisposing conditions (e.g., Paget's disease, prior radiation).

Teriparatide:

Explanation of other options:
Osteonecrosis of jaw (Option A): A well-known complication of bisphosphonates and denosumab.

Net bone loss (Option B): Teriparatide is an anabolic agent that stimulates bone formation, leading to a net increase in bone mass.

Subtrochanteric fracture of the femur (Option D): Associated with long-term bisphosphonate use (Atypical Femoral Fractures).

Key Takeaways:

  • Teriparatide → Risk of Osteosarcoma.
  • Bisphosphonates → Risk of ONJ & Atypical Femur Fractures.

question_text:
A 70-year-old man undergoes routine blood work as part of a health check-up. He has no major complaints except for occasional bone pain. He denies weakness or recent fractures. On physical examination, no focal deficits are noted.
His biochemical profile is as follows:
Serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP): 710 IU/L (↑ elevated)
Serum calcium: 9.2 mg/dL (Normal)
Serum phosphate: 3.5 mg/dL (Normal)
25-hydroxy vitamin D: Normal
Parathyroid hormone (PTH): Normal
X-ray pelvis shows thickened cortices with areas of sclerosis and lysis.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given scenario of occasional bone pain with an isolated increase in ALP is suggestive of Paget's disease.

  • Paget's disease of bone is marked by localised areas of increased bone turnover, resulting in enlarged, thickened bones with abnormal internal structure and increased brittleness.
  • Pathologically, Paget's disease may involve one or multiple sites, beginning at the metaphysis of long bones and advancing toward the diaphysis, leaving altered architecture.
  • It features marked osteoclastic and osteoblastic activity, elevated plasma alkaline phosphatase, and increased collagen crosslinks (CTX).
  • Paget's disease progresses through three stages:
    • Lytic phase
    • Mixed lytic and blastic phase, where osteoblastic activity begins in response to bone resorption by osteoclasts
    • Sclerotic phase
  • The osteolytic stage shows bone resorption by large osteoclasts, replaced by vascular fibrous tissue, alongside new bone formation by osteoblasts, affecting both endosteal and periosteal surfaces.
  • This results in a thick but weak, deformable bone. As osteoclastic activity subsides, new lamellar bone fills resorption cavities, creating a mosaic pattern.
  • In the late stage, bone becomes sclerotic and brittle.
  • Clinically, PDB occurs equally in men and women, rarely before age 50, and may remain localised or widespread.
  • Common sites are the pelvis, tibia, femur, and skull. Many patients are asymptomatic, with diagnosis often incidental via X-ray or elevated alkaline phosphatase.
  • When symptomatic, it causes pain which is worse at rest or in warmth and deformities, especially in the lower limbs.
  • Skull involvement can cause enlargement, ill-fitting hats, or basilar invagination (short neck appearance).
  • Complications include cranial nerve compression (vision loss, facial palsy, deafness), otosclerosis, osteosarcoma, spinal cord compression, and spinal claudication. In some cases, it can lead to high-output cardiac failure.
  • Radiographically, the resorptive phase shows osteolysis in the form of flame-shaped lesions, as shown below, and osteoporosis circumscripta in the skull.
  • It then progresses to thick, sclerotic bone with coarse trabeculation. Stress fractures and deformity may occur, sometimes only recognised after fracture. Radionuclide scans reveal the distribution of active lesions.
  • Biochemically, calcium and phosphate are usually normal, though immobilised patients may develop hypercalcemia. Serum ALP, especially bone isoenzyme, reflects activity and extent, and helps monitor treatment.
  • Treatment with IV zoledronate effectively induces remission, often lasting years, with minimal side effects apart from transient flu-like symptoms.

Explanation of other options:

Osteomalacia (Option A): Osteomalacia is the adult counterpart of rickets, resulting from inadequate mineralisation of bone, leading to incompletely calcified osteoid that softens the skeleton, increasing fracture risk. In adults, calcium remains at the low-normal range due to secondary hyperparathyroidism, with elevated PTH and ALP, low serum phosphate, and markedly reduced 25-OHD levels (typically <10 nmol/L).

Primary hyperparathyroidism (Option B): Primary hyperparathyroidism, most often caused by a solitary adenoma, typically affects middle-aged women and may be asymptomatic or present with hypercalcaemia-related symptoms such as anorexia, abdominal pain, depression, and renal calculi. Biochemical tests reveal hypercalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, elevated serum PTH, and raised alkaline phosphatase in cases with osteitis fibrosa.

Osteoporosis (Option D): Osteoporosis is a condition marked by reduced bone mass and structural defects that make bones fragile and prone to fractures despite being normally mineralised. The cancellous bone becomes porous, and the cortices thinner, but biochemical parameters such as alkaline phosphatase, serum phosphorus, and calcium-phosphorus product remain within normal limits.

question_text: Which vitamin deficiency is primarily responsible for rickets?
explanation:
Explanation:

Vitamin D deficiency is the main cause of rickets, a disorder of growing bones in children characterised by defective mineralisation of the growth plate.

Pathophysiology:

  • Calcipenic rickets: Due to inadequate calcium absorption, often from vitamin D deficiency.
  • Hypocalcemia: Low calcium intake or absorption leads to secondary hyperparathyroidism.
  • Hypophosphatemia: Reduced tubular phosphate reabsorption contributes to defective bone mineralisation.
  • Growth Plate Effects: Decreased apoptosis of hypertrophic chondrocytes, leading to widened, irregular, and poorly mineralised growth plates.

Clinical Features:

  • Bone deformities (e.g., bowed legs, knock knees)
  • Delayed closure of fontanelles
  • Craniotabes (soft skull bones)
  • Rachitic rosary (prominent costochondral junctions)
  • Growth retardation

Explanation for Other Options:

Vitamin A (Option A): Deficiency causes night blindness, xerophthalmia, and keratomalacia, not rickets.

Vitamin B (Option B): Deficiency leads to neurological or haematological disorders (e.g., beriberi with B1, anaemia with B12/folate), not bone disease.

Vitamin C (Option C): Deficiency causes scurvy, characterised by gingival bleeding, petechiae, and poor wound healing, not rickets.

question_text: A middle-aged woman presents with severe pain and deformity in hands and fingers. X Rays of hand shows typical pencil-in-cup type of deformity in DIP. Probable diagnosis would be?
explanation:
Psoriatic Arthropathy

  • Prevalence: Affects 5%-30% of patients with psoriasis.
  • Onset: Typically, skin disease precedes arthritis.
  • Demographics: Equally affects men and women, usually between 30-40 years of age.

Key Clinical Features:

  • Joint Involvement:
    • Characteristic involvement of distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints (rare in other inflammatory arthritis).
  • Nail Changes (in 90% of cases):
    • Pitting, fragmentation, and discoloration.
  • Dactylitis ("Sausage Digits"): Seen in 30% of cases.
  • Enthesitis and Tenosynovitis: Prominent features.
  • Arthritis Mutilans:
    • The most destructive form, causing telescoping (shortening) of digits.

Pathophysiology:

  • Upregulated RANK-L expression in synovium (B-type cells).
  • Marked increase in osteoclast precursors leading to bone erosion.

Radiographic Findings:

  • Pencil-in-Cup Deformity: Typically seen in the DIP joints.
  • Small Joint Ankylosis: Fusion of joints.
  • Osteolysis: Destruction of metacarpal (MC) and phalangeal bones.
  • Periostitis and Bony Enthesitis: Inflammation and bone formation at tendon attachment sites.

Diagnosis:

  • Classic skin lesions of psoriasis aid in diagnosis.

Treatment:

  • Steroids are commonly used for managing symptoms.

Option B: Rheumatoid arthritis Spare Distal DIP Joints.

Pencil in cup deformity is typical for Psoriatic arthritis.

Option C: Haemophilia most commonly involves Knee and other large joints.

Option D: Neuropathic Arthritis typically shows total destruction of foot and ankle joints.

Key Takeaway -

Presentation of psoriatic arthritis is like rheumatoid arthritis - a polyarthritis, distal IP joints of hands involved (unlike rheumatoid arthritis, where these are spared). Classic skin and nail lesions help in diagnosis. Rheumatoid factor is negative. Treatment is by steroids.

question_text: An 80-year-old woman slipped in the bathroom and sustained a left hip injury, resulting in pain and inability to walk. She has no history of osteoarthritis, and examination reveals a shortened and externally rotated left leg. X-ray confirms the diagnosis. How would you approach the management of this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The X-ray reveals a left hip fracture in an elderly woman with a shortened, externally rotated limb after a fall, indicating a displaced femoral neck fracture, for which hemiarthroplasty is the best treatment option.

  • Hemiarthroplasty is a surgical procedure in which the femoral head and neck are substituted with a prosthetic implant, and it is typically the treatment of choice for elderly patients with displaced femoral neck fractures.

Explanations of other options:

Internal Fixation with Cancellous Screws (Option A): This approach can be used for specific hip fractures, but it is generally not suitable for displaced femoral neck fractures, which are more frequently seen in older individuals.

Meyer's Operation (Option B): It consists of surgically cutting and realigning the femur to correct deformity, but this procedure is typically unsuitable for elderly patients with displaced femoral neck fractures due to its invasive nature.

McMurray's Osteotomy (Option D): This procedure requires surgically cutting the femur to realign the deformity, but it is generally not appropriate for older patients with displaced femoral neck fractures because of its invasive nature.

question_text: A 42-year-old female laborer presents with a visible, soft, and fluctuant swelling over the anterior aspect of the knee, located in front of the patella, along with discomfort during knee movement. An MRI is performed.What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Housemaid's knee is the common name for prepatellar bursitis, which involves inflammation of the prepatellar bursa, located between the patella and the overlying skin.
  • It commonly occurs in individuals whose occupation or activities involve frequent kneeling, such as laborers, cleaners, or carpet layers.
  • MRI findings show fluid collection anterior to the patella, confined within the prepatellar bursa. The swelling is typically soft, fluctuant, and superficial, with no joint space involvement.
  • Symptoms include localized swelling, mild discomfort, and sometimes restriction in full knee flexion.

Explanation of other options:

Subdermal abscess (Option B): While an abscess may also appear as a fluid-filled collection, it usually presents with signs of infection (redness, warmth, fever), and irregular margins with possible internal debris or septations on MRI, distinguishing it from a smooth bursal swelling.

Gout (Option C): Gout commonly affects joints like the first metatarsophalangeal joint, not typically the prepatellar region. If it affects the knee, MRI may show tophi with heterogeneous signal intensity or erosive changes, which are not typical of prepatellar bursitis.

Rheumatoid arthritis (Option D): RA causes synovial inflammation, joint space narrowing, and pannus formation, typically within the joint. The prepatellar bursa is extra-articular, and isolated swelling here without joint involvement is not characteristic of RA.

Key Takeaways:

Housemaid's knee (prepatellar bursitis) presents with localized, anterior knee swelling due to repetitive kneeling trauma, confirmed by MRI showing fluid in the prepatellar bursa.

question_text:
A 67-year-old patient with a history of diabetes presents with knee swelling, limited range of motion, and minimal or no pain. The knee X-ray (shown below) demonstrates significant joint changes.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

In a diabetic patient with an arthritic knee showing joint destruction, especially involving the lateral femoral condyle, the most probable diagnosis is Charcot joint (neuropathic arthropathy).

Charcot Joints (Neuropathic Arthropathy) are:

  • Progressive, degenerative, and destructive joint disorders
  • Caused by loss of normal pain sensation and impaired proprioception

Commonly Affected Joints

Aetiology and Mechanism

Radiographic Features:

  • Rapid, severe destruction of the articular surfaces
  • May involve multiple small joints
  • Often shows disorganisation of the joint with subluxation or fragmentation

Rheumatoid Arthropathy (RA) (Option A): It is characterised by bone softening and soft tissue changes, with morning stiffness and symmetrical joint involvement being typical features.

Osteoarthritis (Option B): usually shows joint space narrowing on imaging, which is not seen in this patient, and is associated with activity-related pain.

Psoriatic Arthropathy (Option D): can present similarly to RA but is often accompanied by skin and nail lesions and tends to affect joints asymmetrically.

question_text: An 55 yr old man with chronic lower back pain radiating to both lower limbs consulted an orthopedic surgeon. Xray LS spine lateral which looked as shown. Diagnose the condition.
explanation:
Spondylolisthesis: Pathology & Types

Normal Vertebral Stability:

  • Forward displacement of a vertebral body is prevented by:
    • Articular processes of adjacent vertebrae
    • Intervertebral disc and ligamentous attachments (to a lesser extent)
  • Spondylolisthesis: A condition where a vertebra slips forward over the one below due to a defect in this "check" mechanism.

Types of Spondylolisthesis:

  1. Isthmic Spondylolisthesis (most common type):
    • Involves a lesion in the pars interarticularis.
    • Subtypes:
      • Lytic: Due to a fatigue fracture of the pars interarticularis.
      • Elongated: The pars interarticularis remains intact but is abnormally elongated.
      • Acute fracture: A fracture of the pars interarticularis causing separation.
    • Pathomechanics:
      • The anterior half of the vertebra (including the vertebral body, pedicles, and superior articular facets) slips forward along with the spinal column above it.
      • The posterior half (laminae and inferior articular facets) stays aligned with the vertebra below.
  2. Dysplastic Spondylolisthesis:
    • Least common type.
    • Results from a congenital abnormality in vertebral development, leading to vertebral slippage.
  3. Degenerative Spondylolisthesis:
    • Common in elderly individuals.
    • Caused by osteoarthritis of the posterior facet joints, leading to instability and subluxation.
    • Retrolisthesis (backward displacement) may occur in some cases.
    • Displacement is usually minor, with rare neurological involvement.
  4. Pathological Spondylolisthesis:
    • Results from generalized or localized bone disease that weakens vertebral articulation.
  5. Traumatic Spondylolisthesis:
    • Rare type.
    • Occurs when one vertebra slips over another following trauma or injury

WHY NOT OTHERS

  • Option A - Spondylosis is Degenerative spine disease commonly seen in old age.
  • Option B - Spondylitis is Inflammatory condition involving the spine at a younger age. e.g. ankylosing spondylitis
  • Option C - Spondylolisthesis is forward displacement of a vertebra over the one below it. It commonly occurs between L5-S1, and between L4-L5. Occasionally, the displacement is backwards (retrolisthesis) Hence Correct Option.

Key takeaways:

Spondylolisthesis is forward displacement of a vertebra over the one below it. It commonly occurs between L5-S1, and between L4-L5. Occasionally, the displacement is backwards (retrolisthesis).

question_text: Boutonniere's deformity is seen in?

question_text: All of the following are causes of secondary osteoarthritis of any joint except:
explanation:
Secondary Osteoarthritis (OA)

Definition: Secondary osteoarthritis is a type of OA that results from an underlying primary joint disease, which leads to degeneration of the joint. This degeneration often develops years after the initial condition.

Age of Onset:

  • Can occur at any age after adolescence.
  • Commonly affects the hip joint.

Predisposing Factors:

  1. Congenital Maldevelopment:
    • Example: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH).
    • Impact: Abnormal joint development that predisposes the joint to degeneration.
  2. (Option C) Irregularity of Joint Surfaces from Previous Trauma:
    • Example: Post-traumatic arthritis following intra-articular fractures.
    • Impact: Joint surface irregularities lead to abnormal wear and tear.
  3. Previous Diseases Affecting Articular Surfaces:
    • Examples: Joint infections, Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA), Avascular Necrosis (AVN) (Option A).
    • Impact: These conditions damage the articular surfaces, contributing to secondary OA.
  4. Internal Derangement of the Knee:
    • Example: Presence of a loose body due to synovial chondromatosis. (Option D)
    • Impact: Mechanical disruptions within the joint accelerate cartilage degeneration.
  5. Mal-Alignment:
    • Examples: Bow legs, knock knees.
    • Impact: Abnormal joint alignment leads to uneven stress distribution and increased wear.
  6. Obesity and Excessive Weight:
    • Impact: Increased load on joints accelerates the wear and tear process.

Treatment of Secondary Osteoarthritis (OA)

Pharmacological:

  • Analgesics: Acetaminophen for pain relief.
  • NSAIDs: Ibuprofen, naproxen to reduce pain and inflammation.
  • Topical Agents: NSAIDs and capsaicin creams for localized relief.
  • Intra-Articular Injections: Corticosteroids for inflammation, hyaluronic acid for lubrication.

Surgical:

  • Arthroscopy: Minimally invasive repair of joint damage.
  • Osteotomy: Realignment of bones to correct malalignment.
  • Joint Replacement: Total or partial replacement of the damaged joint.
  • Arthrodesis: Joint fusion (small joints)

Option A, C & D: AVN, Intra Articular Fracture and loose body all three can cause Secondary arthritis.

Key Takeaway -

Secondary OA Causes

  • AVN
  • Post traumatic following Intra articular fracture
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Loose body due to Synovial Chondromatosis.

question_text: A patient with subtalar and tibiotalar arthritis underwent the surgery shown in Figure A. The patient now complains of numbness on the plantar/lateral aspect of his foot including the 4th and 5th toes. Which nerve was most likely injured?

question_text: A young female presents with a loose, hard, mobile swelling in her left knee with complaints of occasional locking of knee joint as well. Investigation of choice for diagnosis of this condition is?
explanation:
Synovial Chondromatosis

Definition:

  • Synovial chondromatosis is a proliferative disorder of the synovial membrane in joints or bursae. It involves the transformation of synovial tissue into cartilaginous nodules or masses.

Key Characteristics:

  • Appearance: Can range from simple metaplasia (transformation of tissue type) of the synovial lining to the development of firm cartilaginous nodules.

Presentation:

  • Age Group: Typically affects individuals around 30 years old.
  • Symptoms: Common symptoms include joint pain, stiffness, and swelling.

Common Locations:

  • Knee: The knee joint is the most frequently affected site.

Imaging Findings:

  • X-rays: Show calcified loose bodies within the joint.
  • MRI: Detects precalcific cartilaginous loose bodies and provides more detailed imaging of the joint structure.
  • USG is of little or no use in synovial chondromatosis.
  • CT scan will give exact diagnosis but will be unable to pick up pre-calcified fragments.

Treatment:

  • Arthroscopic Resection: Removal of rice bodies (small, rounded calcified nodules) and the affected synovial tissue.
  • Synovectomy: Surgical removal of the synovial membrane to prevent recurrence.
  • Option A - X-rays: Show calcified loose bodies within the joint.
  • Option B - USG is of little or no use in synovial chondromatosis.
  • Option C - MRI: Detects precalcific cartilaginous loose bodies and provides more detailed imaging of the joint structure.
  • Option D - CT scan will give exact diagnosis but will be unable to pick up pre-calcified fragments.

Key Takeaway -

Biopsy of the loose bodies and synovium is gold standard but invasive hence MRI is the IOC in diagnosing Synovial chondromatosis.

question_text: All of the following are main cell types found in bones except:
explanation:
Bone cells: There are three main cell types in the bone. These are:

Option A - Osteoblasts: Concerned with ossification, these cells are rich in alkaline phosphatase, glycolytic enzymes and phosphorylases.

Option B - Osteophytes are bone spurs or outgrowths that form along the edges of bones, usually at joints. They are typically associated with conditions like osteoarthritis and are a result of the body’s attempt to repair itself in response to joint damage or degeneration. Osteophytes can vary in size and shape and may cause pain or restrict joint movement if they impinge on surrounding tissues. They are not seen in normal bone.

Option C - Osteoclasts: These are multinucleate mesenchymal cells concerned with bone resorption. These have glycolytic acid hydrolases, collagenases and acid phosphatase enzymes.

Option D - Osteocytes: These are mature bone cells which vary in activity, and may assume the form of an osteoclast or reticulocyte. These cells are rich in glycogen and PAS positive granules.

Key Takeaway –

Osteophytes are bone spurs or outgrowths that form along the edges of bones, usually at joints. They are typically associated with conditions like osteoarthritis and are a result of the body’s attempt to repair itself in response to joint damage or degeneration. Osteophytes can vary in size and shape and may cause pain or restrict joint movement if they impinge on surrounding tissues.

option_b: Global increase in range of motion

explanation:
Sequelae of Septic Arthritis of the Hip in Infants (tom smith arthritis)

  • Description:
    • This condition results from septic arthritis of the hip in infants. (Option D)
    • The head of the femur, which is cartilaginous at this age, is rapidly and completely destroyed by the pyogenic process.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Onset:
      • Acute with rapid abscess formation.
      • The abscess may burst or be incised and typically heals quickly.
      • Often mistaken for a superficial infection.
      • The child may later present with a limp, but usually without pain.
    • Examination Findings:
      • Unstable gait.
      • Affected leg is shorter.
      • Increased hip movements in all directions. (Option B)
      • Positive telescopy test. (Option A)
    • Radiological Findings:
      • X-ray reveals complete absence of the head and neck of the femur. (Option C)
  • Differentiation from Congenital Dislocation of the Hip (CDH):
    • Clinical Similarities:
      • Both conditions can present around the same age.
    • Differentiating Features:
      • In this condition, the acetabulum is normally developed and round.
      • In CDH, the acetabulum is shallow.
      • Complete absence of the femoral head and neck distinguishes this condition from CDH.
    • Treatment - On the lines of any other arthritis.

Key takeaways:

In Tom Smith arthritis, The head of the femur, which is cartilaginous, is rapidly and completely destroyed by the pyogenic process.

  • DDH
  • Tom Smith arthritis

  • Avascular necrosis of femoral head leading to collapse and deformation of femoral head leading to osteoarthritis
  • Mechanism: increased intraosseous pressure leading to blockage of blood supply
  • Risk factors:

question_text: A 12 year girl presents to the ER at night complaining of severe pain in lower third leg with mild swelling. No history of fever, trauma or previous injury. Her parents recollect a similar episode which was treated with Tab. Aspirin by a family doctor. Likely diagnosis would be:
explanation:
Osteoid Osteoma

  • Overview:
    • The most common true benign bone tumor.
  • Pathology:
    • Consists of a nidus of tangled, partially mineralized osteoid trabeculae surrounded by dense sclerotic bone.
  • Clinical Presentation:
    • Age Group: Commonly occurs between 5-25 years.
    • Commonly Affected Areas:
      • Lower extremities, particularly the tibia.
      • Typically located in the diaphysis of long bones.
      • Posterior elements of the vertebrae are also frequently involved.
    • Symptoms:
      • Persistent, nagging pain, often worst at night.
      • Pain is relieved by salicylates (e.g., aspirin).
      • Minimal or no clinical signs; may present with mild tenderness or a palpable swelling if superficial.
  • Diagnosis:
    • X-ray: Reveals a zone of sclerosis surrounding a radiolucent nidus (usually <1 cm).
    • CT Scan: May be needed to detect the nidus if not visible on X-ray due to extensive sclerosis.
  • Treatment:
    • Complete excision of the nidus along with the surrounding sclerotic bone.
  • Prognosis:
    • Good prognosis; it is not a premalignant condition.

Option A: Osteomyelitis present with fever and inflammatory signs like swelling, warmth, Sequestrum and cloaca.

Option C: Osteoclastoma, Epiphyseal Tumor present in 20-40 years female patient with soap bubble Appearance.

Option D: Osteochondroma are small bone tumors occurs in hand and feet.

Key Takeaway -

Ddx of Pain History:

  • Osteoid osteoma - Nagging night pain; relieved by aspirin; no fever
  • TB - Dull aching night pain; not relieved aspirin; mild fever +nt
  • Rheumatoid arthritis - Morning pain along with stiffness
  • Osteoarthritis - Pain usually occurs in the evening/night after prolonged walking throughout the day

question_text: A 73-year-old lady presents with complaints of long-standing back pain and kyphotic posture of her upper body. The X-ray of her spine looks as follows. Which of the following will not be used for treatment of this condition?
explanation:
• The given x ray shows anterior wedging of vertebrae with loss of height and typical cod fish appearance hence she is having severe Osteoporosis

Medical Treatment of Osteoporosis:

The treatment of osteoporosis includes the following approaches:

  1. High Protein Diet
    • Many elderly patients suffer from malnutrition. Increasing protein intake may enhance the formation of the organic matrix of bone.
  2. Calcium Supplementation
    • Though its effectiveness is debatable, calcium supplements may benefit patients with dietary calcium deficiency.
  3. Androgens
    • Androgens have an anabolic effect on the protein matrix of bone and can help reduce symptoms in some cases.
  4. Estrogens (Option D)
    • Estrogens have been shown to prevent further bone mass loss, particularly in postmenopausal osteoporosis.
  5. Vitamin D
    • Administered to boost calcium absorption from the gut, complementing other treatments.
  6. Fluoride
    • Although still under research, fluoride is believed to increase bone crystallinity, slowing bone resorption.
  7. Alendronate
    • Taken once daily on an empty stomach. It is effective but can cause esophagitis as a side effect.
  8. Calcitonin
    • Given via injection, calcitonin helps build bone mass and relieves pain.
  9. Teriparatide (Option A)
    • An anabolic agent that increases osteoblastic activity, leading to new bone formation.
  10. Denosumab (Option B) and Strontium
    • These are antiresorptive agents used to reduce bone resorption.
  • Option A, B & D: Teriparatide, Denosumab and estrogen all 3 are used in managing Osteoporosis.
  • Option C: Methotrexate has no role in management of Osteoporosis. It's used in Rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Key Takeaway -
    • The given x ray shows anterior wedging of vertebrae with loss of height and typical cod fish appearance hence she is having severe Osteoporosis
    • Teriparatide is frequently used these days for increasing healing potential of bones after complex/segmental fractures.
    • Calcitonin can be easily administered through nasal inhalation and has shown good results.

question_text: Earliest radiological feature of tb spine is?
explanation:
• The classic triad of TB spine is disk space reduction, lysis of the vertebra and paravertebral soft tissue abscesses.
  • Disk space reduction is the earliest finding, seen in commoner paradiscal type of tuberculosis. It is due to lack of nutrition or prolapse of nucleus pulposus into soft cancellous deceased body.
  • Thereafter, the contiguous margins of the affected vertebrae get eroded. With further destruction of vertebral body, there is anterior wedging of vertebra leading to kyphotic deformity.
  • Bone and joint tuberculosis constitute 1-4 percent of total number of cases of tuberculosis.
  • Systemic features of infection, such as fever, do not occur commonly in bone and joint
  • Spine is the commonest site of bone and joint tuberculosis.
  • Dorsolumbar spine is the commonest region to get affected; Paradiscal being the commonest type.
  • Reduction of disc space is the earliest radiological sign of TB spine.
  • It is the neurological complications associated with spine TB, which are of serious concern.
  • TB hip is common cause of monoarthritis in children. Early diagnosis can save the joint from developing ankylosis.
  • TB knee is of two types: Synovial and articular.
  • Joints gets affected early, if there is a juxta-articular tubercular osteomyelitis.
  • Treatment is focussed on (a) control of the disease, (b) functional recovery.
  • Healing of tuberculous arthritis occurs by fibrous ankylosis.
  • TB osteomyelitis is common in small bones

question_text: A 65 yr old fell this morning in her bathroom after which she is not able to bear weight on right side and has severe pain. She was brought to the orthopaedic department for further management. PBH AP view shoes right NOF fracture with pre-existing hip joint arthritis. Best plan of management for her would be?
explanation:
Operative Treatment Principles for Fractures:

Fracture Reduction

  • Reduction Maneuver:
    • Perform hip flexion with gentle traction and external rotation to disengage the fragments.
    • Follow with slow extension and internal rotation to achieve reduction.
    • Confirm reduction with AP and lateral imaging.
  • Guidelines for Acceptable Reduction:
    • AP View: Valgus or anatomical alignment should be observed.
    • Lateral View: Maintain anteversion while avoiding posterior translation of the fracture surfaces.

Internal Fixation

  • Multiple Screw Fixation: Option A
    • Most accepted method; screws should cross the fracture site for compression.
    • Typically, three parallel screws are used. Additional screws do not enhance stability and may penetrate the joint.
    • Configuration: Screws should be arranged in an inverted triangular configuration with one screw adjacent to the inferior femoral neck and another to the posterior femoral neck.
  • Sliding-Screw and Side Plate Devices: Option D
    • If utilized, a second pin or screw should be placed superiorly to control rotation during screw insertion.
    • These devices improve resistance to shear forces, particularly in high Pauwel angle fractures.

Prosthetic Replacement Option C

  • Advantages Over Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF):
    • Allows for faster full weight-bearing.
    • Eliminates risks of nonunion, osteonecrosis, and failure of fixation (over 20% to 40% of ORIF cases may require secondary surgery).
  • Disadvantages:
    • More extensive procedure with greater blood loss.

Primary Total Hip Replacement: Option B

  • Recent interest in total hip replacement for acute treatment of displaced femoral neck fractures has increased especially in cases with pre-existing arthritis.
  • Studies indicate better functional results compared to hemiarthroplasty and internal fixation.
  • Eliminates potential acetabular erosion associated with hemiarthroplasty.

Option A: Fixation with Cancellous screws is done when fracture reduction is possible in <60 years patients.

Option C: Bipolar hemiarthroplasty is prefered in >60 years patients without existing arthritis.

Option D: Fixation with dynamic screw is done when fracture reduction is not possible in <60 years patients.

Key takeaways:

Neck of femur fracture management:

  • If age is less than 60 yrs - Fixation with Screws or DHS
  • If age is more than 60 yrs without pre-existing arthritis and not very active lifestyle - Bipolar hemiarthroplasty
  • If age is more than 60 yrs with pre-existing arthritis and active lifestyle - Total hip replacement.

question_text: A mother brings her 7 yr kid with complaints of low grade fever, pain and swelling in the left hip region for 2-3 days. The left lower limb has a FABER attitude with mild decrease in movements. Probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Option A - The child has fever, pain and swelling and FABER deformity. This narrows down the DD towards either septic arthritis or transient synovitis. As the fever is low grade and restriction in movement is mild, transient synovitis becomes the best choice.

Transient Synovitis of the Hip (Observation Hip)

Overview:

  • A non-specific synovitis of the hip commonly seen in children aged 4-8 years.
  • Characterized by painful stiffness of the hip, which typically resolves in 2-3 weeks with rest and analgesics.
  • X-ray and ESR are usually normal.
  • Termed 'observation hip' because it requires careful observation to differentiate from other serious conditions.

Differential Diagnosis:

  1. Early Infective Arthritis: (Option B)
    • May mimic observation hip, particularly in early tuberculosis or septic arthritis.
    • Key differentiating features:
      • High ESR
      • Presence of systemic symptoms (fever, malaise)
      • Persistent signs may require biopsy, especially in regions where tuberculosis is common.
  2. Chronic Synovitis:
    • Mono-articular rheumatoid arthritis can resemble observation hip but persists longer and may have systemic features of rheumatoid disease.
  3. Perthes' Disease: (Option D)
    • In early stages, before X-ray changes are evident, it can resemble transient synovitis.
    • Further follow-up reveals characteristic X-ray changes.
    • The typical findings of advanced burnt out (stage 4) Perthes disease are: femoral head deformity with widening and flattening (coxa plana), proximal femoral neck deformity: coxa magna. "sagging rope sign" (thin sclerotic line running across the femoral neck) indicative of Perthes' disease.

Treatment:

  • Bed rest and analgesics.
  • Recovery usually occurs within a few weeks.

Option A - The child has fever, pain and swelling and FABER deformity. This narrows down the DD towards either septic arthritis or transient synovitis. As the fever is low grade and restriction in movement is mild, transient synovitis becomes the best choice.

Option B - Septic Arthritis Present in 0-5 years with more pronounced sign and symptoms with elevated ESR & CRP.

Option C - Acute OM will present with high grade fever and severe pain with the child looking toxic generally.

Option D: Perthes' Disease - In early stages, before X-ray changes are evident, it can resemble transient synovitis. Further follow-up reveals characteristic X-ray changes indicative of Perthes' disease.

question_text: A 61-year-old woman presents with a one year history of worsening bilateral, anterior knee pain. The pain is increased by climbing stairs. Both knees are stiff for five to 10 minutes in morning. There is no history of knee swelling. The pain is partially controlled by paracetamol 1 g up to four times a day. She has a history of diabetes, and angina. On examination, she is overweight. There is crepitus and during active and passive movement of both knees. There is no knee effusion. A recent knee x ray shows joint space narrowing in the medial tibio-femoral joint. What is the next step in her management?
explanation:
This lady has osteoarthritis.

NICE guidelines recommend formulating individualised management plans for patients with osteoarthritis.

Behavioural change, such as exercise, weight loss and suitable footwear should be encouraged. Comorbidities which compound the effect of osteoarthritis symptoms should be identified and their treatment optimised.

Paracetamol and/or topical NSAIDs (for knee or hand OA) should be offered before considering oral NSAIDs.

If symptoms are not controlled with the above strategies, oral NSAIDs or COX-2 inhibitors (but not etoricoxib) can be used. A proton pump inhibitor should be co-prescribed. The lowest effective dose should be prescribed for the shortest period possible. If the patient is already taking low-dose aspirin, an alternative analgesic should be considered.

Treatments which are not recommended include rubefacients, intra-articular hyaluronan, electro-acupuncture and chondroitin or glucosamine products.

Adjuvants which can be used include opioid analgesics, topical capsaicin and intra-articular corticosteroids.

Application of heat or cold packs, or TENS, can be considered if other strategies are ineffective. Manipulation and stretching can be helpful, particularly for hip osteoarthritis. Bracing/joint supports can be used for patients with biomechanical joint pain or instability.

Patients should be referred for joint surgery if they have already been offered all of the core treatments or if they have refractory joint symptoms which have a substantial impact on their quality of life.

If there is a clear history of mechanical locking, referral for arthroscopic lavage and debridement should be considered.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 371 Pg: 2861

question_text: Wandering acetabulum is seen in
explanation:
Multiple cavitation is typical of tuberculosis. Such cavities are formed in the femoral head and the acetabulum. Eventually, the head or the acetabulum gets partially absorbed. By the constant pull of the muscles acting on the hip, the remaining head of the femur may dislocate from the acetabulum onto the ilium, giving rise to the so-called wandering acetabulum.

The TB HIP progresses through the following clinical stages:

  1. Stage 1 (Stage of tubercular synovitis): Due to synovitis, there is joint effusion and the joint is held in position of maximum capacity, i.e., flexion, abduction and external rotation causing apparent lengthening. On X-ray all that is visible is a widened joint space due to effusion and generalized osteopenia.
  2. Stage 2 (Stage of early arthritis): With advancement of the disease process, there is destruction of articular cartilage. With spasm of flexors and adductors of hip, there is flexion, adduction and internal rotation deformity with apparent shortening. True shortening is also present due to damage to articular cartilage but is less than 1 cm. X-ray shows decrease in joint space and osteopenia.
  3. Stage 3 (Stage of late arthritis): With further destruction, clinical signs of flexion, adduction, internal rotation deformities and apparent shortening are exaggerated. True shortening is more than 1 cm. Here is gross restriction of movements and muscle wasting. X-rays may show complete loss of joint space with destruction of head/acetabulum.
  4. Stage 4 (Late arthritis with subluxation/dislocation): there are flexion adduction and internal rotation deformities with gross shortening. With destruction of acetabulum, femur head and ligaments, the upper end of femur may displace upwards and dorsally leaving the lower part of acetabulum empty but forming a false acetabulum higher up(wandering acetabulum). In some cases, the head and neck of femur gets smaller in size and contained in an enlarged acetabulum(mortar and pestle appearance). Severe destruction of capsule and acetabulum may eventually lead to pathological dislocation of femur head.

question_text: Which of the following is not a common extra articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Uveitis (specifically acute anterior uveitis or iridocyclitis) is not a characteristic feature of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). It is classically seen in Seronegative Spondyloarthropathies such as Ankylosing Spondylitis (associated with HLA-B27).

The ocular manifestations seen in RA include:

  1. Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (Dry eyes): The most common ocular finding (associated with secondary Sjögren's syndrome).
  2. Episcleritis: Benign, self-limiting redness.
  3. Scleritis: painful, correlates with systemic disease activity, can lead to scleromalacia perforans (thinning of sclera).

Explanation of other options:

  • Anemia (Option B): Anemia of chronic disease (normocytic, normochromic) is a common extra-articular manifestation of RA.
  • Splenomegaly (Option C): Occurs in Felty's Syndrome, a severe subset of RA characterized by the triad of Rheumatoid Arthritis, Splenomegaly, and Neutropenia.
  • Amyloidosis (Option D): Long-standing uncontrolled inflammation in RA can lead to Secondary (AA) Amyloidosis, which commonly affects the kidneys (nephrotic syndrome).

Key Takeaways:

  • RA Eye Findings: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (Most Common), Scleritis (Specific).
  • Felty's Syndrome: RA + Splenomegaly + Neutropenia.
  • Caplan's Syndrome: RA + Pneumoconiosis (Lung nodules).

question_text: Piano key sign which is one of the important signs in wrist examination is positive in which condition?
explanation:
Components of the Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex (TFCC)

  • Dorsal and Volar Radioulnar Ligaments
  • Articular Disc
  • Meniscus Homologue
  • Extensor Carpi Ulnaris (ECU)
  • Ulnolunate Ligament
  • Ulnotriquetral Ligament

Variance and Load Distribution

  • Neutral Variance:
    • 80% of compressive loads through the radius
    • 20% through the ulna
  • +2 mm Variance:
    • 60% of loads through the radius
    • 40% through the ulna

TFCC Tears

  • Acute (Class I) Tears:
    • Most commonly avulsions at the ulnar periphery (Type IB)
    • These tears are amenable to repair due to well-vascularized periphery.
  • Degenerative (Class II) Tears:
    • Associated with positive ulnar variance and ulnocarpal impaction syndrome.

Diagnosis and Surgical Treatment

  • Arthroscopy:
    • Gold standard for diagnosis of TFCC tears and ulnar-sided wrist pain.
  • Repair Techniques:
    • No clear clinical outcome difference between open and arthroscopic repair techniques.
    • Surgical treatment options:
      • Peripheral Repair: For acute tears.
      • Central Débridement: For specific cases.

Treatment for Variance-Related Conditions

  • Ulnar Shortening Osteotomy: Recommended when no arthrosis is present.
  • Wafer Resection: Indicated for cases with arthrosis.

Management of Chronic and Osteoarthritis Conditions

  • Chronic DRUJ Instability: Treated with TFCC repair or ligament reconstruction.
  • DRUJ Osteoarthritis (OA):
    • Options include:
      • Hemiresection interposition arthroplasty
      • Darrach resection (suitable for low-demand patients)
      • Sauvé-Kapandji arthrodesis (e.g., for rheumatoid arthritis)
      • Prosthetic arthroplasty

Complications

  • Most Common Complication: Injury to superficial sensory nerves.

Option B, C and D: They do not have a positive piano key sign.

The Piano-Key Sign Test is a test carried out for the clinical assessment of wrist instability. It is used as an indicator for distal radio-ulnar joint instability and tears of the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC)of the wrist.

Key takeaways:

  • The Piano-Key Sign Test is a test carried out for the clinical assessment of wrist instability. It is used as an indicator for distal radio-ulnar joint instability and tears of the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC)of the wrist.
  • The piano-key test involves depressing the distal ulna from dorsal to volar with the hand pronated. A positive result is characterized by painful laxity in the affected wrist compared with the contralateral wrist.

question_text: What factor is associated with a higher risk of dislocation after total hip arthroplasty?
explanation:
Dislocation after total hip arthroplasty is a multifactorial problem.

Numerous risk factors may act independently or cumulatively to increase the risk of this complication. Previous hip surgery of any kind is associated with a twofold increased risk for dislocation.

Other risk factors include

  • Female gender,
  • Impaired mental status,
  • Inflammatory arthritis, and older age.

Numerous studies have shown a lower dislocation rate with a direct lateral approach, although surgical techniques such as capsular repair have significantly lowered the incidence of dislocation after using the posterior approach. Metal-on-metal bearings have been associated with other complications such as adverse tissue reactions but are often used with larger-diameter bearings, which pose a lower risk of dislocation.

Reference: Berry, D. J. (2001). PRIMARY TOTAL HIP ARTHROPLASTY. In M. W. Chapman (Ed.), Chapman's Orthopaedic Surgery (3rd ed., pp. 2769–2794). Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

question_text: A 42-year-old female patient with a family history of ankylosing spondylitis presents with neck pain and stiffness. Her investigations are likely to show all of the following except:
explanation:
Radiology of Ankylosing Spondylitis

  1. Lumbar Spine X-Ray Findings:
  • Squaring of Vertebrae:
    • Vertebrae become squared off due to loss of normal curvature and disc space narrowing.
  • Loss of Lumbar Lordosis:
    • Normal curvature of the lumbar spine is lost, resulting in a more straightened appearance.
  • Bridging Osteophytes (Syndesmophytes):
    • Bony outgrowths form at the anterior aspects of the vertebrae, bridging adjacent vertebrae.
  • Bamboo Spine Appearance: (Option B)
    • The spine takes on a characteristic appearance due to the formation of syndesmophytes and calcification of the anterior longitudinal ligament, resembling bamboo.
  1. Pelvis X-Ray Findings:
  • Haziness of the Sacroiliac Joints:
    • Irregular subchondral erosion and loss of joint definition.
  • Sclerosis and Widening of SI Joints:
    • Increased bone density (sclerosis) and widening of the articulating surfaces.
  • Bony Ankylosis of the Sacroiliac Joints: (Option C)
    • Fusion of the sacroiliac joints, resulting in loss of joint mobility.
  • Calcification of Ligaments:
    • Calcification of the sacroiliac ligament and sacro-tuberous ligaments.
  • Evidence of Enthesopathy:
    • Calcification at the attachment sites of muscles, tendons, and ligaments, particularly around the pelvis and heel.
  1. Peripheral Joints X-Ray Findings:
  • Similar to Rheumatoid Arthritis:
    • X-ray changes can resemble those seen in rheumatoid arthritis, including joint space narrowing and erosions.
  • Formation of Large Osteophytes:
    • Development of large bony outgrowths at the joint margins.
  • Periarticular Calcification:
    • Calcification around the joints, which is less common in rheumatoid arthritis.

Option A, B & C: Positive for HLA B27, Bamboo spine appearance & Bony ankylosis for SI joints all 3 are features of Ankylosing spondylitis.

Key takeaways:

Ankylosing spondylitis:

  • HLA B27 Positivity
  • Bamboo spine Appearance
  • Bony ankylosis of SI Joint
  • Periarticular calcification in peripheral joints,

question_text: 60 years old man with diabetes mellitus presents with painless swollen right ankle joint. Radiograph of ankle joint shows destroyed joint with large number of loose bodies. The most probable diagnosis is?
explanation:
• Charcot joint, also known as a neuropathic joint or Charcot (neuro/osteo) arthropathy, refers to a progressive degenerative/destructive joint disorder in patients with reduced / absent pain sensation and proprioception.
  • The most common cause is diabetes.
  • Most patients present with a limp, difficulty putting on shoes, or soft tissue swelling. But the clinching point is the absence of pain even in the presence of severe deformity and disability.
  • The characteristic physical findings are anesthetic or hypoesthetic feet (100% of patients), bony deformities (69% of patients), and soft tissue swelling (17% of patients). Many patients also have ulceration and abnormal callus formation.
  • The most common bony deformities are abnormal projections on the plantar arch (rocker sole) or other unusual prominence of the dorsal or medial arches of the midfoot or the MTP joint.
  • Treatment is difficult. Bracing is usually advised for some joints. CROW (charcot resistant orthotic walker) is now used for charcot’s joint of foot and ankle.

question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic change in cartilage involved in moderate osteoarthritis?
explanation:
The changes observed in articular cartilage affected by osteoarthritis include:

  • Increased water content (as a result of the disruption in architecture of the matrix molecules),
  • Decreased quantity of proteoglycans,
  • Decreased quantity of collagen with decreases in cross-linking and stiffness associated with degradation,
  • Increased thickness of subchondral bone,
  • Increased chondrocyte activity and proliferation of chondrocytes.

This is different than the changes seen during the natural aging process which include: decreased water content, decreased proteoglycan content and size (decreased length of protein core and GAG chains), normal quantity of collagen, increased collagen stiffness and cross-linking, unchanged chondrocyte activity/proliferation, unchanged thickness of subchondral bone, and decreased ratio of chondroitin sulfate to total glycosaminoglycans.

Incorrect Answers:

Option A: Subchondral bone thickness is increased in osteoarthritis.

Option B: Chondrocyte activity is increased in moderate osteoarthritis.

Option C: Proteoglycan content is decreased in both osteoarthritis and the normal aging process.

Reference: Manish kumar varshney 1st edition page no 1151

question_text: Below figure shows the radiograph of a healthy 52-year-old woman who has severe right hip pain that has been unresponsive to nonsurgical management. What is the most appropriate surgical procedure currently?

question_text: Which of the following is not classified as a seronegative arthritis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Seronegative spondyloarthropathies are a group of inflammatory joint disorders that are characterized by the absence of rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies in the blood, hence the term "seronegative." These conditions often share a genetic link, particularly with the HLA-B27 antigen. Rheumatoid arthritis, in contrast, is the archetypal "seropositive" arthritis, as the majority of patients test positive for RF and/or anti-CCP antibodies.

Explanation of Other Options:

(B) Reactive arthritis: This is a classic example of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy, often triggered by a preceding infection.

(C) Enteropathic arthritis: This form of arthritis is associated with inflammatory bowel diseases (like Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis) and is classified as a seronegative spondyloarthropathy.

(D) Psoriatic arthritis: This is an inflammatory arthritis that occurs in some people with psoriasis and is also a member of the seronegative spondyloarthropathy family.

Key Takeaway:

The term "seronegative arthritis" distinguishes a group of inflammatory arthritides (including psoriatic, reactive, enteropathic arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis) from rheumatoid arthritis. The primary distinguishing feature is the absence of rheumatoid factor in the blood of patients with seronegative conditions.

question_text: Most common joint involved in septic arthritis
explanation:
SEPTIC ARTHRITIS:

  • This is an arthritis caused by pyogenic organisms.
  • Other terms often used to describe this condition are pyogenic arthritis, infective arthritis or suppurative arthritis.
  • It is more common in children and males are more susceptible. Other predisposing factors are poor hygiene, poor resistance, diabetes etc.
  • Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest causative organism.
  • The knee is the commonest joint affected. Other joints commonly affected are the hip, shoulder, elbow etc.
  • As the organism reaches the joint by various routes(hematogenous/direct trauma), there begins an inflammatory response in the synovium resulting in the exudation of fluid within the joint. Joint cartilage is destroyed by inflammatory granulation tissue and lysosomal enzymes in the joint exudate. Outcome varies from complete healing to total destruction of the joint. The latter may result in a complete loss of joint movement(ankylosis).
  • Septic arthritis presents with a severe throbbing pain, swelling and redness of the affected joint. This is associated with high grade fever and malaise.
  • Blood shows neutrophilic leucocytosis. ESR is markedly elevated. A blood culture may grow the causative organism. Joint aspiration is the quickest and the best method of diagnosing septic arthritis. The fluid may show features of acute septic inflammation.
  • Combination of Ceftriaxone and Cloxacillin, in appropriate doses is usually given. These are subsequently changed to specific antibiotics as per aspirate culture and sensitivity reports. The joint must be put to rest in a splint or in traction.

Reference: Maheshwari ortho, 5th edition, Page no. 177.

question_text: What is the end result of untreated septic arthritis?
explanation:

  • Complications of septic arthritis include
    1. Secondary osteoarthritis
    2. Osteomyelitis
    3. Septicemia
    4. Bony ankylosis

question_text: 40 yrs-old-female presents with urine darkening on standing, joint pain and stiffness and pigment deposition in joints. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Individual presenting in 4th decade with joint pain and stiffness and urine darkening on standing and pigment deposition in joints is suggestive of alkaptonuria. Oochronosis(Alkaptonuria):

  • Alkaptonuria is a rare, heritable disorder characterized by the appearance of homogentisic acid in the urine, dark pigmentation of the connective tissues(oochronosis) and calcification of hyaline and fibrocartilage.
  • Inborn error is an absence of homogentisic acid oxidase in the liver and kidney. Those affected usually remain asymptomatic until the 3rd & 4th decade when they present with pain and stiffness of the spine & (later) larger joints.
  • Dark pigmentation of ear cartilage & sclera and staining of clothes by homogentisic acid in sweat. Urine turns dark brown when it is alkalinized or if it is left to stand for some hours.
  • X-ray reveals narrowing & calcification of intervertebral discs. Peripheral joints show chondrocalcinosis and severe osteoarthritis.

Reference: Appley, 9th edition, Page no. 82.

question_text: Differentiating features of psoriatic arthritis from RA is?

    3. Symmetrical polyarthritis similar to RA
    4. Axial involvement similar to ankylosing spondylitis

  • Swelling of fingers can result in sausage digts.
  • X ray of hand shows Pencil in cup deformity.
  • The drug of choice for psoriatic arthritis-Methotrexate

question_text: Most specific antibody in rheumatoid arthritis is?
explanation:
INVESTIGATIONS IN RA

  • Routine blood investigations: Hb may be low; white cell counts are raised along with a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels.
  • Rheumatoid factor (RF): The RF is an IgM autoantibody against Fc region of IgG, seen in almost two-third patients of RA. Its detection can suggest the diagnosis. However, early in the disease the levels are lower, therefore the sensitivity is lower and hence it is not useful for screening purposes.
  • Neither is the presence of RF specific for RA as it can be seen in 5% of healthy population and in diseases like systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), tuberculosis (TB), Sjogren’s syndrome, syphilis, chronic liver disease, sarcoidosis, leprosy, infectious mononucleosis and malaria.
  • Anti-cycliccitrullinated polypeptide (anti-CCP): Anti-CCP antibodies are positive in upto 98% of cases. These are more specific than RA factor and may be positive very early in the course of the disease. Positivity indicates bad prognosis.
  • Antinuclear antibody (ANA) may also be raised in RA.

    • Rituximab- This is a chimeric monoclonal antibody against the CD20 antigen expressed on the surface of B cells
    • Tofactinib is a JAK inhibitor
    • Infliximab, Adalimumab and Etanercept are both TNF-alpha blockers.

question_text: Which of the following medications when combined with methotrexate has been shown to be more effective than methotrexate alone in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis?

question_text: A 46-year-old male is 2.5 years out from a closed subtalar dislocation treated with reduction and casting. His current radiographs are shown in figure A. An MRI is performed which demonstrates broad-based avascular necrosis of the talus. He has attempted bracing, injections and NSAIDs, but continues to be significantly limited. What is the most appropriate surgical management for this patient?

option_d: Total ankle arthroplasty using lateral transfibular approach
explanation:
• This patient has broad-based avascular necrosis (AVN) of the talus with tibiotalar and subtalar arthritis. A tibiotalocalcaneal (TTC) arthrodesis is indicated. A lateral approach allows direct access to the tibiotalar and subtalar joints along with local autograft.
  • Trauma is the most common etiology for AVN, mainly fractures of the talar body or talar neck, and comprises 75% of cases.
    • The treatment options for talar AVN are varied and dependent to a certain extent on the osteonecrosis stage.
    • Early cases can be treated with core decompression, non-vascularized, or vascularized bone graft.
    • In late cases, where structural changes have occurred, treatment modalities are salvage procedures such as arthrodesis techniques.
  • Figure A is an AP and lateral ankle demonstration avascular necrosis of the talus with tibiotalar and subtalar osteoarthritis.
  • Incorrect answers:
    • Answer 1: Using the anterior approach alone would not allow access to the subtalar joint for preparation.
    • Answer 2: This patient has subtalar arthritis in addition to tibiotalar arthritis, a better pain-relieving option for this patient includes an arthrodesis of the subtalar joint.
    • Answer 4: Given the broad-based avascular necrosis of the talus as well as patient's age, total ankle arthroplasty is not the best option for this patient.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 295.

question_text: Condition in which there is anterior or posterior displacement of a vertebra in relation to the vertebrae below:
explanation:
Spondylosis - Degenerative osteoarthritis of the joints of the spinal column.

Spondylitis - is an inflammation of the vertebra. It is usually seen in inflammatory conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis.

Spondylolysis - it is a defect or break in the pars interarticularis of the vertebra. Pars interarticularis is an important structure that links a vertebra to its adjacent vertebrae. Any defect in it can predispose the slipping of one vertebra over its lower vertebra resulting in spondylolisthesis. So, spondylolysis is the precursor of spondylolisthesis.

Spondylolisthesis - The anterior or posterior displacement of a vertebra or the vertebral column in relation to the vertebrae below it.

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th ed, Pg: 283-284.
