question_text: A 55-year-old female presented with back pain for six months. Her CT scan image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The CT scan shows anterior slippage of a vertebra, characteristic of spondylolisthesis.

  • Spondylolisthesis is the forward displacement of one vertebral body over the one beneath it, most commonly at L5-S1 or L4-L5.
  • It can be caused by degeneration, trauma, congenital defects, or pars interarticularis defects.
  • In this patient, the chronic back pain and the CT scan showing vertebral misalignment point to a likely diagnosis of degenerative spondylolisthesis, which is typical in older adults.
  • In this type, the pars interarticularis remains intact, but instability of facet joints due to osteoarthritis leads to vertebral slippage.
  • This form usually does not cause severe neurological issues but may lead to chronic back pain and spinal canal narrowing.

Explanation of other options:

Paget's disease (Option A): Shows thickened cortical bone, coarsened trabeculae, and a "cotton wool" appearance on imaging. The vertebrae are typically enlarged with mixed lytic and sclerotic changes-findings not seen in this case.

Osteoporosis (Option B): Leads to generalized bone thinning, often with vertebral compression fractures, not anterior vertebral slippage as seen in spondylolisthesis.

Renal osteodystrophy (Option D): Associated with chronic kidney disease; radiological signs include subperiosteal bone resorption, rugger-jersey spine, and osteosclerosis, none of which are suggested by the CT findings here.

question_text: A young girl presents with thigh swelling and a discharging sinus, from which a bony fragment has emerged. There is a history of recurrent bone pain and intermittent discharge from the same site. What is the protruding bony fragment most likely?
explanation:
Explanation:

A young girl likely has chronic osteomyelitis, given the history of recurrent bone pain, swelling, and intermittent discharge. The bony fragment protruding through the sinus is most likely a sequestrum.

Chronic osteomyelitis

A dreaded sequela of acute osteomyelitis, often follows an open fracture or an operation.

Predisposing Factors:

  • Often evolves from untreated or inadequately treated acute haematogenous osteomyelitis.
  • Host defense is weakened by scar tissue, devitalized bone, poor vascularization, and non-collapsing cavities.
  • Bacterial persistence: Biofilm formation (glycocalyx) on sequestra or implants; survival inside osteoblasts/osteocytes.
  • High-risk groups: elderly, debilitated, diabetics, patients with peripheral vascular disease, malnutrition, lupus, immune deficiency, substance abuse.
  • Local trauma (open fractures, prolonged surgeries, implants) is the most common precipitating factor.

Pathology:

  • Bone destruction: Localized or diffuse around infection focus or implants.
  • Sequestra: Dead bone fragments in pus-filled cavities, act as bacterial substrate.
  • Involucrum: Reactive new bone forms a sheath around sequestra; large diaphyseal segments may be encased. (Option A ruled out)
  • Sinus formation: Draining pathways through involucrum to skin; may temporarily seal, causing "flare-ups."
  • Cloacae: Openings in the involucrum through which pus or sequestra can drain to the skin surface. (Option B ruled out)

Clinical Features:

  • Recurrent pain, fever, redness, tenderness ("flare").
  • Discharging sinus: Thickened, puckered tissue; seropurulent discharge; skin excoriation.
  • Post-traumatic cases may show bone deformity or non-union.

Imaging:

  • On X-ray, chronic osteomyelitis typically shows dense, devitalized bone (sequestrum) within a lucent cavity, surrounded by reactive new bone (involucrum), sometimes with cloacae for drainage.
    • Gives a bone in bone appearance.
  • Sinogram: May help localize infection.

Management

  • Chronic osteomyelitis is managed with surgery and antibiotics.
  • Surgical intervention involves sequestrectomy and saucerization, aiming to:
    • Drain pus
    • Excise sinus tracts
    • Remove the sequestrum
    • Curette the cavity walls until fresh bleeding appears ("Paprika sign")
    • Saucerization to ensure proper drainage.
  • Local antibiotic therapy can be delivered using PMMA beads loaded with gentamicin or vancomycin.
  • Vacuum-assisted closure (negative pressure wound therapy) may be used to clear slough and promote granulation tissue, with pressures of 50-125 mmHg.

Explanation of other options:

Loose body (Option D): A loose body is a free fragment of bone or cartilage typically found within a joint, often arising from osteoarthritis, osteochondral lesions, or trauma, and is not associated with chronic osteomyelitis.

question_text: A 26-year-old male presents with complaints of chronic lower back pain, which has been progressive for the past 1 year. He also experiences early morning stiffness lasting for 1.5 hours, which is relieved by exercise. He also gives a history of anterior uveitis. Which of the following investigations is most useful for early diagnosis of the underlying condition?
option_c: CT spine of the sacroiliac joint
explanation:
Explanation:

The given clinical vignette of chronic lower back pain in a young male associated with morning stiffness and a history of anterior uveitis is suggestive of ankylosing spondylitis, and among the given options, MRI of the sacroiliac joint is the most useful for early diagnosis.

  • Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease classified under axial spondyloarthropathies, predominantly affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints.
  • It is strongly associated with HLA-B27 and ERAP1, showing a marked familial tendency.
  • It occurs more commonly in males (ratios 2:1 to 10:1), typically presenting between ages 15 and 25.
  • The triggering factor may involve bacterial antigens cross-reacting with HLA-B27 or antigen presentation to T-cells, sometimes following genitourinary or bowel infection.
  • Pathologically, AS is characterised by synovitis of diarthrodial joints and inflammation at fibro-osseous junctions known as enthesopathy, leading to preferential involvement of tendon and ligament insertions.
  • Sacroiliac and vertebral facet joint synovitis results in cartilage destruction and reduced chest expansion. Costovertebral involvement impairs respiratory movement.
  • Disease progression follows three stages: inflammatory cell infiltration and bone erosion, granulation tissue replacement by fibrous tissue, and ossification of fibrous tissue, producing ankylosis.
  • Ossification across discs forms syndesmophytes linking vertebrae, potentially rendering the spine completely rigid.
  • Clinically, AS often begins insidiously in adolescence or early adulthood with intermittent backache and stiffness, worse in the morning and after inactivity.
  • Pain may radiate to the buttocks or thighs, and symptoms progress to continuous stiffness, fatigue, joint pain, swelling, Achilles tendon tenderness, foot strain, or intercostal pain.
  • Extraskeletal manifestations include general fatigue, weight loss, acute anterior uveitis, and, rarely, aortic valve disease, carditis, or apical pulmonary fibrosis.
  • Imaging reveals early sacroiliac joint erosion and fuzziness, progressing to periarticular sclerosis and bony ankylosis.
  • Vertebral changes include squaring, ossification of surrounding ligaments, and syndesmophyte bridging between vertebrae, producing a bamboo spine.
  • X-ray changes include squaring of the lumbar vertebrae and formation of bony bridges between the vertebral bodies known as syndesmophytes.
  • If the bridging occurs at several levels, it results in a bamboo spine as shown below.
  • MRI can detect early inflammatory changes with contrast enhancement. Laboratory findings show elevated ESR and CRP during active disease.
  • Treatment aims to maintain posture and movement, reduce pain and stiffness, and prevent deformity. It includes general posture-preserving measures, NSAIDs for symptom control, TNF inhibitors for severe disease (with IL-17 and IL-12/23 inhibitors in development), and surgery to correct deformity or restore mobility.

Explanation of other options:

Anti-CCP (Option A): Anti-CCP antibodies are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis.

CT spine of sacroiliac joint (Option C): MRI provides a detailed assessment of the sacroiliac joints and can reveal characteristic erosions and signs of inflammation, including bone oedema. Hence, MRI is considered a better investigation compared to CT in diagnosing ankylosing spondylitis.

Bone scan (Option D): Radionuclide imaging of bone is valuable for diagnosing stress or undisplaced fractures undetectable by plain X-ray, identifying small bone abscesses or osteoid osteomas, and assessing loosening or infection around prostheses. It can also detect femoral head ischaemia in Perthes' disease or adult avascular necrosis, and enables early identification of bone metastases. It has limited value in the diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis.

question_text: A patient diagnosed with tuberculous arthritis of the hip complains of hip pain and demonstrates true (actual) shortening of the affected limb. Based on the natural progression of hip tuberculosis, what stage of disease does this presentation represent?
explanation:
Explanation:

Hip pain with true limb shortening is characteristic of Stage III (advanced arthritis) in tuberculous infection of the hip.

Babulkar & Pandey Clinico-Radiological Staging of Hip Tuberculosis


Tuberculous Hip (final phase): The joint typically heals with fibrous ankylosis, resulting in a fibrous, immobile articulation.

Tuberculous Spine (final phase): Healing usually culminates in bony ankylosis, where the affected vertebrae fuse to form a solid bony block.

question_text: A 35-year-old patient presents with complaints of back pain, stiffness, and recurrent episodes of eye pain with redness. On examination, they are found to have anterior uveitis and sacroiliitis. Which of the following HLA is commonly involved?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical triad of inflammatory back pain, anterior uveitis, and sacroiliitis is highly suggestive of Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS), a classic seronegative spondyloarthropathy.There is a very strong association between AS and the HLA-B27 allele, which is present in approximately 90-95% of patients with this condition.

Ankylosing Spondylitis / Marie Strumpell Disease

  • It is a Chronic inflammatory disorder mainly affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints.
  • Leads to pain, stiffness, and eventual spinal fusion (bamboo spine).

Pathophysiology:

  • Inflammation at tendon and ligament attachment sites (entheses).
  • Erosive changes followed by new bone formation.
  • Formation of syndesmophytes results in spinal fusion.

Clinical Features:


Diagnosis:

  • Based on symptoms, imaging, and HLA-B27 status.

Clinical Criteria (Modified New York):

  • Low back pain for more than three months improving with activity.
  • Reduced lumbar spine motion.
  • Decreased chest expansion relative to age and sex.

Radiographic Criteria:

  • Bilateral sacroiliac joint inflammation (grade 2-4) or unilateral (grade 3-4).

Radiological Findings:

  • Sacroiliac joint haziness or blurring.
  • Sclerosis near joints.
  • Syndesmophytes and vertebral squaring.
  • Bamboo spine appearance.
  • Dagger sign, trolley track sign, Romanus lesions (shiny corners).

MRI:

  • Useful for early detection of inflammation.

Clinical Tests:

  • Sacroiliac joint: Gaenslen's, Patrick/FABER, Figure of four, Pump handle tests.
  • Lumbar spine: Schober and modified Schober tests.

Laboratory Tests:

  • HLA-B27 positivity in 90% of cases.
  • Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein during active disease, but may be normal.

Treatment:

Complications:

  • Fragile spinal fractures with minor trauma.
  • Heart issues including valve and conduction problems.
  • Osteoporosis increasing fracture risk.

Explanation of other options:
HLA DQB1 (Option A): Associated with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus and Celiac disease.


HLA DR3 (Option B): Associated with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, Myasthenia Gravis, and Sjogren's syndrome

.
HLA DR4 (Option D): Associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis and Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.

Key Takeaways:

  • Ankylosing Spondylitis is strongly linked to HLA-B27.
  • The classic presentation includes inflammatory back pain, sacroiliitis, and uveitis.

question_text: A 34-year-old male with ulcerative colitis presents with backache and morning stiffness, relieved by exercise. X-ray is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory arthritis primarily affecting the sacroiliac joints and spine. Patients typically present with inflammatory back pain and stiffness, which improves with activity. There is often an association with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Bamboo spine on imaging is a hallmark of advanced disease.

  • Clinical features:Chronic back pain, stiffness, loss of lumbar lordosis, enthesitis, and involvement of peripheral large joints.
  • Extra-articular manifestations:Anterior uveitis (most common), aortic regurgitation, and IBD.
  • Investigations:Positive HLA-B27, elevated ESR and CRP, MRI for early detection of sacroiliitis.
  • X-ray findings:Blurred joint margins, sclerosis, pseudowidening of sacroiliac joints, syndesmophytes, bamboo spine, and dagger sign.

Explanation of other options:

Pott's spine (Option A):

  • Tuberculous spondylitis affecting 1-2 vertebrae
  • Causes vertebral collapse and gibbus deformity
  • Usually focal pain, systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss)
  • Does notcause diffuse spinal stiffness or bamboo spine

Psoriatic arthritis (Option B):

  • Often asymmetric, involves distal interphalangeal joints
  • Features: dactylitis ('sausage digits'), nail pitting, skin lesions
  • Axial involvement less common than AS
  • Typically no strong association with ulcerative colitis

Rheumatoid arthritis (Option D):

  • Chronic symmetric arthritis of small joints of hands and feet
  • Rarely affects axial skeleton
  • Morning stiffness present, but does not improve significantly with activityin the same way as AS

Key Takeaways:

  • AS = HLA-B27 + sacroiliitis + bamboo spine.
  • Strongly linked with IBD.
  • Uveitis = most common extra-articular sign.

question_text: An elderly patient comes to the outpatient department (OPD) with the shown deformity. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image demonstrates a hand deformity with fingers deviating toward the ulnar side, a hallmark feature of rheumatoid arthritis (RA).

Explanations of other options:

Rickets (Option A): Rickets is caused by a lack of vitamin D, calcium, or phosphorus, leading to defective bone mineralisation. It typically manifests as bowed legs, stunted growth, and soft skull bones.

Osteomalacia (Option B): Osteomalacia is caused by inadequate vitamin D or calcium, resulting in bone softening, primarily in adults. It often presents with bone pain, muscle weakness, and an increased risk of fractures.

Osteoarthritis (Option C): Osteoarthritis is a chronic degenerative disorder of the joints that mainly involves the breakdown of articular cartilage, typically presenting with pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility.

question_text: FRAX is
explanation:
Explanation:

FRAX stands for Fracture Risk Assessment Tool.(Option B,C and D ruled out)

It is a calculator that estimates a person's 10-year probability of sustaining a major osteoporotic fracture (spine, hip, forearm, shoulder) or a hip fracture.

Purpose:

  • Estimates the likelihood of experiencing a major osteoporotic fracture or hip fracture within ten years.
  • Assists clinicians in making informed decisions for osteoporosis treatment.

Factors Considered:

  • Age: Fracture risk rises with advancing age.
  • Sex: Women are generally more susceptible due to lower bone density.
  • Height and weight
  • Previous fractures: Fractures after age 50 indicate higher future risk.
  • Family history: Hip fractures in parents increase personal risk.
  • Smoking: Tobacco use reduces bone density, increasing fracture probability.
  • Long-term steroid use: Chronic glucocorticoid therapy weakens bones.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis: Increases fracture risk via inflammation and steroid use.
  • Alcohol intake: More than three drinks per day elevates risk.
  • Bone mineral density: Lower measurements at the femoral neck or spine further increase risk.

Use of BMD in FRAX:

  • Without BMD: Risk is calculated using clinical factors alone.
  • With BMD: Incorporates T-score with clinical data for a more precise estimate.

Results:

  • Provides a 10-year fracture probability as a percentage.
  • Shows both absolute risk and risk relative to the general population.

Key Takeaways:

  • FRAX = Fracture Risk Assessment Tool.

References:

https://frax.shef.ac.uk/FRAX/tool.aspx?country=9

question_text: What is the most common Late complication of this condition, if left untreated?
explanation:
Explanation

The most common late complication of a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, if not properly managed, is cubitus varus, also known as "gunstock deformity."

  • Cause: Malunion following supracondylar fracture of the humerus (particularly extension-type).
  • Appearance: Loss or reversal of the normal carrying angle of the elbow.
  • Timing: Develops as a delayed complication after fracture healing.

Supracondylar fractures of the humerus

  • Mechanism of injury: Fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH).
  • Location: Just above the humeral condyles.
  • Displacement of distal fragment: Posterior shift and tilt, medial shift or tilt, and internal rotation are common.
  • Classification:
    • Type I: Undisplaced fracture
    • Type II: Partially displaced (anterior cortex displaced)
    • Type III: Completely displaced (anterior and posterior cortex)
  • Clinical features:
    • Pain, swelling, and deformity around the elbow
    • Possible nerve injury (most often anterior interosseous nerve, producing hand of benediction sign)
    • Dimple sign due to skin puckering
    • Posterior prominence of the olecranon (S-shaped deformity)
  • Radiographic findings:
    • Fat pad (sail sign) due to effusion
  • Disturbed teardrop sign
  • Crescent sign suggesting varus or valgus tilt
  • Fishtail sign showing irregular widened proximal fragment

Management

  • Undisplaced fractures: Immobilization in an above-elbow plaster slab at 90° flexion.
  • Displaced fractures:
    • Closed reduction and percutaneous K-wire fixation (Type II).
    • Open reduction and internal fixation with K-wires (Type III).
  • Late presentation with swelling: Managed with Dunlop's skin traction or Smith's skeletal traction.

Complications

  • Early: Brachial artery injury, nerve injuries, compartment syndrome (Volkmann's ischemia).
  • Delayed:
    • Cubitus varus (most common, due to malunion)
    • Elbow stiffness
    • Myositis ossificans
    • Volkmann's ischemia

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Pulled elbow (Option A): Refers to subluxation of the radial head, typically in children after a sudden pull on the hand. It is unrelated to supracondylar fractures.

Dinner fork deformity (Option B): Seen after a Colles' fracture of the distal radius, not after supracondylar humeral fractures.

Osteoarthritis (Option D): More common in weight-bearing joints or degenerative joint disease; not the most frequent late complication of supracondylar humerus fractures.

Key Takeaway:

The hallmark late complication of untreated supracondylar fractures of the humerus is cubitus varus (gunstock deformity), caused by malunion leading to loss of the carrying angle.

question_text: Apley's grinding test is used for identifying injuries of which of the following structure?
explanation:
Tests for intraarticular structures of knee

  • ACL: -
    1. Anterior drawer test
    2. Lachman test
    3. Pivot shift test
    4. Bounce home test
  • Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)-
    1. Posterior drawer test
    2. Godfrey’s sag sign
    3. Quadriceps active test
  • Menisci-
    1. McMurray test
    2. Thesaly test
    3. Ege’s test
    4. Apley’s grinding test- Apley’s grinding test involves placing the patient in the prone position with the knee flexed to 90 degrees. The patient’s thigh is then rooted to the examining table with the examiner’s knee. The examiner laterally and medially rotates the tibia, combined first with distraction, while noting any excessive movement, restriction or discomfort. The process is then repeated using compression instead of distraction. If rotation plus distraction is more painful or shows increased rotation relative to the normal side, the lesion is most likely to be ligamentous. If the rotation plus compression is more painful or shows decreased rotation relative to the normal side, the lesion is most likely to be a meniscus injury
  • Collateral ligament-
    • Varus stress test – LCL injury
    • Valgus stress tests – MCL injury
  • Posterolateral comer (PLC)-
    • Dial test
    • External rotation recurvatum test
    • Reverse pivot shift test

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 879.

question_text: Match the following
explanation:
• Neurapraxia (1) - c: Neurapraxia is a temporary block in nerve conduction, usually due to nerve compression or disrupted blood supply without structural damage to the axon.
  • Neurotmesis (2) - d: Neurotmesis is the most severe form of nerve injury, involving the complete destruction of the axon and surrounding encapsulated tissue. This requires surgical intervention for recovery.
  • Axonotmesis (3) - a: In axonotmesis, the axon itself is disrupted, but the surrounding connective tissue (nerve sheath) remains intact, allowing potential regeneration over time.
  • Denervation Hypersensitivity (4) - b: This occurs when there is post-synaptic upregulation of neurotransmitter receptors in response to loss of nerve input (denervation) leading to increased sensitivity.

Why Not Other Options:

  • B (1-d, 2-c, 3-a, 4-b): Incorrect because neurapraxia is not associated with destruction (d) but with compression (c).
  • C (1-a, 2-d, 3-c, 4-b): Incorrect as neurapraxia does not involve axonal disruption (a); this fits axonotmesis.
  • D (1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-c): Incorrect because neurapraxia involves compression, not hypersensitivity (b), and axonotmesis is related to axon disruption (a).

Key Takeaways:

  • Neurapraxia: Temporary, non-destructive nerve injury due to compression.
  • Neurotmesis: Complete nerve destruction requiring surgical repair.
  • Axonotmesis: Axonal disruption with potential for recovery.
  • Denervation Hypersensitivity: Upregulation of receptors after denervation leading to heightened response.

question_text: Match the following according to Seddon's classification for nerve injuries:
explanation:
Seddon's Classification of Nerve Injury

  1. Neuropraxia
    • Definition: The mildest form of nerve injury.
    • Characteristics:
      • Function: Temporary loss of nerve function.
      • Cause: Compression or stretching of the nerve.
      • Recovery: Complete recovery usually occurs within a few days to weeks.
      • Histological Findings: No significant axonal damage; myelin sheath may be affected.
  2. Axonotmesis
    • Definition: Moderate nerve injury.
    • Characteristics:
      • Function: Disruption of the axon with preservation of the nerve sheath.
      • Cause: More severe compression or stretching, causing axonal damage.
      • Recovery: Recovery is generally good with proper intervention, usually occurring over several months.
      • Histological Findings: Damage to the axon with degeneration of distal nerve fibers; the endoneurium remains intact.
  3. Neurotmesis
    • Definition: Severe nerve injury.
    • Characteristics:
      • Function: Complete severance of the nerve, including both the axon and the connective tissue structures.
      • Cause: Severe trauma such as lacerations or avulsions.
      • Recovery: Recovery is poor without surgical intervention, and even with surgery, functional recovery may be incomplete.
      • Histological Findings: Complete disruption of the nerve, including axon, myelin, and connective tissue structures (epineurium, perineurium, and endoneurium).

This classification helps in determining the appropriate management and predicting the potential for recovery based on the extent of never injury.

Key takeaways:

  • According to Seddon's classification, neuroma in continuity is classified in axonotmesis.
  • According to Sunderland's classification, neuroma in continuity is classified as a 4th degree injury.

question_text: A bowling champion presents with complaints of pain and difficult grasping from the dominant thumb. X Ray is normal but clinically it is diagnosed as bowler's thumb. Select true statement about the same:
option_a: 1st MCP joint arthritis due to bowling
explanation:
Bowler's Thumb

  1. Definition and Cause
    • Condition: Perineural fibrosis of the ulnar digital nerve of the thumb.
    • Cause: Repetitive compression of the nerve while grasping a bowling ball.
    • Affected Individuals: Typically bowlers who participate several times a week.
  2. Symptoms
    • Tingling and Hyperesthesia: Sensations of tingling and increased sensitivity around the pulp of the thumb.
    • Palpable Lump: A tender lump may be felt in the affected area.
    • Distal Skin Atrophy: Atrophy or thinning of the skin in the distal region of the thumb may occur.
  3. Management and Prevention
    • Early Awareness: Recognizing the condition early can help prevent worsening.
    • Protective Measures:
      • Shield or Splint: Using a shield or splint can protect the thumb from further compression.
      • Rest from Bowling: Taking a break from bowling allows the affected area to heal and reduces symptoms.
  4. Treatment Options
    • Neurolysis: In some cases, surgical intervention to release the nerve may be necessary.
    • Dorsal Transfer of the Nerve: This procedure may be considered to relieve compression and improve function if conservative measures are not effective.

Option A - 1st CMC is the second most common joint to undergo OA after the knee joint. But not seen in bowler's thumb.

Option B - Bowler's thumb refers to neuropathy of ulnar digital nerve of thumb

Option C - Gamekeeper's thumb refers to tear of ulnar collateral ligament at the 1st MCP joint.

Option D - EPL tenosynovitis is usually seen in cases of rheumatoid arthritis.

Key takeaways:

Bowlers thumb:

  • Perineural fibrosis of the ulnar digital nerve of the thumb due to repetitive movements.
  • Present with Tingling, Hyperesthesia and distal atrophy of skin.
  • Managed with Splint & Neurolysis if Required.

question_text: All of the following are true regarding brachial plexus injury except:
option_a: Dorsal scapular nerve is involved in C5 root lesion
option_b: Positive triple response after histamine injection is seen in pre ganglionic lesion
option_c: Normal SNAPs but loss of sensation on examination indicates postganglionic injury
option_d: Pseudomeningocele formation on MRI is characteristic of preganglionic lesions
explanation:
1. Importance of Anatomy:
    • Knowledge of brachial plexus anatomy is essential for evaluating and diagnosing brachial plexus lesions.
  2. Mechanism of Injury:
    • High-energy trauma is often associated with severe lesions, such as nerve root avulsions.
  3. Diagnosis:
    • Location and Severity Assessment:
      • Differentiate between supraclavicular and infraclavicular injuries.
    • Specific Indicators of Preganglionic Lesions (Nerve Root Avulsions):
      • Horner Sign (Sympathetic Chain Involvement): Ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis.
      • Winged Scapula: Due to involvement of the long thoracic nerve affecting the serratus anterior muscle.
      • Weak Rhomboids: Due to involvement of the dorsal scapular nerve.
      • Motor Deficits with Intact Sensory Function: Indicates that cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia are intact.
      • Electromyography (EMG): Shows loss of innervation to paraspinal muscles.
      • Elevated Hemidiaphragm: Indicates phrenic nerve involvement.
    • Radiographic Evaluation:
      • Complete imaging series including cervical spine, chest, and shoulder girdle.
      • Inspiratory and expiratory chest radiographs to detect paralyzed hemidiaphragm.
      • Transverse spinal process fractures may indicate nerve root avulsions.
      • Scapulothoracic dissociation is often linked to multiple root avulsions and major vascular injury.
    • Advanced Imaging:
      • CT Myelography: Detects nerve root avulsions.
      • MRI: Identifies peripheral neuromas, pseudomeningoceles, and mass lesions.
    • Electrodiagnostic Studies:
      • EMG: Evaluates injury extent, denervation (fibrillation potentials), and monitors recovery.
      • Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS): Assesses injury extent and monitors recovery.
      • Sensory Nerve Action Potentials (SNAPs): Normal SNAPs with loss of sensation on examination indicate preganglionic injury.
      • Somatosensory Evoked Potentials (SSEPs): Assesses nerve root continuity; performed 4–6 weeks after injury (Wallerian degeneration).

Option A - Dorsal scapular nerve arises from ventral ramus of C5 root.

Option B - Histamine test is normal (positive triple response of vasodilation, wheal formation and flare) in preganglionic injuries but in post ganglionic injuries flare is absent.

Option C - Normal SNAPs but loss of sensation on examination indicates preganglionic

Option D - MRI shows pseudomeningocele formation in preganglionic lesions.

Key takeaways:

Brachial Plexus Preganglionic Injury:

  • Normal Histamine test
  • Normal SNAP But loss of sensation.
  • Psuedomeningocele on MRI

question_text: All of these are potential sites of compression of median nerve leading to pronator syndrome except:
explanation:
(Option A) - Osborne ligament compresses the ulnar nerve.

Pronator Syndrome

  • Definition: Compression of the median nerve in the arm/forearm.
  • Potential Sites of Compression:
    • Supracondylar Process:
      • Anterior distal humerus.
      • Seen on lateral radiograph.
      • Present in ∼1% of the population.
    • Ligament of Struthers:
      • Courses between the supracondylar process and medial epicondyle.
    • Bicipital Aponeurosis (Lacertus Fibrosus).
    • FDS Aponeurotic Arch.
    • Between the Two Heads of the Pronator Teres Muscle.
  • Differentiation from Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS):
    • Pronator Syndrome:
      • Proximal volar forearm pain.
      • Sensory disturbances in the distribution of the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve over the thenar region.
      • Decreased sensation over the thenar region.
    • CTS:
      • Normal sensation over the thenar eminence.
  • Provocative Tests:
    • Resisted elbow flexion with forearm supinated (Bicipital Aponeurosis).
    • Resisted forearm pronation with elbow extended (Pronator Teres).
    • Resisted long finger PIP joint flexion (FDS).
  • Nonoperative Treatment:
    • Activity modification.
    • Splints
    • NSAIDs
  • Surgical Treatment (if nonoperative management fails):
    • Release of all potential sites of compression.
    • Success rate is approximately 80% in most series.
  • Associated Conditions:
    • Often associated with medial epicondylitis.

Option B, C & D: Ligament of struthers, Lacertus Fibrosus and FDS Aponeurotic arch all compress median nerve in Pronator syndrome.

Key takeaways

Pronator syndrome - Compression of the median nerve in the arm/forearm.

Potential sites of compression (mnemonic: SLAPS)

  • Supracondylar process: Anterior distal humerus seen on lateral radiograph, in ∼1% of the population
  • Ligament of Struthers: Courses between the supracondylar process and medial epicondyle (Option D)
  • Bicipital aponeurosis (Lacertus fibrosus) (Option B)
  • FDS Aponeurotic Arch (Option C)
  • Between the two heads of Pronator teres muscle

question_text: Which of the following is true regarding nerve grafting?
option_c: Fibrin glue is used during repair
option_d: Anterior interosseous nerve and saphenous nerve used as graft
explanation:
Explanation:
Autologous nerve grafting (most commonly sural nerve) bridges segmental defectsin peripheral nerves when tension-free end-to-end repair isn't possible. This restores continuity for axonal regeneration. Adjuncts such as fibrin glue may be used but do not replace micro sutures. Donor nerves are usually sensory (sural, medial/lateral antebrachial cutaneous)

Explanation of other options:
Used in facial nerve repair (Option B): True in principle (interposition/cable grafts may be used). Not the single best answer vs A, which states the core indication across orthopaedics.
Fibrin glue is used during repair (Option C): Adjunctively true-fibrin glue can reinforce coaptation but does not replace micro sutures; selection depends on surgeon preference.
Anterior interosseous nerve and saphenous nerve used as graft (Option D): Incorrect. Typical donor grafts are sural, medial antebrachial cutaneous, lateral antebrachial cutaneous. AIN is a motor branch (used as a donor nerve for transfers, not as a free graft). 'Saphenous' generally refers to a vein used as a conduit, not the nerve as a standard graft.

question_text: Which of the following is the last symptom to develop in compartment syndrome?
explanation:
The limbs contain muscles in compartments enclosed by bones, fascia and interosseous membrane. A rise in pressure within these compartments due to any reason may jeopardize the blood supply to the muscles and nerves within the compartment, resulting in what is known as “compartment syndrome

Compartment syndrome can be diagnosed early by high index of suspicion. Excessive pain, not relieved with usual doses of analgesics, in a patient with an injury known to cause compartment syndrome must raise an alarm in the mind of the treating doctor. Injuries with a high risk of developing compartment syndrome are as follows:

  • Supracondylar fracture of the humerus
  • Forearm bone fractures
  • Closed tibial fractures
  • Crush injuries to leg and forearm.

Diagnosis of compartment syndrome

  • Normotensive patient
    • Compartment pressure >30 mmHg
  • Hypotensive patient

Delta P (diastolic BP - compartment pressure) <30mmHg

5 p's of compartment syndrome

Pain out of proportion to exam, paresthesias, pallor, pulselessness, paralysis.

Paralysis is last symptom to develop in compartment syndrome.

Reference:Essential orthopedics by Maheshwari 7thedition page no 48.

Meralgia Paresthetica: Overview

Definition:
Meralgia paresthetica is a condition characterized by tingling, burning, and numbness in the skin supplied by the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, which becomes entrapped in the fascia near the anterior superior iliac spine. (Option A)

Causes:

  • Compression Factors: Tight belts, excessive abdominal pannus, and prolonged hip flexion.

Diagnosis:

  • Clinical Evaluation: Based on symptoms and physical examination.
  • Imaging: MRI or CT to rule out other causes.

Treatment:

  • Conservative Measures: Release of compressive devices, postural exercises.
  • Medications: NSAIDs and analgesics for pain relief.
  • Local Treatments: Hydrocortisone injections.
  • Surgical Intervention: Considered if conservative treatments fail.

Prognosis:

  • Most cases improve with non-specific treatments and lifestyle modifications. Surgical decompression may be needed for persistent symptoms.

Option A: Meralgia paresthetica is due to compressive neuropathy of Lateral Cutaneous Nerve of thigh.

question_text: Another name of reflex sympathetic dystrophy in modern orthopaedics is:
explanation:
Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)

  1. Definition and General Features:
    • Abnormal and Excessive Limb Pain: CRPS is characterized by intense and disproportionate pain in a limb.
    • Changes in the Limb: The affected limb shows various changes, including early signs of inflammation.
    • Early Features of Inflammation:
      • Swelling: The limb often becomes swollen.
      • Vasomotor Dysfunction: Abnormalities in blood vessel regulation, leading to changes in skin color and temperature.
      • Sudomotor Dysfunction: Altered sweating patterns in the affected limb.
    • Progression: Over time, inflammation may recede but lead to persistent issues such as:
      • Contracture: Stiffening and shortening of muscles or tendons.
      • Osteoporosis: Thinning of the bone in the affected area.
  2. Types of CRPS
    • CRPS1
      • Former Name: Reflex Sympathetic Dystrophy (RSD). (Option A)
      • Characteristics: No demonstrable nerve damage is observed.
      • Prevalence: More common compared to CRPS2.
      • Prognosis: Generally guarded; recovery can be variable.
    • CRPS2 (Option B)
      • Former Name: Causalgia. (Option D)
      • Characteristics: Identifiable nerve damage is present.
      • Prognosis: Typically very poor, with a less favorable outcome.
  3. Sudek's Osteodystrophy (Option C)
    • Feature of CRPS: This condition is associated with CRPS.
    • Characteristics: Osteoporosis in the bones of the affected region, contributing to bone weakening and increased fracture risk.

Key takeaways:

  • Former name of CRPS 2 is causalgia
  • Former name of CRPS 1 is RSD

question_text: Book test is used to assess the function of adductor pollicis, Which of the following nerves supplies the muscle?

Median Nerve Anatomy and Course

Formation and General Course:

  • Formation: The median nerve is formed by the joining of branches from the lateral and medial cords of the brachial plexus.
  • Arm: It descends adjacent to the brachial artery.

Course in the Forearm:

  1. Entry:
    • Enters the forearm between the two heads of the pronator teres.
  2. Initial Path:
    • Passes deep to the tendinous bridge of the flexor digitorum superficialis in the proximal third of the forearm.
  3. Mid-Forearm:
    • Descends between the flexor digitorum superficialis and flexor digitorum profundus.
  4. Pre-Wrist:
    • Approximately 5 cm above the wrist, it lies on the lateral side of the flexor digitorum superficialis.
  5. Near Wrist:
    • Becomes superficial just above the wrist, lying between the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis and flexor carpi radialis.

Course in the Hand:

  1. Entry to Palm:
    • Passes deep to the flexor retinaculum to enter the palm.
  2. Muscular Branches:
    • A short, stout muscular branch supplies the thenar eminence muscles:
      • Abductor pollicis brevis
      • Opponens pollicis
      • Flexor pollicis brevis
  3. Digital Branches:
    • Divides into 4 to 5 palmar digital branches supplying the skin of the palm.
    • Provides motor branches to the first and second lumbrical muscles.
    • Option A, B and C: FCR, FPL & FDS are supplied by the median nerve.
    • Option D - FCU is supplied by the ulnar nerve.

Key takeaways:

  • Median nerve is known as labourer's nerve as it supplies strong flexors of the forearm which are required for powerful activities.
  • Ulnar nerve is known as a musician's nerve as it supplies small intrinsic muscles of hand required for fine movements.
  • Radial nerve supplies the extensors of the wrist and hand in the forearm.

question_text: If the outer sheath and nerve fibre is intact and the inner axon are damaged, it is known as
explanation:
Seddon's classification: Seddon classifies nerve injuries into three types:

  1. neurapraxia;
  2. axonotmesis; and
  3. neurotmesis.

Neurapraxia: It is a physiological disruption of conduction in the nerve fibre. No structural changes occur. Recovery occurs spontaneously within a few weeks, and is complete.best prognosis. Eg- Saturday night palsy, crutch palsy, tourniquet palsy etc.

Axonotmesis: The axons are damaged but atleast one of the outer coverings of nerve intact. . Wallerian degeneration occurs. Recovery may occur spontaneously but may take many months. Complete recovery may not occur. Neuroma in continuity (progressive tinel's sign present). Rate of regeneration - 1mm/day. Motor march is seen.

Neurotmesis: The structure of a nerve is damaged by actual cutting or scarring of a segment. Wallerian degeneration occurs. Spontaneous recovery is not possible, and nerve repair is required. End neuroma, non progressive tinel's sign, motor march is absent. Worst prognosis

Reference: CAMPBELL OPERATIVE ORTHOPEDICS 14THEDITION PAGE NO 3277+ROCKWOOD AND GREENS FRACTURE IN ADULTS 9THEDITION PAGE NO 1136.

question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents with tingling sensation in the lateral 3 digits along with loss of sensation at the base of the thumb. Which nerve is most likely involved?
explanation:
Explanation:

The median nerve supplies sensation to the lateral three and a half fingers (thumb, index, middle, and half of the ring finger) on the palmar side and also controls the thenar muscles (except adductor pollicis).

Key Features in This Case:

  • Tingling in lateral three digits → Median nerve involvement
  • Loss of sensation at the base of the thumb → Affects the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve, which arises before the carpal tunnel
  • Suggestive of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) → Compression of the median nerve at the wrist
  • Median nerve is Involved in carpal tunnel syndrome, causing tingling in the lateral three digits and thenar sensation loss.

Explanation of other options:

Radial nerve (Option A): Supplies sensation to the dorsum of the hand and controls wrist extension, but does not affect the palmar lateral three fingers.

Ulnar nerve (Option B): Supplies medial 1.5 fingers (ring & little finger), affecting grip strength (intrinsic hand muscles).

Anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) (Option D): A branch of the median nerve but purely motor, affecting flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus, and lateral FDP, with no sensory loss.

Key Takeaways:

The median nerve is responsible for sensation in the lateral three and a half fingers and can be compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome, leading to tingling and sensory loss at the base of the thumb.

question_text: This test is done to identify which nerve injury?
explanation:
• Test shown in image is PEN TEST. used to check function of abductor pollicis longus which is supplied by MEDIAN NERVE.
  • Muscles of the thenar eminence: Out of the three muscles of the thenar eminence, only two can be examined for their isolated action.
  • These are as follows:
  • Abductor pollicis brevis: The action of this muscle is to draw the thumb forwards at right angle to the palm. The patient is asked to lay his hand flat on the table with palm facing the ceiling. A pen is held above the thumb and the patient is asked to touch the pen with tip of his thumb. This is called the 'pen test'
  • Opponens pollicis: The function of this muscle is to oppose the tip of the thumb to other fingers. Apposition is a swinging movement of the thumb across the palm and not a simple adduction. The latter movement is by the adductor pollicis muscle supplied by the ulnar nerve.
  • Major motor branches of the median nerve
    • In the arm - Nil
    • In the forearm - All the flexor muscles of the Proximal forearm, except the flexor carpi ulnaris and medial -half of the flexor digitorum profundus
    • In the hand - Thenar muscles*(three) First two lumbricals
  • The three muscles are flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis and abductor pollicis. Adductor pollicis is not supplied by median nerve

question_text: Most sensitive test for Anterior cruciate ligament tear?
explanation:
• LACHMAN TEST is the most sensitive test for ACL tear,
    • It is done with the knee flexed at 20 degrees, stabilizing the distal femur with one hand and pulling forward on the proximal tibia with the other hand. With an intact ligament minimal translation of the tibia occurs and a firm end point is felt, however with a torn ACL, more translation is noted and the end point is soft or mushy.
    • Further, Lachman test is more comfortable and painless for the patient in comparison to all the other tests, especially in an acute setting.
  • ANTERIOR -DRAWER TEST - is done with the knee at 90° degree of flexion and is not as sensitive as Lachman test but serves as an adjunct in the evaluation of ACL instability
  • Mc murray test and the Apley’s grinding test are used for identifying meniscus tears.
  • Few important points in knee injuries.
    • Blood supply of ACL is primarily derived from Middle genicular artery
    • Anterior cruciate ligament prevents anterior translation and rotation of the tibia on the femur
    • Posterior cruciate ligament prevents posterior subluxation of the tibia on the femur
    • Investigation of choice in Knee joint injury is MRI.
    • Medial meniscus has less mobility than the lateral meniscus and is more susceptible tearing when trapped between the femoral condyle and tibial plateau. Hence medial meniscus in the most commonly injured meniscus.
    • Coronary ligament of the knee are ligaments connecting the menisci to tibia.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 879.

question_text: Below Figure shows an MRI image of an anatomical structure labelled in red. What would be the most appropriate treatment modality if this structure was acutely injured, in isolation, resulting in a partial tear?
option_a: Cast immobilization and non-weight bearing for 2-4 weeks
option_b: Cast immobilization and non-weight bearing for 6-8 weeks
explanation:
• Figure A shows a coronal and axial MRI image of the ankle. The red structure is the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL). The most appropriate treatment of an acute partial or complete ATFL injury would be physical therapy for peroneal strengthening and proprioception.
  • The anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) is the most commonly involved ligament in low ankle sprains.
  • Partial tears of the ATFL are usually categorized as Grade I injuries; which means there is no frank ligamentous disruption and the ankle is relatively stable on examination.
  • Treatment consists of RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation), early protected weight-bearing, and when comfortable, physical therapy for peroneal strengthening and proprioception.
  • Anatomic reconstruction or tendon transfers may be considered if patients continue to have pain and instability despite extensive nonoperative management.
  • Incorrect Answers:
    • Answers A, B: Cast immobilization and non-weight bearing are not recommended. Bracing has been shown to be effective during sport, but weight bearing is recommended.
    • Answer D: Early arthroscopic exploration and repair would not be warranted in an acute, isolated, ATFL injury. Arthroscopy may be indicated in acute or recurrent ankle sprains caused by anteriorinferior tibiofibular ligament impingement or posteromedial impingement lesions of the ankle.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 1261.

question_text: A 28-year-old male laborer suffered a left ankle injury 4 months ago at work while unloading a dolly. He notes difficulty walking and pain with ambulating. Physical exam shows an inability to toe walk on the left, as well as the finding demonstrated in Figure. What other test will be positive and which procedure will likely best result in the restoration of power and function?
option_a: Thompson test, primary repair with synthetic graft augmentation
option_c: Thompson test, VY advancement with tendon transfer
option_d: Thessaly test, VY advancement with tendon transfer
explanation:
• This patient has a chronic Achilles tendon rupture. He would have a positive Thompson (Simmonds) test and would most benefit from a V-Y advancement with FHL tendon transfer given the chronicity of the injury.
  • Chronic Achilles tendon ruptures are challenging conditions for both the patient and surgeon. Functional rehab has shown to be effective for acute ruptures but there seems to be a little role for this in chronic cases unless medical co-morbidities preclude surgery.
  • Primary repairs of chronic injuries are difficult to achieve due to scarring and tendon stump retraction. Instead, local tissue augmentation such as VY advancements allows functional lengthening of the tendon to span this gap. Additionally, tendon transfers allow restoration of plantarflexion strength, with the FHL tendon being the most common transfer.
  • Incorrect Answers:
    • Answer 1: Synthetic graft augmentation has not shown a significant benefit for Achilles ruptures.
    • Answer 2: The Thomas test evaluates for hip flexion contractures.
    • Answer 4: The Thessaly test evaluates for meniscal pathology.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 921.

question_text: Which of the following injuries would require plating of the radius along with closed reduction and evaluation of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ)?

question_text: Most common cause of tardy ulnar nerve palsy is?
option_a: Nonunion fracture lateral condyle of humerus

question_text: All of the following are potential sites of ulnar nerve entrapment leading to cubital tunnel syndrome except:
explanation:
Option B- Ligament of struthers compresses median nerve and not ulnar nerve.

Cubital Tunnel Syndrome

  • Prevalence: Second most common upper extremity compression neuropathy.
  • Anatomy:
    • Floor: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) and elbow joint capsule.
    • Walls: Medial epicondyle and olecranon.
    • Roof: Flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) fascia and arcuate ligament of Osborne.
  • External Compression Sources:
    • Tumors, ganglions, osteophytes, heterotopic ossification (HO), medial epicondyle nonunion.
  • Associations:
    • Burns, cubitus valgus, medial epicondylitis, repetitive elbow stress.
  • Differential Diagnosis:
    • Thoracic outlet syndrome, cervical radiculopathy (C8–T1).
  • Symptoms:
    • Paresthesias in the ulnar 1½ digits and dorsal ulnar hand.
  • Provocative Tests:
    • Cubital tunnel compression, Tinel test, prolonged elbow hyperflexion.
  • Examination Findings:
    • Motor Weakness Signs:
      • Froment Sign: Thumb IP joint flexion during key pinch.
      • Jeanne Sign: Thumb MCP hyperextension with key pinch.
      • Wartenberg Sign: Persistent abduction/extension of small digit.
      • Masse Sign: Flattening of palmar arch and loss of ulnar hand elevation.
    • Atrophy: Interosseous and first web space.
  • Diagnostic Tests:
    • Electrodiagnostic tests with conduction velocity <50 m/sec across elbow indicate diagnosis.
  • Nonoperative Treatment:
    • Activity modification, night splints, FCU stretching, NSAIDs.
  • Surgical Options:
    • Techniques: In situ decompression, anterior transposition, medial epicondylectomy.
    • Outcomes: No significant difference between simple decompression and transposition if no ulnar nerve instability. Higher recurrence rate than carpal tunnel release.
  • Postoperative Considerations:
    • Persistent pain may be due to neuroma formation from iatrogenic injury.

Option A, C & D: Ulnar nerve is compressed by the medial head of triceps, Osborne ligaments and Arcade of Struthers.

Key takeaways

Cubital tunnel syndrome & Sites of compression (mnemonic: AO TEAM)

  • Arcade of Struthers: fascial thickening at hiatus of the medial intermuscular septum as the ulnar nerve passes from anterior to posterior compartment. Location: ≈8 cm proximal to the medial epicondyle
  • Osborne ligament
  • Medial head of Triceps
  • Anconeus Epitrochlearis: Anomalous muscle originating from medial olecranon and inserted on the medial epicondyle
  • Aponeurosis of the proximal edge of FDS or two heads of FCU
  • Medial intermuscular septum

question_text: Anterior cruciate ligament acts by preventing which of the following?
explanation:
• The primary function of ACL is to prevent anterior translation of tibia with respect to femur.
  • ACL takes origin from medial wall of lateral femoral condyle (posteriorly in the area of the inter-condylar notch) and courses anteriorly and medially to insert on the inter-condylar area of the tibia.
  • The ACL is critically important because it prevents the tibia from being pushed too far anterior relative to the femur. It is often torn during twisting or hyperextension injuries of the knee.
  • ACL tear is treated with ACL reconstruction. ACL reconstruction is most commonly done using autograft, meaning, the tissue used for repair is taken from the patient’s body itself. The two most common sources for tissue are the patellar tendon and hamstrings tendon.
  • The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) stretches from medial condyle of femur to the posterior intercondylar area.
  • This ligament prevents posterior displacement of the tibia relative to the femur.

Reference- Maheshwari, 5th ed. pg. 148-149

question_text: A 16-year-old gymnast presents to the emergency department after landing awkwardly on her ankle subsequent to dismounting from the parallel bars. She reports that she felt her ankle 'roll inward,' essentially inverting her ankle as a result of a misaligned axial load. On physical examination of the injured ankle, there appears to be a forward displacement of the talus. Which of the following ligaments has she most likely injured?
explanation:
• The lateral ligaments of the foot are more commonly injured than the medial ligaments since they are weaker.
    • The anterior talofibular ligament is the most common of the lateral ligaments to be injured. In fact ATFL is the most commonly injured ligament in the human body.
    • Injuries to the ligaments about the ankle usually result from inversion and internal rotation of the foot combined with ankle plantar flexion.
    • With complete disruption of the anterior talofibular ligament, forward displacement of the talus in the ankle mortise is present.
    • Lateral ankle sprains represent of all sports-related traumatic lesions
  • The anterior talofibular ligament is the weakest ligament and the therefore are the most frequently torn.
  • There is usually a predictable pattern of progression injury that we see in the ankle. The first ligament to be injured is the anterior talofibular ligament followed by the calcaneofibular ligament and finally, the posterior talofibular ligament.
  • So, ligament strains of ankle are of 3 types based on this progression
    • First-degree sprain is characterized by a partial or complete tear of the anterior talofibular ligament
    • In second- degree sprain both the anterior talofibular and calcaneofibular ligaments are either partially or completely torn.
    • Third-degree sprain consists of injuries to the anterior talofibular, calcaneofibular, and posterior talofibular ligaments.
  • Option B is incorrect. The calcaneofibular ligament is a lateral ligament that is injured frequently, but less frequently than the anterior talofibular ligament.
  • Option C is incorrect. The lateral ligaments are more commonly injured than the medial ligaments since they are weaker. The talonavicular ligament is a medial ligament so it is much less likely to be injured.
  • Option D is incorrect. The lateral ligaments are more commonly injured than the medial ligaments since they are weaker. The tibiocalcaneal ligament is a medial ligament so it is much less likely to be injured.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 1261.

question_text: A 24-year-old male was involved in a motorcycle crash and sustained the injury shown in Figure A. In the trauma bay it was noted that the patient could not extend his wrist. What artery runs with his injured nerve?
explanation:
• The patient has a Holstein-Lewis fracture or fracture of the distal one-third of the humeral shaft associated with neuropraxia of the radial nerve. The profunda brachii artery runs with the radial nerve.
  • The profunda artery and radial nerve exit the triangular interval between the long head of the triceps and the humerus and travel in the spiral groove distally.
  • The nerve crosses the spiral groove and pierces the intermuscular septa 7.5cm proximal to the elbow joint.
  • In this region, the nerve is at risk of injury during humeral shaft fractures.
  • A radial nerve palsy would present with an inability to extend the wrist, thumb and fingers.
  • The vast majority(80-90%) of radial nerve injuries in the setting of humeral shaft fractures recover with expectant management and as such radial nerve injury is not an indication for operative management.
  • Answer 2: The posterior circumflex humeral artery runs with the axillary nerve in the quadrangular space.
  • Answer 3: The scapular circumflex artery runs in the triangular space, without a major nerve.
  • Answer 4: The brachial artery runs on the medial aspect of the arm in close proximity to the ulnar and median nerves.

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th edition, Page no. 94.

question_text: All of the following are possible sites of compression for the ulnar nerve EXCEPT:
explanation:
• Here are five sites of potential ulnar nerve entrapment around the elbow: arcade of Struthers, medial intermuscular septum, medial epicondyle, cubital tunnel and deep flexor pronator aponeurosis.
  • The ulnar nerve emerges from the medial intermuscular septum, under the arcade of Struthers and lies on the medial head of the triceps.
  • At the level of the elbow, the ulnar nerve continues distally toward the posterior aspect of the condylar groove, passing between the medial epicondyle and olecranon to enter the cubital tunnel.
  • The roof is formed by the arcuate(Osborne's) ligament.
  • This ligament blends distally with the antebrachial fascia superficial to the aponeurosis and connects the ulnar and humeral heads of the FCU.
  • The ligament of Struthers is a fibrous band extending from the supracondylar process of the humerus to the medial epicondyle which can cause compression of the median nerve.

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th edition, Page no. 67.

question_text: Guyon's canal is entrapment neuropathy site for which nerve?
explanation:
• Important Sites of Compression for ulnar nerve
  • Arm
    • Arcade of Struthers(the arcade is a thin aponeurotic band lying approximately 8 cm above medial epicondyle, extending from medial head of triceps to the medial intermuscular septum) may be a compression site in cases where a transposition of ulnar nerve has been done as a surgical treatment(not a site in ordinary cases).
  • Elbow
    • Behind medial epicondyle: Cubitus valgus deformity(tardy ulnar nerve palsy) or compression in the cubital tunnel(most common site) when the nerve passes between two heads of FCU.
  • Hand
    • Guyon's canal

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th edition, Page no. 67.

question_text: Cheiralgia paraesthetica is compression neuropathy of which nerve

  • Carpal tunnel syndrome - Median nerve at wrist
  • Pronator syndrome - Median nerve between two heads of pronator teres

question_text: Wrist Drop is a feature of -
explanation:
A) High radial nerve palsy:

This occurs if the nerve is injured in the radial groove.

In this type, all the muscles supplied by radial nerve except the triceps and anconeus are paralysed.

Occasionally, the radial nerve may be injured still higher up, in which case even the triceps may be paralysed. This is called very high radial nerve palsy

B) Low radial nerve palsy:

This occurs if the nerve is injured around the elbow so that the muscles supplied by the radial nerve in the distal arm (brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis) are spared

Low radial nerve palsy may be of two types:

  1. Type I: Injury occurs between the spiral groove and elbow joint.
    1. Muscles involvement is-
      • Elbow extensors(Triceps, anconeus) are spared.
      • Wrist, elbow and finger extensors are paralysed.
      • Sensory loss in first web space(on dorsal side)
  2. ii) Type II: Injury occurs below the elbow joint.
    1. Elbow extensors(triceps, anconeus), Brachioradialis and wrist extensors(ECRL) are spared.
    2. Finger extensors(extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor indicis) and thumb extensors (extensor pollicis longus & brevis) are paralysed.
    3. Sensory loss in first web space(on dorsal side).
      • Clinical features depend upon the site of lesion.
        1. If lesion is high
          • Wrist drop, thumb drop and finger drop.
          • Inability to extend elbow, wrist, thumb & fingers(MP joint)
          • Patient can extend interphalangeal joints due to action of lumbricals and interossei.
          • Sensory loss over posterior surface of arm & forearm and lower lateral half of forearm.
        2. If lesion is low
          • Type I - Wrist drop, thumb drop and finger drop. Elbow extension is preserved. Sensory loss over the dorsum of first web space,
          • Type II - Thumb drop and finger drop Elbow and wrist extension is preserved Sensory loss over the dorsum of first web space.

Reference: Campbell's, 12th ed, Pg: 3100.

question_text: Ulnar paradox is due to
explanation:
Ulnar Paradox:

  • Going by common sense, one would expect that high palsy is associated with greater paralysis and hence should have more clawing while the reverse should be expected in low palsy.
  • However, what is seen is absolutely opposite.
  • Low lesions have greater paralysis than high lesions. this is due to preserved long finger flexor function in low ulnar nerve palsy, as when the injury is distal to elbow many a times the FDP gets spared and causes exaggerated flexion of DIPs, accentuating clawing.

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th edition, Pg: 204.

question_text: In lateral meniscal repair, which structure is at risk?
explanation:
• While repairing lateral meniscus tears, we have to take sutures on the lateral aspect of the knee. Sometimes these sutures pass very close to the head and neck of the fibula putting the common peroneal N at risk.
  • Structures at risk in meniscus repair
    • Medial meniscal repair: Saphenous nerve and vein.
    • In lateral meniscal repair:
      1. Peroneal nerve
      2. Lateral geniculate artery is as it traverses through the posterolateral aspect of capsule at the lateral joint line.
      3. Popliteal vessels are at risk in repair of the posterior horn of lateral meniscus.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 905.

question_text: The picture given below shows a hand following a nerve injury. Identify the nerve:
explanation:
Ulnar Claw Hand:

  • The deformity in the picture is Partial Claw Hand, i.e., Hyperextension of MCP joints and Hyperflexion of interphalangeal joints of ring and little fingers.
  • Clawing of fingers is caused by Lumbrical muscle paralysis. It is also called as Intrinsic Minus Deformity or Duchenne's sign.
  • Lumbricals of little finger and ring figer are supplied by Ulnar nerve.
  • Lumbricals of Index finger and Middle finger are supplied by Median nerve.
  • The ulnar nerve palsy causes partial claw hand involving little and ring fingers; Ulnar nerve and Median Nerve combined injury causes Total claw hand involving all four fingers
  • Knuckle bender splint is used to correct the claw hand deformity.

Reference: Maheshwari Essentials Orthopedics, 5th ed, Pg: 67.

question_text: Identify the object in the given image:
explanation:
Dynamic cock up splint –

A dynamic cock-up splint supports wrist extension while allowing finger movement, commonly used for conditions like wrist drop, radial nerve palsy, or post-stroke rehabilitation.

Features:

  • Spring Mechanism: Assists wrist extension.
  • Adjustable Support: Customizable wrist angle.
  • Functional Design: Stabilizes the wrist while enabling hand movement.

This splint aids in rehabilitation by promoting muscle re-education and preventing contractures, improving daily function as the flexor muscles work well to passively extend the wrist and fingers after active flexion using springs and rubber bands.

Use:

  • Radial nerve injury commonly occurs in humeral shaft fractures especially at the junction of middle and lower thirds of the shaft called the Holstein-Lewis fractures. Most of these injuries are neuropraxia injuries and do not warrant any urgent/active intervention.
  • Radial nerve injury results in wrist and finger drop. Hence Cock-up or Dynamic cock up splints are advised till recovery is achieved to keep the wrist in extension.
  • Dynamic splint gives added advantage of passive finger extension after active flexion hence preventing contractures.

Option A: Cock up splint – Also used in radial nerve palsy. It just keeps the wrist and finger extended. No moving parts are involved.

Option B: VIC splint – Helps to release contracture gradually in VIC.

Key Takeaway -

  • Radial nerve injury commonly occurs in humeral shaft fractures especially at the junction of middle and lower thirds of the shaft called the Holstein-Lewis fractures. Most of these injuries are neuropraxia injuries and do not warrant any urgent/active intervention.
  • Radial nerve injury results in wrist and finger drop. Hence Cock-up or Dynamic cock up splints are advised till recovery is achieved to keep the wrist in extension.
  • Dynamic splint gives added advantage of passive finger extension after active flexion hence preventing contractures.

question_text: Nerve tested by using Clinical test shown in Photograph?
explanation:
• Test shown in the image is to check ulnar nerve palsy and it is called FROMENT SIGN.
  • The patient is asked to grasp a book between the thumb and index finger.
  • Normally, a person will grasp the book firmly with thumb extended, taking full advantage of the adductor pollicis and the first dorsal interosseous muscles.
  • If the ulnar nerve is injured, the adductor pollicis will be paralysed and the patient will hold the book by using the flexor pollicis longus(supplied by median nerve) in place of the adductor.
  • This produces flexion at the inter-phalangeal joint of the thumb This becomes more pronounced if the examiner tries to pull the book out while the patient tries to hold it.
  • This sign is known as 'Froment's sign' or the 'book test'.

  • For ulnar nerve remember:
    • Adductor pollicus
    • Book test - for adductor pollicis
    • Card test - to check palmar interossei
    • Egawa test - to check dorsal interossei
    • Froment sign.

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 7th edition, Page no. 67.

question_text: True about articular cartilage is
explanation:
• Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage
  • It does not have a perichondrium
  • It is avascular
  • It also lacs any nerve supply, hence making it insensitive to pain. So, in arthritic conditions, it is the subchondral bone which gets exposed due to damage to the articular cartilage that causes all the pain.

question_text: A 27-year-old woman got her arm injured as she placed her upper limb outside the window of a moving vehicle and sustained a spiral lower third humerus fracture. She is unable to actively extend her wrist or long fingers and notes numbness in her first dorsal web space. What is the most likely cause of her nerve dysfunction?
option_b: Stretch injury from the fracture displacement
option_c: Crush injury from impact with the vehicle
option_d: Vascular injury from interruption of the blood supply
explanation:
Commonest complication of Humeral Shaft Fractures

Nerve Injury

  • Commonly Affected Nerve: Radial nerve
    • Type of Injury: Typically neurapraxia (stretching leading to temporary nerve damage). (Option A,B,C and D)
    • Causes of Injury:
      • At the time of fracture.
      • During manipulation of the fracture.
      • During healing (nerve entrapment in the callus).
  • Special Fracture Type:
    • Holstein-Lewis Fracture:
      • A spiral fracture at the junction of the middle and distal third of the humerus.
      • Frequently associated with radial nerve palsy.
  • Clinical Presentation:
    • Motor Deficits:
      • Paralysis of wrist, finger, and thumb extensors (wrist drop).
      • Paralysis of brachioradialis and supinator muscles.
    • Sensory Changes:
      • Loss of sensation in a small area on the radial side of the back of the hand (first dorsal web space).

Treatment

  • Early Cases:
    • Closed Fractures: Nerve usually recovers spontaneously.
    • Open Fractures: Surgical exploration is often necessary.
  • Neglected Cases / Complex Injuries:
    • Tendon transfers are performed if nerve repair is impractical.

Tendon Transfer Procedure: Modified Jones Transfer

  • Objective: Use muscles innervated by the median and ulnar nerves to substitute for lost wrist and finger functions.
  • Tendon Transfers:

Key takeaways:

Although certain fracture patterns in the humerus (spiral distal third- the Holstein-Lewis pattern) are more likely to be associated with nerve injuries, the mechanism for most nerve palsies associated with fractures is stretch.

  • A special type of humerus fracture, where there is a spiral fracture at the junction of the middle and distal third, is commonly known to be associated with a radial nerve palsy. This is called the Holstein Lewis fracture.
  • The radial nerve injury results in paralysis of the wrist, finger and thumb extensors (wrist drop), brachioradialis and the supinator. There is a sensory change in a small area on the radial side of the back of the hand.

question_text: Which is not a part of Horner's syndrome?
explanation:
• Enophthalmos and not exophthalmos is a part of Horner's syndrome.
  • Horner's syndrome is composed of the following
    • Ptosis
    • Loss of Ciliospinal reflex
    • Enophthalmos
    • Miosis
    • Anhydrosis
  • It is usually seen in lower brachial plexus palsy, such as Klumpke's palsy, where the T1 nerve root is involved.
  • This is because Horner's syndrome occurs due to the paralysis of the sympathetic nerve to ipsilateral face that arises from T1 nerve root.

Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1537

question_text: Investigation of choice for entrapment neuropathy is
explanation:
• The diagnosis of entrapment neuropathy is based on electrodiagnostic studies(EMG/NCV) and Magnetic resonance imaging(MRI).
  • Entrapment neuropathy is a medical condition caused by entrapment and compression of a peripheral nerve wherever it traverses fibro-osseous tunnels,
  • Sites of entrapment neuropathy are:
    • Carpal tunnel - Median nerve(carpal tunnel syndrome)
    • Cubital tunnel - Ulnar nerve(cubital tunnel syndrome)
    • Guyon's canal - Ulnar nerve(Guyon's canal syndrome)
    • Tarsal tunnel - Posterior tibial nerve(Tarsal tunnel syndrome)
    • Inguinal ligament - Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh(meralgia paraesthetica).
    • Suprascapular notch - Suprascapular nerve
    • Neck of fibula - Common peroneal nerve
    • Fascial tunnel of superficial peroneal nerve - Superficial peroneal nerve
    • Archede of Frohse - Posterior interosseous syndrome
    • Thoracic outlet syndrome - Lower trunk of brachial plexus and rarely subclavian vessels
    • Compression in the foot Digital nerve - Morten's metatarsalgia

Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney, 1st edition, Page no. 1700.

question_text: A patient presents with a far lateral herniation of the L4-5 disc. Which of the following findings is most likely to be present?
explanation:
• At every disc level there is an exiting nerve root and a traversing nerve root. In L4, L5 disc, the exiting nerve root is L4 and traversing root is L5. Similarly in L1, L2 disc the exiting nerve root is L1 and traversing one in L2. This is applicable to all discs below cervical region.
  • There are 2 types of disc herniations - paracentral and far lateral
  • Almost all(>95%) disc protrusions are paracentral in nature and paracentral discs compresses the traversing nerve root.
  • Rarely, there can be a far lateral disc which will compress the exiting nerve root.
  • In this case, there is a far lateral disc so the exiting nerve root will be affected. Here, the L4 nerve root is the exiting root, so ankle dorsiflexion would be weakened.
  • Anterior thigh numbness would be the result of L2 or L3 nerve compression.
  • Extensor hallucis longus weakness would be consistent with L5 palsy.
  • Lateral foot numbness and plantar flexion weakness would be consistent with an S1 nerve root palsy.

Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney, 1st edition, Page no. 1389.

question_text: Sciatic nerve damage most commonly due to which of the following causes?
explanation:
• The most common pathological mechanisms for sciatic nerve injury are compression, traction or direct injury by mechanical disruption as is seen in intragluteal muscle injection or called as Sciatic neuritis.
  • Division of the main sciatic nerve is rare except in gunshot wounds or operative(iatrogenic) accidents.
  • The sciatic nerve is the nerve most commonly injured during total hip replacement.
  • Sciatic nerve is the most common nerve injured by intramuscular injections, especially in children.

Reference: Maheshwari, 5th ed, Pg: 264.

question_text: Glomus cells are found in -
explanation: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Chemoreceptors Arterial chemoreceptors consist of globular aggregations of chemoreceptive cells (glomus cells), and supportive cells, separated from one another by fibrous tissue septa. In these setpa and between glomus cells, numerous capillaries and nerve fibers are seen. The glomus cells have the structure of endocrine amine hormone secreting cells.

question_text: Motor march is seen in:
explanation:
Axonotmesis:

  • PATHOLOGY - Axons broken, nerve intact
  • DEGENERATION - Proximally + distally
  • NEUROMA - Neuroma in continuity
  • PROGNOSIS - Recovery +/-, Motor march +

Neurapraxia:

  • PATHOLOGY - Physiological interruption, anatomically normal
  • DEGENERATION - Nil
  • NEUROMA - Nil
  • PROGNOSIS - Recovery complete within 6 weeks

Neurotmesis:

  • PATHOLOGY - Axons as well as nerve broken.
  • DEGENERATION - Proximally + distally
  • NEUROMA - End or side Neuroma
  • PROGNOSIS - Recovery poor

Nerve regeneration: As regeneration begins, the axonal stump from the proximal segment begins to grow distally.

  • If the endoneural tube with its contained Schwann cells is intact, the axonal sprout may readily pass along its primary course and reinnervate the end-organ. The rate of recovery of axon is 1 mm per day. The muscle nearest to the site of injury recovers first, followed by others as the nerve reinnervates muscles from proximal to distal, the so-called motor march.

Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th ed, Pg: 63.

question_text: Tinel sign is seen in
explanation:
Pathological changes after nerve injury

  • After nerve injury, nerve first degenerates and then tries to regenerate.
  • Nerve degeneration
    • The part of the neurone distal to the point of injury undergoes secondary or Wallerian degeneration, the proximal part undergoes primary or retrograde degeneration upto a single node
  • Nerve regeneration
    • As regeneration begins, the axonal stump from the proximal segment begins to grow distally.
    • If the endoneural tube with its contained Schwann cells is intact, the axonal sprout may readily pass along its primary course and reinnervate the end-organ.
    • The rate of recovery of axon is 1 mm per day.
    • The muscles nearest to the site of injury recovers first, followed by others as the nerve reinnervates muscles from proximal to distal, the so-called motor march.
    • When the skin over the nerve is percussed gently from distal to proximal, the patient gets a tingling sensation if the nerve is recovering.
    • This is called Tinel's sign and is a sign of recovery.

Reference: Essential Orthopedics Maheshwari, 5th edition, Page no. 69.

question_text: Tinel's sign can be used to
option_a: Assess the severity of nerve injury
option_b: Assess the type of nerve injury
explanation:
• Tinel's sign is used to assess regeneration of a nerve after injury.
  • Percussion along the course of a nerve from distal to proximal induces tingling sensation at the site of a neuroma. This is called Tinel's sign.
  • Tinel's sign occurs due to the hypersensitivity of the neuroma that forms after a nerve injury.
  • Tinel's sign can be of 2 types
    • Non - progressive Tinel's sign - It is seen in end neuroma which forms after neurotmesis. This has bad prognosis.
    • Progressive Tinel's sign - It is seen in neuroma of continuity which forms after axonotmesis. Here, the Tinel's sign progresses form proximal to distal as the nerve regenerates. Hence it can be used to assess the progress of nerve recovery.

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 69

question_text: Rate of regeneration of an injured nerve is
explanation:
• Rate of regeneration of an injured nerve is 1 mm per day.
  • Regeneration of nerve happens only in axonotmesis, where at least one of the outer sheaths of the neuron - endoneurium/ epineurium/ perineurium is intact.

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 74

question_text: Which of the following nerve injuries does not produce a neuroma?
explanation:
• Neurapraxia is a physiological disruption of impulse transmission through an injured nerve. There is no anatomical damage. Therefore, there is no neuroma formation.
  • In axonotmesis we get a neuroma in continuity
  • In neurotmesis we get an end neuroma.

Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1534

question_text: True statement about nerve injury is
option_a: NCV is the best predictor of outcome within 48 hrs of injury
option_b: Positive Tinel's sign if present indicates the accurate location of injury
option_c: Traction nerve injuries are indication for emergency surgery
option_d: In all cases of open wounds with clinical signs of nerve injury, nerve exploration must be done
explanation:
• NCV is not the best predictor of outcome within the first 48 hours of nerve injury. EMG is the only investigation useful in the first 48 hours but it is not very reliable.
  • Positive Tinel's sign does not indicate the accurate location of injury. If the nerve is regenerating, then the Tinel's sign will progress from proximal to distal and will not stay at the site of original injury.
  • Traction nerve injuries are usually neurapraxias, which will recover on its own and does not require any surgical intervention.
  • In all cases of open wounds with clinical signs of nerve injury, nerve exploration must be done, so that we can do a primary repair of the nerve (if injured). Primary repair has the best outcome when compared to a delayed nerve repair.

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 72

question_text: Motor march is seen in
explanation:
• Motor march is the progressive recovery of muscles from proximal to distal when a nerve regenerates after injury.
  • It is seen only in axonotmesis where the proximal segment of the nerve regenerates and grows towards the distal segment.
