question_text:
Patient standing on one side has Trendelenburg sign positive. What is the Action of the muscle tested in Trendelenburg test?
1. Abduction
2. Flexion
3. Adduction
4. Internal rotation
explanation:
The Trendelenburg test assesses the function of the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles, which are the primary hip abductors.

  • Action of tested muscles: Abduction of the hip
  • Test interpretation:
    • Positive sign: When the patient stands on one leg, the opposite hip drops due to weakness of the hip abductors on the stance side (gluteus medius/minimus weakness or superior gluteal nerve injury).

Other options:

  • (A) 2, 3 (Flexion, Adduction) - Incorrect
    • Hip flexion (iliopsoas, rectus femoris) and hip adduction (adductors) are not tested in Trendelenburg test.
  • (C) 2, 4 (Flexion, Internal Rotation) - Incorrect
    • Hip internal rotation (gluteus medius/anterior fibers) is a minor function but not the main action tested.
  • (D) 1, 4 (Abduction, Internal Rotation) - Incorrect
    • Abduction is correct, but internal rotation is not the primary function tested.

Reference:Fundamentals of orthopedics by mohindra and jain page no-97

question_text: A 25 year old male presents with weakness of grip after injury. The test shown in the image is positive. Which nerve is injured?
explanation:
• The image shows pen test.
  • Pen test tests for the functioning of abductor pollicis brevis muscle which is supplied by the median N.
  • Pen test is done by hovering a pen above the palm of the patient and asking him to abduct the thumb and touch the tip of the pen. If the patient is unable to do so, then it means that the median N is injured.

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 66

question_text: Ottawa rules are used for
option_a: Deciding when to take x rays in ankle injuries
option_b: Order of reimplantation of an amputated limb
option_d: Rules for investigation modalities in tumors
explanation:
• Ottawa rules are used for deciding when to take x rays in ankle injuries.
  • Ottawa ankle rules are the guidelines for taking ankle x rays in several countries.
  • According to this, X rays are indicated in ankle injuries only if at least one of the following is present
    1. Pain around the medial/ lateral malleolus
    2. Tenderness over the medial/ lateral malleolus
    3. Inability to weight bear immediately after injury
    4. Inability to take 4 steps at the hospital
  • The idea behind the Ottawa rules is to minimize X ray usage and radiation exposure.

Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1386

question_text: The anterior drawer test of ankle done with the ankle in 20 degrees of plantarflexion most effectively tests for injury or laxity or which of the following ligaments shown in Figure?
explanation:
• B points to the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL).
  • The ATFL is the most common ligament injured with ankle sprains and occurs most often with the foot in slight plantar flexion.
  • Plantar flexion of the foot causes the ATFL to become parallel with the axis of the foot and become taut.
  • Acute lateral ankle ligament injuries are very common and can result in chronic instability if left untreated.
  • Conservative measures include functional rehabilitation which is the management of choice for acute and chronic injuries. Surgical intervention is best reserved for high-demand athletes

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 1262.

question_text: A 36-year-old male injured his right arm after a fall. His injury radiograph is shown in Figure A. On physical examination, he was found to have a nerve injury. Which function is the last to return?
option_a: Pain sensation to the radial portion of the dorsum of the hand
option_b: Temperature sensation to the radial portion of the dorsum of the hand
option_c: Sensation of light touch to the radial portion of the dorsum of the hand
explanation:
• This patient sustained a humeral shaft fracture which is associated with radial nerve palsy.
  • Motor function is also last function to return. In the case of a radial nerve injury, this is manifested in a loss of wrist extension.
  • Peripheral nerve injury causes a loss of distal function in the following order: motor function, proprioception, light touch sensation, temperature, pain and sympathetic activity. Nerve function recovery occurs in the reverse order.
  • Therefore, if a patient has a nerve injury, motor function is lost first and is the last to recover. The injury this patient sustained is also known as a Holstein-Lewis fracture.

question_text: A 25-year-old football player sustains a blow to the arm during a match. He develops temporary weakness and tingling, but recovers completely within 6 weeks without surgical intervention. Which of the following best describes neuropraxia?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Neuropraxia is the mildest form of peripheral nerve injury, as described in Seddon's classification.
  • In this condition, the axon remains intact, but there is focal demyelination or damage to the myelin sheath due to compression or ischemia.
  • Conduction block occurs across the site of injury, leading to weakness or sensory loss.
  • Since the axon and endoneurial tubes are preserved, full recovery occurs within weeks to months without Wallerian degeneration.

Explanation of other options:

Damaged axon, intact nerve sheath (Option B): Describes axonotmesis, where axons are damaged but connective tissue sheaths remain intact.

Damaged axon and nerve sheath (Option C): Describes neurotmesis, the most severe form of injury, with a poor prognosis.

question_text: A 28-year-old man falls asleep with his arm compressed against a hard surface after heavy alcohol intake. The next morning, he wakes up with wrist drop and an inability to extend his fingers. In such compressive neuropathies, which of the following represents the correct order of susceptibility of nerve fibres?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical scenario matches the Saturday night palsy, due to compression of the Radial nerve
  • Nerve fibres differ in their susceptibility to compression and hypoxia depending on their size and function. The order of susceptibility is:
    • C fibres (small, unmyelinated, pain and autonomic fibres): Most sensitive to compression and hypoxia, so affected first.
    • B fibres (small, myelinated, preganglionic autonomic fibres): Intermediate susceptibility.
    • A fibres (large, myelinated, motor and sensory fibres): Least susceptible, affected last.

Thus, in compressive neuropathies such as Saturday night palsy, the order of fibre involvement is C < B < A.

Explanation of other options:

A < B < C (Option A): Incorrect, as large A fibres are the most resistant, not the most susceptible.

B < A < C (Option B): Incorrect, as C fibres are more susceptible than B or A fibres.

C < A < B (Option D): Incorrect sequence, as A fibres are less susceptible than B fibres.

question_text: In 1943, Seddon described the basic types of peripheral nerve injury.  These types assist in the assessment, prognosis, and determination of treatment strategy. Some of these injuries lead to irreversible damage, while others are reversible. Clinical history and physical examination are important in assessing the extent and severity of nerve Injury. Which of the following Seddon's peripheral injury types has the best prognosis?
explanation:
• Neuropraxia:
    • This is the mildest and most common type of peripheral nerve injury, caused by transient compression or stretch.
    • It involves focal demyelination at the injury site without disrupting the axon or connective tissues, leading to a temporary blockage of nerve conduction.
    • Motor and sensory loss is temporary, and autonomic function is generally preserved.
    • Recovery is typically spontaneous and occurs within 3 months as the nerve remyelinates, giving it the best prognosis of all types of nerve injury.
  • Axonotmesis:
    • More severe than neuropraxia, it involves complete axon disruption and demyelination, but the surrounding connective tissues remain intact.
    • This results in a complete loss of motor, sensory, and autonomic function.
    • Recovery is possible but depends on the distance from the injury, as regeneration of axons takes time.
  • Neurotmesis:
    • The most severe type, it involves a complete division of the peripheral nerve. The axon and connective tissue are both disrupted.
    • Recovery is not possible without surgical intervention, and the prognosis is poor.
  • Complete Transaction:
    • Refers to a full severing of the nerve, resulting in total loss of function with no possibility of spontaneous recovery.

Why Not Other Options:

  • A. Axonotmesis:
    • Although recovery is possible, it depends on the distance from the injury and takes longer than neuropraxia.
  • C. Neurotmesis:
    • Complete division of the nerve with no spontaneous recovery, making this option have a very poor prognosis.
  • D. Complete Transaction:
    • This implies total disruption of nerve continuity, making recovery impossible without intervention.

Key Takeaways:

  • Neuropraxia is the least severe and has the best prognosis, with spontaneous recovery occurring within months.
  • Axonotmesis and neurotmesis are progressively more severe, with axonotmesis showing some potential for recovery and neurotmesis having a poor outlook.
  • Complete transaction represents total nerve injury with no recovery possible without surgery

question_text: The following clinical finding is observed at rest. Which nerve is most likely involved?
explanation:
Explanation:

The ulnar nerve is responsible for the ulnar claw hand. The ulnar nerve innervates the intrinsic muscles of the hand, including the hypothenar muscles, and the medial two lumbricals.

Injury to the ulnar nerve, such as at the elbow or wrist, can result in ulnar claw hand, where there is hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints (MCP) and flexion of the interphalangeal joints (IP) of the 4th and 5th fingers. This happens because of the unopposed action of the long flexors and extensors due to the loss of ulnar nerve function.

Explanation of other option:

Median (Option B): Median nerve involvement typically leads to "ape hand" deformity or "benediction" hand, not ulnar claw hand. The median nerve controls the flexors of the thumb, index, and middle fingers. Damage to the median nerve causes weakness and loss of opposition of the thumb, which is not seen in ulnar claw hand.

Musculocutaneous (Option C): The musculocutaneous nerve primarily innervates the muscles in the anterior compartment of the arm (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis). It does not contribute significantly to the intrinsic muscles of the hand and would not be involved in ulnar claw hand.

None (Option D): Since the ulnar nerve is responsible for the ulnar claw hand, the answer is not "None."

Key Takeaways:

The ulnar nerve is involved in ulnar claw hand, and this condition is typically seen in cases of ulnar nerve injury.

question_text: What is the likely diagnosis for a 17-year-old male presenting with a painless swelling on the outer aspect of his left knee, as seen in the provided radiograph?
explanation:
Explanation:

The X-ray reveals a clearly outlined bony outgrowth originating from the metaphysis of the distal femur, characteristic of an osteochondroma.


Explanations of other options:

Enchondroma (Option A): Enchondromas are noncancerous cartilage tumours that commonly develop inside the medullary cavity of long bones like the proximal humerus or femur. They are often symptom-free and found incidentally on X-rays.


Chondroblastoma (Option B): Chondroblastomas are uncommon benign bone tumour that originate in the epiphysis of long bones, such as the proximal humerus or femur. Radiographs typically show them as round or oval lytic lesions in the epiphyseal region.

Giant Cell Tumour (Option D): Giant cell tumors are benign bone lesions that usually occur in the epiphysis of long bones, most often the distal femur or proximal tibia. They can present with pain, swelling, and bone destruction, sometimes leading to pathological fractures. On X-rays, they appear as lytic lesions with a characteristic "soap-bubble" pattern.

question_text: Metastasis not found in
explanation: Answer- C. Fibula Metastatic bone disease is the commonest malignancy of bones and is much more common than primary bone tumors. The commonest sites for bone metastases are vertebrae (most common), pelvis, the proximal half of the femur and the humerus. Extremities distal to elbow and knee are least commonly involved sites. Spread is usually via the blood stream; occasionally, visceral tumors spread directly into adjacent bones e.g., the pelvis and ribs.

question_text: Classification system for bone tumors is named after
explanation:
Enneking system is based on knowing the histologic grade of the lesion(G, see below), tumor site(T, intracompartmental or extracompartmental) and metastases(M).

Enneking system is simple and the three broad categories based on low grade(I), high-grade lesion(II) and metastatic lesion(III) are further divided into subgroups based on intracompartmental(IIIA) or extracompartmental (IIIB) location.

In the Enneking system, bone tumors are graded as follows:

  • G0 - Benign lesion
  • G1 - Low-grade malignant lesion
  • G2 - High-grade malignant lesion

Surgical grade depends on histology, however, a higher surgical grade is applied if the radiographic features and clinical behaviour of a lesion indicate an aggressive lesion that is incompatible with its benign histologic features.

Site In the Enneking system, the site and local extent of bone tumors are classified as follows:

  • T0 - A benign tumor that is confined within a true capsule and the lesion's anatomic compartment of origin(i.e., a benign intracapsular, intra compartmental lesion)
  • T1 - An aggressive benign or malignant tumor that is still confined within its anatomic compartment(i.e., an intracompartmental lesion)
  • T2 - A lesion that has spread beyond its anatomic compartment of origin(i.e., an extra compartmental lesion) Metastasis

Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney, 1st edition, Page no. 160.

question_text: Soap bubble appearance is a radiological finding in which bone tumour:
explanation:
Giant Cell Tumor of Bone

  • Characteristics: Giant cell tumours are lytic, eccentric, and expansile lesions, often surrounded by a thin shell of bone, giving a classic 'soap bubble' appearance in radiology.
  • Option A - Also known as Osteoclastoma.
  • Age group - 20-40 years.
  • Common Locations: Typically arise from the epiphysis of long bones, such as:
    • The lower end of the femur
    • The upper end of the tibia
    • The lower end of the radius
  • Clinical Features:
    • Tenderness on firm palpation.
    • Swelling and pain
    • A distinctive 'egg-shell crackling' sensation may be felt.
  • Radiology - Xray shows expansile lytic lesion in epiphyseal region of bone near joints.

Soap bubble appearance.

  • Biopsy - Spindle cells and multinucleated giant cells
  • Treatment - Excision +/- reconstruction using bone graft, Arthrodesis or Arthroplasty.
  • Prognosis - Recurrence following treatment is a serious With every subsequent recurrence, the tumour becomes more aggressive. May show malignant potential.

Option B: Unicameral bone cyst Shows leaf sign.

Option C: Aneurysmal bone cyst Shows Ballooning cortex with blood filled cavity.

Option D: Adamantinoma shows Honey-comb appearance.

Key Takeaway:

The Rule of 'E' for GCT (Giant Cell Tumor):

  1. Epiphysis: Typically occurs in the epiphyseal region of long bones.
  2. Expansile: The lesion is expansile, leading to the thinning of the cortex.
  3. Egg-Shell Crackling: The lesion may exhibit egg-shell cracking on palpation or imaging.
  4. Eccentrically Placed: The tumor is often eccentrically located within the bone.
  5. Excision: Surgical excision is a common treatment option.

explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis, given a painless palpable bony mass arising from the metaphysis in a growing individual with X-ray findings of a cartilage-capped bony outgrowth, is osteochondroma.


Explanations of other options:

Osteosarcoma (Option A): Osteosarcoma is a malignant tumour of bone that commonly arises in the metaphysis of long bones. It typically manifests as a painful, fast-growing swelling. Radiographic findings often show an aggressive, irregular, and destructive lesion with features like cortical disruption, periosteal reaction, and extension into adjacent soft tissue.

Multiple myeloma (Option B): Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells within the bone marrow and does not present as a solid, palpable mass at the metaphysis of long bones. Radiologically, it is characterised by widespread lytic defects in the skeleton, commonly described as 'punched-out' lesions.

Osteoid osteoma (Option D): Osteoid osteoma is a benign bone lesion that presents with localised pain, often relieved by NSAIDs. It is usually located in the cortical region of long bones rather than the metaphysis. On X-ray, it appears as a small radiolucent nidus encircled by dense reactive sclerosis.

question_text:
A 15-year-old cross country runner complains of vague shin pain. A radiograph of the tibia is seen in Figure A.

  • Incorrect Answers:

Only in "unresectable" tumors or situations where resection would be associated with poor functional outcome would Ewing's be treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy without surgical excision.

question_text: An 8-years old boy presents with swelling in mid-thigh region. On examination, femoral thickening was found with Codman's triangle. On aspiration, greyish white liquid was aspirated that showed atypical round cells with MIC-2 positivity. The most likely diagnosis is?
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis of a swelling in mid-thigh region of an 8-years old boy, with femoral thickening with greyish white liquid aspirated from swelling showing atypical round cells with MIC-2 positivity is Ewing's sarcoma.

Ewing's sarcoma: A type of primitive neuroectodermal tumour(PNET) On histopathological examination shows small round cells, which show positive immunohistochemical staining or CD-99 and MIC-2 gene. Although the classical periosteal reaction seen in Ewing's sarcoma is onion peel appearance but sometimes it can present as Codman's triangle.

Ewing's Sarcoma:

  • Arises from endothelial cells of the bone marrow in the diaphysis(medullary cavity) of long tubular bones(especially femur) and flat bones of pelvis.
  • Highly malignant, undifferentiated peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor(PNET)
  • MC site: Diaphysis of femur> fibula> ilium> tibia.
  • Pathology: Arising in medullar cavity usually invade the cortex and periosteum producing a soft tissue mass. Composed of sheets of uniform, small round cells(that are slightly larger than lymphocytes), with pale clear appearing cytoplasm due to presence of glycogen.
  • Cytoplasm is PAS positive and diastase digestible.
  • Presence of Homer-Wright rosettes and pseudo rosette is indicative of neural differentiation(i.e., PNET) Express MIC 2 gene in very high amount, distinguish from other round cell tumors
  • Most definitive test: Demonstration of chromosomal translocation by karyotyping or RT PCR DETECTION OF t(11:22)
  • 80%-90% patient have translocation mostly t(11:22)>t(21:22) and rarely t(7:22).
  • Ewing sarcomas are periodic acid Schiff positive(owing to intracellular glycogen) and reticulin negative.

Clinical Feature: Mostly in males between 10-20 years of age. Pain, swelling, tenderness, urinary/rectal complaints (when ilium involved) pathological fracture. Systemic symptoms such as fever, generalized weakness, weight loss and lab anomalies as anaemia, leukocytosis and raised ESR are hallmark of fulminating course, advanced disease or metastasis.

50% of all metastases occurs to lung and 25% to bone and bone marrow.

Diagnosis: Mottled rarefaction of spongiosa with permeation of overlying cortex, reflecting rapid bone destruction is the principal finding Laminated(layered) periosteal new bone formation known as onion-peel appearance soft tissue mass, indicating neoplasm has perforated cortex

Treatment: Highly radiosensitive(melts on radiotherapy) but overall survival is not much enhanced Chemotherapy is much more effective and include vincristine, actinomycin D, adriamycin, ifosfamide and etoposide. Best results are achieved by: Preoperative chemotherapy then wide excision(or amputation) if tumor is in favorable site and further chemotherapy for 1 years. Radiotherapy followed by local excision if it is in less accessible site and then further chemotherapy for 1 year.

Reference: Maheshwari, Essentials Ortho, 5th edition, Page no. 243.

question_text: A 20-year-old male presents with localized pain that is gradual in onset and has progressively worsened over time. An X-ray reveals a sunburst appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Osteosarcoma is a type of bone cancer most commonly found in adolescents and young adults. It typically presents with gradual onset of localized pain, which worsens over time.
  • The characteristic radiological finding in osteosarcoma is the sunburst appearance on X-ray, which is caused by the tumor's aggressive periosteal reaction.
  • The pain and gradual worsening are key features for this diagnosis.

Explanation of other options:

Ewing sarcoma (Option B): Ewing sarcoma can also present with bone pain, but its radiographic appearance is different. Ewing sarcoma often shows an "onion skin" periosteal reaction on X-ray, which is not consistent with the sunburst appearance seen in osteosarcoma.

Chondrosarcoma (Option C): Chondrosarcoma typically affects older adults and presents with a different radiological appearance, usually showing cartilage calcification or a more radiolucent lesion, which is different from the characteristic sunburst appearance seen in osteosarcoma.

Gout (Option D): Gout primarily affects the joints and is not typically associated with a sunburst appearance on X-ray. It presents with acute pain, usually in the lower extremities, especially the big toe, due to the deposition of urate crystals, not a bone tumor.

Key Takeaways:

The sunburst appearance on X-ray is a classic finding in osteosarcoma, which is the most likely diagnosis in this case.

question_text: The image given below is an xray of a patient diagnosed with osteosarcoma. Select false statements.
option_a: The age of the patient would be around 15-20 yrs
option_b: An irregular destruction in the metaphysis of the femur can be seen
option_c: Typical sun-ray appearance can be seen as the tumor is growing into surrounding soft tissue
option_d: Lytic lesion seen in osteosarcoma is marked by the arrow
explanation:
Radiological Features of Osteosarcoma

1. X-ray Findings

  • Periosteal Reaction:
    • Codman's Triangle: Triangular elevation of the periosteum seen at the tumor's edge.
  • Bone Destruction:
    • Bony Lesions: Destruction of bone with irregular borders.
  • Calcification:
    • Sunburst Pattern: Radiating spicules of calcified bone from the tumor, often seen in aggressive forms.

2. CT Scan Findings

  • Soft Tissue Mass:
    • Extensive Soft Tissue Involvement: Large, heterogeneous mass extending beyond the bone.
  • Bone Matrix:
    • Mineralization: Heterogeneous mineralization within the tumor.

3. MRI Findings

  • Signal Characteristics:
    • T1-weighted Images: Tumor appears low to intermediate signal intensity.
    • T2-weighted Images: Tumor appears high signal intensity due to increased water content.
  • Invasion:
    • Medullary Cavity Involvement: Tumor extending from the cortex into the bone marrow.

4. Bone Scan Findings

  • Increased Uptake:
    • High Radiotracer Uptake: Reflects increased bone activity around the tumor.

Option A: Epiphyseal growth plates visible in femur and tibia hence the patient has not attained skeletal maturity and would be between 15-20yrs of age.

Option B: Distal femur metaphysis shows irregular cortical destruction with periosteal reaction.

Option C: The lateral view of xray shows typical 'Sun-ray appearance' of the tumour into the surrounding tissue.

Option D: The arrow shows the periosteal reaction with new bone formation and not lytic lesion. Lytic lesions can be seen in GCT.

Key Takeaway -

Mnemonic - "OSCAR HAS BONEs"

  • O: Osteosarcoma
  • S: Sunburst pattern (calcification pattern on X-ray)
  • C: Codman's triangle (periosteal reaction seen on X-ray)
  • A: Aggressive (highly invasive tumor with soft tissue involvement)
  • R: Radiological features (X-ray, CT, MRI findings)
  • HA: High ALP (elevated alkaline phosphatase in blood)
  • S: Soft tissue mass (extensive involvement seen on CT)
  • BONEs: BONE marrow invasion (medullary cavity involvement)

    • The x ray finding of endosteal scalloping and punctate calcification is seen in chondrosarcoma.
  • Osteosarcoma and Chondroblastoma are commonly seen in the 2nd decade of life
  • Metastasis does not produce endosteal scalloping and punctate calcification

question_text: Which of the following is a GCT variant?

question_text: Most common site of Admantinoma is
explanation:
Adamantinoma is a low grade malignant tumor most commonly affecting the tibia. It is a diaphyseal tumor.

Tibia (85% cases) followed by fibula is the most common site for adamantinoma of long bones.

It occurs between 20 to 40 years of age.

The swelling is associated with only minimal pain and it increases in size gradually.

Metastasis is not common.

question_text: Which of the following is the most radiosensitive tumor?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most radiosensitive tumour is Ewing's sarcoma, a malignant bone tumour.

Ewing's sarcoma

  • Ewing sarcoma is a malignant tumor of the diaphysis of long bones in children; cell of origin unknown.
  • The classic t(11;22) chromosomal translocation produces the EWS-FLI1 fusion gene, which is responsible for the pathogenesis of Ewing sarcoma.
  • Its the most common malignant bone tumor in the first decade (5-20 years)
  • Most commonly affects the femur
  • Clinical Features:
    • Painful swelling
    • In young children (5-7 years), may mimic acute osteomyelitis: pain, fever, redness, tenderness
    • Aspiration may yield whitish material
    • Laboratory investigation shows elevated WBC, ESR, CRP

X-ray findings

  • Diaphyseal lytic lesion
  • The periosteum may be lifted off in multiple layers, producing an onion-skin appearance.

Histopathology

  • Sheets of small round blue cells with minimal cytoplasm; Pseudo-rosettes may be present
  • Immunohistochemistry: CD99 positive.

Treatment:

  • Highly radiosensitive, but radiotherapy is often avoided in children due to risk of secondary osteosarcoma and long-term effects
  • Most lesions are treated with chemotherapy and surgery

List of Radio-Sensitive Bone Tumors (Mnemonic: HELP)

  • Hemangioma
  • Ewing sarcoma
  • Lymphoma of bone
  • Plasmacytoma

Explanation of other options:

Melanoma (Option B), Osteosarcoma (Option C), Renal cell carcinoma (Option D): All these tumours are moderately to highly radioresistant.

question_text: Which tumour is associated with Codman’s triangle and sunburst appearance?
explanation:
Explanation:
Osteosarcoma classically shows aggressive periosteal reaction with Codman's triangle (periosteum lifted creating an angle) and a sunburst pattern of spiculated new bone radiating from the cortex.

Explanation of other options:
Ewing's (Option B): Onion-skin/lamellated periosteal reaction more typical.
GCT (Option C):Eccentric, expansile lytic lesion at epiphysis; lacks sunburst/Codman's.
Chondrosarcoma (Option D): Rings-and-arcs calcification, endosteal scalloping-not classic sunburst.

question_text: A 20-year-old individual reports painful swelling localised to the index finger near the proximal phalanx, and the accompanying X-ray was obtained. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical features of pain along with a radiolucent lesion with stippled areas in the proximal phalanx of the finger on X-ray suggest an enchondroma.


Explanations of other options:

Osteosarcoma (Option A): Osteosarcoma is a malignant bone cancer that typically occurs in the metaphysis of long bones in young adults. On X-ray, it often presents as a mixed radiolucent and radiopaque lesion with a characteristic sunburst appearance.

Ewing's Sarcoma (Option B): Ewing's sarcoma is a malignant bone tumour that most often arises in the diaphysis of long bones in young individuals. On X-ray, it typically shows a permeative pattern with a characteristic onion-skin appearance.

Osteoclastoma (Option C): Osteoclastoma, also called a giant cell tumour, is a benign bone lesion typically found in the epiphysis of long bones in young adults. On X-ray, it is seen as a solitary, eccentrically positioned lytic lesion with the characteristic 'soap bubble' pattern.

question_text: Absolute contraindication of total hip replacement in adults is:
option_a: Secondary arthritis due to TB hip
explanation:
Absolute Contraindications for Total Hip Replacement (THR):

  • Active Infection (Option B):
    • Description: Active infection of the hip joint or any other region.
    • Rationale: Increases risk of postoperative infections and complications.

Relative contraindications for THR

  • Unstable Medical Illnesses:
    • Description: Any unstable medical conditions that significantly increase the risk of morbidity or mortality.
    • Rationale: May affect the patient's ability to recover from surgery.
  • Asymptomatic Bacteriuria:
    • Description: Presence of bacteria in the urine without symptoms.
    • Rationale: Not associated with increased risk of surgical site infections and is considered a relative contraindication.

Considerations for Specific Conditions:

Healed Tuberculosis (TB) of the Hip: (Option A)

  • Preoperative Requirements:
    • Complete Course of Antitubercular Therapy (ATT): Ensure TB infection is fully treated.
    • Synovial Fluid Biopsy: To rule out latent infection before surgery.
  • Conclusion: Not an absolute contraindication if these conditions are met.

Tom-Smith Arthritis (Sequelae of Septic Arthritis in Infancy): (Option C)

  • Description: Condition where the head of the femur is resorbed due to early septic arthritis, leading to future arthritis.
  • Treatment Considerations:
    • After Infection Resolution: THR is a viable option once skeletal growth is complete and latent infection has been ruled out.

Option A & C: Tom smith and TB Arthritis are Relative contraindications.

Key takeaway:

Active infection is only absolute contraindication to total hip replacement. Healed Tb, Tom smith arthritis and asymptomatic bacteriuria are relative contraindications.

Joint disorders and joint reconstruction

Reference: Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics 14th edition page no. 425

question_text: Which structure is at risk when we place the Hohmann retractor along the anterior rim of the acetabulum, during a total hip replacement surgery?
explanation:
• Placement of a curved cobra or Hohmann retractor in the interval between the anterior rim of the acetabulum and the psoas tendon puts the femoral nerve and vessels at risk.
  • Erroneous placement of this retractor over the psoas muscle can cause injury to the femoral nerve or adjacent vessels.
  • The risk increases with a more inferior placement of the retractor.
  • The safest position is near the level of the anterior superior iliac spine.

Reference: Manish kumar varshney 1st edition page no 1205

question_text: A 65-year-old woman undergoes an uncomplicated right total hip arthroplasty. Preoperatively her right  leg length was 2mm shorter than the left side. On the evening of surgery, she has full motor strength  and intact sensation. On the morning of postoperative day two she develops an inability to dorsiflex her ankle. There is no wound drainage and her anticoagulation levels are within normal limits. What is the next best step in treatment?
option_a: Maintain head of the bed flat with non-weight bearing restrictions
option_c: Place the hip in flexion and the knee in extension
option_d: Place the hip in extension and the knee in flexion
explanation:
• This patient has developed a sciatic nerve palsy of unknown origin.
  • The hip should be placed in extension and the knee flexed to relax the nerve while reversible causes of the palsy are investigated.
  • Sciatic nerve palsy is the most common nerve palsy following total hip arthroplasty.
  • Symptoms may present immediately post-op suggesting iatrogenic injury (retractor placement, cement heat, injury from cup screw placement, cerclage cabling, direct injury, indirect through excessive lengthening, "double crush" in the setting of lumbar spondylosis) or may evolve after surgery.
  • The immediate treatment of a new nerve palsy is to limit tension on the nerve by placing the hip in extension and knee in flexion.
  • The patient may then undergo workup for the cause of new nerve palsy.
  • Expeditious axial imaging may be obtained to evaluate for hematoma. Based on clinical judgment the patient may be taken for decompression of hematoma versus reversal of other causes of nerve compression. Incorrect Answers:
  • Option A: Restricting the patient to head of the bed flat and non-weight bearing would not relieve tension on the sciatic nerve.
  • Option B: An EMG may be indicated eventually, but the next best step is to relieve tension on the sciatic nerve.
  • Option C: Hip flexion and knee extension positioning would put more tension on the sciatic nerve.

Reference: Fundamentals of orthopaedics Mohindra n jain 1st edition page no 397

question_text: When can a femoral external fixator placed for polytrauma as a part of damage control orthopaedics, be safely converted to definitive intramedullary nail fixation?
option_d: At any time as long as the pin sites are clean
explanation:
The advantages of staged treatment in polytrauma cases according to DCO are:

  • Relief of pain, by preventing movement at the fracture.
  • Prevention of further damage to skin, soft tissues and neurovascular bundle of the injured extremity.
  • Prevention of complications such as fat embolism and hypovolemic shock.
  • Transportation of the patient was made easier.

Inflammatory Response After Trauma

  1. Surge in Inflammatory Mediators:
    • Trauma triggers a surge in inflammatory mediators (e.g., cytokines), which peaks between 2-5 days post-injury.
  2. Leukocyte Activation:
    • Following this initial burst, leukocytes become "primed" and are highly susceptible to activation by additional trauma, such as surgery.
    • This heightened state can lead to severe complications, including:
      • Multisystem Organ Failure
      • Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
  3. Management Strategy During Acute Phase:
    • To avoid further physiological stress ("second hit"), traumatologists typically limit interventions to treating only potentially life-threatening injuries during this critical inflammatory window.

Option A, B & D:

Current studies indicate safe conversion of femoral fixators within 3 weeks (Option B,C) and tibial fixators within 7-10 days (Option A) in polytrauma patients if pin sites are clean; otherwise, staged removal with treatment of the pin sites can safely be performed.

Key takeaways:

Current studies indicate safe conversion of femoral fixators within 3 weeks and tibial fixators within 7-10 days in polytrauma patients if pin sites are clean; otherwise, staged removal with treatment of the pin sites can safely be performed.

question_text: Myodesis is contraindicated in amputations done for which condition?
explanation:
• Myodesis is contraindicated in amputations done for ischemic conditions like peripheral vascular disease.
  • Myodesis is the process by which the cut muscle is sutured onto the bone or periosteum after amputation.
  • Myoplasty is the process by which the cut muscle is sutured onto another muscle after amputation.
  • Myodesis is superior to myoplasty in terms of function. However, it is contraindicated in ischemic conditions as it may further reduce the blood flow to the muscles and cause muscle necrosis.

Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1954.

question_text: A 35 yr old is having expansile swelling with egg shell cracking in the lower end of radius. Bone biopsy confirms it to be giant cell tumour. All of the following modalities can be used for treatment except:
explanation:
Treatment Options for Giant Cell Tumor (GCT)

The choice of treatment for GCT is guided by the tumor's location, size, and severity.

Excision

  • Complete surgical removal of the tumor is often preferred when the tumor is accessible and clear margins can be achieved.

Excision with Reconstruction (Option D)

  • Used when extensive bone or joint removal is needed. Common reconstruction techniques include:
    • Turn-O-Plasty: Rotation of bone segments to maintain function.
    • Arthrodesis: Joint fusion to provide stability.
    • Arthroplasty: Joint replacement with prosthetics.
    • Bone Grafting: Filling defects with bone grafts (autografts or allografts).

Curettage with or without Adjuvants

    • Involves scraping out the tumor while preserving the surrounding bone:
      • (Option A) - Cryotherapy: Freezing the tumor cavity to reduce recurrence.
      • Bone Grafting: Filling the cavity after curettage.

Radiotherapy (Option B)

    • Typically used for inoperable tumors or where surgery poses high risks. Radiotherapy helps control tumor growth but is less favored due to the potential risk of malignant transformation.

Amputation (Last Resort)

    • Considered when other treatments fail or the tumor is too extensive, resulting in loss of limb function or severe recurrence.

Option A, B & D: Curettage with cryotherapy, Radiotherapy and Excision with fibula head grafting all three are used in GCT Management.

Option C - Chemotherapy is of no use in GCT.

Key Takeaway -

GCT Management Options: (Chemotherapy Not done)

  • Excision with or without Reconstruction
  • Curettage
  • Radiotherapy
  • Amputation

question_text: All of the following are different surgical approaches to do primary total knee replacement except:
explanation:
Surgical approaches used for doing primary total knee replacement surgery are:

  1. Medial parapatellar (most common) (Option A)
  2. Subvastus (Option B)
  3. Mid-vastus (Option D)
  4. Lateral para patellar (least common)

Quadriceps Snip Approach in Knee Surgery

  • Purpose: Primarily used in revision knee replacement surgery to address fibrotic scarring after primary knee replacement.
  • Applications:
    • Commonly employed in revision knee arthroplasty and for treating stiff knees.
    • Best suited when stiffness originates from proximal causes; if stiffness is distal, a tibial tubercle osteotomy is preferable.
  • Technique:
    • Simple and straightforward to perform, offering good joint exposure in most revision cases or ankylosed knees.
    • Involves cutting the rectus tendon at or near the musculotendinous junction at a 45° angle proximally and laterally, aligned with the vastus lateralis muscle fibers.
    • The tendon should be fully divided, with reattachment of all muscle fibers at the end of the procedure.

Option A, B & D: Medial Parapatellar, Subvastus and Midvastus all 3 approaches are used in primary TKR.

Option C: Quadriceps Snips Surgery approach Primarily used in revision knee replacement surgery to address fibrotic scarring after primary knee replacement.

Key Takeaway -

  • Medial Parapatellar, Subvastus and Midvastus all 3 approaches are used in primary TKR.
  • Quadriceps Snips Surgery approach Primarily used in revision knee replacement surgery to address fibrotic scarring after primary knee replacement.

question_text: A 40-year-old female presents to the physician with a 5-month history of plantar medial heel pain. She notices it immediately on getting out of bed in the morning, but the pain improves after a few steps. The pain is exacerbated throughout her workday to the point where she is unable to finish her work shift. Figure shows a lateral radiograph of the affected heel. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management ?
option_a: Walker boot immobilization with full weight bearing for 4 weeks
option_b: Corticosteroid injection to the plantar fascia
option_c: Surgical release of 50% of the plantar fascia
explanation:
• This is the classic history of plantar fasciitis and the x ray shown calcaneal spur.
  • The typical patient is 40-70 years of age and can point almost directly to the plantar medial heel as the source from where the pain emanates.
  • It is a degenerative process associated with micro-tears of the plantar fascia.
  • It is widely accepted that heel spurs can occur concomitantly with plantar fasciitis, but they are not the etiology of the disorder.
  • Treatment is predominantly aimed at intrinsic toe stretching (Illustration B) combined with Achilles stretching (Illustration A) as gastrocnemius contractures are often found concomitantly.
    • Night splints have also been found to help.
    • If surgery is required because conservative management fails after 6-12 months, only the medial third of the plantar fascia is released so that the medial longitudinal arch is not compromised.

Reference: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter: 17, Pg: 260

question_text: 45-year-old manual labourer presents to the OPD with acute onset back pain that radiates to his right leg after carrying a heavy object. He also has mild weakness with ankle dorsiflexion on that side. What should be his initial treatment? His MRI is shown in Figure
explanation:
• The clinical picture and MRI points towards lumbar IVDP and the first line management for it is bed rest and NSAIDs. Once patient's pain is better, physical therapy is also started.
  • Lumbar disc herniation is the most common cause of radicular pain in the adult working population. 95% of these herniations involve L4/5, L5/S1 lumbar disc spaces.
  • Patients typically present with low back pain and sharp stabbing leg pain with sensory symptoms in a specific dermatomal distribution.
  • Persistent intractable pain following non-surgical treatment during a minimum 6-week period is the most frequent indication for surgery so in this case first we should start with anti-inflammatory medications.

Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney, 1st edition, Page no. 1390.

question_text: A 37-year-old male is struck by a car while walking at night. He is hemodynamically unstable at initial evaluation in the trauma bay. Advanced Trauma Life Support protocols are started, and an initial survey is completed. A chest radiograph and a pelvis AP radiograph (shown below) are obtained. What is the most appropriate next step?
option_a: The patient should be taken directly to the OR for percutaneous placement of a pelvic external fixator
option_b: Dedicated inlet and outlet views of the pelvis to better classify the fracture
option_c: Continued resuscitation and immediate CT of the chest, abdomen and plevis
option_d: Immediate application of pelvic binder, continued resuscitation and re-evaluation of hemodynamic status
explanation:
• Immediate application of pelvic binder, continued resuscitation and re-evaluation of hemodynamic status
  • The patient has an Anterior-Posterior Compression type pelvic ring injury and this injury places the patient at risk of life- threatening hemorrhage.
  • The most appropriate next step in the trauma bay is to place the patient in a pelvic binder in order to minimize pelvic volume and impart stability to the injured hemipelvis. This will also cause tamponade of the bleeding pelvic veins, thereby preventing further internal blood loss.
  • Other options
    • Answer A: While this patient may need to go emergently to the OR for multiple reasons, the work-up needs to be completed. However, the patient’s pelvis should be stabilized with a pelvic binder in the interim.
    • Answer B: These images should be obtained, but the pelvis should be compressed with a pelvic binder first.
    • Answer C: While the pelvis may not be the only location of bleeding, the patient has a known source for bleeding, and it can be quickly stabilized with a pelvic binder. After the pelvic binder is placed, continued resuscitation and investigation of other possible locations of bleeding should occur.

Reference- Maheshwari Essential Ortho 5th edition, page no 125

question_text: A 20 year old woman present with a painless swelling in her left thigh for the last 6 years. It was initially growing slowly but has been static in size for the last 3 years. She does not have any other symptoms. The X ray is given below. What is the next line of management?
option_a: Emergency surgery to excise the tumor
option_c: Core biopsy to confirm the diagnosis
explanation:
• The x ray shows a tumor arising from the metaphysis of the distal femur which is growing away from the knee joint. The tumor has a pedicle and an expanded end. The medullary canal and the cortex of the tumor is continuous with the parent bone. All these findings are seen in osteochondroma.
  • Osteochondroma is a benign tumor which stops growing when the patient attains skeletal maturity.
  • Osteochondromas are almost always asymptomatic and therefore no treatment is required.
  • In this case the patient has no symptoms, hence we can leave the swelling alone. We need to intervene only if any symptoms arise.

Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 248

question_text: A 42-year-old sustains a left finger injury while attempting to catch a baseball for his son. He presents with left, long finger pain and an inability to extend his middle finger at the distal interphalangeal joint. A radiograph after closed reduction and splinting is shown in Figure A. What is the best course of treatment?
option_b: Repeat splinting of the distal interphalangeal joint in extension
option_c: Splinting of the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints in extension
option_d: Fusion of the distal interphalangeal joint
explanation:
• Figure shows a lateral radiograph with a large intra-articular bony avulsion fragment and volar subluxation of the distal phalanx
  • The radiograph depicts a bony mallet injury with volar subluxation of the distal phalanx after splinting of the DIP joint in extension, which is an indication for reduction and pinning.
  • A mallet deformity is caused by disruption of the terminal extensor tendon distal to DIP joint. Occasionally, a bony avulsion of the distal phalanx is noted on radiographs. "Bony" mallet fingers will rarely require surgical fixation.
  • It is important to attempt to splint a bony mallet injury and get a new radiograph prior to making the decision for operative treatment. Indications for surgical management of this condition include volar subluxation of the distal phalanx even after DIP splinting.
  • This patient meets the indications for ORIF and nonoperative modalities would not be appropriate.
  • A DIP fusion in a young patient would not be appropriate.

Reference- Fundamentals of orthopedics Mohindra and Jain page no 86

question_text: Volkmann ischemic contracture (VIC) is a classic complication of untreated acute compartment syndrome in the forearm. Which muscles are the most likely to be affected by this phenomenon?
option_a: Flexor digitorum superficialis and palmaris longus
option_b: Flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis
option_c: Flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus
option_d: Flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum superficialis
explanation:
Long-Term Sequelae of Untreated Acute Compartment Syndrome

Overview

  • Primary Consequences: Muscle fibrosis and Volkmann ischemic contracture.
  • Etiology: Result from unrecognized or untreated acute compartment syndrome leading to advanced myonecrosis and muscle fibrosis.

Volkmann Ischemic Contracture

  • Definition: A classic sequelae of untreated compartment syndrome, particularly in the forearm, characterized by irreversible muscle and nerve damage.

Affected Muscles (Option A, B, C and D)

  • Most Vulnerable:
    • Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP)
    • Flexor Pollicis Longus (FPL)

Classification

  1. Mild Form:
    • Presentation: Mild flexion contractures at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints.
    • Function: Preserved strength and sensation.
  2. Moderate to Severe Forms:
    • Presentation:
      • Worsening contractures affecting multiple joints.
      • Significant sensorimotor deficits.
    • Complications:
      • Chronic pain.
      • Severe hand dysfunction.
      • Intrinsic-minus or Claw Hand Deformity: Characteristic of severe cases, resulting from imbalance between the intrinsic and extrinsic hand muscles.

Treatment Options

  1. Contracture Release and Tendon Transfers:
    • Indicated to improve function in cases of moderate to severe contractures.
    • Goals: Limited functional improvement, especially in severe forms.
  2. Muscle Slides:
    • Utilized to address muscle shortening and improve joint mobility.
  3. Nerve Decompression:
    • Recommended for patients experiencing chronic neuropathic pain.
    • Indication: When muscle fibrosis causes extrinsic compression on already compromised peripheral nerves.
  4. Free Innervated Gracilis Muscle Transfer:
    • Considered in selected severe cases to restore some hand function.

Option A, B & D: Superficial muscle like Flexor digitorium superficialis is not affected hence all 3 are incorrect options.

Key takeaways

  • Early recognition and treatment of compartment syndrome are crucial to prevent long-term sequelae such as Volkmann ischemic contracture.
  • FDP and FPL are most vulnerable to contracture.
  • Surgical interventions aim to restore function, but outcomes are often limited, especially in advanced cases.

question_text: During surgical hip dislocation for the management of femoral acetabular impingement, preservation of what structure is paramount to maintaining vascularity to the femoral head?

DISCUSSION:

  • When a trochanteric osteotomy is performed with the desire to maintain vascularity to the femoral head, as in the approach for a surgical hip dislocation, the deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery must be maintained.
  • This branch courses along the posterior aspect of the greater trochanter, posterior to the tendon of obturator externus, and anterior to the tendons of superior gemellus, obturator internus, and inferior gemellus.
  • It perforates the capsule above the superior gemellus and distal to the tendon or piriformis, before dividing into two to four terminal retinacular branches.

question_text: Triple deformity of knee typically seen in advanced TB knee consists of following components:
option_a: Flexion, anterior subluxation and external rotation
option_b: Flexion, posterior subluxation and internal rotation
option_c: Flexion, posterior subluxation and external rotation
option_d: Extension, posterior subluxation and external rotation
explanation:
Pathology of Tuberculosis of the Knee

Disease Origin:

  • Osseous Tuberculosis:
    • Location: Typically begins in the femoral or tibial condyles; less commonly in the patella.
    • Description: Initial infection starts in the bone.
  • Synovial Tuberculosis:
    • Location: More commonly begins in the synovial membrane.
    • Description: Leads to hypertrophy (enlargement) of the synovium.

Natural History:

  • Early Stages:
    • The disease may be confined to the synovium.
    • Synovial hypertrophy occurs without significant joint damage.
    • Inflammation primarily affects the synovial membrane.
  • Later Stages:
    • Destruction of Articular Cartilage and Bone:
      • The disease progresses to destroy both cartilage and underlying bone.
      • The hypertrophied synovium spreads over and under the cartilage, leading to its destruction.
      • Cartilage detachment exposes the bone.
    • Joint Distension and Subluxation:
      • Prolonged Joint Distension: Due to synovial effusion and pus formation.
      • Destruction of Ligaments: Leads to subluxation of the tibia.
        • The tibia may flex, slip backward, and rotate externally on the femoral condyles (known as triple subluxation).
      • Formation of Abscesses:
        • Pus Formation: Pus may burst out of the joint capsule, resulting in a cold abscess.
        • Sinus Formation: The abscess may eventually lead to the development of a sinus.

Healing:

  • Fibrous Healing:
    • Untreated: The body's attempt to heal can result in fibrosis.
    • Fibrous Ankylosis: The joint becomes stiff and fixed in a deformed position due to the formation of fibrous tissue.

Key takeaways :

  • Long standing distension of the joint and destruction of the ligaments produces subluxation of the tibia. The tibia flexes, slips backwards and rotates externally on the femoral condyles (triple subluxation). (Option A,B, C and D)

question_text: A 40 year old male, diagnosed with stage 2 TB paraplegia was started on ATT 2 weeks back. Since yesterday there is involuntary dribbling of urine into his clothes. What is the next line of management?

explanation:
• In, India we follow the middle path regime for treatment of TB paraplegia.

    2. Worsening of paraplegia while on ATT
    3. Appearance of a new neurological deficit while on treatment

question_text: A 20-year-old man reports painless snapping about the lateral aspect of the right hip. He denies any history of trauma. Examination reveals no limp or tenderness. question_text: Quadriceps active test is used for which ligament injury?
explanation:
• Quadriceps active test is used for identifying PCL tears.
  • Quadriceps active test
    • The quadriceps active test basically starts at the initial position of the sag sign, where the tibia sags down due to PCL tear. In a patient with an intact PCL, when one fires their quadriceps mechanism at 90° of knee flexion, the knee should not move forward noticeably. In patients who have a PCL tear, when the quadriceps mechanism fires, it pulls through the patella, patellar tendon, and ultimately on the tibial tubercle to pull the tibia back to a reduced position. This is the principle behind the quadriceps active test. This test is most useful when there may be a subtle PCL tear.
    • The quadriceps active test is performed with the knee flexed between 80°-90° and in neutral rotation. From this initial position, the patient is then asked to fire the quadriceps muscle while the examiner applies counter pressure against the ankle. As the quadriceps applies pressure through the patella and patellar tendon to pull the tibial tubercle anteriorly, any posterior translation of the tibia on the femur will be reduced back to a normal position.

Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 745

explanation:
• Nucleus displacement: The nucleus is under positive pressure at all times. When the annulus becomes weak, either because a small area of its entire thickness has disintegrated spontaneously or because of injury, the nucleus tends to bulge through the defect. This is called disc protrusion(fig B).
  • This tendency is greatly increased if the nucleus is degenerated and fragmented. Finally, the nucleus comes out of the annulus and lies under the posterior longitudinal ligament; though it has not lost contact with the parent disc. This is called disc extrusion(Fig-c).
  • Once extruded, the disc does not go back. The posterior longitudinal ligament is not strong enough to prevent the nucleus from protruding further. The extruded disc may lose its contact with the parent disc, when it is called sequestrated disc(Fig-d).

question_text: Which of the following sentence is not true about spinal shock?
explanation:
• Bulbocavernous reflex is absent in spinal shock. Root value of bulbocavernous reflex S2-S4.
  • Just after an acute cord injury there is cessation of all activity at and below the level of lesion. This stage of physiological disruption is referred to as "spinal shock". This stage persists for 24-48 hours after which recovery starts and the classical UMN pattern starts evolving.
  • The first reflex to return once the spinal shock is over is "the Bulbocavernosus reflex", hence the presence of this reflex heralds the end of the stage of spinal shock and onset of recovery.
  • Spinal shock is a combination of areflexia or hyporeflexia and autonomic dysfunction that accompanies spinal cord injury. The initial hyporeflexia presents as a loss of both cutaneous and deep tendon reflexes below the level of injury accompanied by loss of sympathetic outflow, resulting in hypotension and bradycardia. Reflexes generally return in a specific pattern, with cutaneous reflexes generally returning before deep tendon reflexes.
  • Initially following the injury, in spinal shock the reflexes are absent. Usually, it returns within 24 hours. Presence of flaccid paralysis after the recovery of spinal shock implies the diagnosis of neurological paralysis

Reference: Ebnezar, 5th edition, Page no. 304.

question_text: Patient presents to the OPD with pain and feeling of buckling of right knee. He gives history of injury during playing hockey 3 months back. On examination, the knee was unstable anteriorly in extension but was stable in 90 degrees of flexion. Probably injury involves:
explanation:
• The ACL ligament is the primary restraint to anterior tibial displacement, accounting for approximately of the resistance to the anterior drawer test when the knee is at of flexion and neutral rotation. ACL has 2 bundles –anteomedial and posterolateral. The anteromedial band is tight in flexion, providing the primary restraint, whereas the posterolateral bulky portion of this ligament is tight in extension. The posterolateral bundle also provides the principal resistance against hyperextension.
  • Therefore in ACL tears
    • Complete ACL tear will produce instability in both flexion and extension.
    • Anteromedial bundle tear will produce instability in flexion 
    • Posterolateral bundle tear will produce instability in extension.

question_text: TRUE about myositis ossificans
option_a: Mature fibroblasts are seen at periphery and proliferating fibroblasts at the center
option_b: Cytological atypia and mitotic figures are seen at periphery and mature fibroblast at the center
option_c: Matures fibroblasts are seen at the center and proliferating fibroblasts at the periphery
option_d: Mature fibroblast along with cytological atypia and mitotic figures are seen at periphery
explanation:
MYOSITIS OSSIFICANS

Zonal phenomenon is a characteristic feature of Myositis ossificans. In the center actively proliferating fibroblast with numerous mitotic figures, cytological atypia and loose random arrangement is found. In the periphery more organized arrangement of mature fibroblast with transformation into mature osteoid is seen. This is in contrast to neoplastic lesion in which more mature cells are seen at the center

More about Myositis Ossificans (Aka Hematoma Ossificans)

It is a benign pathological bone formation (heterotopic ossification) in muscles and other soft tissues Trauma is the most common inciting event, but may occur without trauma in paraplegics, Guillain-Barre (GB) syndrome, acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) encephalopathy, closed head injury, following extensive burns and in a comatose patient. One-third cases are idiopathic.

Most commonly affected muscles are quadriceps, glutei and brachialis. However, the elbow joint is most commonly involved joint by myositis ossificans. After injury, massage to the elbow and vigorous passive physiotherapy may provoke the development of myositis ossificans.

Pathology: It is a calcium hydroxyapatite deposition in soft tissues being composed of a benign matrix rich in fibroblasts and osteoclast like giant cells.

Clinical features: Clinical features are divided into three phases:

Acute phase: After a few days to a few weeks of injury, patient develops pain swelling and stiffness of nearby joints.

Pseudotumoral phase: This comes after 2–3 weeks and characterized by painless hard mass.

Resolving phase: This comes after 3–6 months. Gradual resolution of the lesion may occur in this phase.

Radiology: Initial X-rays are normal. Calcification and mineralization are seen 2–3 weeks after the onset of symptoms and matures in next 3–6 months. Periosteal reaction is seen as laminations. There are three variants of the myositic mass. In stalked variant a peduncle is attached to the underlying bone. In sessile variant, the mass has a broad-based attachment to underlying periosteum. In a third variant bony mass is only attached to involved muscle.

Diagnosis: It can be made on clinical background in association with X-ray features. In doubtful cases diagnosis can be confirmed by biopsy. Biopsy also differentiates it from a bone-forming tumor like osteosarcoma due to the presence of zonal phenomena.

Treatment: In acute cases, treatment consists of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), ice, compression dressing, splintage for the involved limb and active range of motion physiotherapy. Passive stretching should be avoided, rather active exercises are to be encouraged. If required, excision of the ossified mass can be done after maturation, which usually takes a year or so (indicated by decreased levels of alkaline phosphatase and mature bone deposition on X-ray).

Reference- Maheshwari Ortho 5th edition, page number 52

question_text: Which of the following statements about 'Menisci' is not true:
option_a: Medial meniscus is more mobile than lateral
option_b: Lateral meniscus covers more tibial articular surface than medial
option_c: Medial meniscus is more commonly injured than lateral
option_d: Menisci are predominantly made up of Type I Collagen
explanation:
• Medial meniscus is less mobile than the lateral meniscus. This is because the medial meniscus has an attachment on to the medial collateral ligament at the joint line. This fixes the medial meniscus in its place. Lateral meniscus has no such attachment on any ligament and hence free to move.
  • The practical importance of this is that, whenever there is a twisting injury to the knee, the lateral meniscus will move and escape injury, however the medial meniscus cannot move and gets crushed between the tibial and femoral condyles resulting in its tearing. This is the reason why medial meniscus is the most commonly injured meniscus.

Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 901.

question_text: Complete transection of the spinal cord at the C7 level produces all of the following effects except
option_c: Anaesthesia below the level of the lesion
option_d: Areflexia below the level of the lesion
explanation:
• Spinal cord injury is an upper motor neuron lesion so there would be hyperreflexia below the level of lesion
  • Cord transection: In this type, the cord and its surrounding tissues are transected. The injury is unfortunately irreparable. Initially, the motor paralysis is flaccid because the cord below the level of injury is in a state of 'spinal shock'.
  • After some time, however the cord recovers from shock and acts as an independent structure, without any control from the higher centres. In this state, though the cord manifests reflex activity at spinal level, there is no voluntary control over body parts below the level of injury. There is total loss of sensation and autonomic functions below the level of injury.
  • The appearance of signs suggestive of reflex cord activity i.e., bulbo-cavernosus reflex, anal reflex and plantar reflex, without recovery of motor power or sensations is an indicator of cord transection.
  • These reflexes usually appear within 24 hours of the injury. In a few days or weeks, the flaccid paralysis(due to spinal shock) becomes spastic, with exaggerated tendon reflexes and clonus. Involuntary flexor spasms at different joints and spasticity leads to contractures. Sensation and autonomic functions never return.

Reference: Maheshwari Orthopedics, 5th edition, Page no. 276.

question_text: Low serum phosphate and normal calcium levels are found in what common etiology of hereditary rickets?
explanation:
• Low serum phosphate and normal calcium levels are found in X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets.

X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets is the most common form of hereditary rickets. It is an X-linked dominant disorder which has been linked to the PHEX gene.

  • Laboratory findings of this disorder include low serum phosphate, normal serum calcium and 25 hydroxycholecalciferol levels and abnormally low 1, 25-dihydroxyvitamin D3.
  • Answer B: Vitamin D-dependent rickets, type I, is a rare autosomal recessive disorder.
  • Answer C: Vitamin D-dependent rickets, type II, is a rare autosomal recessive disorder, most often caused by mutations in the vitamin D receptor gene.
  • Answer D: Autosomal dominant hypophosphatemia results from a rare mutation in the fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) gene.

Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney, 1st edition, Page no. 98.

question_text: The active form of vitamin-D(calcitriol) is produced by the enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase. What hormone activates this enzyme?
explanation:
• The precursor to calcitriol is stored in the skin where UV exposure converts it to previtamin D3. Then, it is bound to vitamin-D binding protein(DBP) where it is carried to the liver and metabolized to 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
  • When calcium is low, parathyroid hormone(PTH) levels become elevated which activates 1-alpha-hydroxylase which converts it to the active Vitamin D(calcitriol).
  • Its most potent effect is to enhance intestinal calcium absorption through DNA regulation. Illustration shows a diagram of Vitamin D metabolism.

Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney, 1st edition, Page no. 98.

question_text: Which artery labelled in the figure provides the predominant blood supply to the spinal cord?
explanation:
Anterior spinal artery is the predominant blood supply of spinal cord and supplies anterior two thirds of spina cord.

The spinal cord receives its arterial supply from various sources that include:

  1. Vertebral artery
  2. Ascending cervical arteries
  3. Deep cervical artery
  4. Intercostal arteries
  5. Lumbar arterial system
  6. Lateral sacral arteries.

Anatomically, these basically constitute three longitudinal arteries on the surface of spinal cord that supply specific geographical regions of the cord(Figs 22A to C):

  1. Anterior two-thirds by an anterior spinal artery.
  2. Posterior one-third by a pair of posterior spinal arteries.
  3. The lateral columns are supplied by an anastomoses between the spinal arteries known as arterial vasocorona.

Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney, 1st edition, Page no. 1338.

question_text: A 24-year-old man is noted to have a urinalysis that is positive for blood. The microscopic examination of the urine is negative for casts or red blood cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• A urinalysis that is positive for blood does not distinguish between myoglobin and haemoglobin.
  • A microscopic urine exam is necessary for a definitive diagnosis. In a patient with myoglobinuria, a microscopic evaluation will fail to show the presence of red blood cell (RBC) casts or intact RBCs. Gross myoglobinuria can lead to an abnormal coloration of the urine and is typically described as “cola colored.”
  • Hematuria and Renal cell carcinoma would be expected to produce urinalysis and microscopic exam that are positive for RBCs, whereas nephritic syndrome would be expected to have RBC casts.

Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition, page no 526

question_text: What is the incidence of DVT among patients who undergo TKR without any prophylaxis?
explanation:
Thromboembolism: -

  • Common complication after TKR surgery if no prophylaxis is used
  • Rate of pulmonary embolism-1-4.5%, if no prophylaxis is used
  • Rate of fatal embolism-0.1–2%, if no is prophylaxis used
  • Most of the thrombosis affects the distal veins and therefore the risk of fatal embolism is lesser than THR
  • However, the rates may be underestimated because the distal clots can grow proximally into popliteal veins and femoral veins so effect appear late (3–4 weeks after surgery)-delayed deaths at home
  • There is no universally accepted prophylaxis regimen for DVT
  • AAOS guidelines recommend use of multiple measures-physical and pharmacological
  • Early mobilization is the most effective and cheapest modality.
  • Pharmacoprophylaxis can be given by using any of these-UFH, LMWH, Xa inhibitors (including oral), warfarin
  • Physical measures that can be used include calf pumps, anti-DVT stockings etc.

Reference: Manish kumar varshney 1st edition page no 563

question_text: Which of the following processes is involved in age-related intervertebral disc degeneration?
option_a: Increased cell number in the nucleus pulposus
explanation:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF DISK DEGENERATION:

  1. Loss of Proteoglycan - The aggrecan molecules become smaller and get leached from the tissue. This reduces glycosaminoglycans and water holding capacity and thus there is fall in the osmotic pressure of the disk matrix.
  2. Loss of Collagen Fibers - Type II collagen become more denatured and get replaced by type 1 collagen.
  3. Increase in Fibronectin - Fibronectin content increases with increasing degeneration and it becomes more fragmented.
  4. Enzymatic Activity - Increased fragmentation of the collagen, proteoglycan and fibronectin is mediated by increased enzymatic activity including cathepsins, MMPs and aggrecanases.

Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney, 1st edition, Page no. 1353.

question_text: The spinal cord terminates as the conus medullaris at what vertebral level in adults?
explanation:
SPINAL CORD:

  • The spinal cord extends from the level of foramen magnum to the level of the intervertebral disc between 1st and 2nd lumbar vertebra.
  • The spinal cord is 40-50 cm long and 1-1.5 cm in diameter.
  • By weight the spinal cord contributes only 2% of the central nervous system.
  • All the three meninges namely the pia, arachnoid and dura mater cover the spinal cord.
  • It is attached to the dura mater by a series of lateral denticulate ligaments emanating from the pial folds.

Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney, 1st edition, Page no. 1331.
